The proposed Indrio Groves TVC Hamlet PUD requires the rezoning of the subject +/- 1,027.11 acres from AG-1 (Agricultural – 1) to PUD (Planned Unit Development) and approval of the Preliminary Development Plan. This is the first application for the development of a TVC Hamlet since the option was created by amendment of the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code (LDC) in 2024. The proposed Indrio Groves Preliminary Development Plan provides for the development of up to 3,081 dwelling units, including 2,577 single-family dwellings, 214 townhouses, and 328 multifamily apartments, along with other associated improvements.
The Preliminary Plan provides for dedication of right-of-way for Koblegard Road, pursuit of right-of-way for Russos Road, and right-of-way for Spanish Lakes Boulevard, a K-8 school site civic sites and provides for up to 40,000 sq. ft. of commercial uses, including the commitment to provide a childcare center, and the provision of +/-426.5 acres of common open space.
A Hamlet PUD became a development option outside the Urban Services Boundary in the Towns, Villages and Countryside Future Land Use category in the autumn of 2024 when amendments to the Comprehensive Plan and the LDC took effect. The option of rezoning to PUD (Planned Unit Development) was added to the option of rezoning to PTV (Planned Towns and Villages) if increased density is desired, or rezoning to PCS (Planned Country Subdivision), if development with the density recognized by the Transferable Development Value Map was desired.
Pursuant to the adopted Comprehensive Plan policies and the LDC, residential density may be increased from 1 dwelling unit per acre (DU/A) (as provided in the Transferable Development Value Map) to 3 DU/A by providing 10% workforce housing that remains affordable for at least 20 years or 9% workforce housing and a child care center on-site. The minimum amount of open space can be reduced from sixty percent (60%) to forty percent (40%) by the inclusion of open space that is available for active and passive recreation within 1/4 mile of a majority of the residents, civic spaces, and at least one local store to support the daily needs of residents. Density can also be increased to 3 DU/A through the acquisition of transferable development credits, but acquisition of transferable development credits is not required.

description: The St. Lucie Woods Preserve encompasses a 33-acre property in St. Lucie County for an interactive nature preserve designed to accommodate the needs of sensory-challenged individuals, including those with Autism-Spectrum Disorder, as well as the public. Purchased by the County in 2018, the property is located west of Oleander Avenue, north of Prima Vista Boulevard, and south of Midway Road, along the eastern banks of the St. Lucie River just east of the Oxbow Eco-Center & Preserve. Through an extensive public engagement effort facilitated by the Treasure Coast Regional Planning Council, the County has gathered input from a diverse range of partner agencies, industry professionals, and the public to inform the concept plan and program. Through careful programming and management, St. Lucie Woods will allow users to experience nature, learn about natural systems, and enjoy “walk in the woods” in a safe, supportive, and engaging manner. The Concept Plan integrates prior County plans, public input, and best practices to provide a development program that protects and celebrates the site’s environmental resources and identifies locations for various improvements to provide an educational, enriching experience for individuals of all abilities. The Plan includes a welcome center and education building, an “infinity loop trail” with active and passive activities, staff accommodations, and various boardwalk and trail connections to waterfront facilities along the St. Lucie River.

description:
In 1961, St. Lucie County adopted its first set of land development regulations that set minimum requirements for buildable lots, such as lot size, width, and road frontage. Since then, amendments in 1984 and 1990 have updated those standards. As a result, some lots that were once conforming no longer meet current requirements for lot area, width, or minimum road frontage or sometimes a combination of the 3.
A nonconforming lot may still be considered buildable if it was under separate ownership as of July 1, 1984. The key date here is July 1, 1984, which is when the current Land Development Code zoning regulations were adopted. If, on that date, the same owner held two or more adjoining lots, those parcels are treated as a single combined buildable lot and must remain together.
But, if a lot was under separate ownership on July 1, 1984, it may still qualify as buildable—even if it doesn’t meet today’s standards. Lots that don’t conform to the zoning code but are still buildable are called non-conforming lots of record. A nonconforming lot of record (NCLOR) was created if the lot was in existence before the passage of the zoning ordinance or ordinance amendment, and now it fails to comply with related dimensional standards such as minimum lot area, width, or road frontage.

description:
St. Lucie County currently administers several economic incentive programs, including Ad Valorem Tax Abatements (AVTA), the Job Growth Investment Grant (JGIG), and Impact Fee Mitigation (IFM), to encourage targeted industry recruitment, job creation, and capital investment within the County. While these programs have been effective in supporting economic development, the existing evaluation framework relies largely on case-by-case analysis and negotiated terms, which can result in inconsistencies in how incentives are awarded and limited transparency in the decision-making process.
PDS and the EDC previously presented an overview of the County's Economic Incentive Program to the Board, who directed staff to conduct a comprehensive review of the County’s incentive structure to modernize the program and better align incentives with measurable economic outcomes. The proposed updates establish a standardized, points-based scoring system that evaluates projects based on objective criteria, including job creation, wage levels, capital investment, and industry alignment. This scoring framework is intended to serve as the primary basis for determining both eligibility and the level of incentive awarded across all programs.
The revised program also strengthens accountability by directly tying incentive awards to verified performance and establishing clear compliance thresholds. Under the proposed framework, incentive payments are contingent upon the applicant achieving defined performance obligations, with provisions allowing for prorated payments in cases where substantial, but not full, compliance is demonstrated, subject to Board approval.
Additionally, the updates align and integrate the County’s incentive programs under a unified structure, improve administrative consistency, and ensure that incentive levels are commensurate with the economic benefit provided to the County. The proposed changes are intended to enhance transparency, improve return on investment, and provide the Board of County Commissioners with a more predictable and defensible framework for evaluating incentive requests.
Key Revisions to Economic Incentive Program
Establishes a standardized, points-based scoring system to evaluate all incentive applications
Defines the scoring matrix as the primary basis for determining eligibility and maximum incentive levels
Replaces case-by-case negotiation with a consistent, transparent evaluation framework
Ties incentive awards directly to measurable performance metrics, including job creation, wage levels, and capital investment
Introduces a tiered incentive structure based on total score achieved
Aligns all programs (AVTA, JGIG, and Impact Fee Mitigation) under a unified evaluation methodology
Strengthens compliance and reporting requirements, including annual verification of performance obligations
Establishes clear performance thresholds for payment eligibility
Allows for prorated incentive payments when at least 70% of required performance is achieved, subject to Board approval
Clarifies that failure to meet minimum performance thresholds may result in forfeiture of incentive payments for the applicable period
Clearly states that the Board has full discretion to approve, deny or modify incentive agreements and award amounts and may terminate or modify any incentive or exemption in the event of noncompliance
Updates and modernizes the Job Growth Investment Grant (JGIG) structure, including alignment of award amounts with scoring outcomes (and cap increase)
Refines the Ad Valorem Tax Abatement (AVTA) structure, including alignment of exemption duration and value with project score
Formalizes a two-phase AVTA process (preliminary support and final approval by ordinance)
Improves administrative consistency and predictability in evaluating incentive requests
Enhances the County’s ability to ensure a measurable return on investment (ROI) for awarded incentives

description:
The HOME Investment Partnerships Program (HOME) requires participating jurisdictions to reserve a minimum of fifteen percent (15%) of their annual HOME allocation for housing activities undertaken by qualified Community Housing Development Organizations (CHDOs). The St. Lucie HOME Consortium, comprised of St. Lucie County, Martin County, Indian River County, the City of Port St. Lucie, the Village of Indiantown, and the City of Fellsmere, administers HOME funds in accordance with federal regulations at 24 CFR Part 92. St. Lucie County is the lead entity.
In September 2025, the Consortium issued Request for Proposal (RFP) No. 25-084 to solicit proposals from qualified and certifiable CHDOs to undertake the development of affordable single-family homes for homeownership by income-eligible households. Following evaluation by the selection committee and subsequent Board approval to negotiate with the highest ranked proposer, St. Lucie Habitat for Humanity CHDO, Inc. was identified to move forward with project development activities.
Federal HOME regulations require participating jurisdictions to execute written agreements defining both the organizational responsibilities of the CHDO and the specific terms under which HOME funds will be provided for individual projects. To satisfy these requirements, a CHDO Umbrella Agreement and Project-Specific HOME Agreement have been prepared.
The CHDO Umbrella Agreement establishes the organizational framework governing St. Lucie Habitat for Humanity CHDO, Inc.’s participation as a Community Housing Development Organization under the HOME Program. The agreement outlines ongoing compliance obligations applicable to all HOME-assisted activities, including financial management, reporting, monitoring, record retention, and compliance with applicable federal regulations. The umbrella agreement does not authorize funding for a specific project but establishes the framework under which project-specific agreements may be executed.
The Project-Specific Agreement establishes the terms and conditions for the development of HOME-assisted homeownership units by St. Lucie Habitat for Humanity CHDO, Inc. The agreement identifies the project locations, establishes the amount and use of HOME funds, and outlines requirements related to environmental review, site control, reimbursement of eligible costs, property standards, affordability restrictions, income eligibility of the homebuyer, and monitoring by the HOME Consortium.
Through a partnership with the City of Port St. Lucie, three of the project sites will be provided by the City for the development of affordable homeownership units. The remaining two properties are owned by Habitat for Humanity. The projects proposed under this agreement include the following properties:

description:
The Medical Examiner for the 19th Judicial Circuit ("ME"), the District Board of Trustees of Indian River State College (the "Trustees"), and Indian River County, Martin County, Okeechobee County, and St. Lucie County (the "Counties") (the ME, Trustees and Counties will be collectively referred to as the "Parties") entered into a lnterlocal Agreement in 2023 for the purposes of locating, designing, permitting and constructing a new facility for the ME ("New Improvements"). The Parties have since secured a site for the New Improvements through a long-term lease with the Trustees, completed and approved the architectural design, initiated the permitting process, and received an estimated construction cost for the New Improvements from the Architect responsible for designing the New Improvements. Each of the Counties has budgeted and appropriated the monies needed to fund the construction of the New Improvements based on the County share calculation set out in Section 4a ix in the 2023 lnterlocal Agreement.
The construction of the new Medical Examiner Facility was a two-step process which began with an RFQ (RFQ No. 25-066). RFQ No. 25-066 was for contractors to submit qualifications and experience on similar projects. The contractors also had to demonstrate that they had a sufficient number of qualified staff in the applicable disciplines to complete the work within the required time frame and in compliance with State of Florida statutes and standards, as applicable. From this RFQ, the short-listed contractors were invited to participate in the subsequent Invitation to Bid (Bid No., 26-004), at which time pricing would be requested, and the project would be awarded to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder.
On July 20, 2025, RFQ No. 25-066 was issued for the Pre-Qualification of Construction Contractors for Construction Services for the Office of the Medical Examiner Facility.
On August 27, 2025, responses to RFQ No. 25-066, were opened. Seven proposals were received; 638 companies were notified, and 65 documents were distributed.
On October 17, 2025, the selection committee, made up of representatives from the Okeechobee County BOCC, Martin County BOCC, Indian River County BOCC, St. Lucie County BOCC, the Office of the Medical Examiner and Indian River State College, evaluated, ranked and shortlisted the proposals. The short-listed contractors in order of ranking were as follows:Charles Perry Partners, Inc.
Verdex Construction, LLC
Proctor Construction Company, LLC
Paul Jacquin & Sons Construction
On November 4, 2025, Bid No. 26-004 was issued to the four short-listed contractors.
On February 20, 2026, responses to BID No.26-004, Construction of the Medical Examiner Facility, were opened. Four bid documents were distributed to shortlisted contractors and 4 proposals were received. The lowest responsible bid received was submitted by Charles Perry Partners, INC. (CPPI) in the amount of $22,668.662.00. The total bid is inclusive of 10% contingency, permit allowance, and the cost of the public construction bond. The Architect of Record, in their role providing Construction Administration services, was provided the bid documents for review on 2/27/2026 and concluded their review on 3/10/2026. Following this review, the Architect of Record took no exception to the recommendation to award the contract to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder, CPPI. Facilities met with the Architect and CPPI to discuss the project contingency. Based on the straightforward nature of the project scope and site conditions, the parties agreed that a 5% construction contingency would be adequate in place of the originally assumed 10% contingency. With this adjustment taken into consideration, the revised total project cost is estimated to be $21,652,286.00. This revised amount reflects the reduced contingency, permit allowance, and cost of public construction bond, and brings the project into alignment with the approved project budget.

description:
This Public Purpose Lease Agreement for Lease Property (located under the east side of South Bridge to the south of Museum Pointe) was initially entered into between the State of Florida Department of Transportation, Lessor, and the St. Lucie County Port and Airport Authority, Lessee, on July 26, 1996, for a period of twenty (20) years. A Lease Renewal of the original Lease Agreement was executed on December 12, 2016, with the County as Lessee for an additional twenty (20) year period beginning on August 1, 2016, and ending on July 31, 2036.
In 2023, an I-85 bridge collapsed in Atlanta, Georgia, which was caused by a fire beneath the structure. In response, the Federal Highway Administration issued a directive stating: "The discovery of such materials stored underneath a highway bridge should be treated as a critical finding requiring immediate follow-up action in accordance with NBIS Regulations and Guidance and must be reported to the FHWA (23 CFR 650.313(q))." This amendment is pursuant to that directive.
The proposed amendment prohibits the storage of flammable/hazardous items and amends related provisions.

description:
Florida Rock Industries, Inc. dba Vulcan Materials Company (VMC), obtained approval from St. Lucie County (SLC) for a Class II Mining permit to quarry and extract sand, limestone and coquina rock materials in the IX (Industrial Extraction) zoning district “Florida Rock Industries, Inc. Mine” on + 321.5 acres of primary project area with ±44.8 acres of mining expansion area.
VMC commenced the mining operation at its Fort Pierce Quarry located at 14171 Range Line Road pursuant to a Mining Permit issued on January 9, 2025. VMC has voluntarily agreed to contribute corporate foundation funds, annually and for a time through the end of mining at the Fort Pierce Quarry, in an amount of $25,000 (Twenty-five Thousand Dollars and zero cents) to non-profit organizations within SLC as selected by and agreed upon via a Community Advisory Council (CAC).
The CAC is a voluntary organization whose members serve as representatives of a community-based organization and interested stakeholders. Members are free to express their personal ideas and viewpoints, as well as issues raised by friends and neighbors. Members are expected to live and/or work in the immediate vicinity of the Quarry. The CAC would be an advisory group expected to participate in discussions and encouraged to make constructive suggestions to VMC on how to best address questions and concerns about the quarry raised by neighbors. Additionally, the CAC would collectively decide, annually, what local non-profit organizations within SLC should receive donations from VMC totaling $25,000. Once named by the CAC, VMC’s Foundation would disburse funds directly to the selected non-profit organizations in SLC. VMC is committed to listening to and considering all recommendations and providing an open forum to discuss all relevant issues.

description:
In 2013, the Public Works Department learned of the existence of five box culverts beneath Orange Avenue. These culverts are situated within five miles of the St. Lucie and Okeechobee County line and were constructed in the 1960s when Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) owned and built the roadway. The culverts are identified as follows: Culvert A (MP2.2), Culvert B (MP2.3), Culvert C (MP2.7), Culvert D (MP3.0), and Culvert E (MP4.0).
In 2015, an engineering evaluation was conducted and completed on the five culverts to assess their construction, conditions, hydrologic and hydraulic functions, as well as their maintenance needs. This evaluation also examined how these culverts perform during rainfall events and provided a summary of potential alternatives to address any concerns.
Stephen Cooper, PE & Associates, Inc. (SCPE) was awarded the total contract of $174,888.80 for the design and preparation of construction plans. Subsequently, it was decided to remove Culvert C from the project due to the need for a more thorough analysis, coordination with the adjacent Wescott Groves property, and budget considerations.
The project was advertised for construction in November 2024 and awarded to Johnson-Davis, Inc. for a bid of $1,518,000.00. The construction work for the 4 culverts is anticipated to be completed in April 2026.
Coordination meetings were held with representatives from Wescott Groves. A proposal from SCPE was received to complete the design, engineering, permitting, and post-design services of Culvert C for a total of $22,055.00.

description:
The County is planning median beautification and access management improvements along Prima Vista Boulevard, from US Highway 1 to Airoso Boulevard, as part of an Infrastructure Sales Tax Referendum-funded project. These improvements include modifications at the intersection of Prima Vista Boulevard and Floresta Drive. The City of Port St. Lucie has contracted with Consor North America, Inc. to design improvements to Floresta Drive and has agreed to coordinate with the County to incorporate the required intersection improvements at Prima Vista Boulevard.
During the development of the County’s access management design by Kimley-Horn, Inc., design inconsistencies were identified between their plans and Consor’s existing intersection design. In response, St. Lucie County requested a new proposal from Consor to update its plans so that they align with Kimley-Horn’s latest design. Attached is a proposed amendment to the Interlocal Agreement between the County and the City to facilitate this coordination.
Under the proposed amendment, the City would incorporate the additional design work for the Prima Vista Boulevard improvements into its existing contract with Consor. The scope of work is detailed in Exhibit A. The County will reimburse the City of Port St. Lucie for the cost of these design services, not to exceed $27,248.00.

The property owner has petitioned for an amendment of the Comprehensive Plan Future Land Use Map for +/- 75.97 acres located at 5325 Summerlin Road, generally bounded by N. Kings Hwy on the west and Copenhaver Rd. to the east, approximately 600 feet north of Picos Rd.
The proposed amendment is from RU (Residential Urban) and COM (Commercial) to MXD (Mixed Use District), with associated subarea policies regulating industrial uses totaling approximately 836,500 square feet, to be developed pursuant to a Planned Nonresidential Development (PNRD).
On January 13, 2026, the Board held a transmittal hearing and voted to transmit the proposed amendment to the Florida Department of Commerce and other state agencies for review. On February 19, 2026, the Florida Department of Commerce, Department of Environmental Protection, and the Treasure Coast Regional Planning Council provided responses in the form of letters issuing no objections or comments on the proposed amendment. Other agencies offered no responses.
A companion amendment proposes to rezone the properties from AG-1 (Agricultural -1) and RS-2 (Residential Single-Family-2) to PNRD (Planned Non-Residential Development) and approve a preliminary site plan which proposes multiple industrial buildings totaling approximately 836,500 square feet along with associated site improvements such as driveways, parking areas, loading areas, landscape buffers, stormwater ponds, and conservation areas. The application indicates that the project will support Class A targeted industry development.

description:
Lennar Homes, LLC is proposing a rezoning amendment for +/-1,027 acres from AG-1 (Agricultural-1) to PUD (Planned Unit Development) & Preliminary Development Plan, for the Indrio Groves Hamlet PUD. The property has a future land use designation of TVC (Towns, Villages and Countryside).
The proposed Indrio Groves TVC Hamlet PUD requires the rezoning of the subject +/- 1,027.11 acres from AG-1 (Agricultural – 1) to PUD (Planned Unit Development) and approval of the Preliminary Development Plan. This is the first application for the development of a TVC Hamlet since the option was created by amendment of the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code (LDC) in 2024. The proposed Indrio Groves Preliminary Development Plan provides for the development of up to 3,081 dwelling units, including 2,577 single-family dwellings, 214 townhouses, and 328 multifamily apartments, along with other associated improvements.
The Preliminary Plan provides for dedication of right-of-way for Koblegard Road, pursuit of right-of-way for Russos Road, and right-of-way for Spanish Lakes Boulevard, a K-8 school site civic sites and provides for up to 40,000 sq. ft. of commercial uses, including the commitment to provide a childcare center, and the provision of +/-426.5 acres of common open space.
A Hamlet PUD became a development option outside the Urban Services Boundary in the Towns, Villages and Countryside Future Land Use category in the autumn of 2024 when amendments to the Comprehensive Plan and the LDC took effect. The option of rezoning to PUD (Planned Unit Development) was added to the option of rezoning to PTV (Planned Towns and Villages) if increased density is desired, or rezoning to PCS (Planned Country Subdivision), if development with the density recognized by the Transferable Development Value Map was desired.
Pursuant to the adopted Comprehensive Plan policies and the LDC, residential density may be increased from 1 dwelling unit per acre (DU/A) (as provided in the Transferable Development Value Map) to 3 DU/A by providing 10% workforce housing that remains affordable for at least 20 years or 9% workforce housing and a child care center on-site. The minimum amount of open space can be reduced from sixty percent (60%) to forty percent (40%) by the inclusion of open space that is available for active and passive recreation within 1/4 mile of a majority of the residents, civic spaces, and at least one local store to support the daily needs of residents. Density can also be increased to 3 DU/A through the acquisition of transferable development credits, but acquisition of transferable development credits is not required.

description:
This is a request for approval of the Major Site Plan for 36.6 acres located on Kings Hwy., south of Indrio Road, within the Towns, Villages and Countryside (TVC) Future Land Use category. The Plan proposes 165 dwelling units for a density of 4.5 dwelling units per acre. Consistent with the desired street scape in the TVC, all off-street parking is accessed from rear alleys. The Plan will dedicate 2.2 acres for right-of-way to provide for a future east-west road along the southern boundary of the property, consistent with the North County Future Street Network Plan. The Plan provides 16.78 acres of common open space or 48.8% (when measured as a percent of the net site area after dedication of right-of-way). The common open space includes wet and dry detention, perimeter landscaping, a 1.28-acre communal park and another acre within linear parks and pocket parks. The dwellings will be made available for rent.
The Major Site Plan is returning to the Board of County Commissioners for approval, despite being in substantial conformity with the approved Preliminary Development Plan because the Preliminary Development Plan was approved by the Board in December 2024, prior to the effective date of Ordinance 2025-14, which designates as a Minor Site Plan "any development application that is in substantial conformity with a Preliminary Planned Development Plan approved by the Board of County Commissioners after August 1, 2025." Further, while the Land Development Code applicable in the Towns Villages and Countryside Overlay Zone provides for administrative approval of Final Site Plans in the PTV (Planned Towns & Villages) Zoning Ditrict and the PRW (Planned Retail Workplace) Zoning District, that administrative approval process does not extend to Final Site Plans in the PUD Zoning District.

description:
The North Lennard Road MSBU 1 parking and drainage improvements constructed Tilton Road from Silver Oak Drive west to Prima Vista Boulevard. Additionally, a portion of North Lennard Road was extended from the intersection of Tilton Road and Prima Vista Boulevard north, connecting to the existing road in front of Savanna Ridge Elementary School just south of Kitterman Road. The road and drainage project was completed in 2011. After the project was completed, the County began receiving complaints from the owners of the property at 1100 Tilton Road alleging that their property was being flooded as a result of the County Project.
The property owners sued the County for inverse condemnation, alleging that flooding as a result of the construction of the project resulted in a "taking" of the property at 1100 Tilton Road. In 2018, the County settled with the owners of 1100 Tilton Road. The settlement included the County developing a "cure" plan for the flooding. (“Kane cure plan”) The proposed cure plan provided for a culvert extending from the Kane property under Tilton Road allowing stormwater from the property at 1100 Tilton Road to discharge into a drainage structure at the northwest corner of the property at 1103 Tilton Road (“Bessemer property”). The stormwater then would “bubble up” or drain to the south through a pre-existing ditch on the western boundary of the Bessemer property and continuing south to the wetland feature located on and south of the 1103 Tilton Road parcel. A copy of the Kane Settlement Agreement is attached.
In September of 2018, the County's consulting engineering firm Kimley Horn designed the Tilton Road Stormwater Improvement Project ( the "Tilton Road 2018 Project"). This project would have implemented the Kane cure plan. Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer testified they learned of the proposed Tilton Road 2018 Project in approximately 2020 when work crews arrived and began installing silt fences along Tilton Road. The Bessemers' attorney contacted the County on August 25, 2020 objecting to the proposed Tilton Road 2018 Project claiming it intended to force more water from the north of Tilton Road to the south on Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer's Property. Additionally, the owners of 1103 Tilton Road also claimed that the owners of the Kane Properties (1100 Tilton Road) had been pumping water which was accumulating on their land into the catch basins on the north side of Tilton Road, which was then entering the roadway stormwater management system. The claim was that this significantly affected drainage and flooding on Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer's Property (1103 Tilton Road). During the course of time from mid- 2020 through mid- 2022, the Bessemers' engineer, in concert with County staff and professionals, worked on amending the proposed changes to the drainage in the area. As a result of the complaints of the Bessemers, the Kane cure plan was not implemented.
In 2022, Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer filed suit against the County claiming that the flooding on their property resulted in a taking of the front portion of their property. In general, the Bessemers alleged that the County significantly modified the overall conditions of storm water in the area, including Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer's Property, by a permit and work done to change the control elevation of the flood waters as set forth in the South Water Management District Environmental Resource Permit. That permit stemmed from changes considered and studied by the County under an analysis done by Culpepper & Terpening, Inc. in its North Lennard Road Pond 1 Improvements report.
The lawsuit also named the owners of the Kane property as Defendants contending that the pumping of stormwater by the Kanes exacerbated the flooding on their property. The testimony at trial was that during 2020-2022, the Kane Properties were continuing to pump water into the system which inundated Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer's Property anytime there was a significant rain event. In defense, the owners at 1100 Tilton Road claim they were forced to pump water due to the failure of the County to implement the "cure plan" as agreed to in the Kane settlement.
The County in turn filed a third-party action against Culpepper & Terpening, Inc. as design engineers of the Tilton Road project claiming that the drainage portion of the project was negligently designed resulting in flooding in the drainage basin. In 2023, the County settled its claim against Culpepper & Terpening for $850,000.00 which was essentially the policy limits under Culpepper & Terpening’s liability insurance policy. A copy of the Mediated Settlement Agreement is attached.
An inverse condemnation lawsuit requires a two-step process. In Step 1, a circuit judge is required to determine whether there is a "taking" of private property by the government. In general, under Florida law, in order to demonstrate that government action has resulted in a "taking" due to flooding, an owner must prove that the flooding constitutes a substantial interference with the owner's property rights for more than a momentary period and is reasonably expected to recur (the Courts have noted that rain is a condition reasonably expected to recur in the future). If the judge determines that a taking has occurred, the case proceeds to Step 2 which is a jury trial where the jury determines how much damages the property owner has suffered. If the judge determines that a taking has occurred, the government is also responsible for paying the property owner's attorneys' fees and costs in addition to the damages assessed by the jury.
In the current case, the Step 1 hearing took place on September 8th and 9th, 2025. (See attached Final Judgment). The court found the County modified and/ or attempted abatement of the storm water management system affecting Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer's Property in 2011 but also again in 2016, 2018, 2021, and 2022 through June 4, 2024 (the date of completion of Project Two). The Court determined that the period of time (2011 to 2022) the flooding was temporary, occasional, or recurrent, but causing no permanent injury to the land and that the situation involved elements of uncertainty, specifically the County's planned and actual construction of projects which altered or partially abated the causative conditions. Up through June 2024, all of these conditions prevented a reasonably accurate estimate of damages. At the conclusion of Project Two, the flooding around Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer's Property was no longer be "abatable". Prior to that, there were numerous attempts with some limited success to abate the flooding conditions on the Property. There was no physical damage to the Property until the driveway was partially destroyed in 2020 which coincides with the time that the inundations of the overall storm water management system by the County, the pumping by the Kane Parties (which the County permitted or refused to prohibit) and the failed remediation projects made recurring flooding on Mr. and Mrs. Bessemer's Property a permanent taking.
Mediation:
After the Court found a "taking", the parties mediated the case on March 3, 2026 to settle damages for the property owners at 1103 Tilton Road. Outside Counsel recommends settlement. (See attached.)
Settlement is $758,128.50 to the Plaintiffs,the Bessemers, inclusive of property damages, interest, out-of-pocket expenses, attorney fees, court costs, and damages of any nature and survey to be provided by Richard Creech. The County also settled with Kane Defendants a total of $35,000 for attorneys' fees. The basis for this settlement is that but for the County not constructing the Kane cure plan, the Kanes would not have pumped water from their property which caused them to be named in the subject lawsuit thereby incurring significant attorneys’ fees. Kane Defendants will provide release in favor of County and Bessemer. Bessemer and County to split mediator fees.
Settlement contingent on signed release by Bessemer in favor of the County and the Kane defendants. Bessemer to provide signed releases to St. Lucie by Thursday, March 12, 2026. Staff to recommend approval and will agenda this settlement with the St. Lucie County Board on March 17, 2026. Staff needs 30 calendar days to process the check after the item goes to the Board.
Stipulated Final Judgment to include legal description and details for easement.

description:
FPUA is constructing the Mainland Water Reclamation Facility (MWRF) to remove the existing Island Water Reclamation Facility (IWRF) from service, thereby relocating the facility away from its current vulnerable location directly adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon. As part of this effort, FPUA has developed a phased plan to systematically redirect flows from the existing IWRF to the new MWRF, which includes a requested easement through the George Lestrange Preserve to directionally bore an underground 36- inch force main through the preserve as shown in the attached Alternatives Analysis draft February 20, 2026.
Proposed force main alignment:
Since the George Lestrange Preserve property was purchased in partnership with Florida Communities Trust (FCT) under the grant award agreement FCT#02-056-FF2, FCT review and approval is required for the proposed force main. The original Board approved purchase and grant agreement included facilities along the western boundary of the preserve (related to the future Jenkins Road extension), and exiting in the southwest corner of the preserve property. The new route of the proposed force main is generally along the western and southern areas of preserve and the this adjustment and requested easement for the linear facility requires approval by FCT in accordance with Rule 62-818.015(1)(b), F.A.C. One criteria of the subject FCT approval is a letter of support from the County confirming the project partner concurrence with the proposed easement request. An Alternatives Analysis for the subject request has been provided identifying avoidance and minimization of impacts to the preserve associated with the requested easement needed to proceed with the project.
A draft letter of support for the force main alignment through the preserve is included for review and approval by the Board. The draft support letter includes the following conditions of approval, in addition to the Best Management Practices outlined in the Alternatives Analysis:- Updated listed species surveys shall be completed and any gopher tortoise burrows located within the area of impacts shall be relocated in accordance with FWC regulations.
- Establishment of an annual voluntary usage and maintenance fee to the County for the easement and to be used for the continual maintenance and restoration of the George Lestrange Preserve site.
- Creation of a closure schedule for the preserve to the public to accommodate the construction is to be submitted to the County and the schedule shall be limited to the greatest extent feasible.
- All disturbed areas shall be restored in accordance with the management plan.

description:
On August 18, 2020, the County entered into a reimbursement grant contract with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) for an allocation of $1.6M for the Cypress Creek Restoration Project, designed to promote natural area storage, groundwater recharge, rehydration of the historic creek, wetland restoration, habitat enhancement, and improve water quality for St. Lucie County through a series of water control structures. Funding is provided at 100% to cover all design, permitting, and construction costs with no match for the County.
On October 3, 2023, the bid for construction of the project was awarded to Enviro-Tech Systems, Inc. in the amount of $865,305.13 under contract C23-10-873. During construction, it was noted the dimensions in the bidding documents, based on data provided by FDOT, were approximately 6 inches off from the in-field measurements, which required modifications to the weir structure fabrication and concrete capping. Since construction activities were already in progress, including the installation of coffer dams, which restrict area drainage, Change Order No. 1 was issued to address the discrepancies. Additionally, Change Order No. 1 included reincorporation of a series of upstream “ditch blocks” within the County’s preserve area, which were later removed from the construction scope due to permitting delays.
During construction, several issues were identified that required remedial work on the control structures CS-1, Weir #1, and CS-2 to allow for the successful completion of the project while avoiding any adverse impacts to neighboring properties. The proposed Change Order No. 2 will remove the additional 3 ditch blocks from the scope, as detailed in the attached Change Order No. 2, and reallocate those funds to the additional remedial work required for the CS-1 and CS-2 structures.
Additionally, a concurrent Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) outlining the plan revisions and associated remedial work for CS-1 and Weir #1 with Captec Engineering, Inc., and Enviro-Tech Systems, Inc. is attached for review and approval.

description:
Chapter 125, Florida Statutes, and Chapter 553, Florida Statutes, authorize the County to enforce the Florida Building Code and to establish reasonable fees to offset the costs of inspection and enforcement activities. Section 125.56, F.S., specifically authorizes the Board of County Commissioners to establish a schedule of inspection fees to defer the costs of enforcing the Florida Building Code.
Section 553.80(7)(a)2., F.S., further authorizes local governments to use building permit fee revenues for activities related to the enforcement of the Florida Building Code, including but not limited to the construction and renovation of facilities, purchase of hardware and software, and training of personnel necessary to carry out enforcement responsibilities.
The County currently assesses a five-dollar ($5.00) Automated Building Permit Fee on building permits, certificates, and related authorizations. The proposed amendment does not change the fee amount. Instead, it clarifies that the funds collected may be used for authorized enforcement-related purposes consistent with §553.80(7)(a)2., F.S., rather than being limited solely to the County’s automated building permit software and related computer programs.
The amendment provides flexibility to support enforcement operations, including technology improvements, hardware acquisition, facility improvements, and personnel training directly associated with the administration and enforcement of the Florida Building Code.
This draft Resolution implements the Board’s Strategic Plan Priority PT 1.3 — Commitment to Accountability and Fiscal Responsibility — by ensuring fee revenues are administered in compliance with statutory requirements and used solely for authorized enforcement purposes.

description:
On November 12, 2020, the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners adopted the 2020 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan & Reinvestment Strategy (“2020 Port Master Plan”), including reference to the need for a regional stormwater solution for the Port Study Area. The 2021 Port of Fort Pierce Stormwater Master Plan (“2021 Stormwater Master Plan”) was subsequently completed in February 2021 as an extension to an earlier study (September 2017) investigating stormwater options for the Port and the County-owned Harbour Pointe Park. The 2021 Stormwater Master Plan covered Port properties stretching from Taylor Creek to Seaway Drive and sought to identify possible options for offsite "stormwater management areas and/or stormwater park amenities." Three (3) conceptual alternatives were eventually developed in the plan with varying degrees of Port buildout. Two (2) undeveloped parcels, west of the Florida East Coast Railroad (FEC)/US-1 corridors, were ultimately identified as potential sites for a master stormwater management solution.
Work Authorization 04 (Ongoing, Inwood Consulting Engineers) includes additional data collection and analysis to better refine conceptual assumptions used in the 2021 Stormwater Master Plan. This ongoing effort hopes to include further review of the two (2) parcels purchased by the county (west of the FEC/US-1 corridor, off of Avenue O) and provide conceptual pump station and stormwater layouts.
PTGA Grant G3G90 (Financial Project Number 455617-1-94-01) includes $300k from the Department of Transportation to help address the future design phase of the proposed Regional Stormwater project.

description:
In 1996, a bond referendum was approved by St. Lucie County’s BOCC to purchase what now is Harbour Pointe Park (f.k.a. the Cotton Property). The 20-acre tract of land was approved for purchase with the understanding that the property would be used for “…marine commercial, recreation, and tourism…”. Since then, this park has operated as a passive recreational park and lay-down area (periodically) for County-initiated marine construction activities and artificial reef program deployments. The park includes a stormwater pond that services North 2nd Street roadway improvements and currently has limited recreational amenities.
The County’s purchase of the Port Terminal (previously known as the Indian River Terminal) in 2018, included a 10% stake in adjacent lands owned by DBI Inc.; these adjacent lands are immediately north of the County's port terminal and south of Harbour Pointe Park. An exchange agreement to resolve this 10% ownership was ultimately executed in September 2024 and resulted in the County acquiring an additional +/- 6.0 acres of land immediately west of the park; expanding the park’s footprint to approximately +/- 26.0 contiguous acres. This newly acquired land provided the County with an opportunity to decommission the current park entrance (which is established within an easement) and formally pursue an official entrance corridor over county-owned property. Efforts are currently underway to establish said entrance corridor which will connect North 2nd Street directly to the expanded Harbour Pointe Park.
The 2020 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan formally adopted by St Lucie County's BOCC identified a recreational boat ramp facility at the park as a key component to the park’s future development. There has been (and continues to be) a growing demand for boat ramp facilities within the County, and the City of Fort Pierce has expressed similar wants/needs. With a new entrance corridor in mind, funding to prepare a more detailed vision for the proposed boat ramp facility was approved by the BOCC in the FY-2023/24 budget. This funding allowed staff to solicit RFQ No. 24-032 for design and permitting services associated with the proposed Harbour Pointe Regional Boat Ramp and a contract was executed with Taylor Engineering. A conceptual design was subsequently formulated for the BOCC as part of the effort, which garnered consensus from the board on the general size, shape, scale, and boat ramp offerings. This conceptual plan was ultimately used as a template for the current design/permitting efforts underway.
Grant funding from the Florida Inland Navigation District (F.I.N.D.) and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission’s Florida Boaters Improvement Program (FBIP) were previously secured for the design and permitting efforts associated with the proposed regional boat ramp facility ($250,000.00 from both organizations - totaling $500,000.00) and construction funding is now being sought from F.I.N.D. to offset the cost of future construction.
The attached resolution is required to complete a future grant application request.

The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) provided a Seaport Public Transportation Grant Agreement (G2S29) to the County in direct response to terminal improvements proposed by Derecktor Shipyards. The terminal projects, originally identified by Derecktor as Areas 1-4 Improvements, included pavement and drainage improvements to the County’s port terminal space. These improvements were intended to help Derecktor better utilize the recently completed Utility Loop (located along the southern perimeter of the port property) and bring the terminal infrastructure up to par with similar facilities typical of the mega yacht industry. The Grant funds secured in FDOT Seaport Grant G2S29, coupled with the balance of older FDOT Seaport Grant funds previously secured for Derecktor (Grants G2204, G1W17 and G1804), resulted in approximately $2,058,963.00 FDOT funds being made available for the proposed project(s). These state funds require a 50% local match, which brings the total New Improvement Budget to $4,117,926.00 (set to expire on 12/31/2027).
Work Authorization No. 03 with Tetra Tech includes Construction Administrative Services for the bidding and construction oversite of the Derecktor Shipyard Pavement Improvement Project (Area 1) project. Tetra Tech previously assisted the county in the review of the proposed project design (provided by Derecktor Shipyards) and their review of the design has confirmed that the proposed project is consistent with St. Lucie County's overall project goals and objectives for the facility. The project will enhance pavement and drainage features on the southern sections of the county-owned port terminal (where the old packing house was demolished) to support Derecktor's current MRO operation(s). The updates to the terminal are consistent with what patrons of the mega-yacht industry expect from a facility servicing their vessels.
Plans and specifications are substantially complete and regulatory permits have been secured for the project.

description:
St. Lucie County Public Safety utilizes Everbridge (branded locally as Alert St. Lucie) as the primary platform for disseminating time-sensitive emergency alerts and public safety notifications. The Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) currently funds and provides the Everbridge notification system to St. Lucie County at no cost as part of a statewide initiative to standardize emergency communications.
While FDEM provides the platform, the County is responsible for the local administration and governance of the system. This Interlocal Agreement (ILA) formalizes the partnership between the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners, St. Lucie County Fire District, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, and Port St. Lucie Police Department.By executing this agreement, the County authorizes these partner agencies to access the FDEM-provided platform. This ensures:
Immediate Response: Local agencies can launch alerts specific to their jurisdiction (e.g., localized police activity or fire evacuations) without delay.
Coordinated Messaging: Establishes a unified technical framework to ensure consistent public messaging during multi-agency incidents.
State Alignment: Maintains compliance with FDEM requirements for local participation in the statewide notification network.

description:
The Challenge: Evolving Threats in a Growing CountySt. Lucie County is one of the fastest-growing regions in the nation, leading to increased pressure on emergency responders to manage complex hazards. Current methods for identifying unknown substances are often slow and outdated, sometimes requiring samples to be sent hundreds of miles for laboratory testing. This delay results in:Extended business closures and public disruptions.
Prolonged decontamination efforts.
Increased risk of accidental exposure to lethal substances like fentanyl for first responders.
The Solution: Rigaku Handheld Analyzers
The St. Lucie County Fire District proposes the integration of Rigaku advanced handheld analyzers to provide rapid, field-based identification of hazardous materials.Rapid Results: Delivers definitive identification of over 13,000 substances (including explosives, toxic chemicals, and narcotics) in under 60 seconds.
Enhanced Safety: Uses Raman spectroscopy to scan through translucent packaging (liquid, powder, or gel), allowing for identification without direct contact with the substance.
Operational Efficiency: Facilitates swift containment, faster patient triage, and significantly reduced scene times.
Proven Need: These devices are essential for high-profile security; similar technology was utilized during pre-trial hearings at the Alto Lee Adams, Sr. U.S. Courthouse.

description:
Florida Department of Transportation District Four (FDOT) is proceeding with Drainage Improvements for SR 5/US-1 from Edwards Road to Tennessee Avenue project (FPID 441714-1-52-01) and the Outfall for SR 70/Virginia Avenue project (FPID 441715-1-52-01). Within the encompassing projects’ limits, the area is subject to flooding along both US-1 and Virginia Avenue, with both recognized as major hurricane evacuation routes for the City of Fort Pierce. An evaluation was conducted on the existing site conditions in this area to develop a solution to alleviate the chronic flooding issues occurring within FDOT right-of-way. A variety of proposed alternatives were considered, with the preferred concept ultimately to enhance collection and conveyance along US-1, fix adverse grading of the City’s Mayflower Canal, regrade the Savannah Road outfall ditches, as well as provide supplementary drainage bypass pipes to replace the existing deficient (2) 48” pipes that cross underneath (west-east) Sabal Palm Plaza and through FDOT right-of-way, to convey large scale stormwater runoff from the Virginia Avenue East Canal Basin (1,250 acres), to the Virginia Avenue Outfall Canal and ultimately Sand Mine Lake. Drainage bypass pipes are proposed along local Gardenia Avenue (54”) and along SR 70 to US-1 (72”), both of which outfall into the City’s Virginia Avenue Outfall Canal, which flows to Sand Mine Lake.
Stemming from coordination efforts with the City of Fort Pierce, a direct outfall to Sand Mine Lake was added through Indian Hills Drive. This outfall will connect to the proposed 72” bypass pipe conveying runoff from the Mayflower Canal and will run east along Indian Hills Drive to convey a portion of the flows directly to the Lake. This outfall consists of a 48” storm drain pipe combined with French drain cells which will provide water quality pre-treatment prior to outfalling to the Lake, as well as additional stormwater runoff attenuation.
As the site was acquired using Florida Communties Trust (FCT) funding FCT #04-045-FF4, approval of the easement as a linear facility must be made by FCT. A letter of support from County staff is attached as an exhibit to this item.
To accommodate this outfall, a drainage easement is required to extend the 48” storm drain pipe approximately 200’ beyond the limits of Indian Hills Drive right-of-way to outfall into the Lake. County staff was agreeable to the easement being processed as a donation, as the easement was of mutual benefit to the FDOT, City and the County. The outfall easement alignment was refined in coordination with the FDOT Environmental Management Office to eliminate potential environmental impacts, and then sent to the FDOT Right-of-Way Office for final review. FDOT then provided the County with existing right-of-way and title search documentation for reference, as well as the draft easement linework and language for ultimate review and approval. The proposed Easement and supporting documents are attached for review and approval. The Easement has been reviewed and approved by the County Surveyor.

description:
The County Administrator has discussed with the Board the need for a proposed extension to the existing 0.5 percent infrastructure surtax. Proceeds from the surtax, if approved, would be used to improve public roads, reduce traffic congestion, reduce neighborhood flooding, improve local water quality and other similar uses. Implementation of the proposed surtax requires that the Board adopt an ordinance that directs the Supervisor of Elections to schedule a referendum election to allow the qualified electors of the County to vote on the levy of the proposed surtax. It is anticipated that the Cities and the Village will adopt resolutions requesting that the Board adopt an ordinance for a period of ten (10) years. In this regard, attached is a draft ordinance that, if adopted, would direct the Supervisor of Elections to hold a referendum election on November 3, 2026 on the ballot question set out in the draft ordinance. If approved by the voters on November 3, 2026, the proposed surtax would be effective for ten (10) years beginning January 1, 2029. The proceeds would be distributed to the County and municipalities pursuant to the formula set out in Section 218.62, Florida Statutes.
Attached are resolutions from the City of Port St. Lucie, City of Fort Pierce, and the Town of St. Lucie Village endorsing the proposal of the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County, Florida to adopt an ordinance calling for a referendum on the 2026 general election held on November 3, 2026, to allow the electors of the County to consider the continued levy of a one-half cent infrastructure surtax for a period of 10 years.
Attached is draft Ordinance No. 26-004 which, if adopted, will direct the Supervisor of Elections to schedule a referendum election to allow the qualified electors of the County to vote on the levy of the proposed surtax.
The notice of public hearing was published in the St. Lucie News Tribune on March 05, 2026, a copy of which is attached.

description:

The proposed Future Land Use Map Amendment was transmitted to the state land planning agency and the other reviewing agencies. The state land planning agency, or Florida Department of Commerce, identified no comments related to adverse impacts to important state resources and facilities. The Florida Department of Transportation, District 4, filed no comments or objections. The City of Port St. Lucie and Treasure Coast Regional Planning Council provided comments.

description:
Lennar Homes, LLC is proposing a rezoning amendment for +/-1,027 acres from AG-1 (Agricultural-1) to PUD (Planned Unit Development) & Preliminary Development Plan, for the Indrio Groves Hamlet PUD.The property has a future land use designation of TVC (Towns, Villages and Countryside).
The proposed Indrio Groves TVC Hamlet PUD requires the rezoning of the subject +/- 1,027.11 acres from AG-1 (Agricultural – 1) to PUD (Planned Unit Development) and approval of the Preliminary Development Plan. This is the first application for the development of a TVC Hamlet since the option was created by amendment of the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code (LDC) in 2024. The proposed Indrio Groves Preliminary Development Plan provides for the development of up to 3,081 dwelling units, including 2,577 single-family dwellings, 214 townhouses, and 328 multifamily apartments, along with other associated improvements.
The Preliminary Plan provides for dedication of right-of-way for Koblegard Road, pursuit of right-of-way for Russos Road, and right-of-way for Spanish Lakes Boulevard, a K-8 school site civic sites and provides for up to 40,000 sq. ft. of commercial uses, including the commitment to provide a childcare center, and the provision of +/-426.5 acres of common open space.
A Hamlet PUD became a development option outside the Urban Services Boundary in the Towns, Villages and Countryside Future Land Use category in the autumn of 2024 when amendments to the Comprehensive Plan and the LDC took effect. The option of rezoning to PUD (Planned Unit Development) was added to the option of rezoning to PTV (Planned Towns and Villages) if increased density is desired, or rezoning to PCS (Planned Country Subdivision), if development with the density recognized by the Transferable Development Value Map was desired.
Pursuant to the adopted Comprehensive Plan policies and the LDC, residential density may be increased from 1 dwelling unit per acre (DU/A) (as provided in the Transferable Development Value Map) to 3 DU/A by providing 10% workforce housing that remains affordable for at least 20 years or 9% workforce housing and a child care center on-site. The minimum amount of open space can be reduced from sixty percent (60%) to forty percent (40%) by the inclusion of open space that is available for active and passive recreation within 1/4 mile of a majority of the residents, civic spaces, and at least one local store to support the daily needs of residents. Density can also be increased to 3 DU/A through the acquisition of transferable development credits, but acquisition of transferable development credits is not required.

attachments.name: Economic Incentive Program Compliance update FINAL-1

description:
Planning & Development Services is providing an update on the companies that have approved Economic Incentive Agreements with the County that submitted their 2025 Annual Reports but did not meet the job creation requirements specified in their agreements.
As part of the County’s economic incentive programs, participating companies are required to submit annual reports documenting compliance with the terms of their agreements, including job creation targets, wage thresholds, and other performance measures. These reports allow the County to verify eligibility for incentive payments and ensure accountability for public investments intended to support economic development.
Staff’s review of the 2025 Annual Reports identified several companies that did not achieve the required job creation levels during the reporting period. In a number of these cases, the companies have also fallen short of their job creation thresholds in prior reporting years and have previously been granted extensions or adjustments to their performance timelines by the Board.
Given the instances of noncompliance and flexibility already provided, Planning & Development Services is seeking direction from the Board of County Commissioners regarding how the Board would like staff to proceed with these agreements moving forward.
Potential actions may include enforcing the existing provisions of the agreements, which may include termination of the agreements or providing additional time for companies to meet their obligations. Alternatively, the Board may choose to evaluate the circumstances of each company on a case-by-case basis and provide specific recommendations.
Staff will proceed consistent with the Board’s direction and the provisions contained within the approved Economic Incentive Agreements.

Shortly after the Board's approval of the Agreement, County staff submitted an application to the State of Florida Department of Economic Opportunity (DEO).
On January 24, 2017, the Board approved an Amended and Restated Facilities Use Agreement with SFS. This Agreement incorporated changes requested by DEO and Major League Baseball as well as changes negotiated with SFS. Shortly thereafter, on March 17, 2017 the DEO certified the Sports Complex Project. The parties subsequently executed a Spring Training Program Agreement on March 28, 2017.
Attached is a draft copy of the Eighth Amendment to the Amended and Restated Facilities Use Agreement, which, if approved, will add Section 44, New Minor League Building HVAC Units, to the Facilities Use Agreement. This section will clarify responsibilities regarding the New Minor League Building HVAC Units in terms of ongoing maintenance, replacement of the HVAC units, and responsibility of repairs if there is roof damage caused by replacement.

description:
On October 1, 2025, responses to RFA No. 25-013, 25-074, Notice of Funding Availability & Request for Applications (RFA) Regional Opioid Abatement Funding Programs and Services., were opened. Twelve proposals were received; 114 companies were notified, and 41 RFA documents were distributed.
St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioner is the recipient of Opioid Settlement funds resulting from litigation against various opioid distributors and manufactures as a result of the opioid epidemic that has impacted the County.
On November 11, 2021, The State of Florida entered the Florida Opioid Allocation and Statewide Response Agreement with certain Local Governments, the “Florida Plan.” The Florida Plan sets forth a framework of a unified plan for the proposed allocation and use of opioid settlement proceeds on specific Core Strategies and Approved Uses.
On December 14, 2021, St. Lucie County, the City of Fort Pierce, the City of Port St. Lucie, and the St. Lucie County Fire District entered into an Interlocal Agreement Governing the Use of St. Lucie County Regional Opioid Settlement Funds (Primary Interlocal Agreement) authorizing the creation of an Opioid Abatement Funding Advisory Board (OAFAB) by the County via resolution and agreeing to the use of funds within the Florida Plan’s authorized uses. Regional Opioid Settlement funds are intended to meet community needs and may only be used for the approved purposes which include, but are not limited to, opioid-related prevention, harm reduction, treatment, recovery support services, and opioid abatement strategies listed in Schedules A (Core Strategies) and B (Approved Uses) of the Florida Plan and the Primary Interlocal Agreement. Services and programs funded through the Opioid Settlement must be evidence-based, individualized, comprehensive, recovery-oriented, trauma-oriented, and culturally competent. Funds must be used to expand, enhance, or create a new program or service and must not supplant existing funding for a current program or service. St. Lucie County’s regional fund is projected at approximately $17 million over 18 years with diminishing disbursements over time.
The priorities for this funding period are:
Core Strategies:
• Naloxone distribution
• Expansion of medication assisted treatment
• Programs with a focus on pregnant and postpartum women
• Expanding treatment for Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS)
• Expansion of warm hand-off programs and recovery services
• Treatment for incarcerated population
• Prevention programs
• Evidence-based data collection and research
Approved Uses:
Treatment
• Treat opioid use disorder (OUD)
• Support people in treatment and recovery
• Connect people who need help to the help they need (Connections to Care)
• Address the needs of criminal-justice-involved persons
• Address the needs of pregnant or parenting women and their families, including babies with Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS)
Prevention
• Prevent over-prescribing
• Prevent misuse of opioids
• Prevent overdose deaths and other harms (harm reduction)
The County, with administrative support from DOH-St. Lucie, is releasing this RFA as a competitive solicitation for programing and services based on the Florida Plan’s Core Strategies and Approved Uses, the Interlocal Agreement, and the St. Lucie County Regional Settlement Funds Implementation Plan, FY 2025-26.
On June 4, 2024, the St. Lucie Board of County Commissioners (“Board”) entered into an Interlocal Agreement Allocating and Managing St. Lucie County Regional Opioid Settlement Funds with the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County (DOH-St. Lucie). This Interlocal Agreement built upon the Primary Interlocal Agreement of 2021, expanding the OAFAB, assigning administrative support functions for the OAFAB to DOH-St. Lucie, and allocating a portion of the regional opioid settlement funds for community grants.
The purpose of this Request for Applications is for qualified organizations, including for-profit and not-for-profit corporations, and partnerships to provide programs or services that meet the requirements of Core Strategies and Approval Uses (Schedules A and B of the Florida Plan).
Basic eligibility for the organizations includes:
• The proposed programs/services must exclusively serve residents of St. Lucie County.
• The Responder must not discriminate against any person on the basis of age, sex, race, ethnicity, color, religion, national origin, disability, marital status, or sexual orientation in admission, treatment, for participation in its programs, services, activities, and/or employment.
• The mission of the responding organization must be consistent with the goal of addressing the health, economic, and social well-being of St. Lucie County residents in need of opioid and/or substance misuse assistance.
• The responding organization must be incorporated in the State of Florida and/or be authorized to do business in the State of Florida, have a local office/representative and a local phone number for at least three (3) years prior to the date of response.
• The responding organization must agree to all terms and conditions contained in the St. Lucie County Funding Agreement.
On February 18, 2026, the selection committee evaluated the applications that were received and determined that all eleven applicants were responsive. The responsive applicants are as follows:Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County
HANDS of St. Lucie County
Healthy Start Coalition of St. Lucie County
LifeBuilders of the Treasure Coast, Inc.
New Horizons of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee, Inc.
Pinnacle Wellness Group, LLC
Project Lift
RiteLife Services, Inc.
Roundtable of St. Lucie County
Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council
Tykes & Teens, Inc.
The selection committee unanimously recommended awarding to all eleven applicants.

The area is identified in the 2004 SLC Native Habitat Inventory as an “A” based on high-quality native habitat coverage and the potential for rare or endemic species. The preservation of the environmental lands provides for ecological biodiversity; clean air, water, and food; protection of listed species; sustainability; reduced development; and access to green spaces and natural areas for economic prosperity and social well-being.
One hundred fifteen lots have already been acquired. County staff ordered a bulk appraisal of 147 lots in the Turnpike Feeder corridor. Offer letters were sent out to the property owners. Ashok Sardana contacted the County and expressed interest in selling one lot, identified as Parcel ID 1406-333-0008-000-8.
The County presented a Contract for Sale and Purchase to Mr. Sardana for $7,500, which is 100% of the appraised value, as determined by the County’s contracted appraiser, Callaway & Price, Inc. Estimated closing costs are $5,000.
The tax bill for this parcel last year was $9.62. The average property tax bill over the last four years of ownership was $9.23. The Property Appraiser's website estimates a potential county taxable value of $1,000 if this parcel was sold at market value.
Attached for your review and approval is the signed Contract for Sale and Purchase.

title: PUBLIC WORKS

description:
In 2017, Hurricane Irma brought record rainfall to the northern part of St. Lucie County, overwhelming the natural systems and causing significant flooding. Inspections immediately after the storm showed that the flows in Taylor Creek during this event eroded embankments and undermined the approach slabs to the Old Dixie Highway bridge. The bridge was subsequently closed to traffic in January 2018 due to safety concerns.
A damage assessment was performed and the resultant cost to repair the bridge was approximately $800,000.00 (2018 dollars). At the time, the budget for replacement with a new bridge was estimated to be $2,600,000.00 (2018 dollars). Due to the age of the bridge, constructed in 1962, and the lack of sidewalk or shoulder on the deck of the bridge, Public Works recommended, and the Board authorized a contract on March 23, 2021, in the amount of $688,937.00 to design the replacement of the bridge with an entirely new structure. The bridge project is identified as a priority in the infrastructure sales tax project list. The bridge remains in “good to adequate” condition based on the latest FDOT inspection.
Several projects in the vicinity since the time of the original consideration to replace the bridge are now underway and directly impact the value of replacing the bridge. The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) north causeway project will significantly decrease traffic on Old Dixie Highway and the port expansion creates uncertainty for multimodal configurations, connections and locations south of the bridge.
In the 2021 Bridge Inspection Report prepared by the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT), it was noted that the undermining of the south approach was repaired. Subsequent inspection reports have shown little to no change in the condition of the bridge, with the last inspection performed in 2024.
Current costs for replacement of the structure have escalated to nearly $4,000,000.00 (2024 dollars). A recent cost estimate to complete the repairs to the substructure of the bridge by filling the undermined slabs and other recommended repairs approximates the costs at $1,500,000.00 (2024 dollars).
Kimley-Horn has provided a proposal in the amount of $222,395.00 to produce design plans for the repair of the bridge.

attachments.name: Scope - RFQ 25-044 Edwards Road PD&E Study

description:
The Project Development and Environment (PD&E) study is needed to study the future four-lane widening of Edwards Road from S Jenkins Road to 25th Street, approximately 2 miles in length. The PD&E study will meet the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the underlying laws and regulations should any federal or state funding become available. The Edwards Road Jenkins to Selvitz section has been added to the St. Lucie Transportation Planning Organization's Cost Feasible Plan, meaning that projected federal and/or state funding could be received to fund construction over the next 25-year time horizon.
Public Works staff prepared a scope of services for the Edwards Road PD&E request for qualifications (RFQ), to which the County received three engineering proposals. The most qualified consultant was Ardurra Group, Inc. The PD&E study will assess environmental impacts and future growth needs along Edwards Road for the entire 2-mile segment. The study will evaluate the expansion or replacement of the existing bridge over Five-Mile Creek as necessary for the roadway widening.
The study will also include a traffic analysis of the corridor based on future land use and buildout scenarios. Intersection improvements and configurations, including turn lanes and traffic signal(s) will be evaluated based on the County's adopted level of service for roadway facilities.
Five intersections, Edwards Rd. at 25th Street, Edwards Rd. at Selvitz Rd, Edwards Rd. at Rogers Rd., Edwards Rd. at McNeil Rd., and Edwards Rd. at S. Jenkins Rd will be evaluated for lane configuration, delay times and other elements to determine the necessary improvements.
The study will develop alternatives to compare with the no-build option. The study will analyze and assess impacts on the social, economic, cultural, natural, and physical environment in accordance with FDOT policy, procedures, and requirements. Public input in the form of publicly noticed meetings, outreach and other elements to receive feedback from the constituency will be included in the study.

description:
Florida Department of Transportation District Four (FDOT) is proceeding with Drainage Improvements for SR 5/US-1 from Edwards Road to Tennessee Avenue project (FPID 441714-1-52-01) and the Outfall for SR 70/Virginia Avenue project (FPID 441715-1-52-01). Within the encompassing projects’ limits, the area is subject to flooding along both US-1 and Virginia Avenue, with both recognized as major hurricane evacuation routes for the City of Fort Pierce. An evaluation was conducted on the existing site conditions in this area to develop a solution to alleviate the chronic flooding issues occurring within FDOT right-of-way. A variety of proposed alternatives were considered, with the preferred concept ultimately to enhance collection and conveyance along US-1, fix adverse grading of the City’s Mayflower Canal, regrade the Savannah Road outfall ditches, as well as provide supplementary drainage bypass pipes to replace the existing deficient (2) 48” pipes that cross underneath (west-east) Sabal Palm Plaza and through FDOT right-of-way, to convey large scale stormwater runoff from the Virginia Avenue East Canal Basin (1,250 acres), to the Virginia Avenue Outfall Canal and ultimately Sand Mine Lake. Drainage bypass pipes are proposed along local Gardenia Avenue (54”) and along SR 70 to US-1 (72”), both of which outfall into the City’s Virginia Avenue Outfall Canal, which flows to Sand Mine Lake.
Stemming from coordination efforts with the City of Fort Pierce, a direct outfall to Sand Mine Lake was added through Indian Hills Drive. This outfall will connect to the proposed 72” bypass pipe conveying runoff from the Mayflower Canal and will run east along Indian Hills Drive to convey a portion of the flows directly to the Lake. This outfall consists of a 48” storm drain pipe combined with French drain cells which will provide water quality pre-treatment prior to outfalling to the Lake, as well as additional stormwater runoff attenuation.
As the site was acquired using Florida Communties Trust (FCT) funding FCT #04-045-FF4, approval of the easement as a linear facility must be made by FCT. A letter of support from County staff is attached as an exhibit to this item.
To accommodate this outfall, a drainage easement is required to extend the 48” storm drain pipe approximately 200’ beyond the limits of Indian Hills Drive right-of-way to outfall into the Lake. County staff was agreeable to the easement being processed as a donation, as the easement was of mutual benefit to the FDOT, City and the County. The outfall easement alignment was refined in coordination with the FDOT Environmental Management Office to eliminate potential environmental impacts, and then sent to the FDOT Right-of-Way Office for final review. FDOT then provided the County with existing right-of-way and title search documentation for reference, as well as the draft easement linework and language for ultimate review and approval. The proposed Easement and supporting documents are attached for review and approval. The Easement has been reviewed and approved by the County Surveyor.

description:
Funding from this grant supports the operations of route seven of the county's fixed route system. The grant is 100% state funded and does not require a local match.
In July of 2024, St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners approved the St. Lucie Transit Development Plan (TDP). The TDP serves as a guiding document with a ten-year planning horizon and contains a list of prioritized projects and the overall budget for the transit program. The project list includes capital and operating investments such as new service routes, expansion of service, and enhanced infrastructure. The county's existing bus route seven was identified as early as 2009 in the TDP for regional economic development by providing cross-county connectivity. Route seven was implemented in 2015 and is currently in the fourth iteration of route modifications to increase ridership and enhance regional connectivity.
The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Corridor Development Program (CDP) is designed to relieve congestion and improve capacity within an identified transportation corridor by increasing the people carrying capacity of the transportation systems through the use of high-occupancy conveyances. In St. Lucie County, the CDP is intended to strengthen the initial project with improved efficiencies and increased ridership. The CDP covers up to 100% of the total eligible cost of the project.
A local match is not required. FDOT allocated funds in the amount of $300,000.00.
This project is in accordance with the Strategic Plan Policy ECON 2.2.2.
