The proposed project includes approximately 900 linear feet of new boardwalk and replacement of approximately 275 linear feet of existing boardwalk. description:
On September 24, 2025, responses to RFQ No. 25-084, were opened. Two proposals were received; 795 companies were notified, and 12 RFP documents were distributed.
The Treasure Coast HOME Consortium was established in June 2007 in partnership with Indian River and Martin Counties. In June of 2018, Port St. Lucie, Fellsmere, and the Village of Indiantown joined the Consortium. Independently, each jurisdiction would not qualify for HOME funds, but collectively, through the Consortium, they meet the population requirements to receive an allocation. Funds are disbursed between the HOME Consortium members based on HUD's methodology.
St. Lucie County, as the lead agency for the Consortium is pleased to announce the availability of funding to support the development of single-family housing units for homeownership by eligible low-income households (at or below 80% Area Median Income). In accordance with 24 CFR § 92.300, a minimum of 15% of the County’s annual HOME allocation is set aside for Community Housing Development Organizations (CHDOs).
This Notice of Funding Availability and RFP seek proposals from qualified and certifiable CHDOs to undertake new construction and/or acquisition with rehabilitation of single-family homes for sale to income-eligible buyers.
The successful applicant for this RFP will:
1. Acquire and/or develop single-family homes to be sold to households at or below 80% AMI.
2. Comply with all HOME regulations and long-term affordability requirements.
3. Complete CHDO Recertification in accordance with 24 CFR § 92.2 and § 92.300.
4. Ensure timely and cost-effective project completion, with demonstrated capacity and financial systems in place.
5. Income qualify homebuyers as required in HUD 24 CFR Part 5 income regulations.
Eligible activities include:
• New construction of single-family homes;
• Acquisition with rehabilitation of vacant homes;
• Site preparation and infrastructure work related to the project.
All projects must demonstrate:
• Market demand for homeownership at 80% AMI and below;
• A clear path to site control or evidence of property disposition agreements;
• Affordability compliance periods and resale provisions per HOME guidelines.
• Long Term Affordability-In Perpetuity
• Resale Provisions as outlined in § 92.254 Qualification as affordable housing: Homeownership.
Property Details:
The selected proposer will be required to construct at least three (3) single-family homes on the following City of Port St. Lucie-owned parcels:
• 636 SW Curry Street
• 1050 SE Lansdowne Avenue
• 401 SW Duval Avenue
Should the project budget allow, the selected proposer may include additional housing units in their proposal. These may consist of:
• New construction on other suitable sites; and/or
• Acquisition and rehabilitation of single-family homes
All homes must be sold to income-eligible buyers as defined by applicable program guidelines.
On December 2, 2025, the selection committee evaluated and ranked the proposals that were received. The committee members' scores and ranking for each firm are provided in Attachment A.
The short-listed firms in order of ranking are as follows:
St. Lucie Habitat for Humanity CHDO
Community Land Trust of Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast

description:
On August 15, 2025, responses to RFP No. 25-092, IV Therapy and Medical Massage Services, were opened. Three proposals were received; 54 companies were notified, and 24 RFP documents were distributed.
St. Lucie County BOCC maintains a self-insured health plan for its employees as well as the employees of several Constitutional offices. With nearly 2,000 members on the Plan, including both employees and dependents, the County continually seeks innovative solutions aimed at promoting health and wellness. Investing in employee health and wellness is essential for maintaining affordable health plan costs. By prioritizing preventive care, offering wellness programs, and fostering a culture of health, we not only enhance the well-being of our workforce but also reduce long-term healthcare expenses. Healthy employees are more productive, engaged, and less likely to incur high medical costs, which serves to keep the cost of the health plan affordable for its members.
The purpose of this RFP is for an experienced and qualified provider to perform IV infusion therapy and medical massage services to employees and their dependents on the County’s health plan. The objective of these services is to enhance the overall health and welfare of County employees and their dependents by delivering the following services:
IV Therapy Services:Administration of IV fluids, vitamins, and minerals
Customized IV therapy plans tailored to individual health needs
Monitoring and assessment of patients during and after treatment
Education on the benefits and potential risks of IV therapy
Medical Massage Services:Must be deemed medically necessary
Various modalities (e.g., Swedish, deep tissue, sports massage)
Patient education and follow-up care
Recommendations for self-care and wellness practices
On December 15, 2025, the selection committee evaluated the proposals that were received. The committee members' scores for each provider are provided in Attachment A.
The short-listed firms in order of ranking are as follows:Regenerative Medical Group Florida (RMG)
Dr. George Blackwell Inc. d/b/a PSL Health Clinc

attachments.name: C25-12-1099 Shenandoah  - Johnston Rd at C1 & C15 Emergency Culvert Repair

description:
Staff was informed of a depression within the pavement of Johnston Road at FPFWCD Canal 1 (approximately 1 mile south of Indrio Road). Following an investigation by staff, Johnston Road was closed to traffic in October 2025 due to unsafe conditions. Both of the existing 120-inch diameter culvert pipes that extend beneath Johnston Road at Canal 1 are severely deteriorated and will require immediate repair in order to reopen the roadway. Another nearby 72-inch diameter culvert pipe that crosses Johnston Road at Canal 15 is also in very poor condition and will be repaired as part of the project. Various repair alternatives were considered, and the slip-lining method of repair was selected to address all three deteriorated pipes. The proposed slip-lining repair is intended as a temporary measure to address the deteriorated condition of the pipes and to allow the roadway to re-open.
On November 10, 2025, the County Administrator authorized the use of emergency procedures to accelerate the repairs. Per the Purchasing Manual requirements, the County Administrator will request “after-the-fact” approval from the Board of County Commissioners at the next available regular meeting if it is determined that the emergency purchase exceeds the authorization limit.
Staff attended the November 2025 Fort Pierce Farms Water Control District (FPFWCD) Board meeting and garnered their approval of the repair methods, which will include inserting slightly smaller culvert pipes within the deteriorated pipes and grouting the interstitial space between the pipes. Staff has been working on the replacement of these culverts with a bridge project, funded out of the Infrastructure Surtax. At the FPFWCD Board's request, and as a condition of issuing the permit to perform the slip-lining, the County will need to agree to advance the construction funding for the Johnston Road Bridge project to FY27. The design effort is currently 90% complete and is expected to be completed by mid-year 2026. The Johnston Road Bridge project will eliminate the dangerous "s-curve" over Canal 1 by replacing the culverts and straightening the alignment as well as permit future 4-laning of Johnston Road to accommodate future development in the area.

description:
Indrio Savannahs Preserve is a 297-acre natural area purchased for conservation by St. Lucie County through the State of Florida’s Florida Communities Trust Program. The site preserves part of the last remaining North Savannahs freshwater marsh system and includes a large 35-acre man-made lake that was part of a former sand mine. The lake was historically isolated from the surrounding marsh and drainage system, thus limiting water quality treatment and stormwater capacity. The project has connected the northern county drainage basin to the lake and has created a new wetland system near the southern end of the lake to allow for stormwater/water quality improvements.

attachments.name: TDC Memo re TDT Funding Request for Airport Markings Project Dec 2025

description:
As the County continues to prepare for commercial air service at Treasure Coast International Airport, preparations are underway to accommodate the service. These preparations include capital improvements to the airport’s facilities and airfield as well as enhanced security and safety infrastructure improvements.
The County was awarded the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Part 139 Certificate in October 2024. The FAA Part 139 Certification is a rigorous and comprehensive certification process that ensures airports meet stringent federal safety standards. These standards cover various aspects of airport operations, including aircraft rescue and firefighting, wildlife hazard management, emergency planning and the overall condition of the airfield. The certification process involves thorough inspections and continuous compliance with FAA.
Based on the County’s last Part 139 inspection, the findings included a need to correct/enhance the airport markings – this is a requirement under our commercial designation. The airport markings were last completed in 2020. As time has progressed, the markings have faded with the sun. Part of the airport’s Part 139 inspection flagged issues with fading, missing or bleeding reflectivity and incomplete patches. At this time, the markings do not meet the standards for night-time and the reflectivity is not adequate in multiple locations.
On December 10, 2025, the Tourist Development Council unanimously approved using $800,000 from the Tourist Development Tax's 5th cent to help fund the project. Pursuant to County Ordinance 03-12, 33% percent of the County's 5th cent is for capital facilities that promote tourism located north of Midway Road including the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds.

description:
The 2025 Florida Legislature appropriated funds from the Transportation Disadvantaged Trust Fund to administer the Innovative Service Development Grant program.
The legislation (s. 427.0159, F.S.) directs the Commission to award this funding through competitive grants to CTCs for the purposes of providing more cost-effective and time-efficient services to the transportation disadvantaged. These transportation services must address at least one of the following objectives:
- Increase a transportation disadvantaged person’s access to daily activities that could include employment, education, medical and shopping, etc.;
- Enhance regional connectivity and cross-county mobility; or,
- Reduce the difficulty in connecting transportation disadvantaged person's to a transportation hub and from the hub to their final destination.
The St. Lucie County Transit Department was selected and awarded funding for an innovative after-hours transportation program for residents to get to dialysis treatments. The total project cost is $225,000. This amount is comprised of the state allocation of $202,500 from the FCTD with a local match of $22,500 from the Transit MSTU. Funding from this grant will be used strictly for operating costs to purchase transportation trips for individuals who qualify under the transportation disadvantaged criteria from execution date to June 30, 2026. Services will be provided by our contracted provider for the after-hours service.
This project is in accordance with the Strategic Plan Policy PT 1.3.1.

description:
Stormwater culverts direct and channel the flow of stormwater under driveways, roads, sidewalks and other obstructions and are an integral component of stormwater management. Culverts fail over time due to maintenance, environmental or installation issues. Culvert failure can lead to localized flooding which may impede safe conditions of ingress and egress for owners and residents of property in the affected area as well as the traveling public, visitors, emergency responders and other public service providers. Some culvert owners may lack the resources to pay for improvements and repairs.
In 2021, the Board established a voluntary program, Ordinance No. 21-004, to which eligible property owners can apply for and receive funding to improve or repair culverts and then repay this funding through the imposition of a non-ad valorem special assessment against the improved property collected in annual installments on the tax roll.
The attached Resolution No. 2026-3 is the Assessment Resolution as required by County's Ordinance No. 21-004, as amended. The purpose of this resolution relates to the imposition and collection of special assessments to fund stormwater culvert improvements within the Culvert 2026-01 MSBU, determine that real property therein will be specially benefitted, establish the method of assessing the cost of the improvements, approve the assessment roll, and provide an effective date.

The existing facility is 43,112 (gross) square feet, located on a 9.08-acre property within the Urban Service Boundary (USB), zoned IH (Industrial, Heavy), and designated within the IND (Industrial) Future Land Use category.
The Major Adjustment to the Conditional Use Permit is required to allow for the addition of two 78-foot tall towers, addition of a new curing rack building, and minor modifications to the existing building. (Curing racks are constructed to hold and cure products such as concrete cylinders or painted parts.) Per the St. Lucie County Land Development Code Section 11.07.05.E, the modification of the bulk of any one structure by more than 25% requires a major modification to the original Conditional Use permit. description:
On April 23–24, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners held a public Strategic Visioning Workshop to discuss current and future priorities. During this workshop, the Board made several revisions to the adopted Strategic Plan, including a new Vision Statement “Infinite Potential, Creating Endless Opportunities,” and new Mission Statement “Committed To Service, Focused On Our Future, Grounded By Tradition.”
Additionally, the six Strategic Plan Focus Areas were revised to Enhance Public Trust, Economic Prosperity, Quality Infrastructure, Environmental Preservation, Thriving Community, and Health & Safety. The Board also revised its adopted Priorities to Infrastructure, Economic Development & Transit, Tourism, Facilities & Operational Efficiency, Housing Affordability & Workforce Housing, Fiscal Responsibility & Revenue Generation, Environmental Protection, Airport & Seaport Development, and Public Safety.
In the summer of 2025, the County conducted a new community survey. After reviewing and analyzing the results, staff updated the Strategic Plan to reflect community feedback. These updates include revisions to the “Top Priorities Identified By You, Our Constituents”, adjustments to the order and content of Strategic Objectives, and updates to the Appendices.
Staff recommends the Board accept the updated FY2026-2030 Strategic Plan and authorize staff to make minor plan updates to the Appendices and Strategic Goals/Objectives, as needed. Updates will be identified for the Board.

description:
The Opioid Abatement Funding Advisory Board ("Advisory Board"), established in June 2021, advises the Board of County Commissioners on the use of opioid settlement funds in St. Lucie County. The board focuses on prevention, treatment, and recovery strategies, with members appointed by the County Commission, local municipalities, and key community partners.
In collaboration with the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County ("DOH-St. Lucie"), the County has engaged in a solicitation process to disburse the settlement funds, and it has become evident that the most practical and efficient way to disburse the funds is to create a selection committee separate from the Advisory Board that will be tasked with reviewing, analyzing and scoring submissions; change the function of the Advisory Board to that of a committee tasked with, among other things, reviewing and analyzing data, the selection committee's recommendations, and presenting those findings to the Board when necessary.
The attached resolution will change the name of the board, amend its duties, and update the composition. The membership will stay the same, but the voting membership will be limited to the local government stakeholders, with all other members being ex-officio. These changes will help streamline the solicitation process, while keeping a broad range of perspectives at the table and support the County’s ongoing efforts to make thoughtful, collaborative decisions in the fight against the opioid crisis.

description:
St. Lucie County (SLC) received $800,000 in legislative appropriation funding from fiscal year 2023/2024 which was matched with $800,000 of Parks Impact Fees. The funding is supporting the development of ADA-accessible and sensory-­friendly infrastructure for passive recreation at the St. Lucie Woods Preserve located on Oleander Ave., near the Kitterman Rd intersection (fka Myers Stickle). Visitors to the preserve will enjoy nature with amenities specially designed for people with autism spectrum disorder, with ample ADA parking, communication boards, educational signage, nature playscapes, ADA nature trails, boardwalks, a restroom, a river observation area, a pavilion/ outdoor classroom, a kayak stopover, and benches/picnic areas. This site will be the County's first inclusive design preserve and will provide opportunities to connect people with nature, river access, and sensory-friendly amenities specially designed for people with unique abilities and special needs.
This agenda item requests authorization to award of Bid No. 25-090 to Peterson Brothers Construction, LLC, to design, permit and construct several preserve amenities, including 1) the "wilderness" boardwalk, which will span an estimated 1,386 linear feet long and five (5) feet wide, and include four 10’ x 16’ covered sitting/observation areas along the boardwalk, and terminate at the river, 2) a 10' x 16' river overlook/observation deck, 3) a river access boardwalk which will span an estimated 412 linear feet long and 6’ wide, and will terminate at the kayak stop-over, and 4) a kayak stop-over which is intended for kayakers from the river to pull up, tie off their kayak, and exit their boats to enter the preserve, and then return to their kayak. It is not expected that kayakers will carry/pull their kayaks over 400’ from the parking lot to launch from this structure. The kayak stop-over shall accommodate ADA accessibility to the greatest extent feasible, with grabrails and other features that may assist docking a kayak, followed by the kayaker exiting onto the platform.

description:
The County adopted a park impact fee ordinance in 1995 which is set out in Chapter 24, Article VI of the St. Lucie County Code. The park impact fee is affected and collected within the entire County, including, by Interlocal Agreement, areas within the boundaries of all incorporated municipalities of the County.
The County agreed to use the park impact fees collected by the City as follows:Use of Park Impact Fees: Expend or encumber Parks Impact Fee funds collected by the City and remitted to the County within seven (7) years from the date received to pay for land acquisitions or to design, engineer, or construct all or part of the parks improvement projects set out below, including the payment of any debt service which is related to such projects. The County shall determine the allocation of Parks Impact Fee funds to the following parks projects identified in the City's and the County's Parks Master Plan, excluding professional sports facilities and Clover Park:Aquatics facilities,
Land Acquisition,
Oxbow Eco-Center,
Ravenswood Pool improvements and/or expansion,
St. Lucie South County Regional Sports Complex,
The Port St. Lucie Port District,
Torino Regional Park,
Tradition Regional Park,
Trails acquisition, development,
County beaches,
County Fairgrounds, including the proposed Adventure District,
River Park Marina,
Lawnwood Regional Park, or
Any County or City regional park or Special Recreation Area not listed above that is located within the South, Central, or Island Benefit Zones.
The County agreed to allocate four million and 0/100 ($4,000,000) dollars grant to the City for use to construct Torino Regional Park in accordance with the funding agreement attached as 22 Exhibit "C" to the proposed Agreement, dated November 1, 2022.
The term of this proposed Agreement was for five (5) years.
The County and City are requesting to amend the project completion date for two (2) years (December 31, 2027) and increase the funding grant amount to five million dollars for the construction and development of Torino Regional Park. The City agrees to expend or encumber the Grant funds to pay for capital improvements to Torino Regional Park by December 31, 2027.

description:
In 2023, the Board of County Commissioners adopted a Land Development Code Text Amendment that established appropriate construction materials for fences/walls in residential zoning districts. The following language was included in the adopted Ordinance:
Fences that are constructed, in whole or in part, of cattle wire, chicken wire, razor wire or barbed wire or similar materials are not permitted within the RE-1, RE-2, RS-2, RS-3, RS-4, RMH-5, RM-5, RM-7, RM-9, RM-11, RM-15 and HIRD zoning districts. Nontraditional materials, including, but not limited to tires, mufflers, hubcaps, or broken glass are prohibited.
With the recent change, owners within residential zoning districts are prohibited from using predominantly agricultural fence materials.
Through discussions with the Board, staff is proposing an additional amendment to the County's fencing regulations that would allow residential properties within the RE-1, RE-2, R/C, RS-2, RS-3, RS-4, RMH-5, and RM-5 zoning districts, located on a parcel of one (1) acre or greater with a lawfully permitted dwelling unit and on an unpaved, privately maintained road, may construct a fence in whole or in part, of cattle wire, chicken wire, or similar materials. These properties represent a more rural atmosphere with larger parcels and limited subdivision infrastructure (for example, paved roads, lighting and more uniform and smaller lots). If adopted, this section would not apply to razor wire or barbed wire and the fence would need to be maintained and kept free of hazardous protrusions and loose wire.

description:
The Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) provides financial assistance for the removal of derelict vessels. St. Lucie County staff, working in coordination with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), works to identify derelict or at-risk vessels for removal to ensure navigational and environmental safety. Once county staff obtains a derelict vessel removal authorization letter from FWC, staff goes through the process to select a contractor to perform removal efforts.

description:
On August 20, 2019, the St. Lucie County Water and Sewer District approved a contract with CDM Smith, Inc. to perform professional engineering services for Regional Water and Wastewater Treatment Plant Designs (RFQ No. 19-037). One of the elements of the project is the preliminary design of a Low-Pressure Reverse Osmosis (LPRO) Water Treatment Plant (WTP) at the Taylor Dairy Road site. The WTP will utilize mineralized raw water from the Upper Floridan Aquifer (UFA) to be treated with the Low Pressure Reverse Osmosis (LPRO) permeable membranes, which creates a mineralized concentrate as a by-product of the LPRO membrane treatment process. The mineralized concentrate must be properly disposed of by the District.
On September 7, 2021 the Board approved Amendment No. 1 to the August 20, 2019 contract to authorize a pilot testing program for the LPRO Membrane Treatment process using a pilot unit to collect operation data to corroborate the results of the software projections and to produce permeate samples for further testing (blending testing, corrosivity studies, etc.).
On November 2, 2021, the Board approved Amendment No. 2 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. The scope of services in Amendment No. 2 provided for the Underground Injection Control Class I Injection Well Septic Design, Permitting and Bidding Services for disposal of the mineralized raw water concentrate.
On December 6, 2022, the Board approved Amendment No. 3 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. The scope of services in Amendment No. 3 provided for increased compensation and extended the completion date of the project for Raw Water Pipeline and Offsite Production Wells 2 and 4 for Taylor Dairy Road Service Area.
On May 16, 2023, the Board approved Amendment No. 4 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. This amendment increased the compensation and extended the completion date of the project whereby adding the Regional Water Treatment Plant Design for Taylor Dairy Road Service Area to the scope of services.
On July 2, 2024, the Board approved Amendment No. 5 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. This amendment increased the compensation and extended the completion date of the project whereby adding the SFWMD Water Supply Facilities Work Plan update.
On April 22, 2025, the Board approved Amendment No. 6 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. The scope of services for Amendment No. 6 provided for increasing the compensation and extending the completion date of the project whereby adding additional engineering and Construction Administration services.
Attached is a copy of a proposed Amendment No. 7 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. The scope of services for Amendment No. 7 provided for increasing the compensation and extending the completion date of the project whereby adding hydrogeological services assistance, additional engineering and Construction Administration services. The proposed cost of the amendment is an amount not to exceed $1,098,305. The new contract total as amended by Amendment No. 7 is $6,904,082.70.
Funds will need to be transferred from the FG South Water Treatment project to cover this amendment. This is due in part to the bond fund distrubution for the various utility projects was based on initial proposals that were not finalized at the time.

description:
In 2022, St. Lucie County was awarded a CDBG-Mitigation grant in the amount of $600,000 and entered into an agreement with the Florida Department of Commerce (Commerce) to develop a community-wide St. Lucie County Regional Resilience Plan (RRP). The initiative included conducting in-depth Resilience Vulnerability Assessments (RVA) to identify risks and inform potential mitigation and adaptation strategy recommendations as part of the RRP.
Two Vulnerability Assessments were conducted:
1. RVA–FloodFunded through a Florida Department of Environmental Protection Resilient Florida grant.
Analyzed present and future impacts of flooding and sea level rise on critical assets.
Presented to and accepted by the Board in June 2025.
Included as an attachment to the RRP.
2. RVA–Other Hazards (RVA-OH)Funded through the CDBG-Mit grant.
Evaluated vulnerabilities related to inland and storm-surge flooding, high winds, extreme heat, drought, wildfire, and coastal erosion.
A draft version is included as an attachment to the RRP and is currently open for Board feedback.
The RVAs were developed using criteria outlined in State Statute 380.093, F.S. and Federal guidelines. This approach leads to vulnerability assessments that provide the necessary data and corresponding analyses for the County and cities to be eligible and better positioned for future grant funding.
The planning process included extensive community engagement and regular meetings of the St. Lucie Resilience Steering Committee, which played a vital role in shaping the RRP and RVAs. The Steering Committee represented various St. Lucie County, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce and St. Lucie Village departments, as well as local and regional agency staff.
The Regional Resilience Plan represents the first step in developing a comprehensive and collaborative approach to adapt to and mitigate the effects of extreme and disruptive natural events and is another tool that can be used in planning for a resilient community now and in the future.
This project furthers St. Lucie County strategic objectives, including: ES 6.1.1 – Develop a St. Lucie Regional Resilience Plan that addresses natural resources, citizen safety and well-being.
HS 4.2.2 – Support efforts to reduce risks and address storm resilience.
HS 4.4.1 – Identify public safety dangers/hazards that have the greatest impact on health, safety and loss of life and mitigate the negative impacts.

description:
Pursuant to Ordinance No. 24-018, adopted by the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners on June 4, 2024, the Local Option Affordable Housing Tax Exemption Program was created to implement Section 196.1979, Florida Statutes, authorizing local governments to provide ad valorem tax relief for qualifying multifamily developments that offer affordable rental housing. The program was established in response to rising rental costs and the critical shortage of affordable and workforce housing throughout St. Lucie County.
Under the ordinance, multifamily projects containing 50 or more residential units, of which at least 20 percent are restricted to households earning no more than 60 percent of the Area Median Income (AMI), may be eligible for up to a 75 percent County ad valorem tax exemption. Developments in which 100 percent of the residential units are income-restricted to qualified households may receive a full (100 percent) exemption from County levied taxes.
The Community Services Department is designated to administer the program, including application review, eligibility verification, certification, and coordination with the St. Lucie County Property Appraiser’s Office. Certified projects are published annually on the County website to promote transparency and public access to affordable housing information.
The exemption first applies to the 2025 tax roll and will remain in effect through December 31, 2028, unless extended by subsequent action of the Board of County Commissioners.
The 2025 reporting year marks the program’s inaugural implementation. Two projects—Blue Sky Landing I and Blue Sky Landing II, located at 100 and 102 Blue Sky Circle in Fort Pierce—were certified for 100 percent exemption under Ordinance No. 24-018. Together, these developments represent 164 fully affordable rental units, providing safe and stable housing for low-income households while contributing to the County’s broader housing and economic goals.
This initiative reflects St. Lucie County’s commitment to leveraging available state housing tools to preserve and expand the local supply of affordable housing. It directly supports several priorities within the St. Lucie County Strategic Plan, including:
AO 2.1.4 – Support the development of housing for all income levels of the workforce to assist with the attraction and retention of talent.
TC 3.4.1 – Develop and implement a plan to expand affordable, essential, and workforce housing opportunities.
TC 3.4.3 – Develop community-based strategies to address homelessness and unsheltered families.
HS 4.3.1 – Provide economic stability and support services in our community for those individuals and families experiencing vulnerabilities.

description:
St. Lucie County was awarded $250,000 through the Florida Division of Emergency Management’s Hurricane Loss Mitigation Program (HLMP) to complete wind mitigation retrofits on seven single-family homes located in Lakewood Park and owned by the Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council, Inc. (TCHSC). These homes, originally donated by the County in 2014 for use as affordable housing for vulnerable households, are insured by the County, giving the County a direct interest in ensuring they are strengthened against hurricane damage.
The State issued the formal HLMP award letter on July 1, 2025, approving the project scope and budget and authorizing the County to proceed with procurement and construction. The County subsequently executed the HLMP grant agreement (Contract B0255 / Project DEM-HL00121) with the Florida Division of Emergency Management on October 2, 2025, enabling reimbursement for eligible mitigation activities.
To implement the project, the Housing Division issued Invitation to Bid ITB 2026-7, seeking a single licensed contractor to complete all seven mitigation projects. The revised ITB sets a combined funding cap of $247,900. The scope of work for each property includes roof replacement, installation of impact-rated exterior doors and garage doors, improvements to fascia/soffit, drainage and culvert restoration, and compliance with Florida Building Code underlayment requirements.
Bids were due on November 13, 2025, at 2:00 p.m. and four submissions were received. The bid tabulation shows:Byrdson Services, LLC – $314,694.70
KIB Construction Corp. – $244,725.00
De La Hoz Builders, Inc. – $245,168.00
Gentile Corp. – $247,000.00
The lowest responsive and responsible bidder, KIB Construction Corp., submitted a total bid of $244,725.00, which falls within the funding cap of $247,900.
Awarding ITB 2026-7 to KIB Construction Corp. will allow the County to move forward with contracting, permitting, construction, inspections, and reimbursement through the HLMP grant in accordance with the executed State agreement.

description:
The Citizen Advisory Task Force (CATF) was originally established as part of St. Lucie County’s citizen participation structure for the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program. The CATF was referenced in the County’s first Citizen Participation Plan (CPP), adopted on March 21, 1995, through Resolution No. 95-100, which outlined public involvement requirements for federal housing and community development programs.
Since that time, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) has issued multiple updates to 24 CFR § 91.105 governing citizen participation for CDBG and HOME programs. On July 1, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners adopted Resolution No. 25-136, approving a fully updated Citizen Participation Plan that supersedes and replaces the 1995 plan. The amended CPP incorporates all HUD-required provisions—including expanded public notice, public comment procedures, accessibility requirements, and consultation standards—and no longer includes the CATF as part of the County’s citizen participation process.
Additionally, the Florida Department of Commerce (formerly DEO), which administers the Small Cities CDBG program, no longer requires local governments to maintain a Citizen Advisory Task Force to be eligible to apply for funding. With the updated CPP now in effect and the CATF no longer required under federal or state program rules, the CATF is no longer needed to fulfill any statutory or regulatory obligations.
To ensure that the County’s advisory board structure aligns with current federal and state requirements—and to avoid confusion regarding inactive committees—staff recommends formally sunsetting and dissolving the Citizen Advisory Task Force.

Summary - 25-003 Sunrise Blvd @ Edwards Rd Emergency Culvert Repair
Sunrise Blvd Emergency Culvert Repair_PRP Proposal_10-20-25

description:
In early September 2025, Public Works was alerted to a small hole and pavement depression in the southbound left turn lane of Sunrise Boulevard at Edwards Road. An initial inspection by Engineering staff and a local contractor revealed that gaps between segments of a 66-inch concrete stormwater pipe had caused erosion of the foundation soils beneath the roadway. To temporarily stabilize the area and ensure public safety, a concrete slurry mixture was poured into the hole. On September 26, ground penetrating radar (GPR) was used to further assess the site. While no large voids were detected, the scan revealed pockets of very loose, saturated soil along the pipe, confirming that the subgrade conditions posed a significant safety risk.
Engineering staff determined that immediate action was necessary to prevent further erosion and potential collapse of the travel lane. The proposed repairs include sealing the pipe joints and densifying the surrounding soil to restore the structural integrity of the roadway. Public Works acquired administrative approval to proceed with the work under the County’s Emergency Purchase Protocol. Staff is contracting with PRP Construction Group, LLC, to perform the necessary repairs and pavement restoration using available funds from the Stormwater Management Fund Reserve.
This emergency response is critical to maintaining safe travel conditions and avoiding extended lane closures or more costly repairs. The situation meets the criteria for an emergency as defined in the County’s Purchasing Policy, and staff urges prompt authorization to protect public safety and preserve the roadway infrastructure. St. Lucie County entered into an emergency contract C25-10-1019 with PRP Construction Group, LLC to perform the necessary repairs.

description:
On August 1, 1990, the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County, Florida, adopted the St. Lucie County Land Development Code.
On April 2, 2013, the Board adopted a reasonable accommodation ordinance.
"Reasonable Accommodation" is a statutorily established method by which an individual who is disabled and/or handicapped (as those terms are defined in Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and/or the Fair Housing Amendments Act, hereafter "disabled"), or a provider of services to the disabled qualifying for reasonable accommodations under the referred statutes, can request a modification or alteration in the application of a specific Code provision, rule, policy, or practice, to them. The proposed accommodation sought by the disabled individual must be reasonable and necessary to afford such person an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
On December 6, 2022, the Board adopted a reasonable accommodation ordinance that changed the appeal body from the Board of County Commissioners to the Circuit Court.
In the 2025 Legislative Session, the legislature passed an act relating to certified recovery residences, Section 397.487 (15)(a), F.S. This new legislation requires, by January 1, 2026, the governing body of each county or municipality shall adopt an ordinance establishing procedures for the review and approval of certified recovery residences within its jurisdiction. The ordinance must include a process for requesting reasonable accommodations from any local land use regulation that serves to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence. The proposed ordinance addresses the statutory requirement.
Staff finds the proposed Land Development Code (LDC) Text Amendment is consistent with LDC Section 11.06.03. — Standards of Review, and consistent with Florida Statutes.

description:
On August 1, 1990, the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County adopted the St. Lucie County Land Development Code to implement the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan. Goal 2.1 of the Transportation Element within St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan requires that the County provide a safe and efficient integrated multi-modal transportation system which addresses the future needs of St. Lucie County for movement of people and goods, and which considers social, economic, energy and environmental effects including greenhouse gas emissions of the transportation system. The Board is obligated to maintain concurrency in accordance with level of service standards as established by the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan. Goal 6.1 of the Conservation Element within the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan requires that the natural resources of St. Lucie County shall be protected, appropriately used, or conserved in a manner which maximizes their functions and values. The proposed ordinance provides for the improvement of certain essential infrastructure without mitigation to balance and minimize threats of degradation to the health, safety and welfare of the county's citizens.
In this regard, please find attached a draft ordinance, which, if adopted, would provide clarification on the removal of native vegetation for the construction of any non-site-related roadway extensions or expansions, identified in the County's Right-of-Way Protection Plan or the Jenkins Road Area Plan (special district) and prescribed by a site plan approval, site development permit or roadway improvement agreement, provided the roadway will be dedicated to and is agreed to be accepted by St. Lucie County for perpetual ownership and maintenance; with the roadway accepted at such time the improvement serves as a thoroughfare for the County's overall roadway network. Additionally, the draft ordinance would provide clarification on the removal of native vegetation for road construction within an existing County right-of-way. The proposed changes allow this road work to be conducted and exempt from mitigation.
The ordinance, if adopted, will also provide an exemption for vegetation removal activities associated with the operation and maintenance of a water control district system for drainage purposes. Lastly, the ordinance incorporates an exemption established by Section 163.045, F.S., which addresses the removal of a native tree on a residential property with a single-family, detached dwelling unit, if the property owner possesses documentation from an arborist certified by the ISA or a Florida licensed landscape architect that the tree poses an unacceptable risk to persons or property. A tree poses an unacceptable risk if the removal is the only means of practically mitigating its risk below moderate, as determined by the tree risk assessment procedures outlined in Best Management Practices - Tree Risk Assessment, Second Edition (2017).
Staff finds the proposed Land Development Code (LDC) Text Amendment is consistent with LDC Section 11.06.03. - Standards of Review.

description:
Road Impact Fees in St. Lucie County were first adopted in 1985 and implemented in 1986 as an important source of revenue to use in funding the infrastructure necessitated by new growth. Since then, the County has continued to periodically update its Road Impact Fee Study, last updated and adopted on April 19, 2022. The County engaged Nilgün Kamp, AICP, with Tindale Oliver (n.k.a. Benesch) to provide the 2022 update.
The County has strived to work with municipalities to streamline the collection of County Impact Fees whereby a developer or builder pays only the permitting agency. The County's Road Impact Fee Interlocal Agreement with the City of Fort Pierce has been in place since September 13, 2005, and with the City of Port St. Lucie (PSL) since April 19, 2022.
With a population of approximately 394,000, St. Lucie County ranks 20th out of 67 Florida counties in population. The County is continuing to experience population growth, with a projected county-wide increase of 145,000 persons by 2050, or an average annual growth rate of 1.2 percent as estimated by the Bureau of Business & Economic Research (BEBR), ranking 7th among Florida counties. St. Lucie County ranked 13th for residential permitting in 2024, indicating high levels of new development. This continuing growth requires additional public capital facilities. With this continued growth and significant increases in construction costs, the County retained Benesch in 2025 to update the impact fee study to reflect the most recent data available. Along with the updated study, the County retained Benesch to provide an extraordinary circumstances analysis of the new or increased impact fees. The County and Benesch previously hosted two public workshops to discuss the findings of extraordinary circumstances, necessitating the increase in impact fees. The County can use the extraordinary circumstances clause within the statute, to adopt updated Multi-modal Road Impact fees prior to the four-year timeframe for any fee increases and possibly adopt fees at levels higher than the 50-percent increase limit.
As specified in Section 163.31801, F.S., each local government that adopts and collects an impact fee must ensure that the calculation of the impact fee is based on a study using the most recent and localized data available within 4 years of the current impact fee update and the new study must be adopted within 12 months of the initiation of the new impact fee study if the local government increases the impact fee. The local government must provide notice at least 90 days before the effective date of imposing a new or increased impact fee. Impact fees must be proportional and reasonably connected to, or have a rational nexus with, the need for additional capital facilities and the increased impact generated by the new development.
As stated, St. Lucie County’s Road Impact Fee was initially implemented in 1986 to assist the County in providing adequate transportation facilities for expected growth. The most recent study update for these fees was completed in 2022, with the calculated rates adopted in 2022 at 75% of the maximum allowable (capped at a 50% increase and discounted to 75%) and phased-in over four (4) years, with October 1, 2025, being the start of the fourth year. Additionally, these rates only assessed impacts on State and County Roads proportionally by municipality based on VMT (vehicle miles traveled).
As provided in Section 163.3180, F.S., if a local government elects to repeal transportation concurrency, the local government may adopt an alternative transportation system that is mobility-plan and fee-based or an alternative transportation system that is not mobility-plan and fee-based. The local government may not use an alternative transportation system to deny, time, or phase an application for site plan approval, plat approval, final subdivision approval, building permits, or the functional equivalent of such approvals, provided that the developer agrees to pay for the development’s identified transportation impacts via the funding mechanism implemented by the local government.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed HB 479, which defined Mobility Fees/Mobility Plan (an alternative transportation system mobility study developed using a plan-based methodology and adopted into a local government comprehensive plan that promotes a compact, mixed use, and interconnected development served by a multimodal transportation system in an area that is urban in character, or designated to be urban in character, as defined in s. 171.031) and allows only the local government issuing a building permit to collect for transportation impacts. HB 479 requires cities and counties to enter into an interlocal agreement to define any fees for transportation impacts and determine a methodology for the distribution of any revenues. If there is no agreement in place by October 1, 2025, or if an existing agreement is terminated, only the local government issuing the building permit may collect for transportation impacts based on a developer's traffic impact study or a city or county's mobility fee less a 10% discount to the developer.
Currently, road impact fee revenues are St. Lucie County’s primary funding source for new road construction and lane addition improvements. County fuel tax revenues are dedicated to maintenance (like road resurfacing), operations, and debt service payments. Local option sales tax revenues have been mostly allocated to non-capacity projects. Without a transportation impact fee program, the County would not be able to construct planned capacity addition projects included in the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP), and other priority projects unless an alternative revenue source, such as additional sales tax or dedicated millage, is identified. In the absence of impact fee revenues or alternative new/additional funding that would replace impact fee revenues, the level of service is likely to degrade with roads becoming more congested and travel times getting longer.
Although the County’s Road Impact Fee Ordinance requires the road impact fees to be reviewed every five years, to address requirements of recent legislative changes, the County accelerated the update to the road impact fee study prior to the five-year update schedule due to exponential increases in population countywide and construction costs.
At the December 10, 2024, Informal BOCC meeting, Benesch presented mobility fee, multimodal fee and impact fee information as well as discussed the recent legislative changes. The Board discussed multiple options during the Informal meeting. As such, Benesch provided a scope of work to conduct a Transportation Study that included methodologies for Mobility Fees, Impact Fees, and Multimodal Fees. Including all three (3) options allows the Board to consider alternative methods to capture travel demand revenue from future development. Road impact fees can be spent on roadway capacity expansion improvements. With a multi-modal fee or mobility fee, impact fee revenues can be spent on standalone sidewalk, bicycle, and transit improvements that add other capacity to the transportation network (in addition to roadway capacity expansion improvements). With impact fees, the County can utilize concurrency, which allows the county to deny development applications where road capacity is not available to meet the travel demands of the new development. However, recent legislative changes also require local governments to allow development if the development addresses its proportionate share requirements. With multi-modal fees, concurrency remains as well, while it is repealed with mobility fees. Mobility fees are a pay-and-go system and require the County to remove concurrency from its comprehensive plan.
On June 10, 2025, Benesch presented to the Board of County Commissioners at a Special Informal Board Meeting and discussed Road Impact Fees, Multimodal Fees, and Mobility Fees. The Board indicated interest in moving forward with the creation of a Multimodal Fee, and developing scenarios for varying rates for new development inside the Urban Service Boundary vs. outside the Urban Service Boundary.
On July 17, 2025, the County staff and Benesch hosted the first of two Public Workshops to discuss the findings of extraordinary circumstances necessitating the adoption of updated Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee rates.
On July 17, 2025, County staff and Benesh presented the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study, including the recommended rates, to the Planning and Zoning Commission at their regularly scheduled meeting. The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4 to 1 to recommend the Board adopt the Multi-modal Road Impact fee at 100% of the study's recommended rate.
On August 14, 2025, County staff presented the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study and recommended rates to the Treasure Coast Builders Association (TCBA) membership.
On August 15, 2025, County staff presented the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study and recommended rates to the St. Lucie County Citizens Budget Committee. The Committee unanimously passed a Resolution, recommending the BOCC vote to approve 100% of the study's recommended Multi-modal Road Impact Fee rates.
On August 19, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners heard the 2nd of two Public Workshops to discuss the findings of extraordinary circumstances necessitating the adoption of the updated Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee rates.
On August 19, 2025, the Board continued the first reading of the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Ordinance to the September 16, 2025 regularly scheduled Board meeting.
On September 8, 2025, the Draft Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study was updated using the most recent version of the Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) 12th Edition, released in August 2025. This update resulted in trip generation rate reductions for a number of land uses (ex. office and industrial), which lowered the recommended rates identified in the Multi-Modal Road Impact Fee Study.
On September 10, 2025, at 5:30 P.M., County staff and Benesch hosted a virtual public meeting with interested stakeholders to present the updated Multi-modal Road Impact Fee Study and revised recommended fee rates.
On September 16, 2025, at the regularly scheduled Board of County Commissioners meeting, County staff and Benesch presented an update on the County's Multi-modal Impact Fee Study and the first reading of the proposed Multi-modal Impact Fee Ordinance. At the meeting, the BOCC provided direction and passed a motion to hold a Special Informal Meeting in November 2025 and schedule the 2nd reading of the Draft Multi-modal Road Impact Fee Ordinance for the regularly scheduled BOCC meeting on December 2, 2025.
On November 18, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners held a Special Informal Meeting where direction was provided to staff to prepare the draft ordinance to have the multi-modal impact fee rates reflect a 50% increase over the existing road impact fee rate, and a 25% increase for Multi-purpose Recreational Center and Restaurant uses. The restaurant land use category was added for the purposes of the 2025 Impact Fee study to capture the actual traffic demand created by this use. With the limitation of increasing the rate to 25%, the rate falls below the retail/shopping center rate (currently used to calculate impact fees for restaurants), therefore this use type has been eliminated from the Draft Ordinance. Additionally, on November 18, 2025, the Board directed staff to draft the Ordinance to reflect a 4-year phase in of the fee increases and consider an implementation date for the revised fees on October 1, 2026.

attachments.name: Updated Final - ST. LUCIE COUNTY COPCN ORDINANCE

description:
St. Lucie County is statutorily authorized and required under Chapter 401, Florida Statutes to regulate and ensure the quality, adequacy, and necessity of emergency and non-emergency ambulance transport services. Currently, these services are regulated under Article III, "Life Support Services," of Chapter 18 of the County Code. The current regulatory framework has been reviewed to ensure it meets the evolving needs of the County's population and modern emergency medical services (EMS) standards. The review indicated a need to modernize the criteria for service provision and clearly delineate the roles of all providers within the County's EMS system.
The proposed Ordinance is a complete repeal and replacement of the existing Article III, Chapter 18. Its primary purpose is to enhance the protection of the public health, safety, and welfare of St. Lucie County residents by establishing a robust and transparent system for the issuance of Certificates of Public Convenience and Necessity (COPCN).
The new ordinance implements a clear, two-tiered system for ambulance services:
Class A Certificate (Exclusive Emergency): This certificate is granted exclusively to the St. Lucie County Fire District (or its designee) for the provision of all 911-initiated emergency Advanced Life Support (ALS) and Basic Life Support (BLS) pre-hospital transport services. This solidifies the Fire District's role as the sole emergency service provider.
Class B Certificate (Non-Emergency): This certificate is required for all other entities (private companies, hospitals, etc.) providing non-emergency interfacility transfers or other transfers not initiated through the 911 system and not requiring ALS care.
Four-Year Application Cycle: Class B Certificates will now be issued for a term of four (4) years, with a mandated application period only occurring every fourth year (August 1–30). This process is tied to a formal Needs Assessment Survey conducted by the Public Safety Director to ensure continuous public need.
Enhanced Review Process: The new ordinance formalizes the advisory role of the Emergency Medical Services Advisory Council (EMSAC), which will review all applications against specific legislative standards, including financial fitness, operational readiness, and impact on existing services—before making a recommendation to the Board.

description:
Historically the County has been responsible for the cost of HIV medications for inmates and our agreement with the new inmate medical provider (NaphCare) has the same provision. Because the cost of HIV medication is very high, the County entered into an agreement with Midway Specialty Care Center ("Midway") to provide a more cost-effective means of providing HIV physician services and medications. Currently, the contract is structured to provide Midway with a stipend of $350.00 per eligible HIV/AIDS inmate per month for HIV medication and physician services. Bridge medications needed for those inmates waiting to be evaluated by Midway are currently purchased by the County from Midway at their 340b pass-through cost.
However, Midway has informed the County that the provisions underlying their ability to provide medication for $350 per month have changed, and they are no longer able to provide physician services and HIV medication for $350 per inmate per month. In addition, Midway has also informed the County that inmates seen at the jail no longer qualify for the reduced 340b drug pricing. Midway is still alible to provide physician services for inmates living with HIV/AIDS for $75 per office visit.
Staff is seeking to amend our agreement to remove any language related to Midway providing services at a rate of $350 per month per eligible inmate, as well as any language regarding the County purchasing medication from them.

attachments.name: Nineteenth Judicial Circuit - County Funded Employees

description:
The County is a political subdivision of the State of Florida and given those powers and responsibilities enumerated in Chapter 125, Florida Statutes. The County and the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit ('Circuit") are empowered to enter into interlocal agreements pursuant to Section 163.01, Florida Statutes. Section 29.0081(1), Florida Statutes, provides that counties and the chief judge of a judicial circuit may enter into an agreement where the county funds the cost of personnel positions to assist in the operation of the circuit. Section 29.0081(2), Florida Statutes, provides that personnel whose employment is funded under the agreement are hired, supervised, managed, and fired by personnel of the judicial circuit. The Circuit has requested that the County enter into an agreement to consider funding personnel positions. The County and the Circuit entered into an Interlocal Agreement on April 8, 2008 (hereinafter “Agreement”), a copy of which is attached, to clarify the parties’ responsibilities with regard to these personnel positions and desire to amend the Interlocal Agreement.
Attached is a copy of a draft First Amendment to the April 8, 2008 Interlocal Agreement between the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit and St. Lucie County for County—Funded employees for the Board's consideration. The Amendment provides the following:
COUNTY FUNDING OBLIGATIONS
The County agrees to annually consider the Circuit’s proposed budget which may include a request for funding personnel positions. If the County agrees to fund personnel positions to assist in the operations of the Circuit in accordance with Section 29.008(2), Florida Statutes, the County will include the salaries and benefits cost associated with these personnel positions within its budget. The County shall be considered the employer for purposes of Section 440.10, Florida Statutes and Chapter 443, Florida Statutes, in accordance with Section 29.008(2), Florida Statutes. Upon the effective date of the First Amendment Agreement, the County shall transfer all personnel files for County-funded Circuit employees to the Circuit.
CIRCUIT OBLIGATIONS
County-funded Circuit employees shall be hired, managed, supervised, and terminated by Circuit personnel as provided in Section 29.0081(2), Florida Statutes, and shall be considered employees of the Circuit, except as provided in Section 440.10 and Chapter 443, Florida Statutes. These employees shall be subject the provisions in the State Courts System Personnel Regulations Manual and any local personnel policies of the Circuit. When transferring between the County and the Circuit, these employees shall be credited for prior State of Florida service when calculating total years of service for the purposes of determining personnel-related benefits and calculation of accrued leave. The Circuit shall be responsible for compliance with all federal and state labor laws and shall indemnify the County from any liability under such laws, as provided in Section 29.0081(2), Florida Statutes, and authorized by Section 768.28(19), Florida Statutes. The Circuit shall also be responsible for determining any pay increases, and if needed, these pay increases shall be included in the Circuit’s proposed budget submitted to the County for these personnel positions each year.

description:
The Fiscal Year 2026 budget included $600,000 in funding to support the Housing Hub operated by the Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council (TCHSC).
St. Lucie County proposes to enter into an agreement with Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council, Inc. (TCHSC) for the continued operation of the Housing Hub program for homeless individuals. This initiative provides shelter for men and women, offering services such as case management, benefit enrollment, healthcare access, mental health services, employment support, and rental assistance. The agreement allocates $600,000 in funding for fiscal year 2026, with up to 15% available for administrative costs. The program aims to facilitate the transition of participants into permanent housing through comprehensive support and outreach efforts. description:
In July 2022, the Board of County Commissioners approved a Professional Services Agreement (C22-07-513) with The Counseling Center, Inc., d/b/a Integrated Healthcare Systems, to provide licensed mental and behavioral health services for veterans and other vulnerable populations in St. Lucie County.
The First Amendment, executed in December 2023, extended the term of the program through FY 2024 to allow completion of services under the existing budget.
The Second Amendment, approved in April 2024, reduced the total program budget by $80,000.00 and extended the term through December 31, 2026, or until the revised budget was expended.
Staff evaluated and realigned the remaining American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds supporting the Veterans Mental Health Program. Adjustments were made to redirect resources from contract labor toward professional services to better meet the needs of veterans seeking clinical evaluations and counseling. All expenditures remain within the $200,000.00 allocation previously approved by the Board for the ARPA-funded Veterans Mental Health initiative.
The proposed Third Amendment updates the agreement to reflect a revised program budget of $218,633.00 ($138,633.00 for the ARPA funded portion and a not-to-exceed amount of $80,000.00 for FY 2026). This amount includes all costs associated with continued delivery of behavioral health services to veterans.
Since its launch, the Veterans Mental Health Program has helped 123 veterans obtain service-connected disability benefits at varying levels—30%, 50%, 70%, and 100%. To calculate the financial impact, each veteran’s monthly benefit amount is recorded and totaled, then multiplied by twelve to estimate the annual value. Using the minimum compensation rates for each disability level, the program currently generates over $2 million per year in recurring benefits for local veterans. The actual total is even higher, as many veterans receive additional compensation based on dependents or special circumstances. This program not only accelerates access to mental health assessments—reducing wait times from 18 months to an average of just 76 days—but also provides lasting financial stability and support for St. Lucie County veterans and their families.
To sustain this successful initiative, the FY 2026 budget includes $80,000.00 in recurring funds to continue expedited mental health assessments and counseling services for veterans. This funding aligns with the County’s Strategic Plan objectives, specifically HS 4.3.1 to provide economic stability and support services in our community for those individuals and families experiencing vulnerabilities.

description:
Pursuant to Section 420.9076, Florida Statutes, local governments receiving State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) funding are required to establish an Affordable Housing Advisory Committee (AHAC). On May 27, 2008, the Board of County Commissioners adopted Ordinance No. 08-023 establishing the St. Lucie County AHAC to review and recommend specific actions to encourage or facilitate affordable housing opportunities.
The AHAC is charged with evaluating local policies, procedures, ordinances, land development regulations, and comprehensive plan provisions that impact the cost and availability of affordable housing. Each year, the committee must prepare and submit a report to the Board of County Commissioners (BOCC) identifying recommended actions or initiatives to promote affordable housing, consistent with state requirements.
The 2025 AHAC Recommendation Report was adopted by the Committee at a duly noticed public hearing held on October 8, 2025, following a series of meetings held throughout the year. The report includes findings and recommendations addressing the eleven statutory incentives outlined in Section 420.9076(4), Florida Statutes, as well as additional local recommendations to further support affordable housing development within St. Lucie County
Consistent with Incentive J: Preparation of a printed inventory of locally owned public lands suitable for affordable housing, and pursuant to Section 125.379, Florida Statutes, the County prepared and adopted an inventory list of all County-owned and dependent special district properties appropriate for affordable housing. On September 5, 2023, the Board approved Resolution No. 23-141, formally establishing the inventory of publicly owned properties suitable for affordable housing. The inventory satisfies both state statutory requirements and AHAC Incentive J, ensuring that publicly owned land resources are evaluated and made available for potential affordable housing development.
Key recommendations in the 2025 report include:
Expedited Permitting: Amend Resolution No. 10-060 to expand expedited permit review to all documented affordable housing projects, not only those receiving County grant funds.
Fee Reductions: Explore creation of a local Housing Trust Fund and survey peer jurisdictions for effective fee waiver or offset programs.
Parking and Setbacks: Formalize provisions in the Land Development Code allowing greater flexibility in parking and setback standards for affordable housing near transit or shared-parking areas.
Flexible Lot Configurations: Allow zero-lot-line configurations for qualifying affordable housing developments.
Periodic Policy Review: Establish a recurring five-year review process for County codes and ordinances to identify and amend provisions that may inadvertently increase housing costs.
Transit Proximity Incentives: Develop policies to encourage affordable and workforce housing within one-half mile of major transportation and employment centers, including potential density bonuses and reduced parking requirements.
In addition, the AHAC reaffirmed its recommendation to create an Affordable Housing Navigator/Advocate position to assist developers and nonprofit organizations in navigating housing programs and local processes, and to establish an Affordable Housing Developer Toolbox webpage on the County’s website.
It is important to note that this report was prepared prior to the County’s Evaluation and Appraisal Review (EAR)-based Comprehensive Plan Amendments currently underway. The EAR-based amendments included incorporating the statutory definition for affordable housing, consideration of development patterns which support multimodal solutions and mixed-use development options as well as connectivity with transit locations - consistent with the AHAC recommendations. As the EAR process advances, future updates to housing-related goals, objectives, and policies may be made to align with evolving state statutes and local planning priorities.
The 2025 AHAC Recommendation Report aligns with the County’s Strategic Plan goals to expand affordable and workforce housing opportunities (TC 3.4.1, AO 2.1.4) and to develop community-based strategies addressing housing affordability and stability.

The Community Services Block Grant (CSBG) program is administered regionally in partnership with St. Lucie, Martin, and Okeechobee Counties. In coordination with the Florida Department of Commerce (FloridaCommerce), staff have undertaken a comprehensive update of subrecipient agreements to ensure consistency with current federal regulations and reporting standards.
The Amended and Restated Interlocal Agreement with Martin County incorporates federally required elements outlined in 2 CFR 200 and 45 CFR 75, including:
The subrecipient’s unique entity identifier (UEI);
The subaward period of performance start and end dates;
The amount of federal funds obligated by this action and in total; and
Mandatory federal contract provisions such as Equal Employment Opportunity, Clean Air Act, Byrd Anti-Lobbying Amendment, Debarment and Suspension, and related clauses.
The updated agreement also aligns with the County’s umbrella agreement with FloridaCommerce and incorporates other revisions to strengthen program administration. Key updates include detailed monitoring and reporting requirements, current public records language consistent with Chapter 119, Florida Statutes, and clarified indemnification, record retention, and training provisions.
Approval of the amended agreement will ensure continued compliance with federal and state requirements and maintain the County’s eligibility to administer CSBG funds on behalf of the tri-county region.

description:
On November 5, 2019, St. Lucie County conveyed the property located at 1511 Emerald Terrace, Fort Pierce (Parcel ID 2409-820-0009-000-2) to St. Lucie Habitat for Humanity, Inc. for the development of permanent affordable housing.
The County Deed includes a reverter clause stating that, “in the event the Grantee fails to utilize the property for affordable housing, the Grantee agrees to convey the property back to St. Lucie County.”
The lot is approximately 0.33 acres and is zoned Single Family Moderate Density (SF-Moderate) within the City of Fort Pierce. Habitat has reported that, after presenting the site to at least five eligible homebuyers, none have been willing to purchase a home on this parcel.
Habitat has requested approval from the County to sell the property and use the net proceeds exclusively to construct other affordable homes within St. Lucie County. This approach would preserve the County’s intent that the property support affordable housing, while allowing Habitat to reinvest the proceeds into viable projects elsewhere in the community.
Since the County’s state and federal housing allocations are restricted to unincorporated areas, this parcel—located inside Fort Pierce city limits—cannot be directly developed with SHIP or HOME programs administered by the County. Habitat’s proposal would therefore allow the site’s value to continue serving local affordable housing goals without requiring the County to repossess and maintain the property.

description:
On April 18, 2023, St. Lucie County, the City of Fort Pierce, and the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency (FPRA) entered into an Interlocal Agreement to collaborate on the Moore’s Creek Redevelopment Project, also known as the Avenue D Model Block Project. This initiative is designed to foster affordable and workforce housing, job creation, and economic growth while preserving the historic and cultural character of the Avenue D corridor.
Following a Request for Information (RFI No. 23-054) and Request for Proposals (RFP No. 24-044) process led by St. Lucie County, the Board of County Commissioners, the City of Fort Pierce, and the FPRA each approved the selection of Pinnacle Communities II, LLC to develop the project site. The proposed development will include approximately 90 affordable multifamily rental units and associated site improvements designed to enhance the neighborhood and support community revitalization.
To facilitate project implementation, the County and FPRA have each agreed to lease their respective parcels to Pinnacle at Moore's Creek, LLC (or its assigns) under a jointly executed Ground Lease. The lease encompasses approximately 3.01± acres—including 2.30± acres owned by the County (Parcel ID: 2410-601-0181-000-2) and 0.71± acres owned by the FPRA (Parcel IDs: 2410-601-0182-000-9 and 2410-601-0183-000-6)—for the development of the affordable housing project. The lease term is ninety-nine (99) years, commencing upon financial closing and execution of a Development Agreement.
Under the terms of the lease, the Lessee will pay a capital lease payment equal to $10,000 per residential unit constructed on the site, as evidenced by building permits issued by the City of Fort Pierce. The total capital lease payment will be distributed proportionately to each entity based on the land contributed. In addition, the annual base rent is set at $1.00 per year for the entire lease term, paid in full at closing.
The project will be developed in accordance with the approved site plan and consistent with the Lessee’s proposal submitted under RFP No. 24-044. For the first fifty (50) years of the lease term, all residential units will be restricted to households earning at or below 80% of the Area Median Income (AMI), ensuring long-term affordability.
Staff has coordinated with the County Attorney’s Office, the FPRA, and the City of Fort Pierce in the preparation and review of the lease. The proposed lease reflects the terms negotiated between the parties in accordance with the Interlocal Agreement and supports the County’s strategic objectives to expand affordable housing opportunities, strengthen community partnerships, and promote redevelopment within the Avenue D corridor.
This initiative directly supports the Thriving Community goal of the St. Lucie County Strategic Plan, specifically Objective TC 3.4.1 – Develop and implement a plan to expand affordable, essential, and workforce housing opportunities and Objective TC 3.4.4 – Seek out and leverage state and federal funding sources to expand the housing inventory and improve housing affordability.

description:
On April 18, 2023, St. Lucie County, the City of Fort Pierce, and the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency (FPRA) entered into an Interlocal Agreement to collaborate on the Avenue D Model Block Project, a redevelopment initiative designed to promote affordable and workforce housing, stimulate economic activity, and revitalize the Avenue D corridor. The partnership established a phased approach to guide coordinated planning, procurement, and redevelopment efforts among the three entities.
Following the completion of Phase 1 (Request for Letters of Interest) and Phase 2 (Request for Proposals), the County—serving as lead procurement agency—issued RFP No. 24-044. After a competitive solicitation process, Pinnacle Communities II, Inc. (“Pinnacle”) was recommended by the selection committee and subsequently approved by all three entities as the development partner for the project. Pinnacle will construct approximately 90 affordable multifamily rental units and related site improvements on parcels owned by the County and FPRA within the Avenue D corridor.
The First Amendment to the Interlocal Agreement updates and expands upon the 2023 agreement to reflect the completion of prior phases and to define the responsibilities of each entity during future stages of development. Notably, the City of Fort Pierce is no longer a participating property owner in the initial phase of development, as City-owned parcels were removed from the project area. The City remains a party to the Agreement for coordination, permitting, and potential participation in later phases.
Under the amended agreement, St. Lucie County and FPRA will continue as the lead property owners for Phase 3 (Lease Negotiations) and Phase 4 (Lease Approval). The parties will collaborate to prepare and execute a 99-year ground lease with Pinnacle to establish site control and enable financing through the Florida Housing Finance Corporation.
Phase 5 (Financial Contributions) formalizes each party’s financial commitments in support of the project’s competitive housing credit application. St. Lucie County has allocated $460,000 as its Local Government Area of Opportunity (LGAO) funding contribution for Phase 1 of the development. For future phases, the City or FPRA may, at their discretion and subject to funding availability and requisite approvals, consider providing a LGAO contribution. This statement of intent is non-binding and does not obligate any party to provide or approve future funding. No additional funding commitment beyond the County’s allocation is required for the construction of the project
Subsequent phases address the negotiation of a Development Agreement, site plan and permitting approvals, construction, and continued coordination among the parties to ensure successful project implementation. The amendment also clarifies termination provisions and ensures continued alignment with St. Lucie County’s strategic goals to expand affordable housing opportunities, strengthen intergovernmental partnerships, and promote revitalization within the Avenue D corridor.
