description:
On July 23, 2025, responses to RFQ No. 25-064, Community Land Trust Partner, were opened. Two proposals were received; 885 companies were notified, and 25 RFP documents were distributed.
The purpose of this RFQ is for St. Lucie County to partner with a qualified Community Land Trust (CLT) to develop and steward permanently affordable, owner-occupied housing opportunities for households with an income earning range between 80% and 120% of the Area Median Income (AMI).
In accordance with guidance from the Florida Community Land Trust Institute, the County emphasizes that the CLT must reflect a thorough understanding of Florida-specific community land trust practices, including compliance with Section 193.018, Florida Statutes, which governs the valuation and taxation of CLT properties. The selected CLT must use a 99-year renewable ground lease structure and resale restrictions to ensure homes remain permanently affordable to future income-qualified buyers. The CLT should demonstrate the capacity to educate buyers on the benefits and limitations of shared equity homeownership, provide pre- and post-purchase counseling, and support long-term stewardship.
St. Lucie County is experiencing significant population growth, rising housing costs, and a constrained supply of housing options for middle-income households. As identified in the 2024 Housing Needs Assessment, households earning between 80% and 120% of the Area Median Income (AMI) are underserved by existing affordable housing programs yet often cannot afford market-rate options. To address this gap, the County seeks to partner with a qualified Community Land Trust (CLT) to develop and steward permanently affordable, owner-occupied housing opportunities for households within this income range. The CLT will play a critical role in ensuring long-term affordability through ground lease models and stewardship services.
On September 8, 2025, the selection committee evaluated and ranked the proposals that were received. The committee members' scores and ranking for each firm are provided in Attachment A.

description:
Indian River Estates is an existing 1,300 acre subdivision located in unincorporated St. Lucie County. Indian River Estates is bounded by North St. Lucie River Water Control District (NSLRWCD) Canal 22 to the west, Midway Road to the north, and the Savannas Preserve State Park (Savannas) to the south and east. Drainage within the subdivision is divided along a north-south axis. Most of the subdivision drains east toward the Savannas, but a portion of the stormwater runoff flows west to the North St. Lucie River Water Control District Canal 22 and Canal 23.
Development of the subdivision started in the 1950s and is mostly built out. Since Indian River Estates predates modern stormwater regulations, the development does not have the typical stormwater management facilities associated with newer subdivisions. The subdivision frequently experiences flooding issues due to inefficient drainage collection and conveyance, flat topography, high groundwater levels, and tailwater influences from the Savannas. Additionally, high water levels within Indian River Estates can result in untreated stormwater discharges to the Savannas, contributing to degradation of water quality. Easy Street, the southernmost street in the subdivision, historically experienced the worst flooding issues due to lower elevations and its proximity to the Savannas.
The County has designed and constructed a large-scale drainage retrofit to improve drainage and reduce flooding occurrences. Phase 1 improvements, including a stormwater pump station, force main and treatment pond, were completed in 2009. Phase II improvements, designed by Inwood Consulting Engineers, were completed in 2015. Phase 2 added a gravity storm sewer collection system, swale grading improvements, and modifications to the outfalls to the Savannas. These projects have improved drainage conditions within Indian River Estates, but flooding and inefficient drainage is still a concern in the low-lying areas along Easy Street and in western portions of the subdivision.
Phase 3 improvements are a continuation of the St. Lucie County’s investments to date. The project seeks to build on the improvements initiated under previous phases by addressing three main elements:
Evaluate the drainage along Easy Street. Provide recommendations to reduce road flooding during heavy rain events.
Address interactions of flow between Indian River Estates and the Savannas. Evaluate options to reduce/ prevent backflow from the Savannas.
Address internal block drainage systems that are located outside the limits of Phase 2. Provide cost-effective recommendations and designs to improve drainage efficacy.
On October 17, 2023, the Board was presented with and approved three drainage improvement alternatives that were recommended by the design team and County staff.
The project was advertised on September 7, 2025, and the bids were opened on October 8, 2025. Five bids were received, and the lowest responsible bidder was Johnson-Davis, Inc. with a total bid amount of $417,879.00.

attachments.name: BIE - Ordinance No. 25-XXX - Amending Reasonable Accommodation Section 7.10.30

description:
On August 1, 1990, the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County, Florida, adopted the St. Lucie County Land Development Code.
On April 2, 2013, the Board adopted a reasonable accommodation ordinance.
"Reasonable Accommodation" is a statutorily established method by which an individual who is disabled and/or handicapped (as those terms are defined in Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and/or the Fair Housing Amendments Act, hereafter "disabled"), or a provider of services to the disabled qualifying for reasonable accommodations under the referred statutes, can request a modification or alteration in the application of a specific Code provision, rule, policy, or practice, to them. The proposed accommodation sought by the disabled individual must be reasonable and necessary to afford such person an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
On December 6, 2022, the Board adopted a reasonable accommodation ordinance that changed the appeal body from the Board of County Commissioners to the Circuit Court.
In the 2025 Legislative Session, the legislature passed an act relating to certified recovery residences, Section 397.487 (15)(a), F.S. This new legislation requires, by January 1, 2026, the governing body of each county or municipality shall adopt an ordinance establishing procedures for the review and approval of certified recovery residences within its jurisdiction. The ordinance must include a process for requesting reasonable accommodations from any local land use regulation that serves to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence. The proposed ordinance addresses the statutory requirement.
Staff finds the proposed Land Development Code (LDC) Text Amendment is consistent with LDC Section 11.06.03. — Standards of Review, and consistent with Florida Statutes.

BIE - Ordinance No. 25-XXX - Amend the Text of LDC - Tree Mitigation Exemptions

description:
On August 1, 1990, the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County adopted the St. Lucie County Land Development Code to implement the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan. Goal 2.1 of the Transportation Element within St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan requires that the County provide a safe and efficient integrated multi-modal transportation system which addresses the future needs of St. Lucie County for movement of people and goods, and which considers social, economic, energy and environmental effects including greenhouse gas emissions of the transportation system. The Board is obligated to maintain concurrency in accordance with level of service standards as established by the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan. Goal 6.1 of the Conservation Element within the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan requires that the natural resources of St. Lucie County shall be protected, appropriately used, or conserved in a manner which maximizes their functions and values. The proposed ordinance provides for the improvement of certain essential infrastructure without mitigation to balance and minimize threats of degradation to the health, safety and welfare of the county's citizens.
In this regard, please find attached a draft ordinance, which, if adopted, would provide clarification on the removal of native vegetation for the construction of any non-site-related roadway extensions or expansions, identified in the County's Right-of-Way Protection Plan or the Jenkins Road Area Plan (special district) and prescribed by a site plan approval, site development permit or roadway improvement agreement, provided the roadway will be dedicated to and is agreed to be accepted by St. Lucie County for perpetual ownership and maintenance; with the roadway accepted at such time the improvement serves as a thoroughfare for the County's overall roadway network. Additionally, the draft ordinance would provide clarification on the removal of native vegetation for road construction within an existing County right-of-way. The proposed changes allow this road work to be conducted and exempt from mitigation.
The ordinance, if adopted, will also provide an exemption for vegetation removal activities associated with the operation and maintenance of a water control district system for drainage purposes. Lastly, the ordinance incorporates an exemption established by Section 163.045, F.S., which addresses the removal of a native tree on a residential property with a single-family, detached dwelling unit, if the property owner possesses documentation from an arborist certified by the ISA or a Florida licensed landscape architect that the tree poses an unacceptable risk to persons or property. A tree poses an unacceptable risk if the removal is the only means of practically mitigating its risk below moderate, as determined by the tree risk assessment procedures outlined in Best Management Practices - Tree Risk Assessment, Second Edition (2017).
Staff finds the proposed Land Development Code (LDC) Text Amendment is consistent with LDC Section 11.06.03. - Standards of Review.

description:
St. Lucie County (SLC) received $800,000 in legislative appropriation funding from fiscal year 2023/2024 which was matched with $800,000 of Parks Impact Fees. The funding will support ADA-accessible and sensory-friendly infrastructure for passive recreation at the County preserve located on Oleander Ave., near the Kitterman Rd intersection. The funding will aid in the development of the preserve for visitors to enjoy nature with amenities specially designed for people with Autism Spectrum Disorder, including parking areas, interpretive signage/communication boards, nature trails, boardwalks, a restroom, a river observation area, a pavilion/ outdoor classroom, nature play areas, a kayak stopover, and benches/picnic areas. This site will be the County's first inclusive design preserve and will provide opportunities to connect people with nature, river access, and sensory-friendly amenities specially designed for people with unique abilities and special needs.
This agenda item requests authorization to "piggyback" on the Lake County Contract #22-908B to purchase a Pre-Cast "Triple Plumbed Restroom" per Proposal #KT-2025-063 from Leesburg Concrete Company.
The 33-acre property, purchased in 2015 for $457,533, will be preserved in perpetuity primarily for managing and maintaining the high-quality native habitats that provide ecological benefits (clean air, carbon sequestration, aquifer recharge, water quality improvements, wildlife habitat, etc.). A priority goal in ERD is to provide a variety of passive recreation opportunities without negatively impacting the natural resources within the natural areas we manage. This site contains 20 acres of floodplain forest, 11 acres of pine flatwoods, and 2 acres of river oxbows that are all in very good condition. SLC's preserve system facilitates physically active and healthy lifestyles through access to greenways and trails, which are an essential component in walkable community designs. Preserves play a significant role in connecting residents and visitors to the County's natural and human heritage by telling the story of the land, water and people. Being outdoors, in nature, helps to cultivate knowledge, nurture a sense of wonder, and inspire stewardship of the natural world through education, artistic expression, physical activity, and is shown to improve mental health/wellness. The proposed amenities will provide opportunities to connect people to the North Fork of the St. Lucie River, through passive and active programming, will instill a sense of place, stewardship, and community cohesiveness.

attachments.name: WA#01 - Oxbow Eco-Center Expansion with attachment

description:
The purpose of this work authorization is to establish a contract with Peacock Architects for professional architectural services to create a conceptual site plan and schematic design for the expansion of the Oxbow Eco-Center. The expansion includes an approximately 10,000 SF new Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) building, adjacent to the existing Oxbow Eco-Center.
This conceptual site plan and schematic design will include 3D renderings and materials designed to inspire capital fundraising efforts. It is the intention to fund the building construction without the use of taxpayer dollars. Grants and private donations through a professionally led capital fundraising campaign will be the primary source of funds.
The Oxbow Eco-Center’s visitation and program services have outgrown the facility space. Over 1.25 million people have visited the site since it opened in 2000, with an estimated 50,000 visiting Oxbow just last year. With projected population growth, community needs for programming and facility use are expected to grow with it. We currently do not have the capacity to host weddings, birthday parties, large professional functions, and/or events due to space limitations and/or ongoing programs, although we consistently receive requests for such facility use rentals. With a new building, these requests could be accommodated, opening a new source of revenue for St. Lucie County.
This project is in accordance with Strategic Plan Policy TC 3.3.1 – Identify and expand year-round economic impact opportunities in parks, recreation, tourism, culture and education with related community partners and businesses. This directly supports the goal of creating a revenue-generating facility by focusing on economic impact through tourism, recreation, and education — all of which can be served by an expanded Nature Center used for events, rentals, exhibits, or programming.
The primary focus will be to provide a conceptual site plan and space plan for the new LEED building, which will include the following program: Classrooms, Workshops, Offices, Event Space (Used for events i.e. weddings etc.), Catering Kitchen, Outdoor space, and Ancillary spaces to accommodate the program as needed. With an additional building, the current Oxbow facility would be able to extend public hours. Instead of serving as both a visitor center and classroom / program space, it could serve solely as a visitor center with nature exhibits, a gift store, and live animals for the public to enjoy, without needing to close or redirect the public when programs are in session.

description:
The purpose of this project was to construct improvements to the existing water control structure for the pond located at the northeast corner of the Bell Avenue and South 25th Street intersection. The proposed modifications were designed to provide additional water quality treatment and nutrient removal within the existing stormwater pond without increasing losses in the system or altering the flood or water quality elevations.
The prior water control structure design was prone to clogging with dirt and debris at the intake and was challenging to maintain. The modifications reoriented the structure and added extra measures to prevent clogging, as well as making maintenance easier. During construction, an intake pipe was added to improve drainage into the pond and slope protection measures were also incorporated to improve the overall resiliency of the structure.
The total amount for this project was $144,802.90, which includes the full contingency amount of $13,163.90.
Staff monitored the construction and determined the project was completed in conformance with the plans and specifications. The project was completed within budget.

description:
Staff have been monitoring two critical culvert crossings under N. FFA Road at NSLRWCD Canals 44 and 45, with video inspection and periodic visual inspections of the roadway at the crossings.
Over the past few years, both locations exhibited small depressions reoccurring just outside the edge of pavement, above or alongside the culvert pipes, which is indicative of soil traveling into a severely deteriorated section of the aged metal pipes and/or a partial collapse of the pipe.
Prior rainfall events, including Hurricane Milton, had increased the intensity of the depressions at these two culverts, to the point where the roadway integrity was threatened. County Administration approved staff recommendations to proceed with the emergency replacement/rehabilitation of the culverts and the restoration of the roadway pavement.
The total amount for this project was $830,599.00, including $75,509.00 in contingency, of which, $12,796.50 was used. The actual total construction cost was $767,886.50, which was $62,712.50 under budget.
Staff monitored the construction and determined the project was completed in conformance with the plans and specifications.

description:
The SLCSO’s FY 2024–2025 Budget Request (please see Attachment 1) included a Supplemental Budget Appropriation for:
Contingency Budget for FRS – $500,000.
Typically, the State of Florida implements revised employer contribution rates for FRS each July. These adjustments are mandatory and apply to SLCSO personnel. While this year’s rate increase was moderate compared to prior years and less than previously projected as part of the FY 24-25 budgeting process, it still significantly impacted the agency’s personnel costs.
As you know, the SLCSO Budget does not currently include a dedicated contingency fund for these types of mid-year cost increases.
Utilizing the published contribution rates pre- and post-increase, the SLCSO Finance Division calculated the variance for each employee of the SLCSO’s General Fund (BOCC-funded) over the July-August-September period and resulting sum, sharing the calculation worksheets with County staff.
Please note that the calculated total of $242,394.26 does not include:
Special Revenue Fund employees (e.g., School Resource Deputies).
FRS contributions related to overtime activity (which was excluded from the scope of the analysis).
However, it does include the one case at the SLCSO in which the employer contribution decreased as a result of the new rates.
As you may recall, the FRS shortfall was anticipated during the original budgeting process and referenced in the SLCSO’s FY 2024–2025 Budget Request under a contingency amount of $500,000. Accordingly, the SLCSO is now requesting that $242,394.26 of that anticipated amount be formally appropriated to ensure continued compliance with FRS mandates and end of year budgeting requirements. The FY 24-25 books are kept open for up to ​one month following ​September ​30.

description:
During the summer of 2025, ETC Institute administered a community survey for St. Lucie County. The purpose of the survey was to assess resident satisfaction as part of the County’s on-going effort to identify and respond to the needs of the community.
The seven-page survey, cover letter and postage-paid return envelope were mailed to a random sample of households in St. Lucie County. The cover letter explained the purpose of the survey and encouraged residents to either return their survey by mail or complete the survey online.
The goal was to receive 600 completed surveys. This goal was far exceeded, with 709 households completing the survey. The results for 709 households have a 95% level of confidence with a precision of at least +/-3.7%.
The percentage of “don’t know” responses have been excluded from many of the graphs and the benchmarking data shown to facilitate valid comparisons between county services. Since the number of “don’t know” responses often reflect the utilization and awareness of county services, the percentage of “don’t know” responses have been provided in the tabular data section of the Community Survey Findings report.
Major Findings:
Most respondents (77%) rated their overall quality of life in St. Lucie County as either “good” (53%) or “very good” (24%).
The three items’ respondents thought will be most important to the overall quality of life in St. Lucie over the next 10 years (rating “important” or “very important”) are public safety (96%), infrastructure (95%), and balancing the impacts of growth (92%).
When asked to rate their satisfaction with aspects of their customer experience, respondents were most satisfied (rating “satisfied” or “very satisfied”) with the courtesy of the county employees (83%), timeliness of county employees’ response (74%), and the ease of contacting the employee needed (74%)
Highly rated areas include “would you recommend the Library to family and friends” at 94% positive, “access to parks and green spaces” at 78% positive / 92% positive with neutral responses, and “the County’s hurricane/storm response efforts” at 78% positive / 95% positive with neutral.
Areas of opportunity identified include “availability of housing options at varying price points to rent” at 12% positive / 37% positive with neutral, “availability of housing options at varying price points to purchase” at 19% positive / 45% positive with neutral, and “ability to earn a living wage” at 26% positive / 60% positive with neutral.
For historical reference, the most important issue residents identified facing St. Lucie County in the 2022 Community Survey was also Housing Affordability and the Cost of Living.
The full report includes an executive summary of the methodology and major findings, charts depicting the overall results of the survey, benchmarking analysis, Importance-Satisfaction for investments, tabular data, and a copy of the survey that was distributed.

description:
In 2021, the County was awarded a Community Development Block Grant-Mitigation (CDBG-MIT) grant, administered through the FL Department of Economic Opportunity (now Florida Commerce), in the amount of $210,000.00 for the purposes of developing an infrastructure plan incorporating land use planning, comprehensive planning, resiliency planning, and mitigation planning. The plan shall include updated mapping and elevation data to revise the County's Right-of-Way Protection Plan based on sea level rise projections, the need for and location of future stormwater capacity, elevated road sections, and mitigation needs for public infrastructure within the ultimate County Right-of-Way. The plan has the potential to assist the county's elected and appointed officials in mitigating the impacts of sea level rise and natural disasters. As a match to the awarded grant, the County committed $40,000.00 in funds.
Subsequently, in November 2022, the County selected and entered into a contract with The Corradino Group, Inc. to provide the services outlined in the Scope of Services for the awarded grant. The services included in the contract are as follows:Project Management
Typical Street Sections and Street Map Update
Sea Level Rise Projections and Mobility Network Water Storage Designs
Right-of-Way Cross-Sections with Stormwater Mitigation Techniques
Right-of-Way Acquisition Strategies
Multi-Modal Master Street Grid Maps
Draft Comprehensive Plan Policies
Public Engagement
Reporting
On September 10, 2024, PDS and the Corradino Group provided the BOCC with an introduction and an update on the project and discussed the next steps.
The purpose of this agenda item is to provide the Board with a summary of the plan and identify the cause-and-effect relationship of infrastructure investment as future conditions evolve with sea level rise, flooding impacts and natural climate disasters.

description:
As part of St. Lucie County's commitment to a resilient future, the update to the Stormwater Master Plan (SMP) has been underway for two years. This presentation will share the goals and objectives of the plan, cover some of the key data points that helped to shape the plan and will provide a current snapshot and future steps to complete the update to the plan.
The previous version of the County's stormwater plan was completed in 1992 and although it is relevant, the outputs and assumptions are no longer as useful due to the changes in future land use and growth patterns the area has experienced since that time. Furthermore, the tools to model present and future scenarios have evolved. This update uses the latest in hydrologic and hydraulic (H&H) modeling to look beyond today's conditions and plan effectively for the next 20-year cycle of growth.
Public Works staff has been aided by the consultant team led by Tetra Tech, Inc. and this update to the Board will show the work completed to date and the preliminary results of the Stormwater Master Plan.

description:
The County's Public Works Department is responsible for the maintenance of 600 miles of roads, 110 miles of sidewalks, 28 bridges and roughly 70 traffic signals. Circa 2006-2008, with the world's economy in a plunge, the County's restructuring in response to the great recession greatly constrained available revenues. As costs of labor and materials continue to rise, the existing revenue from fuel tax became insufficient to sustain proper preventative maintenance of the County's infrastructure.
The 2018 voter-approved half-cent infrastructure surtax has provided St. Lucie County and the cities of Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie much-needed revenue towards critical infrastructure projects. With an estimated 15–20 percent of revenue coming from tourists, this additional resource has helped make headway against the backlog of deferred maintenance that has languished since the great recession.
The focus of the surtax was and is projects that deliver "better roads, more sidewalks and cleaner rivers". The Board will be provided a review of the framework of the surtax, an update on the proceeds and expenditures and cover key projects that could not have been completed without the surtax proceeds.
The upcoming November 2026 general election provides an opportunity for the voters of St. Lucie County to continue the surtax, should the Board of County Commissioners elect to place the item on the ballot. Staff will explore the next suite of potential projects that could be recipients of surtax proceeds and seek Board direction.

description:
St. Lucie County developed the Sunshine Kitchen Food Business Incubator (Sunshine Kitchen) in 2018 with a US Economic Development Administration grant. The Sunshine Kitchen Food Business Incubator, a 10,000-square foot facility providing year-round, 24-hour-a-day access to users to prepare, produce, package, and market food business items, has been operating since September 2018. The Sunshine Kitchen was created as a community kitchen concept where food entrepreneurs could develop their products in a commercially-equipped shared-use kitchen. The concept follows other business incubation methodologies that provide start-up businesses with management guidance, technical assistance, and relatively low-cost facilities in which the entrepreneur can develop their venture until the company is strong enough to secure its own brick-and-mortar or conventional commercial space. The Sunshine Kitchen continues to grow and serve numerous entrepreneurs, with over 120 clients currently.
The use of kitchen facilities directly impacts costs related to staff workload, contract labor, utilities, supplies, equipment maintenance, cleaning and security. As such, the Board adopted a fee schedule via Resolution 2024-184 on October 1, 2024. The adoption of the uniform fee schedule was necessary for the efficient administration of the Sunshine Kitchen and is in the public interest. It is in the best interests of the general public to charge a fee for services provided by the County, so that those parties deriving the benefit(s) from County-provided services pay for the costs of providing those services. It is appropriate to maintain a fee schedule to properly reflect the technical and operational costs incurred by the County in providing use of the kitchen facilities and rates that are sustainable to the community.
In 2024, the Sunshine Kitchen applied for and was awarded a United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Rural Development Grant (RBDG) for $225,000.00, to assist with the purchase and installation of additional refrigeration and freezer storage. The installation of an outdoor refrigeration and freezer storage unit has been completed and is available for Kitchen users to lease. This additional cold storage allows the Sunshine Kitchen to expand services to clients and the use of the walk-in cooler requires a key/access card for security purposes. The users are provided the initial key at no cost, but the attached fee resolution establishes a few for replacement keys/access cards.
Further, based on feedback and engagement with the clients, the Sunshine Kitchen is expanding the online payments with an option to pay via credit card, subject to third-party convenience fee. Lastly, the attached fee resolution updates the 2% annual adjustment included in the previous resolutions.

description:
The final surveys, conservation easement and Preserve Area Management and Monitoring Plan (PAMMP) documentation have been reviewed by staff and the remaining acreage required by Oak Ridge Ranches is 125.6 acres to satisfy the mitigation requirements. This includes 107.5 acres of habitat to be mitigated plus the quantified acreage from the grading for drainage, which is 18.1 acres, bringing the total acreage to 125.6 acres. This agenda item is to accept a payment of $1,888,721.30 (125.6 acres x $15,037.59/acre) dollars from Oak Ridge Ranches, LLC to satisfy their remaining mitigation and reimburse a portion of the County purchase of the 399-acre Junior Louis Ranch, LLC property.
Oak Ridge Ranches:
The Oak Ridge Ranches development is located north of Glades Cut Off Road, and West of and adjacent to the future extension of Range Line Road.
On October 12, 2023, the Board of County Commissioners approved the Comprehensive Plan Future Land Use Map Amendment for the Oak Ridge Ranches MXD Activity Area via Ordinance 23-015.
On October 12, 2023, the Board of County Commissioners granted a change in zoning to the PUD Zoning District with an associated Preliminary PUD (Master) Site Plan for +/- 3,229.27 acres which encompass the Oak Ridge Ranches PUD via Resolution No. 23-201.
On November 12, 2024, the Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 2024-229 approving Phase 1 (A) Final Site Plan within the project known as Oak Ridge Ranches PUD, which included condition 26 requiring conveyance of a Conservation Easement over the core onsite preserve areas for the Phase 1(A) site plan along with a Preserve Area Management and Monitoring Plan (PAMMP) to St. Lucie County prior to commencement of development. This Resolution also included condition 24 with “The remaining ±107.5 acres of required tree mitigation shall be satisfied via the applicant purchasing land off-site with the equivalent acreage and similar ecological value (i.e., comparable upland habitat) to be conveyed fee simple to St. Lucie County for ownership and management.”
On January 21, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 2025-30 accepting a Conservation Easement and Preserve Area Management and Monitoring Plan (PAMMP) from Oak Ridge Ranches, LLC, associated with Phase 1(A)/Spine Road. The Conservation Easement and PAMMP covered the core onsite preserve areas, which is comprised of four (4) primary areas known as CE, CW, SW, and Wildlife Corridor. The Conservation Easement and PAMMP consists of both native upland habitat and jurisdictional wetlands and their associated upland buffers, totaling ±266.2 acres, ±160.3 acres, and ±61.2 acres respectively, when combined equates to ±487.7 total acres placed under Conservation Easement.
On August 5, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 2025-159 accepting a Conservation Easement and Preserve Area Management and Monitoring Plan (PAMMP) from Oak Ridge Ranches, LLC, for areas outside the Phase 1(A)/Spine Road. The Conservation Easement and PAMMP covered the remaining twenty (20) preserve areas consisting of both native upland habitat and jurisdictional wetlands and their associated upland buffers, totaling ±92.3 acres and ±89.8 acres, and ±37.2 acres respectively, when combined equates to ±219.3 total acres placed under Conservation Easement.
Junior Louis Ranch, LLC:
At the April 15, 2025 Informal Meeting, the Board of County Commissioners “discussed the opportunity to preserve 400 acres of land on the western side of the County, off Okeechobee Road and immediately north of the Cypress Creek Preserve and the Pineland Preserve, slightly to the east. The property is listed on environmentally sensitive land, with quality habitat. The property, initially listed at $10 million and relisted at $7.6 million, has been appraised at $6 million, which is approximately $15,000 per acre. To acquire the property, funding would need to be moved from the Reserves. The County has an opportunity with Oak Ridge Ranches, where they have some additional [m]itigation that needs to be completed, which is 125 – 130 acres that needs to be satisfied. In partnership with Oak Ridge Ranches, they would be investing just under $2 million at the acreage rate to help purchase and protect the land.” After discussing the proposal, the Board reached a consensus of 4 to 1 to move forward and make an offer.
On May 6, 2025, the Board of County Commissioners approved the Contract for Sale and Purchase - Junior Louis Ranch, LLC - Parcel ID 3119-111-0001-000-2. The property consisted of 399.50 +/- acres and lies west of Okeechobee Road and just east of the Okeechobee/St. Lucie County line. The agenda item included:
Oak Ridge Ranches, LLC "(Kolter) is the main developer of the Oak Ridge Ranches Project (Project) located off Glades Cut Off Road and Range Line Road. The Project includes the preservation of 376.5 acres of environmentally sensitive lands, including wetlands, wetland buffers, upland habitats and the 101’ wildlife corridor onsite, via a recorded conservation easement. There is an additional approximately 107.5 acres of habitat to be mitigated plus the quantified acreage from the grading for drainage, which is currently estimated to be 125-130 acres inclusive of both impacts. The County has been coordinating with Kolter on satisfying its remaining preservation through the purchase of land off-site with the equivalent acreage and similar ecological value (i.e., comparable habitat). Kolter has indicated a desire to satisfy the remaining mitigation through a financial contribution to this purchase for the equivalent acreage required to be mitigated.
…There are potential future revenue sources that may be available to reimburse some of the cost of the land, including:
• Contribution from Oak Ridge Ranch to meet their environmental mitigation obligations. They may contribute approximately $1.8-1.9 million to this purchase.
• Future reimbursement from grants”
On July 9, 2025, the County closed on the acquisition of the Junior Louis Ranch, LLC property for a land purchase price of $6,000,000 for 399 acres (approx. $15,037.59/acre). The total purchase cost with closing costs was $6,055,949.16 (approx. $15,177.82/acre).

description:
On August 1, 1990, the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County adopted the St. Lucie County Land Development Code to implement the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan. Goal 2.1 of the Transportation Element within St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan requires that the County provide a safe and efficient integrated multi-modal transportation system which addresses the future needs of St. Lucie County for movement of people and goods, and which considers social, economic, energy and environmental effects including greenhouse gas emissions of the transportation system. The Board is obligated to maintain concurrency in accordance with level of service standards as established by the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan. Goal 6.1 of the Conservation Element within the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan requires that the natural resources of St. Lucie County shall be protected, appropriately used, or conserved in a manner which maximizes their functions and values. The proposed ordinance provides for the improvement of certain essential infrastructure without mitigation to balance and minimize threats of degradation to the health, safety and welfare of the county's citizens.
In this regard, please find attached a draft ordinance, which, if adopted, would provide clarification on the removal of native vegetation for the construction of any non-site-related roadway extensions or expansions, identified in the County's Right-of-Way Protection Plan or the Jenkins Road Area Plan (special district) and prescribed by a site plan approval, site development permit or roadway improvement agreement, provided the roadway will be dedicated to and is agreed to be accepted by St. Lucie County for perpetual ownership and maintenance; with the roadway accepted at such time the improvement serves as a thoroughfare for the County's overall roadway network. Additionally, the draft ordinance would provide clarification on the removal of native vegetation for road construction within an existing County right-of-way. The proposed changes allow this road work to be conducted and exempt from mitigation.
The ordinance, if adopted, will also provide an exemption for vegetation removal activities associated with the operation and maintenance of a water control district system for drainage purposes. Lastly, the ordinance incorporates an exemption established by Section 163.045, F.S., which addresses the removal of a native tree on a residential property with a single-family, detached dwelling unit, if the property owner possesses documentation from an arborist certified by the ISA or a Florida licensed landscape architect that the tree poses an unacceptable risk to persons or property. A tree poses an unacceptable risk if the removal is the only means of practically mitigating its risk below moderate, as determined by the tree risk assessment procedures outlined in Best Management Practices - Tree Risk Assessment, Second Edition (2017).

description:
On August 1, 1990, the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County, Florida, adopted the St. Lucie County Land Development Code.
On April 2, 2013, the Board adopted a reasonable accommodation ordinance.
"Reasonable Accommodation" is a statutorily established method by which an individual who is disabled and/or handicapped (as those terms are defined in Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and/or the Fair Housing Amendments Act, hereafter "disabled"), or a provider of services to the disabled qualifying for reasonable accommodations under the referred statutes, can request a modification or alteration in the application of a specific Code provision, rule, policy, or practice, to them. The proposed accommodation sought by the disabled individual must be reasonable and necessary to afford such person an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
On December 6, 2022, the Board adopted a reasonable accommodation ordinance that changed the appeal from the Board of County Commissioners to the Circuit Court.
In the 2025 Legislative Session, the legislature passed an act relating to certified recovery residences in Section 397.487(15)(a), F.S. This new legislation requires, by January 1, 2026, the governing body of each county or municipality shall adopt an ordinance establishing procedures for the review and approval of certified recovery residences within its jurisdiction. The ordinance must include a process for requesting reasonable accommodations from any local land use regulation that serves to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence. The proposed ordinance addresses the statutory requirement.

description:
St. Lucie County applied for funding under the FFY 2023–2024 Florida Small Cities Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) – Housing Rehabilitation category through the Florida Department of Commerce (FloridaCommerce). The County’s application requested $850,000 in federal CDBG funds to address the rehabilitation or demolition/replacement of substandard housing units for low- and moderate-income households in unincorporated St. Lucie County.
The proposed project, as outlined in the application, includes:
Rehabilitation or demolition/replacement of a minimum of 11 housing units, of which at least 5 units will serve low-income households and at least 2 units will serve very low-income households.
Funding allocation of $711,500 for housing rehabilitation or demolition/replacement, $11,000 for temporary relocation assistance, and $127,500 for program administration.
Leveraging of $50,000 in State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) funds to support additional project costs.
All housing units rehabilitated or replaced under this program will comply with local, state, and national housing codes and meet the federal National Objective to benefit low- and moderate-income persons.
Following submission and review of the County’s grant application, FloridaCommerce awarded the County the requested funding. A Subgrant Agreement (Contract No. 26DB-H03; FLAIR Contract No. H2614) was issued between FloridaCommerce and St. Lucie County.
The Agreement provides up to $850,000 in federal CDBG funds, effective October 1, 2025, through October 31, 2028, to implement the Housing Rehabilitation project. The County is required to comply with all federal and state regulations, including financial management, reporting, civil rights, fair housing, and monitoring provisions, as set forth in the Agreement and incorporated attachments
Approval of this agenda item will authorize execution of the Subgrant Agreement, enabling the County to begin program implementation and deliver much-needed housing rehabilitation assistance to income-eligible households.

attachments.name: WA#04 2nd Amendment - White City Park Shoreline with attachment

description:
White City Park is one of St. Lucie County's oldest parks and is located in the middle of the County off Midway Road on the St. Lucie River. Over the years this Park's shoreline on the east side of the park along the St. Lucie River has experienced significant erosion largely due to the constant flow of the river, tidal changes, and boat traffic. The shoreline is relatively unprotected from tide and wave action other than by vegetation. No structure currently exists to protect or stabilize the shoreline. In recent years, this erosion has become severe enough to encroach on the Park's entrance road leading to the boat ramp. Therefore, it is crucial that this shoreline is stabilized to restore the shoreline, entrance road and prevent further erosion.
Parks and Recreation previously submitted and was awarded a FIND WAP (Florida Inland Navigational District Waterway Assistance Program) Grant to help cover the costs for Phase I of this project which was survey, design and engineering. Phase I was completed in FY'24.
In order to help fund Phase II, construction, St. Lucie County Parks and Recreation Department applied and was awarded a matching $400,000 FIND (Florida Inland Navigational District) Grant. This matching grant along with County funds will allow for $800,000 to be available to complete this project which includes: design, Shoreline Stabilization structures to be constructed per design, and the original access road to be restored to original condition and use. The construction bid was awarded on 6/3/25 for the Shoreline Stabilization Project Phase II to SoCal Shaker Plate & Construction Site Services, LLC for $287,573.00. Construction is estimated to begin in early fall.
With further analysis, staff have verified that the remaining grant funding can be used to extend the project limits of shoreline protection Phase II, and allow additional areas of embankment to be reinforced and armored to help reduce erosion from boating activities and storm events. In addition, this will provide protection of the entry roadway, as the original Phase II construction provides.
The attached First Amendment to Work Authorization No.4 for Dredging & Marine Consultants, under Contract C20-01-167, will provide design, permitting, and construction administrative services for the extension of these limits to the Shoreline Stabilization Project Phase II not to exceed $59,890.00. The 400,000 FIND (Florida Inland Navigational District) Grant will cover half of the costs for the amendment to this agreement.
After review from the Development Review Committee via an application for a shoreline variance permit, it was determined by the Building Department that a No-Rise report and certificate is required by the applicant (Parks and Recreation) for the project’s original limits, the extended limits to the Shoreline Stabilization Project as was proposed in September, and future improvements to the park. In addition, it is required our EOR provide a floodway analysis that demonstrates that the proposed work will not increase the design flood elevation more than 1 foot (305 mm) at any point within the jurisdiction of the applicable governing authority. The attached Second Amendment to Work Authorization No.4 for Dredging & Marine Consultants, under Contract C20-01-167, will provide data collection, the preparation and submittal of a no-rise certification determination to FEMA needed to continue this project in the construction phase as it was awarded since June, and Hydraulic Modeling Analysis. The total amount for this proposed work is not to exceed $29,015.00. FIND (Florida Inland Navigational District) Grant will cover half of the costs for the amendment to this agreement, as well.
meeting: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
title: White City Park Shoreline Stabilization Phase II - 2nd Amendment to Work Authorization No.4 to Contract C20-01-167

attachments.name: Derecktor Restated and Amended Funding Agreement 9.9.25 (Final)

description:
The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) provided a Seaport Public Transportation Grant Agreement (G2S29) to the County in direct response to proposed terminal improvements by Derecktor Shipyards. The terminal projects, originally identified by Derecktor as Areas 1-4 Improvements, included pavement and drainage improvements to the County’s port terminal space. These improvements were intended to help Derecktor better utilize the recently completed Utility Loop (located along the southern perimeter of the port property) and bring the terminal infrastructure up to par with similar facilities typical of the Mega Yacht industry. The Grant funds secured in FDOT Seaport Grant G2S29, coupled with the balance of older FDOT Seaport Grant funds previously secured for Derecktor (Grants G2204, G1W17 and G1804), resulted in $2,058,963.00 FDOT funds being made available for the proposed project(s). These state funds require a 50% local match, which brings the total New Improvement Budget to $4,117,926.00 (set to expire on 12/31/2027).
The proposed 2025 Amended and Restated Grant Funding Agreement (FDOT Grant No.’s G2204, G1W17, G1804, and G2S29) with Derecktor Shipyards is being proposed to the Board to encourage timely completion of the proposed project and amends Section 2 (Payment of Local Match for New Improvements) of the previous 2024 agreement (March 3, 2025, Agenda Item 2024-64436). This project hopes to complete the mutually beneficial port terminal improvement project (known as Area 1 Improvements) for the benefit of both parties. This amendment requires Derecktor to commit $1,000,000.00 towards the proposed project (as a local grant match) and includes a monthly repayment option proffered by Derecktor (similar to the one used to complete the port's Utility Loop), as identified in Exhibit B of the agreement. A local grant match for the balance of the proposed project (up to $1,058,963.00) would be the responsibility of the County.
Once permits are attained and the final construction plans have been mutually approved by both parties, the County will publicly advertise the project through a competitive bidding process and hire a consultant to assist with the timely execution of the project (construction administration).
Derecktor’s failure to meet the deadlines and repayment obligation in the proposed 2025 agreement will be treated as an “Event of Default” under Paragraph 7 of the April 16, 2019, Lease and Franchise Agreement. Execution of the agreement will ensure that previously secured grant funding for the project is used to improve the County’s Port Terminal.

Public Safety will piggyback Sourcewell Contract # 042021-MOT, in which discounted pricing has been established.

description:
Since 1999, the Treasure Coast Sports Commission (TCSC) has been the official organization to attract youth, amateur and other sporting events that generate room nights and positive economic impact to St. Lucie County. During the budgeting process, the St. Lucie County Tourist Development Council (TDC) provides a recommended amount of annual funding to the organization to help achieve its mission of attracting sports tourism to the County and region. Through June of fiscal year 2025, the TCSC helped support 45 sporting events that took place in St. Lucie County or economically impacted St. Lucie County. The events generated an estimated 16,787 room nights and an estimated $25.8 million in total economic output to St. Lucie County.
On June 11, 2025, the TDC unanimously approved annual grant funding in the amount of $275,000.00 to the Treasure Coast Sports Commission for fiscal year 2026. The funding amount will be divided into separate grant agreements for 1. Administrative Costs and 2. Bid Fees & Grants.
Administrative Costs - $120,000.00
This grant agreement in the amount of $120,000.00 will be dispersed in quarterly payments of $30,000.00 upon receipt of a written report detailing TCSC's performance measures. The written reports will include activity relating to events, sales, ROI analysis, etc. including, but not limited to:
Number of events held in St. Lucie County
Name/location of venue(s) utilized
List of participating hotels and/or vacation rentals
Number of room nights generated
Estimated economic impact of event
Amount of funding provided for event
ROI analysis of events funded
Number of sales leads generated
Number of sales calls made
Number of event bids submitted
Number of site visits hosted
Amount of sponsorship funds raised beyond County funding
The grant funding shall be limited to operational expenses for TCSC staff salaries, office supplies, equipment, marketing and advertising costs. Grant funds shall not be used for certain types of expenditures such as staff travel expenses outside the County including but not limited to mileage reimbursement, hotel rooms, flights, car rentals, meals, meal allowances, per diem and tolls.
Bid Fees & Grants - $155,000.00
This grant agreement in the amount of $155,000.00 shall be dispersed in three payments of $60,000.00, $55,000.00, and $45,000.00 and used for bid fees and grants for sporting events taking place in St. Lucie County. Any additional funds requested from the County above this amount will require matching funds. Matching fund amounts will be determined on a case by case basis depending on the prominence of the event, its fundraising potential and other determining factors.
Please note: Funds used for these grants come from the County's Tourist Development Tax which is paid by local hotels, vacation rentals, RV parks and other overnight accommodation businesses. Local property taxes and/or sales taxes are not used.

Culverts fail over time due to maintenance, environmental or installation issues. Culvert failure can lead to localized flooding which may impede safe conditions of ingress and egress for owners and residents of property in the affected area as well as the traveling public, visitors, emergency responders and other public service providers. Some culvert owners may lack the resources to pay for improvements and repairs.
In 2021, the Board established a voluntary program, Ordinance No. 21-004, to which eligible property owners can apply for and receive funding to improve or repair culverts and then repay this funding through the imposition of a non-ad valorem special assessment against the improved property collected in annual installments on the tax roll.

description:
Section 125.5801, Florida Statutes, authorizes counties to require criminal history records checks for employees in positions determined by the Board of County Commissioners to be critical to security or public safety as well as appointees and private contractors with access to any public facility or publicly operated facility which the Board finds to be critical to security or public safety. As provided in the statute, such screening requires fingerprint-based state and national criminal history checks through the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. A county must adopt an ordinance referencing Section 125.5801 in order to access the FBI's criminal history records. A copy of Section 125.5801 is attached for reference.
On January 7, 2003, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 03-07 which met the above-referenced requirements. In August 2025, Human Resources contacted the Florida Department of Law Enforcement ("FDLE") regarding updating the County's Originating Agency Identifier ("ORI") number and/or apply for a FL9 number so that our Human Resources department can directly receive Level 2 background screening results. It was advised by the FDLE that our current Ordinance No. 03-07 has the language "or his designee" after the word "County Administrator" that is too broad and does not ensure that the designee will not be a private entity/citizen. It was recommended that this language be removed and replaced with "or Human Resources and Risk Management Director".
The attached Ordinance No. 25-021, if adopted, would amend the language as recommended by FDLE. There is also language that has been amended so that the verbiage is congruent with § 125.5801, Florida Statutes, as updated by Chapter 2013-116, Laws of Florida. Notice of the public hearing was published in the St. Lucie News Tribune as required by state law.

description:
The Florida Legislature adopted Chapter 2002-169, Laws of Florida, as amended by Chapter 2013-116, Laws of Florida, which laws provided that a county may require, by ordinance, state and national criminal history screening for:Any position of county employment or appointment, whether paid, unpaid, or contractual, which the governing body of the county finds is critical to security or public safety;
Any private contractor, employee of a private contractor, vendor, repair person, or delivery person who is subject to licensing or regulation by the county; or
Any private contractor, employee of a private contractor, vendor, repair person, for-hire chauffeur, or delivery person who has direct contact with individual members of the public or access to any public facility or publicly operated facility in such a manner or to such an extent that the governing body of the county finds that preventing unsuitable persons from having such contact or access is critical to security or public safety.
As authorized by State Law, St. Lucie County Ordinance No. 03-07 required criminal history record checks for certain employees, appointees, and private contractors. County Ordinance No. 03-07, as amended by County Ordinance No. 25-021, which the Board adopted during today's Public Hearing, provides for the County to identify positions of County employment or appointment that are critical to security or public safety and further identify those County facilities that are critical to security or public safety.
Attached is a copy of Resolution No. 25-205, which, if adopted, will identify a list of positions of County employment or appointment that are critical to security or public safety and further identify those County facilities that are critical to security or public safety.

description:
Treasure Coast Risk Management Program (“TRICO”) is a cooperative of local governments created under Chapter 163, Florida Statutes. TRICO manages a combined risk management program for St. Lucie County, Martin County, the City of Port St. Lucie and the City of Stuart.
TRICO was established in 1987 by interlocal agreement to finance losses which cannot be prevented; involving property, operational interruption, liability and risks for each member, for amounts within Florida’s sovereign immunity law and workers' compensation. Most of the risk management for each member is performed by and through TRICO but each member entity has ultimate responsibility for its own management of risks and the purchasing of excess insurance for specific risks. A copy of the 1987 interlocal agreement is attached.
Based on the Roper & Roper, P.A. Opinion on Applicability of Section 624.4621, F.S. to TRICO (attached), it does not appear that the Board is required to appoint a Board member to serve on TRICO. The Interlocal Agreement creating TRICO does, however, provide that the Board may appoint a Board member or senior staff member to serve on TRICO. If the Board desires that a Board member serve on TRICO, then the Board could select a Board member to serve. In the alternative, the Board should select a senior staff member to serve on TRICO.

description:
Since September 14, 2004, the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners has been televising and live streaming County Commission meetings on its local government access channel. Three (3) of the five (5) current cameras in the Commission Chambers have begun to fail and display pixelated images when televising various meetings. These cameras are nearly 10 years old and need to be replaced / upgraded to provide better picture quality for our various televised meetings, including the Board of County Commission Meetings, Planning & Zoning and Code Compliance.
Staff recommends replacing these as soon as possible for several reasons, including the importance of making sure meetings are properly televised to comply with our Strategic Plan of "Enhancing Public Trust." Additionally, due to changing federal tariffs, the cost for electronics are expected to increase in the coming months.
The bid process opened on Wednesday, August 27, 2025, with thirty-five (35) companies notified and two (2) companies bidding on the project. Encore Broadcasting was the lowest responsive bidder. The cost to purchase and install the six (6) 4K Panasonic cameras is $73,233.

description:
On April 2, 2024, the Board of County Commissioners (BOCC) approved Resolution 24-070, which amended Resolution 24-030 and established the current framework for the St. Lucie County Homeless Advisory Committee. Since that time, the Committee has continued to review its roles, responsibilities, and membership structure to ensure broad representation of key stakeholders engaged in addressing homelessness within the community.
To strengthen cross-sector collaboration and ensure that perspectives essential to both prevention and intervention are represented in policy discussions, the Committee recommended expanding its membership by adding two new seats:
A representative from law enforcement, to provide input on public safety concerns and the intersection between homelessness and the criminal justice system; and
A representative from a faith-based organization, to recognize the significant role faith-based partners play in providing shelter, outreach, and supportive services.
The proposed resolution implements this recommendation by amending Resolution 24-070 to update the Committee’s roles and responsibilities and expand the Committee’s composition to fourteen (14) members. An adjustment to the quorum has been made as well to coincide with the increased membership. Additionally, the resolution removes the Secretary as an officer as County staff fulfill this role. These adjustments are intended to enhance the Committee’s ability to develop actionable strategies, foster collaboration, and provide comprehensive recommendations to the BOCC for addressing homelessness in St. Lucie County.

description:
In 2005, St. Lucie County funded the Juvenile Assessment Center (JAC) as an eighteen-month pilot project. In 2007, the Board again funded the JAC, with two-thirds of the funding being provided by the cities of Fort Pierce and Port Saint Lucie along with court fine contributions. On April 27, 2010, the Board terminated the contract with the vendor who operated the JAC and entered into an agreement with the Department of Juvenile Justice (DJJ) to operate the JAC.
The JAC is a 24-hour central receiving and booking program serving juveniles throughout St. Lucie County. After taking juveniles to the JAC, law enforcement officers can return to assigned duties within approximately 15 minutes, thereby saving an average of three (3) hours per juvenile case. Prior to the JAC, officers had to take the juveniles to the jail for booking. The jail is not currently able to accommodate juveniles. Once a juvenile arrives at JAC, they are electronically fingerprinted and photographed. The juveniles are then screened to determine if they are going to be placed in the detention center. Attached is a copy of the proposed Interagency Agreement with the DJJ to operate the JAC for an annual amount of $185,576.04.
Since DJJ is a Department of State Government, this agreement can be approved without a Request for Proposal (RFP).

description:
Section 125.5801, Florida Statutes, authorizes counties to require criminal history records checks for employees in positions determined by the Board of County Commissioners to be critical to security or public safety as well as appointees and private contractors with access to any public facility or publicly operated facility which the Board finds to be critical to security or public safety. As provided in the statute, such screening requires fingerprint-based state and national criminal history checks through the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. A county must adopt an ordinance referencing Section 125.5801 in order to access the FBI's criminal history records. A copy of Section 125.5801 is attached for reference.
On January 7, 2003, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 03-07 which met the above-referenced requirements. In August 2025, Human Resources contacted the Florida Department of Law Enforcement ("FDLE") regarding updating the County's Orinating Agency Identifier ("ORI") number and/or apply for a FL9 number so that our Human Resources department can directly receive Level 2 background screening results. It was advised by the FDLE that our current Ordinance No. 03-07 has the language "or his designee" after the word "County Administrator" that is too broad and does not ensure that the designee will not be a private entity/citizen. It was recommended that this language be removed.
The attached draft Ordinance, if adopted, would amend the language as recommended by FDLE. There is also language that has been amended so that the verbiage is congruent with § 125.5801, Florida Statutes, as updated by Chapter 2013-116, Laws of Florida.

description:
On December 12, 2023, the County and the Sheriff entered into an Interlocal Agreement to transfer management of inmate medical services at the St. Lucie County Jail from the Sheriff to the County. On July 25, 2024, the County entered into a Health Services Agreement with NaphCare, Inc. to be the medical services provider at the Jail after consultation with the Sheriff. If an inmate requires care outside of the Jail, the inmate must be transported to a hospital or other medical facility, requiring a deputy to accompany the inmate. Per the Interlocal Agreement, the Sheriff pays its deputies overtime for guarding the inmates at outside facilities when necessary. The original agreement provided that the Sheriff would invoice the County monthly for such overtime costs, and capped the annual overtime costs allowed at $100,000.00 per year, with an option to review the limit on an annual basis. This amendment will eliminate monthly invoicing, provides for two payments of $250,000.00 to cover the increase in such costs for the upcoming fiscal year, and provides for a one-time year end true-up of $450,000.00 to cover the costs for FY2024-2025.
The amendment also adds language regarding collaboration between the parties to address concerns raised by the Sheriff regarding the medical provider or its medical operations, and states the County will consult with the Sheriff or his designee on any proposed changes to processes or procedures that may adversely affect Jail operations.

description:
On May 21, 2025, responses to RFQ No. 24-010 25-051, Professional Engineering & Architectural Services – Museum Pointe Park Redevelopment, were opened. Seven proposals were received; 819 companies were notified and 87 RFQ documents were distributed.
The scope of services for this contract will be for a qualified engineering firm to provide engineering and architectural services for the design and permitting of various project elements at Museum Pointe Park in Fort Pierce, Florida. The objective of the Museum Pointe Park Redevelopment Project is to enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the County-owned park, while supporting the Port of Fort Pierce’s current Mega-Yacht Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO) operation(s). The County’s adjacent riparian areas at the park are underutilized, and the strategic redevelopment of this waterfront space will improve the aesthetic of the park, increase parkgoer usership/enhance parkgoer experience, support future port development, and possibly create revenue streams for St. Lucie County.
Project elements associated with the Museum Pointe Park Redevelopment Project include 1) a floating dock marina, 2) a multi-story structure – marina clubhouse and office spaces, 3) an event center and associated restaurant venue, and 4) a dedicated fishing pier. All redevelopment elements are expected to utilize existing park infrastructure (to the greatest amount practicable) before considering any new modifications and/or improvements to the site that may be required to design and/or permit new project elements. The objective is to integrate most, if not all, of the proposed elements into one final redevelopment vision that revitalizes the western section of the county park.
On July 2, 2025, the selection committee evaluated and ranked the proposals that were received. The committee members' scores and ranking for each firm are provided in Attachment A.
The short-listed firms in order of ranking were as follows:
WJ Architects, LLC
K2M Design, Inc.
Brooks + Scarpe Architects, Inc.
Edgewater Resources
BEA Architects, Inc.
CPZ Architects, Inc.
CPH Consulting, LLC
On August 22, 2025, as part of the evaluation process, the top four ranked firms were invited to presentations. The committee members’ scores and final ranking for the three firms are provided in Attachment A.

description:
The County is responsible for the repair and maintenance of 28 bridges. These structures require regular upgrades, repairs, and rehabilitation to maximize their safety and service life.
The Range Line Road Bridge over South Florida Water Management District (SFWMD) C-23 Bridge Repairs project addressed deficiencies identified within the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Bridge Inspection Report. The project consisted of bridge deck repairs, guardrail repairs, pile jacket(s) installation, resurfacing a section of the roadway, and replacing the existing bank stabilization material with rubble riprap.
On June 2, 2024, Bid No. 24-069 was advertised for bids for the construction of the repairs for Range Line Road over SFWMD C-23 Bridge.
On July 10, 2024, bids were opened. Three bids were received, and the lowest responsive and responsible bidder was Ferreria Construction Company Inc. of Hobe Sound in the amount of $866,250.00.
The total amount for this project was $866,250.00, including $78,750.00 in contingencies, of which $44,917.00 was used.
Staff monitored the construction and determined the project was completed in conformance with the plans and specifications. The project was completed under budget with a remaining amount of $111,599.95.

description:
Edwards Road is a major east-west arterial roadway connecting US Highway 1 to other major north-south corridors including South 25th Street and Jenkins Road.
On Friday, July 18, 2025, Public Works was notified of a small hole that was observed in the pavement of the outside westbound travel lane on Edwards Road, between Sunrise Boulevard and South 25th Street. Based on an initial investigation conducted by the Public Works Engineering staff, the existing culvert pipes were determined to have deficiencies causing erosion of soil beneath the pavement and the nearby sidewalk. A steel plate was placed over the hole in the pavement as a temporary safety measure.
Staff received administrative approval to repair the joints in the 66-inch reinforced concrete pipe and associated settlements based on the County’s Emergency Purchase protocol in the purchasing manual. The administrative approval memo signed on July 22, 2025 by the County Administrator is attached to this agenda item. The culvert repair work was expedited to avoid collapse of the westbound travel lane of Edwards Road as well as to prevent a more costly roadway restoration repair. PRP Construction Group, LLC, was contracted to perform the repairs and restoration of the pavement at this location on Edwards Road for a final amount of $183,364.50. Construction materials testing was performed by Terracon in the amount of $3,705. The preliminary engineer’s estimate for the project was $200,000.00, so the project was completed within reasonable expected expenditures.
The County's Purchasing Manual (Section 20.4c) provides that if the emergency purchase exceeds the County Administrator's authorization limit, the County Administrator will request "after the fact" approval from the Board at its next regularly scheduled meeting.
meeting: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
title: After the Fact Approval and ratification of Emergency Contract with PRP Construction Group LLC for the Edwards Road Emergency Culvert Repair Construction Project
