description:
Road Impact Fees in St. Lucie County were first adopted in 1985 and implemented in 1986 as an important source of revenue to use in funding the infrastructure necessitated by new growth. Since then, the County has continued to periodically update its Road Impact Fee Study, last updated and adopted on April 19, 2022. The County engaged Nilgün Kamp, AICP, with Tindale Oliver (n.k.a. Benesch) to provide the 2022 update.
The County has strived to work with municipalities to streamline the collection of County Impact Fees whereby a developer or builder pays only the permitting agency. The County's Road Impact Fee Interlocal Agreement with the City of Fort Pierce has been in place since September 13, 2005, and with the City of Port St. Lucie (PSL) since April 19, 2022.
With a population of approximately 385,000, St. Lucie County ranks 19th out of 67 Florida counties in population. The County is continuing to experience population growth, with a projected county-wide increase of 145,000 persons by 2050, or an average annual growth rate of 1.2 percent as estimated by the Bureau of Business & Economic Research (BEBR), ranking 7th among Florida counties. St. Lucie County ranked 13th for residential permitting in 2024, indicating high levels of new development. This continuing growth requires additional public capital facilities. With this continued growth and significant increases in construction costs, the County retained Benesch in 2025 to update the impact fee study to reflect the most recent data available. Along with the updated study, the County retained Benesch to provide an extraordinary circumstances analysis of the new or increased impact fees. The County intends on using the extraordinary circumstances clause within the statute, to adopt updated Road Impact fees prior to the four-year timeframe for any fee increases and possibly adopt fees at levels higher than the 50-percent increase limit.
As specified in Section 163.31801, F.S., each local government that adopts and collects an impact fee must ensure that the calculation of the impact fee is based on a study using the most recent and localized data available within 4 years of the current impact fee update and the new study must be adopted within 12 months of the initiation of the new impact fee study if the local government increases the impact fee. The local government must provide notice at least 90 days before the effective date of imposing a new or increased impact fee. Impact fees must be proportional and reasonably connected to, or have a rational nexus with, the need for additional capital facilities and the increased impact generated by the new development.
As stated, St. Lucie County’s Road Impact Fee was initially implemented in 1986 to assist the County in providing adequate transportation facilities for expected growth. The most recent study update for these fees was completed in 2022, with the calculated rates adopted in 2022 at 75% of the maximum allowable (capped at a 50% increase and discounted to 75%) and phased-in over four (4) years, with October 1, 2025, being the fourth year. Additionally, these rates only assessed impacts to State and County Roads proportionally by municipality based on VMT (vehicle miles traveled).
As provided in Section 163.3180, F.S., if a local government elects to repeal transportation concurrency, the local government may adopt an alternative transportation system that is mobility-plan and fee-based or an alternative transportation system that is not mobility-plan and fee-based. The local government may not use an alternative transportation system to deny, time, or phase an application for site plan approval, plat approval, final subdivision approval, building permits, or the functional equivalent of such approvals provided that the developer agrees to pay for the development’s identified transportation impacts via the funding mechanism implemented by the local government.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed HB 479, which defined Mobility Fees/Mobility Plan (an alternative transportation system mobility study developed by using a plan-based methodology and adopted into a local government comprehensive plan that promotes a compact, mixed use, and interconnected development served by a multimodal transportation system in an area that is urban in character, or designated to be urban in character, as defined in s. 171.031) and allows only the local government issuing a building permit to collect for transportation impacts. HB 479 requires cities and counties to enter into an interlocal agreement to define any fees for transportation impacts and determine a methodology for the distribution of any revenues. If there is no agreement in place by October 1, 2025, or if an existing agreement is terminated, only the local government issuing the building permit may collect for transportation impacts based on a developer's traffic impact study or a city or county's mobility fee less a 10% discount to the developer.
Currently, road impact fee revenues are St. Lucie County’s primary funding source for new road construction and lane addition improvements. County fuel tax revenues are dedicated to maintenance (like road resurfacing), operations, and debt service payments. Local option sales tax revenues have been mostly allocated to non-capacity projects. Without a transportation impact fee program, the County would not be able to construct planned capacity addition projects included in the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP), and other priority projects unless an alternative revenue source, such as additional sales tax or dedicated millage, is identified. In the absence of impact fee revenues or alternative new/additional funding that would replace impact fee revenues, the level of service is likely to degrade with roads becoming more congested and travel times getting longer.
Although the County’s Road Impact Fee Ordinance requires the road impact fees to be reviewed every five years, to address requirements of recent legislative changes, the County accelerated the update to the road impact fee study prior to the five-year update schedule due to increased growth and construction costs.
At the December 10, 2024 Informal meeting, Benesch presented mobility fee, multimodal fee and impact fee information as well as discussed the recent legislative changes. The Board discussed multiple options during the Informal meeting. As such, Benesch provided a scope of work to conduct a Transportation Study that includes methodologies for Mobility Fees, Impact Fees, and Multimodal Fees. Including all three (3) options allows the Board to consider alternative methods to capture travel demand revenue from future development. Road impact fees can be spent on roadway capacity expansion improvements. With a multi-modal fee or mobility fee, impact fee revenues can be spent on standalone sidewalk, bicycle, and transit improvements that add other capacity to the transportation network (in addition to roadway capacity expansion improvements). With impact fees, the County can utilize concurrency which allows the county to deny development applications where road capacity is not available to meet the travel demands from new development. However, recent legislative changes also require local governments to allow development if the development addresses its proportionate share requirements. With multi-modal fees, concurrency remains as well; while it is repealed with mobility fees. Mobility fees are a pay-and-go system and require the County to remove concurrency from its comprehensive plan.
On June 10, 2025, Benesch presented to the Board of County Commissioners at a Special Informal Board Meeting and discussed Road Impact Fees, Multimodal Fees, and Mobility Fees. The Board indicated interest in moving forward with the creation of a Multimodal Fee, and developing scenarios for varying rates for new development inside the Urban Service Boundary vs. outside the Urban Service Boundary.
On July 17, 2025, the County staff and Benesch hosted the first of two Public Workshops to discuss the findings of extraordinary circumstances necessitating the adoption of updated Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee rates.
On July 17, 2025, County staff and Benesh presented the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study, including the recommended rates, to the Planning and Zoning Commission at their regularly scheduled meeting. The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4 to 1 to recommend the Board adopt the Road/Multi-modal fee at 100% of the recommended rate.
On August 14, 2025, County staff presented the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study and recommended rates to the Treasure Coast Builders Association (TCBA) membership.
On August 15, 2025, County staff presented the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study and recommended rates to the St. Lucie County Citizens Budget Committee. The Committee unanimously recommended the Board vote to approve the recommended Impact/Multi-modal Impact Fee rates.

description:
As of July 1, 2022, Section 553.899, Florida Statutes imposed a statewide structural inspection program for aging condominium and cooperative buildings to ensure that buildings are safe for continued use.
In the 2025 legislative session, HB 913 was passed and signed into law by the Governor, requiring the Board of County Commissioners to adopt an ordinance requiring associations and any other owners that are subject to milestone inspection requirements to commence repairs within 365 days after a phase two inspection is received. ​
As of July 1, 2025, St. Lucie County is required to adopt an ordinance requiring condominium associations, cooperative associations, or any other owners subject to Section 553.899 F.S. to schedule or commence repairs for substantial structural deterioration within a specified timeframe after the County receives a Phase Two inspection report. The adoption of this Ordinance is necessary to amend the St. Lucie Land Development Code pursuant to statutory requirements and is in the best interest of the health, safety, and general welfare of existing and future residents of St. Lucie County.

description:
The St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners established the Homeless Advisory Committee (HAC) through Resolution No. 22-124 to provide recommendations and implementation strategies to prevent and end homelessness in St. Lucie County. The Committee comprises representatives from local government, social services, education, health, housing, business, and individuals with lived experience.
As required, the HAC submits an Annual Report to the BOCC each year on or before September 30. The Committee formally adopted its 2024–2025 Annual Report on August 20, 2025.
Key community accomplishments during the past year include:
Expansion of coordinated entry systems to improve access to shelter and housing resources.
Increased permanent housing placements and positive housing exits through the Housing Hub, which achieved an 83% street-to-housed rate and 79% overall positive exit rate.
Delivery of critical services by partner agencies, including rental assistance, utility assistance, mental health services, employment readiness programs, and student support through the McKinney-Vento program.
Launch of new initiatives, including the GraceWay Village Family Restorative Shelter and a Veterans Shelter repurposed from an existing motel to provide targeted services.
The report also identifies ongoing challenges such as the shortage of affordable housing, limited funding and employment opportunities, gaps in behavioral health services, and systemic barriers to long-term housing stability.
Looking ahead, the HAC recommends strengthening partnerships with local governments, nonprofits, law enforcement, and faith-based organizations; expanding affordable housing opportunities; enhancing data collection and sharing; and continuing public education to reduce stigma around homelessness. Planned next steps include adding new committee seats for faith-based and law enforcement representatives, developing safe parking partnerships, and expanding homeless data collection.

description:
Many times, people decide to purchase property without contacting the County to determine if they are able to construct their desired building on the parcel. This presentation is an effort to try and prevent instances where people unknowingly invest in property where development is restricted, due to inconsistencies with the County's Land Development standards.
In 1961 St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners adopted Land Development Regulations for Unincorporated St. Lucie County. Since the adoption of the original Land Development Regulations, the County has implemented amendments to zoning regulations in 1984 and 1990. These regulations provide the minimum requirements for development of property, specifically the Lot Size and Dimensional Requirements for a buildable parcel within the zoning district in which the lot is located.
A nonconforming lot was created before the passage of a zoning ordinance or ordinance amendment that now fails to comply with related dimensional standards such as minimum lot area, width, or frontage.

description:
The Airport's Part 139 (Commercial Airline Service) annual inspection was conducted on March 3-5, 2025.
As noted in this most recent FAA Part 139 certification inspection, the airport needs to address various airfield pavement markings lacking adequate retro reflectivity due to missing or deteriorated glass beads. In accordance with 14 CFR Part 139.311 and FAA Advisory Circular 150/5340-1M, all airfield markings must be maintained in a condition that ensures visibility under all weather and lighting conditions, including at night, which requires proper application of reflective glass beads.
The FAA annual inspection report requires the airfield markings to be corrected before the next FAA annual Part 139 inspection in March 2026. This Atkins Work Authorization is for the Design, Bidding, and Construction Oversight to redo the entire airfield pavement markings and glass beads for reflectivity (safety) at night.

The Florida Development Finance Corporation (the “FDFC”) was created by the Florida Development Finance Corporation Act, Chapter 288, Part X, Florida Statutes (the “Act”) which provides, in part, that the Issuer may issue bonds to finance and refinance projects for the benefit of Florida businesses to enhance the economic development of the State of Florida (the “State”), provided that the FDFC has entered into an interlocal agreement with the local governmental agency in which the project will be located. Waste Pro USA, Inc., on behalf of itself and one or more of its affiliates has requested the issuance of the Issuer’s Solid Waste Disposal Revenue Bonds (Waste Pro USA, Inc. FDFC and Waste Pro USA have requested that the Board consent to the issuance of the Bonds. Attached is proposed Resolution No. 25-172, which, if adopted, would provide the Board's consent to the issuance of the Bonds in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $6,000,000.00. description:
The Property Acquisition Division became aware of a 4.47 acre parcel scheduled for a Tax Deed Sale on September 8, 2025, encumbered with a Conservation Easement in favor of the County, copy attached.
Public Works staff discussed the potential for this property to be purchased and staff made the determination that the County should participate in the Tax Deed Sale for the 4.47 acres based on the following criteria:
• The surrounding neighborhood, between Weatherbee Road and Midway Road, west of North St. Lucie River Water Control District (NSLRWCD) Canal No. 22 is underserved from a drainage standpoint. The area has been identified as a location for a potential capital project in the ongoing update of the St. Lucie County Stormwater Master Plan.
• The parcel is low-lying and appears to consist of lake/wetland areas, making development potential low without significant expense.
• The low-lying nature of the property presents an opportunity to drain surrounding road(s) into a potential future stormwater treatment area.
• The adjacent Canal No. 22 to the east could serve as an outfall.
• Adjacent undeveloped property could enhance the footprint if opportunity to acquire presents itself.
Public Works has Stormwater MSTU funds in a land acquisition account for this purpose and would recommend using those funds, with Board approval, to complete the transaction.
The Board's support has allowed the Public Works team to deliver tremendous success with recent similar purchases, resulting in projects such as Melville Stormwater Treatment Area (STA) Phases I and II and the Sheraton Plaza STA to be constructed. These projects not only meet the goals of better water quality for our watershed, they serve as community amenities and enhance neighborhoods, resulting in higher quality of life for County residents.
On July 22, 1986, the Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 86-156 changing the Zoning classification from RS-3 (Residential, Single Family 3) to RM-11 (Residential Multiple Family 11).
On August 26, 1986, the Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 86-181 granting Site Plan approval for a project known as Gator Lake Residences subject to a condition prior to the issuance of any building permits, for any portion of this site, the developer shall grant to St. Lucie County a Perpetual Conservation Easement, or similar document acceptable to St. Lucie County for the 3.61 acres east of Regina Drive, as identified on the site plan.
On October 21, 1986, the Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 86-235 accepting the Conservation Easement from Triple A Development Associates.
On August 25, 1987, the Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 87-160 granting a Site Plan extension for a project known as Gator Lake Residences. The Site Plan approval has expired as no building permits have been issued no further extensions have been granted.
Due Diligence
The County contracted with Callaway & Price, Inc. to appraise the 4.47 acre parcel.

Discussion
In the event the Board determines to authorize the County staff to bid at the Tax Deed Sale, County staff has determined that the County will need to take the following statutory steps:
• The County must register before the public sale
• The County must deposit 5% of the County's estimate of the County's highest bid with the Clerk prior to the public sale
• If the County is the successful (i.e. highest) bidder, the County must deposit the balance of the purchase proceeds by 2:00 p.m. on the day after the public sale (in this case by September 9, 2025, at 2:00 p.m.)
All of the Clerk public sales are now digital. Because of this, the Board will need to establish bidding parameters in advance of the public sale date. The Board will also need to designate County staff members to attend the Clerk public sale on behalf of the County.
Attached, for Board consideration, is a copy of Resolution No. 2025-176, which, if adopted, would authorize the Property Acquisition Manager to attend the September 8, 2025, Clerk public sale and bid on behalf of the County.

attachments.name: WA#04 1st Amendment - White City Park Shoreline with attachment

description:
White City Park is one of St. Lucie County's oldest parks and is located in the middle of the County off Midway Road on the St. Lucie River. Over the years this Park's shoreline on the east side of the park along the St. Lucie River has experienced significant erosion largely due to the constant flow of the river, tidal changes, and boat traffic. The shoreline is relatively unprotected from tide and wave action other than by vegetation. No structure currently exists to protect or stabilize the shoreline. In recent years, this erosion has become severe enough to encroach on the Park's entrance road leading to the boat ramp. Therefore, it is crucial that this shoreline is stabilized to restore the shoreline, entrance road and prevent further erosion.
Parks and Recreation previously submitted and was awarded a FIND WAP (Florida Inland Navigational District Waterway Assistance Program) Grant to help cover the costs for Phase I of this project which was survey, design and engineering. Phase I was completed in FY'24.
In order to help fund Phase II, construction, St. Lucie County Parks and Recreation Department applied and was awarded a matching $400,000 FIND (Florida Inland Navigational District) Grant. This matching grant along with County funds will allow for $800,000 to be available to complete this project which includes: design, Shoreline Stabilization structures to be constructed per design, and the original access road to be restored to original condition and use. The construction bid was awarded on 6/3/25 for the Shoreline Stabilization Project Phase II to SoCal Shaker Plate & Construction Site Services, LLC for $287,573.00. Construction is estimated to begin in early fall.
With further analysis, staff have verified that the remaining grant funding can be used to extend the project limits of shoreline protection Phase II, and allow additional areas of embankment to be reinforced and armored to help reduce erosion from boating activities and storm events. In addition, this will provide protection of the entry roadway, as the original Phase II construction provides.
The attached First Amendment to Work Authorization No.4 for Dredging & Marine Consultants, under Contract C20-01-167, will provide design, permitting, and construction administrative services for the extension of these limits to the Shoreline Stabilization Project Phase II not to exceed $59,890.00. The 400,000 FIND (Florida Inland Navigational District) Grant will cover half of the costs for the amendment to this agreement.
This Project Funded by FIND Grant and White City Park Reserves.

description:
Stormwater culverts direct and channel the flow of stormwater under driveways, roads, sidewalks and other obstructions and are an integral component of stormwater management. Culverts fail over time due to maintenance, environmental or installation issues. Culvert failure can lead to localized flooding which may impede safe conditions of ingress and egress for owners and residents of property in the affected area as well as the traveling public, visitors, emergency responders and other public service providers. Some culvert owners may lack the resources to pay for improvements and repairs.
In 2021, the Board established a voluntary program, Ordinance No. 21-004, to which eligible property owners can apply for and receive funding to improve or repair culverts and then repay this funding through the imposition of a non-ad valorem special assessment against the improved property collected in annual installments on the tax roll.
The attached Resolution No. 2025-167 is the Assessment Resolution as required by County's Ordinance No. 21-004, as amended. The purpose of this resolution relates to the imposition and collection of special assessments to fund stormwater culvert improvements within the Culvert 2025-06 MSBU, determine that real property therein will be specially benefitted, establish the method of assessing the cost of the improvements, approve the assessment roll, and provide an effective date.

description:
In 2018, after the County received ballots indicating that majority of affected property owners supported the creation of a Municipal Services Benefit Unit (“MSBU”) to fund Ft. Pierce Farms Water Control District (“FPFWCD”) annual fees, the Board approved Resolution No. 2018-258, the Initial Assessment Resolution. The Initial Assessment Resolution described the property to be located within the Lakewood Park Drainage MSBU, provided for the imposition of special assessments therein, estimated the cost to be funded through special assessments, established the method of apportioning the special assessment among affected real property, directed the assessment coordinator to prepare a preliminary assessment roll, approved the interlocal agreement with FPFWCD, approved the interlocal agreement with the Tax Collector, authorized staff to take such actions as may be necessary in furtherance of the project, and established a public hearing.
In 2019, the Board held a public hearing to consider comments from affected property owners prior to approving Resolution No. 2019-019, the Final Assessment Resolution. The Final Assessment Resolution determined that real property within the Lakewood Park Drainage MSBU would be specially benefited by the improvements, ratified and confirmed the Initial Assessment Resolution, approved the assessment roll, imposed assessments upon all property described in the assessment roll and provided the method for collection.
As per the Initial Assessment Resolution, Section 3.04 (D), each year the annual assessment shall be increased as necessary to reimburse the County for costs incurred in designing and constructing any improvements necessary or desirable to accomplish the drainage objectives of the Interlocal Agreement; as well as, developing and collecting the assessment for each fiscal year. In 2019, property owners within the MSBU were notified the maximum annual assessment amount that could be assessed against their parcel (without the Board conducting another public hearing) was $25.04. As a result of increases in FPFWCD fees, the proceeds of the special assessments are no longer sufficient to fund the cost of providing drainage improvements within the MSBU. description:
Pursuant to Chapter 38, Code of Ordinances and Compiled Laws of St. Lucie County, the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners (the Board) has the authority to impose annual assessments for solid waste (garbage and recycling) collection, disposal and administrative services, facilities or programs against certain property within St. Lucie County.
The Board initially levied recurring annual assessments on residential properties within the County Solid Waste Urban Service Area for the purpose of including solid waste fees on property tax bills on September 14, 2004. This method of collection is in lieu of the garbage hauler billing property owners directly for garbage and recycling services. The state statute authorizing collection of special assessments on the tax bill (section 197.3632, Fla. Stat.) requires notice to affected property owners and a public hearing in certain instances where the amount of the annual assessment is increased.
On July 1, 2025, the Board adopted Resolution No. 25-061 ("Preliminary Assessment Resolution") which initiated the process required to impose solid waste assessments for the fiscal year commencing October 1, 2025 ("Fiscal Year 2025-26"). The Preliminary Assessment Resolution scheduled a public hearing for September 2, 2025 to consider adopting a final resolution approving the solid waste assessment roll for Fiscal Year 2025-26, and directed the mailing and publication of notice for affected property owners.
The attached Solid Waste Final Assessment Resolution concludes the process required to impose solid waste assessments for the fiscal year commencing October 1, 2025 (Fiscal Year 2025-26) at a rate of $468.00 per dwelling unit. The resolution also provides that the maximum rate that can be charged in future fiscal years without further notice is $485.00 per dwelling unit, approves the assessment roll for said fiscal year to be collected and directs delivery of this roll to the Tax Collector for collection of the assessments on the 2025 property tax bill. For Fiscal Year 2025–2026, the assessment rate is established at $468.00, an increase from the prior year’s rate of $385.44. The maximum assessment rate authorized for future fiscal years remains unchanged from the previous year. At the public hearing, the Board may vote to assess a lower rate of assessment for Fiscal Year 2025-26.
The purpose for this action is to provide residential property owners and occupants proper, safe and cost effective disposal of residential waste and recyclable materials generated on such property.

description:
The St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan is the policy document used to provide guidelines for growth management within St. Lucie County. The Comprehensive Plan establishes the policies and public improvements to maintain and enhance the quality of life for St. Lucie County residents, protect natural resources and promote sound long-term economic development, while recognizing the differing needs and values of the County's unique communities and diverse land area. Every 7 years, the County is required to review the Comprehensive Plan through the Evaluation and Appraisal Review (EAR) process. This is a required part of the State's growth management process and is a mechanism for determining whether the need exists to amend the County's Comprehensive Plan to be consistent and responsive to State Statutory changes.
St. Lucie County is undertaking an update to its Comprehensive Plan in accordance with Florida Statute requirements and is seeking input on those changes from the public and the Planning and Zoning Commission (Local Planning Agency) and the Board of County Commissioners. The Board of County Commissioners will consider transmittal and adoption of these proposed changes to the Florida Department of Commerce.
Section 163.3191, F.S., requires local governments to evaluate whether amendments to their comprehensive plan are necessary to reflect changes in state requirements, in accordance with a schedule posted by the state land planning agency (Department of Commerce). St. Lucie County was required to notify the Department of Commerce by Oct. 1, 2024, as to the determination if changes were necessary to the Plan.
The County sent the Department of Commerce a letter on Sept. 19, 2024, identifying that amendments were necessary to address changes in state requirements and that the County may also consider amendments to address issues of local concern. Based on the notification timeframe, the County has a deadline of September 30, 2025, to transmit Comprehensive Plan updates to the Department of Commerce. If the County fails to submit its update to the Comprehensive Plan by September 30, 2025, the County may not amend its Comprehensive Plan until it complies with this requirement. (§163.3191(4), F.S.)
The County Comprehensive Plan has 14 elements and a Port sub-element. The County is working on updates to all elements except for two, the Rural Lands Stewardship Area Element and the Property Rights Element. The vast majority of the proposed changes involve the inclusion of statutory changes and references, removal of obsolete text and data and replacement with more current text and data. Within these documents, deletions are presented in strikethrough, and additions are underlined.
Staff recommends the BOCC approve the transmittal the EAR-based amendments to the State Land Planning Agency and other State reviewing agencies; including a separate affidavit, signed by the Chair of the Board of County Commissioners, attesting that all elements of its comprehensive plan comply with Section 163.3191, F.S., and that the plan contains the minimum planning period of 10 years, citing the 2024 Bureau of Economic and Business Research, Florida Estimates of Population 2024 (April 1, 2024) and the Projections of Florida Population by County, 2025–2050, with Estimates for 2023 (January 2024, Volume 57, Bulletin 198) as the source of the population projections used in establishing the 10-year planning period.

description:
The Environmental Resources Department is working toward the goal of acquiring lots within a 486-acre subdivided area northwest of Turnpike Feeder Road that contains approximately 215 lots total. The area is identified in the 2004 SLC Native Habitat Inventory as an “A” based on high-quality native habitat coverage and potential for rare or endemic species. The preservation of the environment lands provides for ecological biodiversity; clean air, water, and food; protection of listed species; sustainability; reduced development; and access to green spaces and natural areas for economic prosperity and social well-being.
Ninety-two lots have already been acquired. County staff ordered a bulk appraisal of 147 lots in the Turnpike Feeder corridor. Offer letters were sent out to the property owners. Elizabeth Hedges Falvey, acting as Power of Attorney on behalf of Mr. Hedges, contacted the County and expressed interest in selling two lots, identified as Parcel IDs 1406-313-0003-000-1 and 1406-313-0002-000-4.
The County presented a Contract for Sale and Purchase to Ms. Falvey for $14,250, which is 100% of the appraised value, as determined by the County’s contracted appraiser, Callaway & Price, Inc. Ms. Falvey submitted a counter-offer of $16,000, which is within the range of value identified by the County's appraiser. Estimated closing costs are $5,000.
The tax bill for each parcel last year was $67.33. The average property tax bill over the last four years of ownership was $31.03 per parcel. The Property Appraiser's website estimates a potential county taxable value of $1,000 if each parcel was sold at market value.
Attached for your review and approval is the signed Contract for Sale and Purchase.

description:
St. Lucie County was recently awarded $250,000 through the Florida Division of Emergency Management’s Hurricane Loss Mitigation Program (HLMP) under agreement number B0255, project number DEM-HL00121. This competitive, state-funded grant program supports mitigation measures that strengthen residential structures against hurricane-related hazards.
The County’s application proposed critical wind mitigation upgrades to seven single-family homes in the Lakewood Park neighborhood. These homes are owned by the Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council and leased to low-income households participating in a permanent supportive housing program. The planned improvements include roof system upgrades, impact-rated windows and doors, structural reinforcements, and drainage enhancements designed to meet or exceed Florida Building Code requirements.
These retrofits will significantly enhance the safety and resilience of the housing stock serving vulnerable residents with incomes at or below 50% of the area median income. Strengthening these homes will reduce potential storm damage, protect life and property, and promote long-term housing stability in an area highly susceptible to hurricane-force winds and localized flooding.
The HLMP contract requires Board approval before execution. Once approved, staff will proceed with procurement and implementation following the terms and conditions outlined in the agreement.

description:
On February 5, 2025, responses to RFA No. 25-013, Program Administrator Services – Property Assessment Clean Energy (PACE), were opened. Four proposals were received; 1,045 companies were notified, and 26 RFA documents were distributed.
The purpose of this Request for Applications is for a qualified organization(s) to act as a program administrator for PACE financing of qualifying improvements in the County. Qualifying improvements shall have the same meaning assigned in s. 163.08 of the PACE Statutes. The Sustainability District is interested in providing residents with choices among multiple PACE programs with proven records of success. Program Administrators may serve on a non-exclusive basis, at the sole discretion of the County.
The Sustainability District anticipates that Administrators shall perform all necessary PACE functions, including but not limited to, levy and collection of assessments through an already-established levy and collection entity, interaction with County Constitutional officers (Tax Collector and Property Appraiser), administration, partnership with municipalities and financing of qualifying improvements.
The Sustainability District will consider any PACE program structure in response to this Request for Applications, subject to the requirement that the Administrator either provides the financing necessary or partners with a bank or other lender to provide the financing. The term “Administrator” means the program administrator as such term is defined s. 163.08(2) together with any financing partner engaged or procured by the program administrator and any third-party administrator engaged by the Administrator pursuant to s. 163.084 of the PACE Statutes.
Administrators will be compensated through proceeds of funds disbursed pursuant to financing agreements and/or annual assessments paid by property owners who participate in the PACE program. The Sustainability District expects that applicants will already have designed and implemented a PACE program in other jurisdictions.
On May 9, 2025, the selection committee evaluated the applications that were received and made a recommendation to invite three of the four applicants to presentations and interviews. The short-listed firms were as follows: Florida Development Finance Corp.
Florida Green Finance Authority
Ygrene Energy Fund Florida, LLC
The selection committee unanimously decided to exclude the fourth applicant, Florida PACE Funding Agency, from further consideration due to on-going ligation with St. Lucie County and other Florida government agencies.
On June 17, 2025, as part of the evaluation process, the three applicants were invited to presentations and interviews. After the presentations concluded, the selection committee deliberated in a publicly noticed meeting and recommended the award of contracts to the three applicants:
Florida Development Finance Corp.
Florida Green Finance Authority
Ygrene Energy Fund Florida, LLC

description:
Tornadoes from Hurricane Milton in October 2025 caused significant damage to vegetation, structures, and various critical infrastructure in the northern and eastern parts of Lakewood Park. Eastwood Canal parallels Eastwood Drive and serves as a primary drainage canal for the central and eastern Lakewood Park community. The canal suffered significant damage from a tornado, including uprooted and fallen trees, accumulation of windblown debris, and several localized erosion washouts.
The diminished stormwater conveyance capacity of the Eastwood Canal poses a threat to the health, welfare, and safety of the residents within Lakewood Park. St. Lucie County sought Federal grant funding assistance for the recovery effort and successfully acquired an Emergency Watershed Protection (EWP) Program grant from the United States Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) for $223,296.70.
The Eastwood Canal Restoration Project will remove fallen trees and storm debris within and along the approximate 2.2 miles of canal. The project also includes several repairs to the drainage outfalls and improvements to the canal bank slopes, resulting in more resilient infrastructure for the County’s critical stormwater management system.
The project was advertised on July 20th, 2025, and the bids were opened on August 8th, 2025. Three (3) bids were received, and the lowest responsible bidder was Environmental Land Development (ELD) with a total bid amount of $168,410.00.

description:
Brightline began operations of its high-speed rail service through St. Lucie County in September 2023. The close proximity of the rail crossings to Old Dixie Highway in the St. Lucie Village area created significant safety concerns due to the fast pace of the trains and the limited space for vehicular traffic attempting to clear the tracks between Old Dixie Highway and the railroad crossings. To improve safety at the roadway crossings, the County is currently designing the installation of traffic light signalization at the seven (7) roadway crossing locations along Old Dixie Highway. The traffic signals will be integrated into the preemption timing of the railway system to ensure vehicles can safely clear the crossing ahead of oncoming trains.
Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. (KHA) was awarded the design services contract (Contract C22-11-1011 W.A. No. 2) in the amount of $575,180. KHA has completed 80% design plans and recently attempted to submit a single FEC permit application for all seven of the crossings which were included in their approved contract. FEC informed KHA that they now require a separate $15,000 permit fee for each of the seven railroad crossings. KHA submitted a request for Amendment No. 1 to their contract for the additional FEC permit fees and associated processing services at a total cost of $105,000. County staff have reviewed the supporting documentation provided by KHA for Amendment No. 1 to permit the FEC signal preemption permits at the seven signals along Old Dixie Highway and recommends to move ahead with the proposed amendment.

description:
The Keen Bridge Replacement project is in the final closeout stages and is under budget by more than $1,045,000 (Infrastructure Sales Tax funds). These funds would normally be transferred to the Infrastructure Sales Tax Reserve account, but Public Works believes the best use of part of these funds is to move $100,000 to the bridge repair account (43108) which is also funded by Infrastructure Sales Tax.
The justification for this is that the county maintains 28 roadway bridges. In 2020, two (2) bridges were classified as structurally deficient, meaning repairs and/or replacements should be undertaken within 6 years. An additional 18 bridges needed to be repaired. While the Board has approved using infrastructure sales tax as a funding source to accommodate the expensive task of designing and performing the repairs, this critical infrastructure is crucial to the movement of people, goods, and services countywide and it is a key priority to complete these projects expeditiously. Based on our current projections, the scheduled bridge repairs may be completed by FY27, two years ahead of schedule. This additional $100,000 helps expedite this milestone.

description:
As the County continues to prepare for commercial air service at Treasure Coast International Airport, preparations are underway to accommodate the service. These preparations include capital improvements to the airport’s facilities as well as enhanced security and safety infrastructure improvements.
At this time, renovations of the main terminal are in process to accommodate passengers, TSA and commercial airline service. The main terminal is currently undersized for modern commercial airline service. There were approximately 50 seats in the current passenger seating area and this renovation project will greatly increase passenger capacity without changing the footprint of the existing structure. By eliminating walls and converting office space to passenger areas, the terminal can more than double its capacity. The project will also add the required TSA space and electrical requirements for commercial airports, as well as convert existing space into airline ticket counters and rental car locations.
On June 12, 2024, the Tourist Development Council unanimously approved using $300,000 from the Tourist Development Tax's 5th cent to help fund the project. Pursuant to County Ordinance 03-12, 33% percent of the County's 5th cent is for capital facilities that promote tourism located north of Midway Road including the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds.

description:
This workshop is in accordance with Section 163.31801, F.S., to allow the Board to consider the "extraordinary circumstances" clause to have the option to adopt updated fees prior to the four-year limit for any fee increases and possibly adopt fees at levels higher than the 50% increase limit.
In June 2021, Florida House Bill (HB) 337 was signed by the Governor, which revised F.S. 163.31801 (Florida Impact Fee Act) to place limits on impact fee increases while allowing local governments to exceed these limits if the following is fulfilled:
1. A demonstrated needs study justifying any increase more than those authorized that has been completed within 12 months before the adoption of the impact fee increase and expressly demonstrating the extraordinary circumstances necessitating the need to exceed the phase-in limitations.
2. No less than two publicly noticed workshops dedicated to extraordinary circumstances.
3. Approval of the impact fee increase ordinance by at least a two-thirds vote of the governing body.
Facing continued growth and significant increases in construction costs, St. Lucie County retained Benesch in 2025 to update the impact fee study to reflect the most recent data available. The County is also interested in using the extraordinary circumstances clause to have the option to adopt updated fees prior to the four-year limit for any fee increases and possibly adopt fees at levels higher than the 50-percent increase limit.
The first public workshop to discuss the County's extraordinary circumstances was held on July 17, 2025. A Public Hearing is required to adopt an Ordinance that re-establishes or increases Road/Multi-modal Impact Fees; that Public Hearing is tentatively scheduled for September 2, 2025, at 6:00 P.M.

attachments.name: Transportation Impact Fee Extraordinary Circumstances Report

description:
Road Impact Fees in St. Lucie County were first adopted in 1985 and implemented in 1986 as an important source of revenue to use in funding the infrastructure necessitated by new growth. Since then, the County has continued to periodically update its Road Impact Fee Study, last updated and adopted on April 19, 2022. The County engaged Nilgün Kamp, AICP, with Tindale Oliver (n.k.a. Benesch) to provide the 2022 update.
The County has strived to work with municipalities to streamline the collection of County Impact Fees whereby a developer or builder pays only the permitting agency. The County's Road Impact Fee Interlocal Agreement with the City of Fort Pierce has been in place since September 13, 2005, and with the City of Port St. Lucie (PSL) since April 19, 2022.
With a population of approximately 385,000, St. Lucie County ranks 19th out of 67 Florida counties in population. The County is continuing to experience population growth, with a projected county-wide increase of 145,000 persons by 2050, or an average annual growth rate of 1.2 percent as estimated by the Bureau of Business & Economic Research (BEBR), ranking 7th among Florida counties. St. Lucie County ranked 13th for residential permitting in 2024, indicating high levels of new development. This continuing growth requires additional public capital facilities. With this continued growth and significant increases in construction costs, the County retained Benesch in 2025 to update the impact fee study to reflect the most recent data available. Along with the updated study, the County retained Benesch to provide an extraordinary circumstances analysis of the new or increased impact fees. The County intends on using the extraordinary circumstances clause within the statute, to adopt updated Road Impact fees prior to the four-year timeframe for any fee increases and possibly adopt fees at levels higher than the 50-percent increase limit.
As specified in Section 163.31801, F.S., each local government that adopts and collects an impact fee must ensure that the calculation of the impact fee is based on a study using the most recent and localized data available within 4 years of the current impact fee update and the new study must be adopted within 12 months of the initiation of the new impact fee study if the local government increases the impact fee. The local government must provide notice at least 90 days before the effective date of imposing a new or increased impact fee. Impact fees must be proportional and reasonably connected to, or have a rational nexus with, the need for additional capital facilities and the increased impact generated by the new development.
As stated, St. Lucie County’s Road Impact Fee was initially implemented in 1986 to assist the County in providing adequate transportation facilities for expected growth. The most recent study update for these fees was completed in 2022, with the calculated rates adopted in 2022 at 75% of the maximum allowable (capped at a 50% increase and discounted to 75%) and phased-in over four (4) years, with October 1, 2025, being the fourth year. Additionally, these rates only assessed impacts to State and County Roads proportionally by municipality based on VMT (vehicle miles traveled).
As provided in Section 163.3180, F.S., if a local government elects to repeal transportation concurrency, the local government may adopt an alternative transportation system that is mobility-plan and fee-based or an alternative transportation system that is not mobility-plan and fee-based. The local government may not use an alternative transportation system to deny, time, or phase an application for site plan approval, plat approval, final subdivision approval, building permits, or the functional equivalent of such approvals provided that the developer agrees to pay for the development’s identified transportation impacts via the funding mechanism implemented by the local government.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed HB 479, which defined Mobility Fees/Mobility Plan (an alternative transportation system mobility study developed by using a plan-based methodology and adopted into a local government comprehensive plan that promotes a compact, mixed use, and interconnected development served by a multimodal transportation system in an area that is urban in character, or designated to be urban in character, as defined in s. 171.031) and allows only the local government issuing a building permit to collect for transportation impacts. HB 479 requires cities and counties to enter into an interlocal agreement to define any fees for transportation impacts and determine a methodology for the distribution of any revenues. If there is no agreement in place by October 1, 2025, or if an existing agreement is terminated, only the local government issuing the building permit may collect for transportation impacts based on a developer's traffic impact study or a city or county's mobility fee less a 10% discount to the developer.
Currently, road impact fee revenues are St. Lucie County’s primary funding source for new road construction and lane addition improvements. County fuel tax revenues are dedicated to maintenance (like road resurfacing), operations, and debt service payments. Local option sales tax revenues have been mostly allocated to non-capacity projects. Without a transportation impact fee program, the County would not be able to construct planned capacity addition projects included in the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP), and other priority projects unless an alternative revenue source, such as additional sales tax or dedicated millage, is identified. In the absence of impact fee revenues or alternative new/additional funding that would replace impact fee revenues, the level of service is likely to degrade with roads becoming more congested and travel times getting longer.
Although the County’s Road Impact Fee Ordinance requires the road impact fees to be reviewed every five years, to address requirements of recent legislative changes, the County accelerated the update to the road impact fee study prior to the five-year update schedule due to increased growth and construction costs.
At the December 10, 2024 Informal meeting, Benesch presented mobility fee, multimodal fee and impact fee information as well as discussed the recent legislative changes. The Board discussed multiple options during the Informal meeting. As such, Benesch provided a scope of work to conduct a Transportation Study that includes methodologies for Mobility Fees, Impact Fees, and Multimodal Fees. Including all three (3) options allows the Board to consider alternative methods to capture travel demand revenue from future development. Road impact fees can be spent on roadway capacity expansion improvements. With a multi-modal fee or mobility fee, impact fee revenues can be spent on standalone sidewalk, bicycle, and transit improvements that add other capacity to the transportation network (in addition to roadway capacity expansion improvements). With impact fees, the County can utilize concurrency which allows the county to deny development applications where road capacity is not available to meet the travel demands from new development. However, recent legislative changes also require local governments to allow development if the development addresses its proportionate share requirements. With multi-modal fees, concurrency remains as well; while it is repealed with mobility fees. Mobility fees are a pay-and-go system and require the County to remove concurrency from its comprehensive plan.
On June 10, 2025, Benesch presented to the Board of County Commissioners at a Special Informal Board Meeting and discussed Road Impact Fees, Multimodal Fees, and Mobility Fees. The Board indicated interest in moving forward with the creation of a Multimodal Fee, and developing scenarios for varying rates for new development inside the Urban Service Boundary vs. outside the Urban Service Boundary.
On July 17, 2025, the County staff and Benesch hosted the first of two Public Workshops to discuss the findings of extraordinary circumstances necessitating the adoption of updated Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee rates.
On July 17, 2025, County staff and Benesh presented the Road/Multi-modal Impact Fee Study, including the recommended rates, to the Planning and Zoning Commission at their regularly scheduled meeting. The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4 to 1 to recommend the Board adopt the Road/Multi-modal fee at 100% of the recommended rate.

description:
In June of this year, the County purchased and closed on the building located at 8881 U.S. 1. The occupancy plan for this building includes relocating the Tax Collector and the Veteran's Services Department from Dorothy Jo Conrad Annex to the building located at 8881 U.S. 1. On July 22, 2025, the Board approved the sale of the Dorothy Jo Conrad Annex to the City of Port St. Lucie. The City agreed to lease the Annex back to the County for a period of 18 months to allow the County time to remodel the 8881 building. The Tax Collector is willing to contribute up to six million and 00/100 ($6,000,000) towards the renovation of the building located at 8881 U.S.1 pursuant to an interlocal agreement which will be a separate agenda item for Board consideration at the August 19, 2025 meeting.
Proposal for Architectural Services Space Needs Analysis
The County will need to retain an architect to (1) to perform an assessment of existing conditions and a program and space/needs assessment for the building usage; and to follow, (2)design the proposed renovations to the County building due to the scope and extent of the renovations. In 2024, the County advertised a Request for Qualifications (RFQ 24-025) for Architects willing to provide continuing architectural services to the County. The firm of Edlund, Dritenbas, Binkley Architects & Associates, P.A. (the "Firm") submitted a response to the RFQ and was ultimately selected as one of the firms that made the shortlist. On April 23, 2024, the Board approved the shortlist and also approved entering into contracts with the shortlisted firms including the Firm. Under the RFQ, and recently amended Competitive Consultant's Negotiation Act ("CCNA"), Florida Statutes Section 287.055, the County may use its continuing Architects for projects in which the estimated construction costs does not exceed $7.5 million. Per County staff, the budget and the preliminary considerations of cost are under this CCNA cap.
Attached to this memorandum is a copy of a July 24, 2025 Proposal for Architectural Services Space Analysis study for the County owned building at 8881 S. US HWY 1. The proposed lump sum fee for the study is $160,000.00. Estimated reimbursable expenses are $2,500.00. A reasonable time of performance will need to be included in the work authorization referenced below.
Construction Management RFQ
County staff is also recommending that the County utilize the Construction Manager at Risk procurement method to select a construction manager to perform the renovations. Since this project is a significant renovation of an existing building, procuring a Construction Manager now allows the ​County to engage the Construction Manager to coordinate with the Architect in the development of final construction documents, providing a contractor's input on existing conditions, price, schedule and market conditions.

description:
The Florida Development Finance Corporation (the “FDFC”) was created by the Florida Development Finance Corporation Act, Chapter 288, Part X, Florida Statutes (the “Act”) which provides, in part, that the Issuer may issue bonds to finance and refinance projects for the benefit of Florida businesses to enhance the economic development of the State of Florida (the “State”), provided that the FDFC has entered into an interlocal agreement with the local governmental agency in which the project will be located. The FDFC and the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County, Florida (the “Board”) have previously entered into an Interlocal Agreement, dated November 27, 2007, which permits the FDFC to issue bonds to finance and refinance projects located within the jurisdictional limits of St. Lucie County, Florida (the “County”) subject to the Board’s reserved right to consent to each such project.
Brightline Holdings LLC, or one or more of its affiliates, subsidiaries or related entities (collectively, the “Borrower”) has requested the issuance of the Issuer’s revenue bonds in the amount of up to $400,000,000 (the “Bonds”), to directly or indirectly (i) finance or refinance the cost of (or reimburse itself for prior expenditures for) the design, development, acquisition, construction, renovation, improvement and equipping of its privately owned and operated intercity passenger rail system extending approximately 320 miles from Miami to Tampa, Florida, with passenger trains capable of operating thereon at top speeds in excess of 150 miles per hour, and with stations located or potentially located in Miami, Aventura, Fort Lauderdale, Boca Raton, West Palm Beach, Brevard County, the Treasure Coast Region, Orange County, and Tampa, Florida, and elsewhere along the rail corridor, including, without limitation, supplemental safety improvements to the corridor within the County and improvements to the rail bridge over the St. Lucie River, (ii) fund debt service reserves, if any; (iii) fund capitalized interest on the Bonds, if any; and (iv) pay costs associated with the issuance of the Bonds (collectively, the “Project”).
FDFC and Brightline Holdings, LLC have requested that the Board consent to the issuance of the Bonds. Attached is proposed Resolution No. 25-158, which, if adopted, would provide the Board's consent to the issuance of the Bonds in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $400,000,000.00. The proposed bond issuance is a "conduit" bond with no liability on the part of the County. Pursuant to Section 3 of the Resolution, the County shall have no responsibility with respect to the repayment of the Bonds. The Bonds and the interest thereon shall not constitute an indebtedness or pledge of the general credit or taxing power of the County but shall be payable solely from the revenues pledged therefor pursuant to financing agreements entered into by and among the Issuer and the Borrower and/or parties other than the County prior to or contemporaneously with the issuance of the Bonds. The Resolution also provides that the approval given herein shall not be construed as (a) an endorsement of the creditworthiness of the Borrower or the financial viability of the Project or the St. Lucie County Facilities, (b) a recommendation to any prospective purchaser of the Bonds, (c) an evaluation of the likelihood of the repayment of the debt service on the Bonds, or (d) an approval of any necessary rezoning applications nor for any other regulatory permits relating to the St. Lucie County Facilities or the Project and the County shall not be construed by reason of its adoption of this resolution to have made any such endorsement, finding or recommendation or to have waived any of the County's rights or estopping the County from asserting any rights or responsibilities it may have in that regard.

attachments.name: BIE - Ordinance No. 25-XXX - Amending the County's PACE Program

description:
The Board adopted Ordinance No. 10-025 on June 15, 2010, which created the St. Lucie County Sustainability District for the purpose of establishing a "PACE Program" for efficiency, renewable energy other improvements through the imposition of property assessed clean energy non-ad valorem special assessments, consistent with and in furtherance of the state energy efficiency policy objectives.
PACE programs allow a property owner to participate in the Energy Financing Program by applying for funding, and if the application is approved, by entering into a financing agreement with the District setting forth the terms and conditions by which funding is made available for qualifying improvements and by which the funding is repaid over time through PACE assessments collected in annual installments on the ad valorem property tax bill.
Since that time, the County and the District have successfully administered a PACE program for the benefit of the District citizens and property owners, and have adopted and implemented various consumer safeguards similar to those in effect in other PACE programs in the State of Florida and nationally.
County staff is recommending that the Board amend and restate the District Ordinance in order to (i) update the provisions thereof for consistency with subsequent amendments to state statutes regarding PACE programs, (ii) ratify and confirm County intent that the District shall be the sole authorized provider of PACE services within the boundaries of the District, unless the County and/or District have entered into and Interlocal agreement authorizing a program administrator other than the District to provide such services, (iii) revise the boundaries of the District to include only the unincorporated area of the County, and (iv) make conforming changes to the consumer protections and safeguards previously adopted and implemented thereunder.
A copy of a proposed ordinance is attached. The proposed ordinance was drafted by the County's special assessment counsel. County staff is recommending that staff provide a copy of the proposed ordinance to the four (4) PACE proposers for review before the ordinance is scheduled for public hearing.

attachments.name: Oak Ridge Ranches - Partial Road Impact Fee Credit Agreement - Road Improvement - FINAL

description:
On October 12, 2023, the Board approved a Proportionate Share and Impact Fee Credit Agreement ("Agreement") between Oak Ridge Ranches, LLC ("Developer") and St. Lucie County. Section 163.3180(5)(h)1., Fla. Stat., provides that local governments that continue to implement a transportation concurrency system, must allow an applicant to satisfy the transportation concurrency requirements of the local comprehensive plan, if the applicant in good faith offers to enter into a binding agreement to pay for or construct its proportionate share of required improvements.
The Agreement determined that adequate transportation public facilities and services are or will be available ("Concurrency") for the development of the Oak Ridge Ranches PUD. The traffic generated by the PUD development which exceeds capacity level of service standards as indicated in the Transportation Element of the Comprehensive Plan will be mitigated by the Developer through a schedule of committed roadway construction projects or payments or alternative conditions, with improvement triggers (trips), as provided in the Transportation Mitigation Schedule, attached as Exhibit "E" to the Agreement.
The Agreement provided for credits against road impact fees for certain of the roadway construction projects, which includes County and City roadways, and also provided the Developer the option of obtaining credit upon completion of the roadwork improvements or upon bonding those improvements. Upon completion of the roadwork improvements the Developer agrees to provide County staff proof that the City of Port St. Lucie has accepted the improvements for City roadways along with invoices reflecting the cost of the improvements in sufficient detail for pre-audit and post-audit purposes.
By signing the Agreement, the Developer made a binding commitment for itself and its successors and assigns the PUD and the Development Property to the County to construct a portion of the regional transportation facilities necessary to mitigate the impacts of the PUD pursuant to Section §163.3180(5)(h)., Fla. Stat. (2025).
One of the committed roadway construction projects that is eligible for road impact fee credits is the expansion of Crosstown Parkway to the intersection of Range Line Road. The Developer is in the process of constructing the improvements to Crosstown Parkway and anticipates completing those improvements in the fall of this year. Due to timing of the Development, the Developer is proposing to bond a portion of the improvements in the amount of $4,000,000.00 as allowed by the Agreement to obtain Partial Road Impact Fee Credits. A copy of a proposed partial Road Impact Fee Credit Agreement is attached. As indicated above, upon completion of the improvements to Crosstown Parkway, the Developer will provide County staff with proof of acceptance of the improvements by the City of Port St. Lucie along with detailed invoices reflecting the cost of the improvements in sufficient detail for pre-audit and post-audit purposes, and to assure compliance with impact fee credits issued pursuant to section 24-264 of the County Code of Ordinances.

description:
As of July 1, 2022, Section 553.899, Florida Statutes imposed a statewide structural inspection program for aging condominium and cooperative buildings to ensure that buildings are safe for continued use.
In the 2025 legislative session, HB 913 was passed and signed into law by the Governor, requiring the Board of County Commissioners to adopt an ordinance requiring associations and any other owners that are subject to milestone inspection requirements to commence repairs within 365 days after a phase two inspection is received. ​
As of July 1, 2025, St. Lucie County is required to adopt an ordinance requiring condominium associations, cooperative associations, or any other owners subject to Section 553.899 F.S. to schedule or commence repairs for substantial structural deterioration within a specified timeframe after the County receives a Phase Two inspection report. The adoption of this Ordinance is necessary to amend the St. Lucie Land Development Code pursuant to statutory requirements and is in the best interest of the health, safety, and general welfare of existing and future residents of St. Lucie County.

attachments.name: WA#01 - Palm Garden Drainage Improvements with attachment

description:
Palm Gardens is a residential subdivision located just east of US 1 and just south of Midway Road in Ft. Pierce. Dominated by single-family residences, the community has limited drainage infrastructure and has historically suffered from roadway and other nuisance flooding during major rain events. The primary existing drainage features found in Palm Gardens include a privately owned lake, located in the central portion of the subdivision, and FPFWCD Canal #22, located along the eastern edge of the subdivision. Due to limited drainage infrastructure, the community is unable to drain efficiently. The County has historically installed a temporary stormwater bypass pump to draw down the lake each hurricane season, which requires personnel to operate and must be continuously checked during extreme weather. The feasibility study will explore options to improve drainage and eliminate the need for pumping to prevent the threat of the lake overflowing into the surrounding community.
A formal proposal to complete the feasibility study was received and staff have negotiated with the consultant to arrive at a recommended amount of $149,819.00. The proposed project will be an initial study to research viable options to increase drainage capacity and improve water quality in the Palm Gardens neighborhood. Up to three (3) conceptual alternatives will be evaluated. Each alternative will address permitting requirements, right-of-way needs, long-term maintenance, construction and all associated costs. Conceptual drawings of one alternative will include the County purchasing undeveloped properties for future retention pond sites. Ardurra anticipates completing the scope of services within approximately fourteen (14) months of the notice to proceed. Additional Board action will be required for any future land acquisition, design or construction associated with the project.

attachments.name: BIE - Ordinance No. 2025-016 - Amending St. Lucie County Code Chapter 32

description:
An Ordinance to Amend St. Lucie County Code Chapter 32 "Public Property", Article IV "Public Conduct" to conform the Code to statutory requirements prohibiting public sleeping or camping, delegate authority to the Parks and Recreation Director or his/her designee to approve Group Functions held on County Property, and to codify the permit process and delegation of authority to the Tourism and Venues Director or his/her designee for events held at the Fairgrounds.
In 1982, the County passed Ordinance 82-10 which created the Public Conduct article in the Code of Ordinances, which is applicable to all properties and facilities, including, but not limited to, buildings, parks, preserves, playgrounds, and recreation areas owned or leased by the County. Ordinance 82-10 included prohibitions for overnight camping in the areas regulated by the article (all properties and facilities), unless specifically authorized. This prohibition remains today.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed Chapter 2024-11, creating Section 125.0231, F.S., related to unauthorized public camping and public sleeping. The proposed ordinance further refines the existing County Code to utilize the terms/text from Section 125.0231, F.S.
The ordinance also amends Section 32-98 regarding permits for group events or functions and the use of County properties and facilities which may be issued by the Parks and Recreation Director or his/her designee.
Further, the ordinance creates Section 32-103 regarding the use of the Fairgrounds. The amendment provides that permits for events at the Fairgrounds may be issued by the Tourism and Venues Director or his/her designee. Additionally, the ordinance establishes a process to host sales events for vehicles, recreational vehicles, motorcycles, and vessels at the Fairgrounds. Currently, Section 8.02.02 of the Land Development Code provides for these sales events on property having a CG, IL or IH zoning designation. The Fairgrounds has a zoning designation of I (Institutional).
Community events, agricultural exhibits, commercial events, vehicle and vessel sales events, trade shows, entertainment and/or musical events, sporting events, expos, and similar exhibitions are typically held at the fairground facilities. Providing for these uses and sales events allows the County to expand the usage opportunities for both residents, businesses and traveling events. Local and traveling events can have a significant economic impact, bringing tourism and revenue.

description:
On March 18th, the BOCC adopted Resolution 2025-068 which established policies for commission meeting protocols, procedures and decorum, and rules of decorum for public participation at commission meetings.
The policies and procedures were developed in conformance with the provisions of Section 125, F.S., and Section 286, F.S., to ensure good order and discipline, proper decorum, as well as orderly and efficient meetings so that BOCC business may be completed efficiently, effectively, and timely. These policies and procedures have been incorporated into the agenda packets for commission meetings and added to the County website since adoption of the Resolution.
Related to meeting policies, the BOCC also discussed commission meeting scheduling and times at its January 14, 2025, and May 13, 2025 meetings. This discussion pertained to adjusting the commission meeting times to better accommodate public feedback and engagement and to make the meetings more efficient.
The current BOCC meeting schedule includes three weeks of meetings - the first Tuesday at 6 PM for a regular meeting, the second Tuesday at 9 AM for an informal meeting, and the third Tuesday at 9 AM for a regular meeting. The BOCC discussions revolved around consolidating meetings by adjusting the second Tuesday to hold an informal at 9 AM and a regular meeting at 3 PM. Additionally, there was discussion for the third Tuesday to include a regular meeting at 3 PM and an informal meeting on the same day at 9 AM or 1 PM. The suggested consensus was to plan for an informal meeting at 1 PM, followed by the BOCC regular meeting at 3 PM on the same day. The 3 PM regular meeting would run through 5 PM and recess before resuming for public hearings at 6 PM.
This item includes an updated meeting schedule to accommodate an informal meeting on the third Tuesday at 1 PM and a regular meeting at 3 PM, with a start date of October 1, 2025. This provides for a week separation between commission meetings to finalize agendas and allow time for meetings and review of agenda items. If needed, the second week of the month can incorporate a rescheduled Planning and Zoning meeting (held on Thursday evenings).
Based on the adjustments, the October BOCC meetings will be:October 7, 2025 Regular meeting at 6 PM
October 21, 2025 Informal meeting at 1 PM
October 21, 2025 Regular meeting at 3 PM
The November and December meetings with the reorganization meeting and holidays will be:November 4, 2025 Regular meeting at 6 PM
November 18, 2025 Reorganization meeting at 9AM
December 2, 2025 Regular meeting at 6 PM
December 9, 2025 Informal meeting at 1 PM
December 9, 2025 Regular meeting at 3 PM
The attached also includes an updated Resolution with updated commission meeting time references in Exhibit A. There are no changes to Exhibit B.

attachments.name: Memo to apply FDEP Wetland Restoration and Protection Grant for George Lestrange

description:
On 7/24/24, the Environmental Resources Department (ERD) submitted the George Lestrange Oxbow Restoration project to the FDEP Wetlands Restoration and Protection Grant Program to complete construction of the previously designed and permitted restoration project under the American Rescue Plan in partnership with Ducks Unlimited, a non-profit organization partnering with the County on the grant and project implementation. The FDEP Wetland Restoration and Protection Grant funding source allows local governments and non-state entities to apply for a 50/50 cost share for wetlands restoration and protection projects.
To be eligible, the applicant must identify at least 50% cost-share (non-state funds) and priority is given to projects that benefit fish and wildlife habitat, water quality, water storage, water conservation, or flood attenuation and to projects where at least $200,000 in non-state funds will be provided. As part of the American Rescue Plan funding, the County completed 100% design and permitting of the George Lestrange Oxbow Restoration project, which will reconnect the historic main river course of Ten Mile Creek to provide additional water storage while increasing water quality and wildlife habitat.
The total construction cost of the project is estimated at $1.14 million. The County expended approximately $480,000 via American Rescue Plan funding on design and permitting which will count towards the required 50/50 match. The remaining matching funds required in the amount of $330,000 will be provided from the Tree Fine and Mitigation Fund.
On 3/26/25, the ERD received notification that the submitted application would be funded in the amount of $810,000 to reconnect the historic main river course of Ten Mile Creek to provide additional water storage while increasing water quality and wildlife habitat. The requested approval for this grant agreement will allow for successful completion of the construction of this project in partnership with FDEP and Ducks Unlimited as detailed in the attached agreements.

description:
On April 18, 2023, the Board approved the short-listed firms and authorized staff to enter contract negotiations with the highest-ranked firm, Wharton-Smith, Inc. for the Progressive Design-Build Services of the South Central County Water & Wastewater Treatment Facilities(hereinafter "Project")
On July 18, 2023, the Board approved the contract with Wharton-Smith, Inc. for these progressive services. The contract approval included compensation in the amount of $4,301,938 for the initial design and reconstruction services fees to commence this multi-phase Project.
On March 22, 2024, the Board approved Amendment No. 1 to the July 18, 2023 Contract for a new contract total of $4,890,634 (an increase of $588,696). Amendment No. 1 provided additional funding for the construction of the UFA test/production well and various site work.
On July 2, 2024, the Board approved Amendment No. 2 to the July 18, 2023 Contract in the amount of $6,840,877. That amendment covered the anticipated tasks for the Design-Builder to complete the final design and reconstruction activities to produce the Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) associated with the Central County Water and Wastewater Treatment Facilities.
The County did not proceed with Amendment 3 as some of the tasks were not needed and others were then included within Amendment #4 as it was already being processed.
Amendments #4 and #5 were both net zero budget amendments that had no overall budget increases. These amendments clarified certain line items within the Schedule of Values involving various tasks and allowances in order to correctly track invoicing and payments. These were both executed through Administration.
For the next phase of Project development, attached is a copy of the draft Amendment No. 6 to the July 18, 2023 Contract in the amount of $12,186,964.00. The scope of services for this amendment includes three pipelines in and around the Tropicana wastewater facility as well as the interim headworks for the current facility. The scope also includes the construction of two additional Upper Florida Aquifer (UFA) raw water wells (UFA-1 and UFA-3) at the Central Water Treatment Plant. The amendment also clarifies the line item schedule of values that were updated under previous zero dollar amendments.
Additional amendments are expected, as the final GMP packages are not expected until late 2025 or early 2026. These packages would cover the main construction of both the water treatment and wastewater facilities.
Various aspects of the Amendment have been reviewed by the outside counsel firm of Nelson Mullins, the law firm involved in the procurement and contracting for this Project.
