description:
This is a request for a Roadway Improvement and Impact Fee Credit Agreement (Agreement) between Sunrise Residential, LLC and St. Lucie County.
The Sunrise Residential Planned Development includes the development of up to 1,500 dwelling units and 100,000 SF of commercial use on a total of approximately 516.95 acres, as more particularly described in the Sunrise PD, with a buildout date of 2044. The project is located within the municipal limits of the City of Fort Pierce, and is more specifically located on the north side of Midway Road, approximately 1 mile +/- west of I-95.
Sunrise Residential PD, Developer seeks with Agreement, to obtain a determination by the County that adequate public transportation facilities and services are or will be available (“Concurrency”) for the development of the Sunrise Residential PD. The traffic generated by the development which exceeds capacity level of service standards as indicated in the Transportation Element of the Comprehensive Plan will be mitigated by the development through a schedule of committed roadway construction projects or payments or alternative conditions, with improvement triggers (trips), as provided in the Transportation Mitigation Schedule, attached herein as Exhibit “B” related to impacts of the Sunrise Residential PC pursuant to Chapter §163.3180(5)h. Fla. Stat. (2024). Specifically, these improvements are related to the following roadway corridors identified in the County’s comprehensive plan transportation element and/or the St. Lucie TPO’s Long Range Transportation Plan:
Arterial A: Construct a 4-Lane Road from Midway Road to Northwest Property Line
Arterial A & Midway Road: Construct North Leg of Intersection
Midway Road & I-95 southbound Ramps: Add a 3rd eastbound through lane

BIE - Ordinance No. 25-012 - Anchoring Limitation Areas

description:
Attached is Ordinance No. 25-012 that, if adopted, would amend the St. Lucie County Code, Chapter 50 (Waterways) by creating: • ARTICLE III – ANCHORING LIMITATION AREAS
• SECTION 50-31 DEFINITIONS
• SECTION 50-32 APPLICABILITY
• SECTION 50-33 DESIGNATED ANCHORING LIMITATION AREAS
• SECTION 50-34 ANCHORING RESTRICTIONS IN ANCHORING LIMITATION AREAS
• SECTION 50-35 EXEMPTIONS
• SECTION 50-36 ENFORCEMENT
Increased boating traffic within the Fort Pierce Inlet has led to an increase in long-term mooring/anchoring within internal segments of Fort Pierce Harbor. Mooring within and adjacent to the primary federal navigation channel (and associated turning basin) poses a substantial navigation risk for boaters and the Port of Fort Pierce’s current mega yacht operation. These risks prompted further investigation to promote safe navigation within and adjacent to the inlet’s main navigation corridors. Two (2) Anchoring limitation Areas (per Section 327.4108 of Florida Statute) are proposed to help address St. Lucie County and City of Fort Pierce’s marine navigation concerns.
The Anchoring Limitation Areas (ALAs) as proposed will define an area in which a person may not anchor a vessel for more than forty-five (45) consecutive days in any six (6) month period, without leaving all anchoring limitation areas for at least twenty-four (24) hours and traveling to an area that is at least one (1) nautical mile away from all anchoring limitation areas, subject, however, to the exemptions in Section 327.4108(4)-(5), Florida Statutes. Two areas of navigable waters have been identified that satisfy the criteria set forth in Section 327.4108, Florida Statutes, for establishing anchoring limitation areas: each area has significant recreational boating traffic, each area is less than 100 acres in size, the combined size of the areas is less than 10 percent of St. Lucie County’s navigable-in-fact waterways, and none of the areas include a mooring field or marina.
This ordinance will be implemented via an Interlocal Agreement between St. Lucie County (County) and the City of Fort Pierce (City), with the City being primarily responsible for patrolling/policing of the ALAs, including all future coordination with pertinent law enforcement to enforce restrictions, and the County establishing the ALAs, acquiring the necessary permits, licenses, or approvals from federal, state, and local agencies and being responsible for the repair and ongoing maintenance of all signage and buoys marking the ALAs.

description:
An Ordinance to Amend the St. Lucie Code to Repeal Chapter 36 "Roads and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" and to Create a New Chapter 36 "Road and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" to Codify Rights of Way Permit and Revocable License Agreement Provisions.
At December 10, 2024 BOCC informal meeting, the BOCC discussed the details and process of obtaining Right-of-Way (ROW) Permits in the County. Staff highlighted the common problems with ROW permits, such as incomplete applications and safety issues. It was mentioned that there is no current fee structure for ROW permits and there are limited resources available with only one permit technician and one inspector causing challenges in tracking permit-related issues. Other potential issues with ROW permits may include unauthorized work, damage to the road, sidewalk, etc., inadequate erosion protection, and public safety issues. The BOCC discussion included an ordinance review and the need for potential code changes to address the issues, inclusion of public notification, updating the fee schedule, and creating a GIS map for public information.
The ordinance amends Chapter 36 "Roads and Bridges" by repealing Chapter 36 "Roads and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" and creating a new Chapter 36 "Road and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" to codify Rights of Way Permits and Revocable License Agreement processes and provisions.

description:
An Ordinance to Amend St. Lucie County Code Chapter 32 "Public Property", Article IV "Public Conduct" to conform the Code to statutory requirements prohibiting public sleeping or camping, delegate authority to the Parks and Recreation Director or his/her designee to approve Group Functions held on County Property, and to codify the permit process and delegation of authority to the Tourism and Venues Director or his/her designee for events held at the Fairgrounds.
In 1982, the County passed Ordinance 82-10 which created the Public Conduct article in the Code of Ordinances, which is applicable to all properties and facilities, including, but not limited to, buildings, parks, preserves, playgrounds, and recreation areas owned or leased by the County. Ordinance 82-10 included prohibitions for overnight camping in the areas regulated by the article (all properties and facilities), unless specifically authorized. This prohibition remains today.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed Chapter 2024-11, creating Section 125.0231, F.S., related to unauthorized public camping and public sleeping. The proposed ordinance further refines the existing County Code to utilize the terms/text from Section 125.0231, F.S.
The ordinance also amends Section 32-98 regarding permits for group events or functions and the use of County properties and facilities which may be issued by the Parks and Recreation Director or his/her designee.
Further, the ordinance creates Section 32-103 regarding the use of the Fairgrounds. The amendment provides that permits for events at the Fairgrounds may be issued by the Tourism and Venues Director or his/her designee. Additionally, the ordinance establishes a process to host sales events for vehicles, recreational vehicles, motorcycles, and vessels at the Fairgrounds. Currently, Section 8.02.02 of the Land Development Code provides for these sales events on property having a CG, IL or IH zoning designation. The Fairgrounds has a zoning designation of I (Institutional).
Community events, agricultural exhibits, commercial events, vehicle and vessel sales events, trade shows, entertainment and/or musical events, sporting events, expos, and similar exhibitions are typically held at the fairground facilities. Providing for these uses and sales events allows the County to expand the usage opportunities for both residents, businesses and traveling events. Local and traveling events can have a significant economic impact, bringing tourism and revenue.

description:
Section 327.4108, Florida Statutes, authorizes counties to establish Anchoring Limitation Areas subject to the requirements contained therein. Section 163.01, Florida Statutes, authorizes public agencies to enter into an interlocal agreement to provide for the efficient use of resources. The City of Fort Pierce ("the City") has requested the County's assistance in establishing one or more Anchoring Limitation Areas in Fort Pierce Inlet, Fort Pierce, on behalf of the City as depicted in Exhibit "A" of the attached Interlocal Agreement. The City is willing to assist the County in implementing and enforcing the established Anchoring Limitation Area(s).
The City shall have the following duties and responsibilities:The City will assist in processing the permits, licenses, or approval applications for the establishment of the Anchoring Limitation Area(s) including, but not limited to, signage and buoy permits from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, where necessary and proper, as determined by the County Administrator, or designee, or as required by law.
The City shall be primarily responsible for patrolling/policing of established Anchoring Limitation Area(s), including all future coordination with pertinent law enforcement to enforce restrictions as set forth in Section 327.4108, Florida Statutes. The County shall maintain concurrent jurisdiction for future enforcement of the restrictions of the Anchoring Limitation Area(s) but will only provide supporting services on a case-by-case basis at the discretion of the County.
The City has the right to retain subcontractors to perform the obligations set forth in this Section, although the City shall remain solely liable for performance under this Agreement. The City may not, under any circumstances, assign any right or interest in the Interlocal Agreement to any third party.
The City shall provide a sufficient marine vessel and sufficient staff and resources to provide daily patrol and coordination for enforcement of the adopted Anchoring Limitation Area(s) and shall actively coordinate with relevant law enforcement to establish specific protocols for tracking and citing all marine vessels moored within these areas. The City staff shall coordinate with the County staff to review the patrolling/policing/enforcement elements of the adopted Anchoring Limitation Area(s) on an annual basis. The review may include details on the effectiveness of the adopted Anchoring Limitation Area(s) and provide an opportunity for both Parties to discuss the expansion/reduction of these areas.
The County shall have the following duties and responsibilities:The County shall amend the St. Lucie County Code to establish the proposed Fort Pierce Inlet Anchoring Limitation Area(s), as depicted in Exhibit A of the Interlocal Agreement.
The County shall coordinate on establishment of an anchoring limitation area with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission as required by Section 327.4108, Florida Statutes.
The County shall be solely responsible for the repair and ongoing maintenance of all signage and buoys marking the Anchoring Limitation Area(s), as well as continued compliance with all conditions of the required permits, licenses, and approvals from federal, state, and local agencies related to the Anchoring Limitation Area(s).
The County shall acquire and pay all costs associated with necessary permits, licenses, or approvals from federal, state, and local agencies for the construction of proposed Anchoring Limitation Area(s) including, but not limited to, signage and buoy permits from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). For all permits, licenses, or approvals that are required to be issued to the County, the County will submit the applications, and pay all associated application fees.
The County shall provide and pay all costs associated with the provision and installation of all necessary signage and buoys to mark the proposed Anchoring Limitation Area(s). The County shall undertake and be solely responsible for all such provision and installation.
The attached Interlocal Agreement, if approved, will implement Ordinance No. 25-012 which is the subject of a public hearing on today's Board agenda.
The Interlocal Agreement is scheduled for review and approval with the Fort Pierce City Commission at the July 21, 2025 City Commission Regular Meeting.

description:
In 2002, the County acquired the site where the Dorothy Jo Conrad Annex is currently located for a purchase price of $320,000.00. After the County closed on the purchase, the County retained an architect and a contractor to design and construct the building that is currently located on the site. The building is currently occupied by the St. Lucie County Tax Collector and the St. Lucie County Veteran's Services Department.
In June of this year, the County purchased and closed on the building located at 8881 U.S. 1. The occupancy plan for this building includes relocating the Tax Collector and the Veteran's Services Department from Dorothy Jo Conrad Annex to the building located at 8881 U.S. 1. The County's Facilities Department has estimated that it will take 18 months to renovate the building at 8881 U.S. 1 so that the building can be used by the Tax Collector and Veteran's Services. The 18-month period is a "worst case" scenario. County staff's intention is to move the Tax Collector and Veteran's Services Department as soon as possible and well in advance of the 18-month period.
County staff has entered into discussions with City of Port St. Lucie staff about the possibility of the City purchasing the Dorothy Jo Conrad Annex from the County. The City is interested in purchasing the Annex because the Annex is adjacent to the City owned "City Center" complex. County and City staff were able to negotiate a proposed Purchase and Sale and Leaseback of the building so that the Tax Collector and the Veteran's Services Department can remain in the building, once sold, until the new building at 8881 U.S. 1 is ready for their occupancy. A copy of the Proposed Purchase and Sale Agreement and a proposed Lease are attached to this agenda item for the Board's review and consideration. A brief description of the proposed Agreement and Lease follows:
Purchase and Sale Agreement
As indicated in the Agreement, the County proposes to sell the property where the Annex is located for a purchase price of $4,372,695.20. The purchase price was established based on an appraisal completed in July 2024 by Parrish & Edwards, Inc. which determined that the "as is" market value of the Annex property was $4,200,000.00. The proposed Agreement also includes a payment of $427,304.80 from the City to the County in satisfaction of the City's obligations pursuant to the June 11, 2021 City Center Settlement Agreement.
The Agreement provides that the County is selling the property "as is". The Agreement also provides for the City, at its option, to perform inspections and due diligence during a 90-day inspection period. If the City is satisfied with the results of its inspections and due diligence, the closing will take place 30 days after the expiration of the inspection period. At closing, the County will be responsible for paying:one-half of the cost of any documentary stamps or other transfer tax
one-half of the cost of recording the Deed
one-half the costs of the title search fees and the premium for the insurance of an owner's policy of title insurance to the City
one-half of the closing or escrow fees of the Closing Agent
The Agreement also provides for a lease back of the Annex to the County.
Lease
After the County closes on the sale of the Annex to the City, the City will lease the Annex back to the County for a period of 18 months for a total rent of $1.00. During the Lease term the County is responsible for all repairs and maintenance of the Annex.

description:
The County and the City of Port St. Lucie ("City") entered into an Amended and Restated Interlocal Agreement dated February 11, 2019 concerning the management and disposal of the Solid Waste that the City collects and delivers to the County's Solid Waste management and disposal system ("system"). In November 2024 the County notified the City that the County did not intend to renew the Amended and Restated Interlocal Agreement when it expires on September 30, 2025. As a result, County Public Utilities staff along with County Administration staff met with City staff to negotiate a new interlocal agreement. The proposed new interlocal agreement is attached to this memorandum and discussed below.
Proposed Interlocal Agreement
An outline of the business terms negotiated by Public Utilities and Administration follows:The City agrees to deliver its Municipally Collected Solid Waste and Recyclable Materials to the County's System.
The County agrees to accept and manage the Solid Waste and Recyclable Materials that the City delivers.
The City may divert up to 80% of its Yard Waste to other locations of the City's choice, but each Fiscal Year the City must deliver at least 20% of its Yard Waste to the County's System.
The County will accept only those Recyclable Materials that are identified in Exhibit "A" to the Interlocal Agreement.
The County will charge and the City will pay the following rates (Per Ton Fee) for the County's services:
Class I Waste (per ton)Yard Waste (per ton)Recycling (per ton)C&D (per ton)October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2035$69$59$35$59Beginning on October 1, 2027, the County may adjust the Per Ton Fee, but only if the County also adjusts the Per Ton Fee applicable to the residents of the unincorporated areas of the County. The Per Ton Fee, as adjusted, that is applicable to the City shall be equal to the Per Ton Fee, as adjusted, that is applicable to the residents of the unincorporated County. The adjustment (i.e., the percentage change) to the Per Ton Fee in any Fiscal Year shall be equal to the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index ("CPI") during the prior Fiscal Year; provided, however, a single adjustment shall not be greater than three percent (3%) of the then current Per Ton Fee.
The County and the City will share the net proceeds (profits) from the County's recycling program. The County shall receive one-half (50%) of the net revenue. The City shall receive part or all of the remaining one-half (50%) of the net revenue, subject to the provisions in Exhibt C (Section 5) of the interlocal agreement. The City's share of the net revenue shall be prorated, based on the percentage of the total tonnage of Program Materials and segregated cardboard (Old Corrugated Cardboard or "OCC") delivered by the City in relation to the total tonnage of such materials received by the County from all sources during the applicable Fiscal Year. The formula for calculating the City's share shall be as follows:
City Share = (City Tons ÷ Total Tons) x 50% x Net Revenue
For example, if during a given Fiscal Year, the City delivers 6,000 tons of Program Materials and segregated OCC to the County, and the total combined tonnage from all sources is 10,000 tons, then the City's portion would be 60% of the total tonnage. If the net revenue for that Fiscal Year is $200,000, the City's share of the net revenue would be: (6,000 ÷ 10,000) x 50% x $200,000 = $60,000.
The term of the Interlocal Agreement shall start on October 1, 2025, and end on September 30, 2035.

description:
This is an Amendment to the FDOT Grant Agreement G3778 FM 451557-1 ARFF (Aviation Rescue Fire Fighting) Truck Replacement for $800,000.00 which was accepted on the 11/12/2024 Board Agenda. This amendment is for additional funds of $800,000.00; for a total grant of $1,600,000.
This project will replace the existing 2006 Oshkosh Striker 1500 ARFF (Aviation Rescue Fire Fighting) truck with a newer unit as the existing truck is approaching the end of its useful life.
ARFF trucks are different from traditional Fire Trucks because Airport emergencies present different types of scenarios and require a unique response. ARFF trucks need to be able to maneuver through ditches and rough terrain and carry a larger water tank, capable of holding thousands of gallons. ARFF trucks are exceptional because they have great acceleration, despite their size and weight. They are fitted with powerful, high-capacity pumps which spray water and foam from turrets which reach long distances. One of the FAA requirements during their annual Commercial Service Part 139 inspection is the ARFF truck must make it to the end of the longest runway and begin spraying water before 3 minutes to pass this part of the inspection.

description:
Pursuant to Chapter 38, Code of Ordinances and Compiled Laws of St. Lucie County, the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners (the Board) has the authority to impose annual assessments for solid waste (garbage and recycling) collection, disposal and administrative services, facilities or programs against certain property within St. Lucie County.
The Board initially levied recurring annual assessments on residential properties within the County Solid Waste Urban Service Area for the purpose of including solid waste fees on property tax bills on September 14, 2004. This method of collection is in lieu of the garbage hauler billing property owners directly for garbage and recycling services. The state statute authorizing collection of special assessments on the tax bill (section 197.3632, Fla. Stat.) requires notice to affected property owners and a public hearing in certain instances where the amount of the annual assessment is increased.
The attached Solid Waste Preliminary Assessment Resolution initiates the process required to impose solid waste assessments for the fiscal year commencing October 1, 2025 (Fiscal Year 2025-26) at a rate of $468.00 per dwelling unit. The resolution also provides that the maximum rate that can be charged in future fiscal years without further notice is $485.00 per dwelling unit, directs the County Administrator to prepare a preliminary assessment roll for said fiscal year to be collected on the 2025 property tax bill, and establishes a public hearing on the assessments to be held on September 2, 2025 at 6:00 p.m. or as soon thereafter as may be heard. At the public hearing, the Board may vote to assess a lower rate of assessment for Fiscal Year 2025-26.
The purpose for this action is to provide residential property owners and occupants proper, safe and cost effective disposal of residential waste and recyclable materials generated on such property.

The contract for the construction project is known as contract #20240082, Floresta Drive Improvement Project Phase 3 (the "Construction Contract"). The Construction Contract requires the Construction Contractor to furnish the City with an acceptable recorded Performance and Payment Bond complying with the statutory requirements set forth in Section 255.05, Florida Statutes, in the amount of one hundred percent (100%) of the Construction Contract price per Section X of the Construction Contract. description:
The County and ACR Acquisition, LLC (aka ACR Properties, LLC) entered into a Settlement Agreement Including Impact Fee Credit Agreement dated November 16, 2009 (the "Agreement").
The Agreement established Credits for roads impact fees and parks impact fees.
The Florida Legislature adopted Chapter No. 2019-165, Laws of Florida, which became effective on June 28, 2019, and which provides as follows with respect to impact fee credits:
If a local government increases its impact fee rates, the holder of any impact fee credits, whether such credits are granted under s. 163.3180, s. 380.06, or otherwise, which were in existence before the increase, is entitled to the full benefit of the intensity of density prepaid by the credit balance as of the date it was first established. This subsection shall operate prospectively and not retrospectively.
The County increased some of its road impact fee rates effective November 1, 2019 (the "Roads Impact Fee Rate Increase") by virtue of Ordinance No. 19-012, which was adopted by the Board on July 2, 2019.
The County and ACR Acquisition, LLC desire to document how the new Impact Fee Credit Law will be applied to the Credits in connection with the Road Impact Fee Rate increase and any future increases in road impact fee rates or parks impact fee rates (including, without limitation, any annual increases in such rates based on changes in the Consumer Price Index).
Attached is the proposed First Amendment to the November, 16, 2009 Settlement Agreement. In response to the new impact fee credit law, ACR Acquisition, LLC proposes (1) to freeze the amount of Road Impact fees for any proposed "increase" authorized by the County's ordinance to the applicable fee that was in effect prior to the rate increase and (2) as to any impact fee rate decreases to apply the Impact Fee Credits against the decreased impact fee rate in lieu of the rate that was in effect prior to the rate decrease. Examples of the proposed use are set out in Section 2c of the Draft First Amendment.

attachments.name: City of Port St. Lucie - 22 - 2A - Hog Pen Slough

description:
Hog Pen Slough is a drainage channel that conveys water from the Savannas State Preserve, unincorporated County parcels, and the City of Port St. Lucie parcels to the North Fork of the St. Lucie River. Home sites that drain to Hog Pen Slough were developed prior to water quality regulation and without a collective stormwater management system to treat surface runoff. Municipal sewer is not available in the area, so aging septic tanks are the sole means of treating wastewater. During periods of heavy rains, neighborhoods within the Hog Pen watershed, particularly near the Silver Oak Drive and Tilton Road area, experience extended periods of standing water. This causes elevated mosquito breeding, higher likelihood of groundwater contamination, and a reduction in the quality of life for County residents.
Surface water quality testing by the City of Port St. Lucie indicated that elevated levels of fecal coliform and nitrogen were found in the downstream extents of Hog Pen Slough. This has prompted plans for a stormwater treatment area (STA) to capture and detain flows prior to release into the North Fork of the St. Lucie River. An 11-acre parcel currently owned by the City is adjacent to Hog Pen Slough and would serve as the location for the STA.
On January 25, 2022, the Board approved an interlocal agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie. The interlocal agreement memorialized a partnership with the City of Port St. Lucie to allocate $150,000.00 of American Rescue Plan funding towards the design of the STA. This funding was intended to accelerate the project schedule, which was currently planned for FY25/26 in the City's CIP, but had a commitment from City staff to move up the timeline. Project design budget was $300,000.00 with a 50/50 split envisioned by City and County. Final construction costs were not known at the time the original interlocal agreement was approved. The project was submitted by the City to the County's Local Mitigation Strategy (LMS) thereby opening up the project to future funding streams. The Interlocal Agreement was recorded on April 12, 2022, and provided for a two-year term with a provision allowing extension of the term.
The City has experienced delays in completing the design of the STA within the two-year term, so that it is necessary to extend the term of the Interlocal Agreement to December 31, 2025.

description:
Permission to Advertise - Ordinance to Amend the St. Lucie Code to Repeal Chapter 36 "Roads and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" and to Create a New Chapter 36 "Road and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" to Codify Rights of Way Permit and Revocable License Agreement Provisions.
At December 10, 2024 BOCC informal meeting, the BOCC discussed the details and process of obtaining Right-of-Way (ROW) Permits in the County. Staff highlighted the common problems with ROW permits, such as incomplete applications and safety issues. It was mentioned that there is no current fee structure for ROW permits and there are limited resources available with only one permit technician and one inspector causing challenges in tracking permit-related issues. Other potential issues with ROW permits may include unauthorized work, damage to the road, sidewalk, etc., inadequate erosion protection, and public safety issues. The BOCC discussion included an ordinance review and the need for potential code changes to address the issues, inclusion of public notification, updating the fee schedule, and creating a GIS map for public information.
The draft ordinance amending Chapter 36 "Roads and Bridges" provides for additional detail and criteria when requests are submitted to utilize the County’s rights of way or easements. The additional detail is proposed to promote public health, safety, and welfare of the citizens of St. Lucie County.
The amendment includes the creation of Sections 36-1 through 36-14, establishing purpose, the applicability of the chapter; establishing definitions, right of way permit application and revocable license agreement requirements; authorizing the public works director, or his or her designee to review, issue or revoke right of way permit applications and revocable license agreements; providing for exemptions from permitting and emergency permit exemptions; providing for the collection of fees; establishing prohibited activities and penalties and for the removal and abandonment of facilities; establishing permittee qualifications; defining installation, construction, and restoration of right of way requirements; and establishing an appeals process.
The amendment also includes that “depending on the nature of the work, the permittee may be obligated to provide notice prior to any construction to all adjacent owners of real property. If obligated to provide notice, the permittee may be required to notify adjacent property owners with the use of mailers, neighborhood flyers, variable message signs or other similar methods.”

title: Permission to Advertise - Ordinance to Amend the St. Lucie Code to Repeal Chapter 36 "Roads and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" and to Create a New Chapter 36 "Road and Bridges" Article 1, "In General" to Codify Rights of Way Permit and Revocable License Agreement Provisions

description:
Permission to Advertise - Ordinance to Amend St. Lucie County Code Chapter 32 "Public Property", Article IV "Public Conduct" to conform the Code to statutory requirements prohibiting public sleeping or camping, delegate authority to the Parks and Recreation Director or his/her designee to approve Group Functions held on County Property, and to codify the permit process and delegation of authority to the Tourism and Venues Director or his/her designee for events held at the Fairgrounds.
In 1982, the County passed Ordinance 82-10 which created the Public Conduct article in the Code of Ordinances, which is applicable to all properties and facilities, including, but not limited to, buildings, parks, preserves, playgrounds, and recreation areas owned or leased by the County. Ordinance 82-10 included prohibitions for overnight camping in the areas regulated by the article (all properties and facilities), unless specifically authorized. This prohibition remains today.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed Chapter 2024-11, creating Section 125.0231, F.S., related to unauthorized public camping and public sleeping. The draft ordinance further refines the existing County Code to utilize the terms/text from Section 125.0231, F.S.
The draft ordinance also amends Section 32-98 regarding permits for group events or functions and the use of County properties and facilities which may be issued by the Parks and Recreation Director or his/her designee.
Further, the draft ordinance creates Section 32-103 regarding the use of the Fairgrounds. The amendment provides that permits for events at the Fairgrounds may be issued by the Tourism and Venues Director or his/her designee. Additionally, the ordinance establishes a process to host sales events for vehicles, recreational vehicles, motorcycles, and vessels at the Fairgrounds. Currently, Section 8.02.02 of the Land Development Code provides for these sales events on property having a CG, IL or IH zoning designation. The Fairgrounds has a zoning designation of I (Institutional).
Community events, agricultural exhibits, commercial events, vehicle and vessel sales events, trade shows, entertainment and/or musical events, sporting events, expos, and similar exhibitions are typically held at the fairground facilities. Providing for these uses and sales events allows the County to expand the usage opportunities for both residents, businesses and traveling events. Local and traveling events can have a significant economic impact, bringing tourism and revenue.

description:
The Florida Legislature passed Chapter 2025-164, LOF (SB 784), which amends the platting provisions within Section 177.071, F.S., and has an effective date of July 1, 2025.
Section 177.071, Florida Statutes, as amended, requires that plats and replats be administratively approved by a designated authority of the local government, and no further action or approval by the governing body is required if the plat or replat complies with the statutory requirements.
The amended statute requires that each local government designate, by ordinance or resolution, an administrative authority and official responsible for reviewing, processing, and administratively approving plats and replats.
The Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County ("Board") desires to comply with the requirements of Section 177.071, Florida Statutes, and facilitate the efficient review and approval of plats and replats.
The Board hereby designates the Deputy County Administrator or designee as the administrative official authorized to approve, approve with conditions, or deny plat and replat submittals in accordance with Section 177.071 and based on compliance with the requirements of Section 177.091, Florida Statutes.

description:
The Environmental Resources Department is working toward the goal of acquiring lots within a 486-acre subdivided area northwest of Turnpike Feeder Road that contains approximately 215 lots total. description:
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) requires all jurisdictions that receive Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME Investment Partnerships Program (HOME) funds to adopt and maintain a Citizen Participation Plan (CPP) in accordance with 24 CFR Part 91. The purpose of the CPP is to ensure meaningful involvement by residents—particularly low- and moderate-income individuals, minorities, persons with disabilities, and non-English speakers—in the planning, implementation, and assessment of HUD-funded programs.
St. Lucie County originally adopted its CPP on March 21, 1995, through Resolution No. 95-100. Since that time, HUD has issued updated regulations, most notably through a final rule effective August 17, 2015, which strengthened citizen participation requirements. These changes include enhanced access for persons with limited English proficiency, additional consultation requirements with public housing agencies and broadband providers, and expanded procedures for public comment and complaint response.
To remain in compliance with federal regulations and continue receiving HUD funding, St. Lucie County has revised its Citizen Participation Plan to reflect the updated requirements. The amended plan outlines procedures for public hearings, publication of draft plans and substantial amendments, and provision of reasonable accommodations. It also ensures public access to information and outlines complaint and technical assistance procedures.
Staff recommends the Board approve the updated Citizen Participation Plan by resolution to formally adopt the revisions and maintain compliance with HUD regulations.

description:
The Florida Department of Commerce has issued an updated Community Action Agency (CAA) Subgrant Umbrella Agreement, to align with revised federal and state requirements for the Community Services Block Grant (CSBG). This agreement supersedes prior agreements and is effective July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026, with options for renewal for up to three additional years.
The revised agreement incorporates extensive updates recommended by KPMG LLP, who was engaged by FloridaCommerce to improve clarity, standardize compliance procedures, and align the contract with current federal and state program requirements. Key changes include:Consolidation and standardization of program income and interest from cash advance provisions.
New data security, integrity, and privacy compliance requirements, including obligations for the use of the Commerce-provided case management system.
Strengthened requirements for business continuity planning and operational transparency.
Updates to audit thresholds and financial documentation protocols.
Enhanced branding, outreach, and website requirements to align with FloridaCommerce public communication standards.
Revisions to CSBG scopes of work to reflect updated definitions, participant eligibility requirements, deliverable timelines, and monitoring procedures.
As a designated subrecipient of CSBG funds, St. Lucie County must execute the updated agreement to continue receiving federal funding to support essential community services. In accordance with Section 29(a) of the agreement, a signed certification letter from the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners is also required and had been attached. The letter affirms that the County has the legal authority to receive the funds, has authorized execution of the agreement, and that the undersigned official has the legal authority to bind the County to its terms.

meeting: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
title: PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT SERVICES

description:
St. Lucie County first adopted Road Impact Fees in 1985 and implemented them in 1986 as an important source of revenue to use in funding the infrastructure necessitated by new growth. Since then, the County has continued to periodically update its Road Impact Fee Study, last updated and adopted on April 19, 2022. The County engaged Nilgün Kamp, AICP, with Benesch to provide the 2025 update.
The County has also worked with municipalities to streamline the collection of County Impact Fees whereby a developer or builder pays only the permitting agency. The County's Road Impact Fee Interlocal Agreement with the City of Fort Pierce has been in place since September 13, 2005, and with the City of Port St. Lucie (PSL) since April 19, 2022.
With a population of approximately 385,000, St. Lucie County ranks 19th out of 67 Florida counties in population. The County is continuing to experience population growth, with a projected county-wide increase of 145,000 persons by 2050, or an average annual growth rate of 1.2 percent as estimated by the Bureau of Business & Economic Research (BEBR), ranking 7th among Florida counties. St. Lucie County ranked 13th for residential permitting in 2024, indicating high levels of new development. This continuing growth requires additional public capital facilities. With this continued growth and significant increases in construction costs, the County retained Benesch in 2025 to update the impact fee study to reflect the most recent data available. Along with the updated study, the County retained Benesch to provide an extraordinary circumstances analysis report of the new or increased impact fees. The County is using the extraordinary circumstances clause to adopt updated fees prior to the four-year limit for any fee increases and possibly adopt fees at levels higher than the 50-percent increase. Because the County is using the extraordinary circumstances exception, a study had to be completed within the past 12 months demonstrating extraordinary circumstances. Also, two public workshops must be scheduled to discuss the extraordinary circumstances and the increase in impact fee rates must be approved by 2/3 of the BOCC. The two required public workshops are scheduled for July 17, 2025, and August 19, 2025.
As specified in Section 163.31801, F.S., each local government that adopts and collects an impact fee must ensure that the calculation of the impact fee is based on a study using the most recent and localized data available within 4 years of the current impact fee update and the new study must be adopted within 12 months of the initiation of the new impact fee study if the local government increases the impact fee. The local government must provide notice at least 90 days before the effective date of imposing a new or increased impact fee. Impact fees must be proportional and reasonably connected to, or have a rational nexus with, the need for additional capital facilities and the increased impact generated by the new development.
As stated, St. Lucie County’s Road Impact Fee was initially implemented in 1986 to assist the County in providing adequate transportation facilities for expected growth. The most recent study update for these fees was completed in 2022, with the calculated rates adopted in 2022 at 75% of the maximum allowable (capped at a 50% increase and discounted to 75%) and phased-in over four (4) years, with October 1, 2025, being the fourth year. Additionally, these rates only assess impacts on State and County Roads proportionally by municipality based on VMT (vehicle miles traveled).
As provided in Section 163.3180, F.S., if a local government elects to repeal transportation concurrency, the local government may adopt an alternative transportation system that is mobility-plan and fee-based or an alternative transportation system that is not mobility-plan and fee-based. The local government may not use an alternative transportation system to deny, time, or phase an application for site plan approval, plat approval, final subdivision approval, building permits, or the functional equivalent of such approvals, provided that the developer agrees to pay for the development’s identified transportation impacts via the funding mechanism implemented by the local government.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed HB 479, which defined Mobility Fees/Mobility Plan (an alternative transportation system mobility study developed using a plan-based methodology and adopted into a local government comprehensive plan that promotes a compact, mixed-use, and interconnected development served by a multimodal transportation system in an area that is urban in character, or designated to be urban in character, as defined in s. 171.031) and allows only the local government issuing a building permit to collect for transportation impacts. HB 479 requires cities and counties to enter into an interlocal agreement to define any fees for transportation impacts and determine a methodology for the distribution of any revenues. If there is no agreement in place by October 1, 2025, or if an existing agreement is terminated, only the local government issuing the building permit may collect for transportation impacts based on a developer's traffic impact study or a city or county's mobility fee less a 10% discount to the developer.
Currently, road impact fee revenues are St. Lucie County’s primary funding source for new road construction and lane addition improvements. County fuel tax revenues are dedicated to maintenance (like road resurfacing), operations, and debt service payments. Local option sales tax revenues have been mostly allocated to non-capacity projects. Without a transportation impact fee program, the County would not be able to construct planned capacity addition projects included in the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP), and other priority projects unless an alternative revenue source, such as additional sales tax or dedicated millage, is identified. In the absence of impact fee revenues or alternative new/additional funding that would replace impact fee revenues, the level of service is likely to degrade with roads becoming more congested and travel times getting longer.
Although the County’s Road Impact Fee Ordinance requires the road impact fees to be reviewed every five years, to address requirements of recent legislative changes, the County accelerated the update to the road impact fee study prior to the five-year update schedule due to increased growth and construction costs.
At the December 10, 2024, Informal BOCC meeting, Benesch presented mobility fee, multimodal fee and impact fee information as well as discussed the recent legislative changes. The Board discussed multiple options during the Informal meeting. description:
On February 28, 2024, responses to RFQ No. 24-032 for Professional Engineering Services associated with the Harbour Pointe Regional Boat Ramp project were opened. The outlined scope of services for the RFQ included the design and permitting of a regional boat ramp facility including (but not limited to) boat ramps and supporting bulkhead, dredging design (and possible mitigation designs/plans), floating docks and/or tending docks, restroom facilities, parking area(s), and associated civil infrastructure. Four proposals were ultimately received, and Taylor Engineering was selected and offered Contract C24-06-879 to help the County design/permit the proposed boating facility.
To ensure future design efforts ultimately address stakeholder/end-user needs, and to ensure that the design best reflects the Board of County Commissioners purpose for the underlying lands, an initial conceptual design phase (identified as a “Stage 1” effort) was scoped and initiated prior to the official design/permitting effort. This pre-design effort was seen as essential to ensure that the proposed boat ramp facility was properly sized and sited and that the planform of the facility included all the amenities that would be expected by future patrons of the facility.
The Stage 1 Conceptual Design phase was concluded on April 15, 2025, when the BOCC reached consensus on the Preferred Alternative (Conceptual) Plan presented by Staff and Taylor Engineering during a BOCC informal meeting. As such, PIB Staff/Taylor Engineering were tasked with formulating a subsequent “Stage 2” effort for the design and permitting associated with the Preferred Alternative (Conceptual) Plan as presented to the BOCC. Amendment No. 2 to Contract C24-06-879 with Taylor Engineering includes those design and permitting efforts required for all three (3) phases of project development which were presented to the BOCC during the April meeting. A copy of the presentation is attached for reference purposes.
It should be noted that increased boater access to the Intracoastal Waterway/Atlantic Ocean has been a topic of discussion in our region for many years and that a boat ramp facility at Harbour Pointe Park was formally adopted by the BOCC in the 2020 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan and Reinvestment Strategy. It should also be noted that a majority of the proposed project footprint is proposed to be constructed within land originally purchased for recreational and commercial purposes (consistent with future port development). Therefore, the proposed facility is consistent with the purpose of the underlying land and in line with the development vision for Harbour Pointe Park.
The objective of the project is to create a world-class recreational boat ramp facility for our community that addresses the current boat trailer parking space deficit within our region, while also promoting the future development of Harbour Pointe Park. The proposed project will create a unique destination for our residents and visitors and could provide unique revenue streams for the Port that can be used to offset future maintenance of the facility.

description:
In May 2020, St. Lucie County engaged a consulting team comprised of Atkins (acting as prime) & Moffatt & Nichol (acting as subconsultant) to prepare a new Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan through a publicly engaged plan-making process. That process ultimately resulted in the 2020 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan and Reinvestment Strategy, which was accepted by the BOCC by resolution on November 5, 2020, and subsequently adopted into the County’s Comprehensive Plan in June 2021 via ordinance 2021-010.
Every five years, Florida seaports are required to update their long-range plan to identify and guide port investments, to ensure alignment with local comprehensive planning and other regional initiatives. Section 163.3178(2)(k), F.S., specifically requires the coastal management of the comprehensive plan to include a comprehensive master plan (port master plan) prepared by each deepwater port. Additionally, the port master plan is one of the requirements to obtaining Florida Seaport Transportation and Economic Development (FSTED) Program funds. The proposed 2025 update is primarily being pursued to conform with State requirements but also provides an opportunity for the County and its constituents to add to the possible vision for the Port. The 2025 Master Plan Update looks to further develop the 2020 Master Planning effort by adding current activities and project initiatives that have become relevant since its adoption. The effort will also look to expand on possible market opportunities with the inclusion of a flexible working waterfront module that could help support Florida’s Spaceport System. The ultimate goal of the update is to refresh the Port’s vision and explore current market trends/conditions that may impact future port development.
It should be noted that the 2020 Master Plan identified a road-map to achieve a truly diverse working waterfront that embraces new industries and opportunities, centered on expanding economic and social benefits for the citizens and businesses found in St. Lucie County and along the Treasure Coast.
The 2020 Master Plan detailed a multi-faceted vision for the Port that called for:The creation of the Treasure Coast’s premier center for yacht, shipbuilding, and related marine maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) facilities; and,
Investment in County-owned Harbour Pointe Park to emerge as a recreational end-destination with both recreational and commercial elements, including the possibility of a public marina, boat ramp, education center, and upgraded park; and,
Advancement of a new wharf and surrounding uplands dedicated to the support of small import/export marine-dependent businesses within the center region of the Port Study Area.
The 2025 Master Plan update will further expand on those visions provided in the 2020 Master Plan by:Recognizing recent activities, outcomes, and drivers that have/or will influence future port development since the 2020 Master Plan was adopted; and,
Exploring possible developing markets, including a specific Space Florida Alternative within the Port Study Area; and,
Identifying nearby development and/or redevelopment initiatives that should be incorporated into the Master Plan update for future planning purposes.
A Port Master Plan Advisory Committee, including staff representatives from St. Lucie County, the City of Fort Pierce, the Transportation Planning Organization, the Treasure Coast Regional Planning Council, and the Fort Pierce Utilities Authority was formulated during the 2020 update, and the 2025 update looks to replicate this coordination to ensure continuity between the plans. The proposed effort also includes one in-person workshop to be held during the Facility Requirement Phase of development, where stakeholder input can be submitted and discussed for any new marine facility planning modules that may be proposed.
Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Public Transportation Grant Agreement (PTGA) XXXXX (Financial Project # 455616-94-01) – Port Master Plan Update was recently received for the proposed effort and includes $75,000.00 (50%) from FDOT, requiring a $75,000.00 (50%) local match share (totaling $150,000.00).
Work Authorization No. 1 with Atkins/Realis (C23-08-745) includes those efforts required to complete the 2025 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan Update.
Disclosure: Please note that during the proposal preparation process, a key technical lead (Mr. John Corley) for this assignment resigned from AtkinsRéalis and went to Kimly-Horn. Given Mr Corley's historical knowledge of the 2020 Port of Fort Pierce Master Planning effort, it was self-evident that the County’s Ports, Inlet & Beaches group (Port) would be best served by keeping him as the key technical lead on the project, rather than engaging a new person from AtkinsRéalis. Given the Port’s motivation to preserve the project’s completion schedule to meet the state’s 5-year masterplan requirement and the Port’s current comprehensive plan update timelines, AtkinsRéalis agreed to partner with the consulting firm that employs Mr. Corley to ensure timely delivery and continuity of end products (without increasing any fees).
Kimley Horn will be providing 93% of the proposed scope and Atkins Realis will be providing quality assurance throughout the course of the effort.

The applicant for 360 Energy Solutions received Site Plan approval through the County on October 23, 2024. The project is located at 3701 Hammond Road.
Per Land Development Code Section 7.05.041:
All residential developments required to obtain site plan approval located within the Urban Service Boundary and all non-residential developments above 6,000 square feet located within the unincorporated area of St. Lucie County and within the Urban Service Boundary are required to design and construct sidewalks within the right-of-way of all streets and roadways that abut or lie within the perimeter of the property.

Per Land Development Code Section 7.05.04.A.4h:
The Board of County Commissioners shall authorize total or partial relief from the requirements of sidewalk construction if it finds, after receiving the recommendation of the Development Review Committee and based on conditions peculiar to the proposed development, that the proposed sidewalk construction is not in the best interest of the County, the applicant shall pay a fee-in-lieu to the County for sidewalk and/or greenways and trails construction. If the fees are not used to design, acquire needed right-of-way or construct sidewalks within ten (10) years from the date of payment, the developer may request a refund.
The applicant has provided a cost estimate for the Fee-in-Lieu of construction. The Hammond Road sidewalk would be 6 feet wide by approximately 141 linear feet, resulting in a total cost of $4,700.00.

description:
The Board of County Commissioners have expressed the desire to increase public participation in the planning process and has recommended requiring community participation meetings for certain development applications, prior to the application being heard at a Public Hearing.
The proposed Ordinance ensures community participation in the development review process for certain development application types and establishes requirements for public participation meetings within the Land Development Code. The Planning & Zoning Commission recommended the mailed notice for the required Community Meeting be expanded to all owners within 1,000 ft. if the petition site is inside the Urban Service Boundary and 1,500 ft. if the petition site is outside the Urban Service Boundary. During the 1st Reading of the Draft Ordinance, the BOCC accepted the P&Z Commission's recommendation and the Ordinance has been updated to reflect the expanded mailed notice distances.
The proposed Ordinance also establishes that uses which are permitted as-of-right, which do not require special permits or variances, can proceed as a minor site plan and are therefore eligible for administrative approval. Also, the proposal seeks to allow development applications that are in substantial conformity with a Preliminary Planned Development Plan approved by the Board of County Commissioners to be processed as a minor site plan.
This proposal also recognizes the Live Local Act, which was approved by the Florida Legislature in 2023 (Ch. 2023-17, LOF) and further refined in 2024 (Ch. 2024-188, LOF) to increase the availability of affordable housing options. The Live Local Act preempts local regulations for certain housing developments in areas zoned for commercial, industrial, or mixed use and requires administrative approval and no action by the Board. This proposal looks to update our Land Development Code accordingly by recognizing Live Local projects meeting the provisions of Section 125.01055, F.S. are to be reviewed and approved administratively through a Minor Site Plan.
The proposal also includes deleting provisions pertaining to the Development of Regional Impact provisions that are no longer consistent with Florida Statutes and updates obsolete department names and titles in Sections 11.02.04, 11.02.06, 11.02.08 and 11.02.09.

description:
Road Impact Fees in St. Lucie County were first adopted in 1985 and implemented in 1986 as an important source of revenue to use in funding the infrastructure necessitated by new growth. Since then, the County has continued to periodically update its Road Impact Fee Study, last updated and adopted on April 19, 2022. The County engaged Nilgün Kamp, AICP, with Tindale Oliver (n.k.a. Benesch) to provide the 2022 update.The County has also strived to work with municipalities to streamline the collection of County Impact Fees whereby a developer or builder pays only the permitting agency. The County's Road Impact Fee Interlocal Agreement with the City of Fort Pierce has been in place since September 13, 2005, and with the City of Port St. Lucie (PSL) since April 19, 2022.
With a population of approximately 385,000, St. Lucie County ranks 19th out of 67 Florida counties in population. The County is continuing to experience population growth, with a projected county-wide increase of 145,000 persons by 2050, or an average annual growth rate of 1.2 percent as estimated by the Bureau of Business & Economic Research (BEBR), ranking 7th among Florida counties. St. Lucie County ranked 13th for residential permitting in 2024, indicating high levels of new development. This continuing growth requires additional public capital facilities. With this continued growth and significant increases in construction costs, the County retained Benesch in 2025 to update the impact fee study to reflect the most recent data available. Along with updated study, the County retained Benesch to provide an extraordinary circumstances analysis report of the new or increased impact fees. There is interest in using the extraordinary circumstances clause to have the option to adopt updated fees prior to the four-year limit for any fee increases and possibly adopt fees at levels higher than the 50-percent increase limit.
As specified in Section 163.31801, F.S., each local government that adopts and collects an impact fee must ensure that the calculation of the impact fee is based on a study using the most recent and localized data available within 4 years of the current impact fee update and the new study must be adopted within 12 months of the initiation of the new impact fee study if the local government increases the impact fee. The local government must provide notice at least 90 days before the effective date of imposing a new or increased impact fee. Impact fees must be proportional and reasonably connected to, or have a rational nexus with, the need for additional capital facilities and the increased impact generated by the new development.
As stated, St. Lucie County’s Road Impact Fee was initially implemented in 1986 to assist the County in providing adequate transportation facilities for expected growth. The most recent study update for these fees was completed in 2022, with the calculated rates adopted in 2022 at 75% of the maximum allowable (capped at a 50% increase and discounted to 75%) and phased-in over four (4) years, with October 1, 2025, being the fourth year. Additionally, these rates only assessed impacts to State and County Roads proportionally by municipality based on VMT (vehicle miles traveled).
As provided in Section 163.3180, F.S., if a local government elects to repeal transportation concurrency, the local government may adopt an alternative transportation system that is mobility-plan and fee-based or an alternative transportation system that is not mobility-plan and fee-based. The local government may not use an alternative transportation system to deny, time, or phase an application for site plan approval, plat approval, final subdivision approval, building permits, or the functional equivalent of such approvals provided that the developer agrees to pay for the development’s identified transportation impacts via the funding mechanism implemented by the local government.
In 2024, the Florida Legislature passed HB 479, which defined Mobility Fees/Mobility Plan (an alternative transportation system mobility study developed by using a plan-based methodology and adopted into a local government comprehensive plan that promotes a compact, mixed use, and interconnected development served by a multimodal transportation system in an area that is urban in character, or designated to be urban in character, as defined in s. 171.031) and allows only the local government issuing a building permit to collect for transportation impacts. HB 479 requires cities and counties to enter into an interlocal agreement to define any fees for transportation impacts and determine a methodology for the distribution of any revenues. If there is no agreement in place by October 1, 2025, or if an existing agreement is terminated, only the local government issuing the building permit may collect for transportation impacts based on a developer's traffic impact study or a city or county's mobility fee less a 10% discount to the developer.
Currently, road impact fee revenues are St. Lucie County’s primary funding source for new road construction and lane addition improvements. County fuel tax revenues are dedicated to maintenance (like road resurfacing), operations, and debt service payments. Local option sales tax revenues have been mostly allocated to non-capacity projects. Without a transportation impact fee program, the County would not be able to construct planned capacity addition projects included in the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP), and other priority projects unless an alternative revenue source, such as additional sales tax or dedicated millage, is identified. In the absence of impact fee revenues or alternative new/additional funding that would replace impact fee revenues, the level of service is likely to degrade with roads becoming more congested and travel times getting longer.
Although the County’s Road Impact Fee Ordinance requires the road impact fees to be reviewed every five years, to address requirements of recent legislative changes, the County accelerated the update to the road impact fee study prior to the five-year update schedule due to increased growth and construction costs.
At the December 10, 2024 Informal meeting, Benesch presented mobility fee, multimodal fee and impact fee information as well as discussed the recent legislative changes. The Board discussed multiple options during the Informal meeting. As such, Benesch provided a scope of work to conduct a Transportation Study that includes methodologies for Mobility Fees, Impact Fees, and Multimodal Fees. Including all three (3) options allows the Board to consider alternative methods to capture travel demand revenue from future development.
Road impact fees can be spent on roadway capacity expansion improvements. With a multi-modal fee or mobility fee, impact fee revenues can be spent on standalone sidewalk, bicycle, and transit improvements that add other capacity to the transportation network (in addition to roadway capacity expansion improvements). With impact fees, the County can utilize concurrency which allows the county to deny development applications where road capacity is not available to meet the travel demands from new development. However, recent legislative changes also require local governments to allow development if the development addresses its proportionate share requirements. With multi-modal fees concurrency remains as well; while it is repealed with mobility fees. Mobility fees are a pay-and-go system and requires the County to remove concurrency from its comprehensive plan. A comparison of impact fees, multi-modal and mobility fees, as well as next steps for each, are discussed in the presentation by Benesch.

description:
The St. Lucie County Regional Resilience Vulnerability Assessment (RVA) Draft Report was presented to the Board of County Commissioners at the April 15, 2025 Informal Meeting. In addition, the Draft Report was presented to the City of Port St. Lucie, City of Fort Pierce and Town of St. Lucie Village in April, as well as at three community stakeholder meetings in May 2025. The Draft Report was updated with minor changes / clarifications, and finalization of the ranking matrix to produce the St. Lucie County Regional Resilience Vulnerability Assessment Final Report. Staff is seeking BOCC acceptance of this Final Report.
In 2023, St. Lucie County entered into a grant agreement with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) for two Resilient Florida Program grant awards, to develop a community-wide Resilience Vulnerability Assessment (RVA) that analyzes current and future flood impacts on critical assets throughout the County. The project included interactive community presentations, and regular meetings of the St. Lucie Resilience Steering Committee which played a vital role in shaping the RVA. The Steering Committee represented various St. Lucie County, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce and St. Lucie Village departments, as well as local and regional agency staff.
The Resilient Florida Program was created by State Statute 380.093, F.S. and includes a mechanism for both planning and infrastructure grant funding, as well as setting specific criteria for conducting vulnerability assessments. The St. Lucie County Regional Resilience Vulnerability Assessment Final Report was prepared based on the criteria and standards set forth in state law and provides the necessary data and corresponding analyses for the County and cities to be eligible for future Resilient Florida infrastructure funding. It represents the first step in developing a comprehensive approach to mitigate and adapt to the effects of extreme and disruptive flood events and is another tool that can be used in planning for a sustainable and resilient community.
This project furthers the goals and objectives of the St. Lucie County Strategic Plan, particularly: ES 6.1.1 – Develop a St. Lucie Regional Resilience Plan that addresses natural resources, citizen safety and well-being; RI 5.3.4 – Actively seek resilience and other funding opportunities to increase resiliency and sustainability of infrastructure and facilities; and HS 4.4.3 – Ensure that public infrastructure is well maintained, resilient and prepared to undergo the challenges of an emergency event.

description:
On February 12, 2025, the Tourist Development Council unanimously approved the purchase and customization of a mobile visitors center (MVC). An MVC will be used to promote tourism and inform visitors already in St. Lucie County and the cities about things to do, places to go, events happening, etc. The MVC can also travel to nearby target markets to increase awareness and draw interest to St. Lucie County.
Brick and mortar visitor centers/tourist information centers are slowly becoming a thing of the past, however, information still needs to be conveniently available. An MVC will allow Visit St. Lucie to have a presence in both north and south County and at special events. The MVC will go beyond information-sharing; it’s a catalyst for visitor engagement. Activating the MVC will enable Visit St. Lucie to reach more visitors (in-market and out-of-market) to promote tourism-related businesses and generate more foot traffic to our industry partners such as hotels, attractions, restaurants, etc. Finally, the MVC will enable Visit St. Lucie and the County to be a more visible part of the community and educate residents on the value of tourism in the local economy (i.e. local tax savings).
The request for bids, St. Lucie County Bid No. 25-049, for the Purchase and Build-Out/Customization of a New Ford Transit or Cargo Van, was opened on April 6, 2025. The bids were reviewed by staff and found that the highest bidder, at $183,800, was unable to meet all requirements, including the delivery date. The low bidder, Defined Designs of Grafton, Ontario, submitted its bid at $179,700 and was able to meet all requirements. The bidder's information was complete and in order. Staff hereby requests the Board's approval to award the contract for St. Lucie County Bid No. 25-049 to Defined Designs.

description:
Treasure Coast International Airport recently obtained a Part 139 Commercial Airline Service Certification on October 2, 2024. The Airport terminal is undergoing renovations for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and future commercial air service, as needed with the Part 139 certification.
On November 12, 2024, the Airport terminal building renovation project was awarded to Perez-Borroto Construction LLC dba TrueBuild Group. The County also authorized Avcon Work Authorization #5 for the airport terminal renovations Construction Administration Services on February 4, 2025. Avcon is responsible for project observation of the progress, quality, and quantities of the executed work and to determine, in general, if the work is proceeding in accordance with the Contract Documents and to review and advise the County on change order requests.
The Airport terminal building was originally built in 1962 and has had additions and renovations, with the most significant renovation in 2011. Fourteen years later, as the contractor progresses with the terminal renovation, multiple unforeseen circumstances, such as ceiling height discrepancies, uneven subfloor, crack membranes, a water leak inside a wall, a roof leak allowing water to accumulate in an AC duct, high moisture levels in the concrete slab necessitating a moisture vapor treatment to the existing slab, and the need for additional fire rated walls, are being uncovered. These items have been reviewed by Avcon to verify the necessity, justification and compliance with the contract details. The County’s Project & Construction Manager, in the Facilities Department, has also been brought in for further reviews and coordination with the contractor and Avcon.
Bid No. 25-001 and subsequent Contract C24-11-1024 with Perez-Borroto Construction LLC dba TrueBuild Group for the Airport terminal renovations was awarded for $1,318,628.00 and did not include a contract contingency. We are requesting an Owner's Contingency in the amount of $25,475.25. The use of those funds shall only be approved by the County Administrator and used for unforeseen issues that are discovered during the remainder of the project schedule. The use of an Owner's Contingency will allow the project to continue without delay. If any portion of the Owner's Contingency is used, the final contract amount will be brought back to the Board for ratification once the project is complete. Pursuant to the Purchasing Policy Manual, a contingency in the amount of 10% of the project total could have been included in the bid and subsequent contract.
Due to the age of the terminal building and the unexpected items being uncovered after demolition, staff is requesting a change order in the amount of $106,387.55 plus an additional Owner's Contingency of $25,475.25 to avoid work stoppage or additional costs to the County as a result of the delay. The Project Manager and Avcon have maintained a running list of items with Avcon documentation on approval or disapproval. An Owner's Contingency will alleviate time delays for Change Orders and potentially further costs with demobilizations and remobilizations. The amount of change order #03 and the requested Owner's Contingency added together would have equaled an original 10% contract contingency of $131,862.80, which is the permissible percentage included in the Purchasing Policy Manual.

description:
The Housing Finance Authority of St. Lucie County (the “Authority”) is proposing the issuance of Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $28,000,000. The bonds will finance the rehabilitation of Orchard Grove Apartments, a 234-unit affordable rental housing development located at 1810 Woodland Circle, Vero Beach, Florida 32967. The development will be owned and operated by Vero Beach Leased Housing Associates IV, LLLP, a Florida limited liability limited partnership, and/or its affiliates, and will provide housing for persons of low to moderate income.
Although the project is located in Indian River County, that county does not have a housing finance authority. At the request of the developer, the St. Lucie County Housing Finance Authority agreed to serve as the bond issuer. This agreement was formalized during the Authority’s meeting on May 15, 2025. Additionally, the Indian River County Board of County Commissioners approved Resolution No. 2025-018 on May 6, 2025, granting St. Lucie County’s Authority the legal authority to operate within Indian River County for the purpose of issuing bonds for this specific project.
​
In compliance with Section 147(f) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, the Authority held a TEFRA (Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act) public hearing on June 2, 2025. Notice of the hearing was published on May 22, 2025, in the St. Lucie News Tribune. No adverse public comments or objections were received at the hearing, and there was no indication that the bonds should not be issued.
​
The St. Lucie County Housing Finance Authority was established on July 22, 1980, by Ordinance No. 80-3 of the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners, pursuant to the Florida Housing Finance Authority Law (Chapter 159, Part IV, Florida Statutes).
Local housing finance authorities (HFAs) are authorized entities created to provide financing for the development and preservation of affordable housing. They may issue tax-exempt bonds and employ other financial mechanisms to support housing efforts in their communities.
Please note: This proposed bond issuance does not involve or rely upon any St. Lucie County general funds. All financing and associated costs will be borne by the developer and private market participants.

description:
In March 2025, St. Lucie County entered into a cost-share agreement with the Indian River Lagoon Council for the habitat restoration of Walton Scrub Preserve. St. Lucie County was awarded $925,961 over three years as part of the $9.4 million NOAA Transformational Habitat Restoration grant received by the Indian River Lagoon Council in August 2024. Walton Scrub Preserve is one of fifteen sites selected throughout the Indian River Lagoon and only one of two located in the southern region.
The provisions in the approved agreement (Contract # IRL2024N-10 and Encumbrance # GL01-2402) outline two subcontracts for implementing the restoration project; one with Indian River State College (IRSC) and the other with Sea & Shoreline, LLC.
Sea & Shoreline, LLC. will be responsible for the design, engineering and permitting of the shoreline restoration to include the installation of three quarter-acre oyster reefs, shoreline plantings, and one acre of seagrass. The total contract price for Sea & Shoreline, LLC will be $693,000 over the 3-year grant period.
Staff is requesting approval of a bid waiver to enter a three-year contract with Sea & Shoreline, LLC as outlined in the Transformational Habitat Grant agreement and as approved by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the grant proposal which was awarded to the Indian River Lagoon Council in August 2024. Additionally, Sea & Shoreline will be managing two other seagrass restoration sites in Indian River County as part of the broader Transformational Habitat Grant, which will provide consistency in restoration practices across the region and better accuracy in the determination of success rate factors. Sea & Shoreline will be working closely alongside the IRSC Biology Department and capstone students who will be subcontracted to conduct monitoring, data collection and data analysis. Sea & Shoreline and IRSC have a separate, formal partnership designed to foster scientific discovery and research efforts, particularly utilizing faculty, staff, and students. This pre-existing relationship will help to ensure positive collaboration and productivity for the Walton Scrub Restoration.
Denial of the bid waiver will result in an estimated 8-to-10-month delay which will push the project completion past the grant deadline.

This proposal includes the electrical wiring and water piping, the delivery and installation of (2) new Aquifer Wells and the installation of a new submersible well pump. Replacing the wells will offer the heater/chiller unit more energy efficiency by using the infinite energy source, this allows the geothermal heater/chiller to operate efficiently and effectively all year-round. Once the Aquifer wells and pump is installed, the heater/chiller unit will be operational, allowing the Aquatic facility to meet the demands for pool programming, increase pool operations, and improve public infrastructure, which will enhance public safety and benefit the overall well-being for the County's residents.

description:

At the event, free laundry and drying services were given to everyone who attended the event. While everyone was appreciative, one woman in particular was overcome with emotion at the kind gesture.
