description:
The C-25 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area (STA) project is being managed by the South Florida Water Management District (SFWMD) on 1,583 acres in northern St. Lucie County, an important component of the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP). The C-25 Reservoir and STA project is in a suite of projects known as the Indian River Lagoon-South project to support the health of the St. Lucie Estuary and the Indian River Lagoon along Florida's Treasure Coast. The C-25 Reservoir and STA will capture, store, and treat local stormwater runoff from the C-25 Canal. The project reduces the rate of harmful flows to downstream estuaries and improves water quality in the estuary and lagoon.
The primary haul route for the construction of the C-25 Reservoir and STA project includes Angle Road between Godwin Road and Kings Highway. The majority of Angle Road west of Kings Highway was resurfaced (full-depth reclamation and double chip seal) in 2023, except for an approximate 0.7-mile segment between Old FFA Road and the Florida Turnpike Overpass, which is an old chip-sealed pavement section in generally poor condition. The County requested that the project include a budget amount for resurfacing the old chip-sealed segment of Angle Road at project completion. A Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) was prepared by South Florida Water Management District to accept a cash payment of $150,000 for the resurfacing of Angle Road. As part of the MOA, the County will continue to maintain the pavement on Angle Road throughout the project duration, which is estimated to be completed in 2029.

description:
The Board of County Commissioners have expressed the desire to increase public participation in the planning process and has recommended requiring community participation meetings for certain development applications, prior to the application being heard at a Public Hearing.
The proposed Ordinance ensures community participation in the development review process and establishes requirements for public participation meetings within the Land Development Code.
The proposed Ordinance also establishes that uses which are permitted as-of-right, which do not require special permits or variances, can proceed as a minor site plan and are therefore eligible for administrative approval. Also, the proposal seeks to allow development applications that are in substantial conformity with a Preliminary Planned Development Plan approved by the Board of County Commissioners to be processed as a minor site plan.
This proposal also recognizes the Live Local Act, which was approved by the Florida Legislature in 2023 (Ch. 2023-17, LOF) and further refined in 2024 (Ch. 2024-188, LOF) to increase the availability of affordable housing options. The Live Local Act preempts local regulations for certain housing developments in areas zoned for commercial, industrial, or mixed use and requires administrative approval and no further action by the Board. Therefore, this proposal looks to update our Land Development Code accordingly by recognizing Live Local projects meeting the provisions of Section 125.01055, F.S. are to be reviewed and approved administratively through a Minor Site Plan.
The proposal also includes deleting provisions pertaining to the Development of Regional Impact provisions that are no longer consistent with Florida Statutes and updates obsolete department names and titles in Sections 11.02.04, 11.02.06, 11.02.08 and 11.02.09.

attachments.name: RLS 24-279 Waterway Anchoring Limitation Zone - Ordinance - FINAL 4.11.25

description:
Permission to Advertise is requested for the attached ordinance that, if adopted, would amend the St. Lucie County Code, Chapter 50 (Waterways) by creating:
• ARTICLE III – ANCHORING LIMITATION AREAS
• SECTION 50-31 DEFINITIONS
• SECTION 50-32 APPLICABILITY
• SECTION 50-33 DESIGNATED ANCHORING LIMITATION AREAS
• SECTION 50-34 ANCHORING RESTRICTIONS IN ANCHORING LIMITATION AREAS
• SECTION 50-35 EXEMPTIONS
• SECTION 50-36 ENFORCEMENT
Increased boating traffic within the Fort Pierce Inlet has led to an increase in long-term mooring/anchoring within internal segments of Fort Pierce Harbor. Mooring within and adjacent to the primary federal navigation channel (and associated turning basin) poses a substantial navigation risk for boaters and the Port of Fort Pierce’s current mega yacht operation. These risks prompted further investigation to promote safe navigation within and adjacent to the inlet’s main navigation corridors. Two (2) Anchoring limitation Areas (per Section 327.4108 of Florida Statute) are proposed to help address St. Lucie County and City of Fort Pierce’s marine navigation concerns.
The Anchoring Limitation Areas (ALAs) as proposed will define an area in which a person may not anchor a vessel for more than forty-five (45) consecutive days in any six (6) month period, without leaving all anchoring limitation areas for at least twenty-four (24) hours and traveling to an area that is at least one (1) nautical mile away from all anchoring limitation areas, subject, however, to the exemptions in Section 327.4108(4)-(5), Florida Statutes. Two areas of navigable waters have been identified that satisfy the criteria set forth in Section 327.4108, Florida Statutes, for establishing anchoring limitation areas: each area has significant recreational boating traffic, each area is less than 100 acres in size, the combined size of the areas is less than 10 percent of St. Lucie County’s navigable-in-fact waterways, and none of the areas include a mooring field or marina.
This ordinance will be implemented via an Interlocal Agreement between St. Lucie County (County) and the City of Fort Pierce (City), with the City being primarily responsible for patrolling/policing of the ALAs, including all future coordination with pertinent law enforcement to enforce restrictions, and the County establishing the ALAs, acquiring the necessary permits, licenses, or approvals from federal, state, and local agencies and being responsible for the repair and ongoing maintenance of all signage and buoys marking the ALAs.
meeting: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting

description:
As part of the strategic long-range transportation network for St. Lucie County, the extension of St. Lucie Boulevard west of Emerson Avenue is reflected in the St. Lucie Transportation Planning Organization (TPO)’s plan and shown in the adopted Right of Way Protection Plan map in the St. Lucie County Land Development Code. The St. Lucie Boulevard Extension (the Airport Connector) will provide an east-west connector in the northern area of St. Lucie County. This connector will provide access to I-95 and the Florida Turnpike for residents in northern St. Lucie County and southern Indian River County.
The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) District Four completed an assessment to evaluate the implications of extending St. Lucie Boulevard (CR-608) to connect with I-95 in 2021.
More recently, St. Lucie County partnered with St. Lucie Transportation Planning Organization (TPO) to complete a study of alignment alternatives for a new roadway, known as the Airport Connector, that will connect the proposed I-95 and Turnpike Interchanges in Northern St. Lucie County, known as the Northern Connector, to the Treasure Coast International Airport. Both the Airport Connector and the Northern Connector are identified as Cost-Feasible Projects in the TPO’s SmartMoves 2045 Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP). The draft study has been completed and is being presented for review and recommendation of a Preferred Alternative for the new roadway.
The attached draft the Treasure Coast Airport Connector Alternative Alignment Study analyzes the alternative design routes and a “No-Build” alternative for a 4-lane arterial roadway connecting I-95 to the Immokalee Road and Kings Highway Intersection. A total of nine alternative alignments across two general areas were analyzed. The long-range planning, public safety, environmental impacts, right-of-way acquisition, and costs of each of the alternatives were evaluated as part of the analyses. Based on the analyses, one alternative alignment, known as Alternative Alignment D, is being recommended in the Study as the Preferred Alternative for the Treasure Coast Airport Connector (TCAC).
At the April 8, 2025 meeting, the TPO Board recommended approval of the study and selected Alignment D as the preferred alternative for the TCAC.

description:
On May 23rd and May 24th, the Board of County Commissioners held a public Strategy (Strategic Visioning) Workshop to discuss current and future priorities. During this workshop, the Board made several revisions to the adopted Strategic Plan, including updates to the Vision Statement, Mission Statement, Strategic Plan Focus Areas, and Board Priorities.
As directed during the workshop, staff has compiled a one-page updated overview document for review and adoption. The one-page overview for consideration features the new Vision Statement “Infinite Potential, Creating Endless Opportunities,” and the new Mission Statement “Committed To Service, Focused On Our Future, Grounded By Tradition.” Additionally, the six Strategic Plan Focus Areas have been revised to Enhance Public Trust, Economic Prosperity, Quality Infrastructure, Environmental Preservation, Thriving Community, and Health & Safety. The Board also revised its adopted Priorities to Infrastructure, Economic Development, Tourism, Facilities & Operational Efficiency, Housing Affordability & Workforce Housing, Fiscal Responsibility & Revenue Generation, Environmental Protection, Airport & Seaport Development, and Public Safety.
Staff will continue to update the full Strategic Plan and will bring back an updated edition for Board review and adoption once results from the 2025 Community Survey are compiled. A draft of the survey instrument is included in this item for the Board’s consideration and adoption.
Previously, the National Research Center conducted a community survey in the summer/fall of 2019 and the county worked to create a new strategic plan. In June of 2020, the Board approved and adopted the St. Lucie County Strategic Plan. In late 2022, another community survey was completed and in March 2023, the Strategic Plan was updated with minor edits to reflect the input received. In July of 2024, the Board revised the plan, with the primary change featuring the separation of Environmental Stewardship and Resilient Infrastructure into two separate focus areas and the identification of 10 budget priorities. The Board further discussed their budget priorities on December 10, 2024, January 14, 2025, and February 11, 2025. In February, the Board identified 12 budget priorities. In the May 2025 strategy workshop, the Board further refined their priorities to nine (9) budget priorities.

description:
The Medical Examiner is an independent contractor for our District 19 Medical Examiner services and serves a population of approx. 739k across four counties, has a staffing level of 19 and a salary of $367k. The Medical Examiner reached out to discuss workload, her compensation and a potential salary adjustment based on the district workload and industry standards. After reviewing the workload for the District 19 office and the 2023 Annual Report by the Medical Examiners Commission, the report demonstrated the necessity to re-evaluate the salary of the Medical Examiner.
Dr. Aronica’s currently salary is $367,143, and she initially sought an increase to be compensated at $515,000 and after discussions reduced the request to $495,000 ($127,854 increase). Okeechobee County and Martin County both voted unanimously to approve the request and on April 8, 2025, Indian River County voted unanimously against the requested increase.
Representatives from our partner counties met and discussed the request by Dr. Aronica for a salary adjustment. Chair Fowler, and I met representatives from Indian River County, Martin County, Okeechobee County, on Friday, April 25, 2025.
During the discussion, representatives of our partner counties expressed the desire to retain Dr. Aronica as the District 19 Medical Examiner, of which her salary was the primary discussion point. Halfway through the meeting, Dr. Aronica was invited into the meeting to join the discussion. Dr. Aronica noted since her tenure the office eliminated the backlog of cases, the office was accredited, and the office had applied and received $380,000 in grants to offset the budget for capital such as vehicles and a new electronic record database, as well as fund a part-time IT employee.
Additionally, Dr. Aronica noted she's been involved in working with the design team to ensure the District builds an appropriate facility specific to the needs of the community, and with that she's been judicious in monitoring costs. In addition to her 23 years of experience, she is tripled board certified, and she's seeking to be reasonably and fairly compensated for her experience and work thus far, in alignment with industry standards. Lastly, Dr. Aronica emphasized she appreciates her position and the community and does not want to leave.
After Dr. Aronica stepped out of the meeting, the discussion concerning her salary adjustment continued. Concerns were expressed that the loss of Dr. Aronica would affect the current level of service, require a search for a replacement that may take 6 to 9 months, and the future base salary may be close to Dr. Aronica's current request, but for a medical examiner potentially with less experience and standing.
During the meeting the consensus between the four-county representatives was to offer Dr. Aroncia a salary of $460,000 annually, which represents a $92,857 salary increase. The increase is distributed between the counties as follows: St. Lucie County is 46.41%, Indian River County is 25.27% , Martin County is 21.28% and Okeechobee County is 7.04%.
Th representatives of the Martin and Okeechobee counties acknowledged the need of all parties to the Interlocal Agreement to consent to the decision, and offered if Indian River County was unable or unwilling to fund its share of the salary increase (at $460,000) the three other counties would fund the difference amongst themselves. The group expressed that this was not their preference but felt it necessary to retain Dr. Aronica.
In summation, Martin County, Indian River County and Okeechobee County have approved the Annual Salary of $460,000 for the Medical Examiner to be effective June 1, 2025.

description:
St. Lucie County (SLC) received legislative appropriation funding from fiscal year 2023/2024. The funding will support ADA accessible and sensory friendly infrastructure for passive recreation at the County preserve located on Oleander Ave., near the Kitterman Road intersection, currently known as Myers-Stickle Preserve. The funding will aid in the development of the preserve for visitors to enjoy nature with amenities specially designed for people with Autism Spectrum Disorder and various levels of unique abilities, including parking areas, interpretive signage, trails, boardwalks, a restroom, river observation areas, an outdoor classroom, nature playgrounds, a kayak launch, and picnic facilities. This site will be the County’s first inclusive design preserve with river access and will provide amenities specially designed for people with unique abilities and special needs.
This agenda item requests authorization to contract with Masteller & Moler for $85,320 for professional engineering design, permitting, bidding, and construction administration and observation services and to allocate $565,000 to cover the estimated construction cost necessary to bring in water and wastewater utilities and the construction of a new lift station at the Myers-Stickle Preserve.
The 33-acre property, purchased in 2015 for $457,533, will be preserved in perpetuity primarily for managing/maintaining high-quality native habitats that provide ecological benefits (clean air, carbon sequestration, aquifer recharge, water quality improvements, wildlife habitat, etc.). A priority goal in ERD is to provide a variety of passive recreation opportunities without negatively impacting the natural resources within the natural areas we manage for the public. This site contains 20 acres of floodplain forest, 11 acres of pine flatwoods, and two acres of river oxbows that are all in very good condition. SLC's preserve system facilitates physically active and healthy lifestyles through access to greenways and trails, which are an essential component in walkable community designs. Preserves play a significant role in connecting residents and visitors to the County’s natural and human heritage by telling the story of the land, water and people. Being outdoors, in nature, helps to cultivate knowledge, nurture a sense of wonder, and inspire stewardship of the natural world through education, artistic expression, physical activity, and is shown to improve mental health/wellness. The proposed amenities will provide opportunities to connect people to the North Fork of the St. Lucie River, through passive and active programming, will instill a sense of place, stewardship, and community cohesiveness.

description:
Impact fees in St. Lucie County was first adopted as follows: Parks (1996), Library (1996), Public Buildings (1996), and Law Enforcement (2004). The County has continued to periodically update these impact fees. The last study was updated on April 19, 2022. Pursuant to Florida Statute Section 163.31801 (Impact Fees), fees must be updated once every (4) four years and must be adopted within 12 months of initiation. This contract will allow the County to update its current impact fees.
Additionally, the St. Lucie County Fire District has requested to piggyback on this contract in order to update the Fire/EMS impact fee study, which was last adopted on September 6, 2022. The County and the Fire District are proposing to enter into an Interlocal Agreement for the Fire District's portion of the Impact Fee Study ($62,724.00).

description:
Article III of Chapter 24 of the St. Lucie County Code of Ordinances (Fire/EMS Protection Impact Fee), specifically Section 24-51(c), establishes, "...the county fire district is the sole provider of fire/emergency medical services in the county." Additionally, Section 24-51(d) provides, "the county must collect fire/EMS protection impact fees in order to provide the fire district with funds to adequately provide fire/EMS services for all county residents, including residents of the cities. Development within the cities impacts the fire/EMS capital needs of the fire district. "
In 2000, the County adopted a Fire/EMS Protection Impact Fee to address the impact of growth and demand on the Fire District to provide Fire/EMS protection services. The current Fire/EMS Protection impact fees are based on a May 2022 study prepared by Dr. James C. Nicholas, and were adopted by the County Board of Fire Commissioners (Fire Board) on June 20, 2022, and subsequently by the Board of County Commissioners (BOCC) on July 21, 2022.
The Fire District is in need to update their FIRE/EMS Protection Impact Fee study concurrently with the County's update of the studies for Library, Public Buildings, Parks, and Law Enforcement Impact Fees. In order to accommodate the request to utilize the County's Impact Fee consultant, this Interlocal Agreement identifies that the Fire District is responsible for remitting the cost of their portion of the FIRE/EMS Impact Fee ($62,724.00), being completed by Alfred Benesch & Company.

description:
The Board of County Commissioners previously approved a contract with ROK Technologies to migrate and host the County's Geographic Information Systems (GIS) data in a Cloud-based environment on 5/21/2024.
A change to ROK Technologies Master Service Agreement has been provided to the County, making this contract renewal necessary.
Background:
As the County continues to leverage Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for critical data analysis and decision-making processes, the need for reliable and secure hosting solutions for our ArcGIS Enterprise environment has become increasingly apparent. The availability of our GIS systems and services is essential to several integrated systems, including EnerGov (Online Permitting/Land Use Management), Public Works Department's Work Order/Asset Management system, and OneSolution OSSI (Computer Aided Dispatch). To maintain and enhance the efficiency, security, and scalability of our GIS infrastructure, the GIS Division has previously contracted with ROK Technologies to manage the hosting of our ArcGIS Enterprise environment.
This contract with ROK provides several benefits, including:
Enhanced Security and Compliance
Improved Reliability and Uptime (GIS services will be available should our network be compromised or be offline for any reason)
Comprehensive 24/7 Support
Scalability and Flexibility
In addition, there are avoided costs, including the cost of replacing servers/hardware and professional services or additional staff for ArcGIS Enterprise administration. Many organizations employ a full-time ArcGIS Administrator; this role is currently being filled by existing staff to the detriment of other projects. The time spent on ArcGIS Enterprise and database administration is easily equal to 1 FTE.

description:
As a recipient of Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Urbanized Area Formula Grant funds, St. Lucie County's Transit Department is required to develop a PTASP and update the safety performance targets yearly.

The PTASP rule became effective on July 19, 2019. FTA subsequently published two Notices of Enforcement Discretion, ultimately extending the PTASP compliance deadline to July 21, 2021 for recipients and subrecipients unable to certify compliance with the PTASP regulation. On February 17, 2022, the FTA published a Dear Colleague Letter to inform the transit industry about the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law changes to Public Transportation Agency Safety Plan (PTASP) requirements. The new requirements apply to transit agencies with an Agency Safety Plan (ASP) in place under the PTASP regulation (49 CFR Part 673).

description:
Chapter 50, Florida Statutes, Legal and Official Advertisements, provides that, effective January 1, 2023, a governmental agency may publish certain statutorily required legal advertisements, publications, or notices on the publicly accessible website of the county in which it lies if doing so would cost less than publishing legal notices in a newspaper. The County has determined that the cost of publishing legal advertisements and public notices on the publicly accessible website of the county is less than the cost of publishing legal advertisements and public notices in a newspaper.
The proposed ordinance creates a new Section 11.00.05 of the St. Lucie County Land Development Code to allow advertisements, publications or notices that are currently required or permitted to be published in a newspaper by county ordinance, resolution, board policy, or administrative procedure, or otherwise, to instead be published on the County’s official website or other private website designated by the County for the publication of legal notices and advertisements that is accessible to the public via the internet, pursuant to Chapter 50, Florida Statutes.
The proposed ordinance serves a public purpose by reducing the costs of County legal advertisements and public notices and by making County legal advertisements and public notices more accessible to the public.

attachments.name: Petition for Dissolution of Reserve Community Development District #2

description:
The Reserve Community Development District #2, a local unit of special-purpose government organized and existing in accordance with Chapter 190, Florida Statutes (the “District”), has filed the attached petition with the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County, Florida, to adopt an Ordinance for the purpose of dissolving the District in accordance with Section 190.046(10), Florida Statutes. The Petition sets out that:
1. The District was established by St. Lucie County Ordinance Board of County Commissioners No. 99-029, amending Chapter 1-6.5, “Community Development” of the Code of Ordinances of St. Lucie County by adding Sections 1-6.5-70 through 1-6.5-73 to establish the District.
2. The boundaries of the District are located wholly within the boundaries of unincorporated St. Lucie County, Florida (the “County”) as set forth in the Legal Description (Exhibit “A”) and the Map of Reserve Community Development District (“Exhibit “B”), both of which Exhibits are attached hereto and incorporated herein by reference.
3. Section 190.046(10), Florida Statutes, provides that, upon petition of the District, the Board of County Commissioners may adopt an ordinance dissolving the District when the District has no outstanding financial obligations and no operating or maintenance responsibilities. Prior to the adoption of the ordinance dissolving the District, ownership of all infrastructure improvements owned by the District will be transferred to other entities and all other financial obligations of the District will be satisfied, so that at the time the District is dissolved, the District will have no further outstanding financial obligations or operating or maintenance responsibilities. A copy of an updated balance sheet for the District dated February 28, 2025, is attached hereto as Exhibit “C.”
4. The District Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution 2025-03 on November 21, 2024, authorizing the filing of this Petition to Dissolve, having determined that the District meets the criteria for dissolution as provided in Section 190.046(10), Florida Statutes, and the termination of the District will not harm or otherwise injure any interests of the landowners of the District, nor harm nor otherwise injure any interests of any other party within or without the District. A copy of Resolution 2021-09 is attached hereto as Exhibit “D” and incorporated herein by reference.
Also attached is draft Ordinance No. 25-008, which, if adopted, would dissolve the Community Development District. County staff has previously determined has no real property or other asset that it purposes to transfer to the County. All improvements funded by the District bonds are owned and maintained by one or more property owner associations within the District. description:
Stormwater culverts direct and channel the flow of stormwater under driveways, roads, sidewalks and other obstructions and are an integral component of stormwater management. Culverts fail over time due to maintenance, environmental or installation issues. Culvert failure can lead to localized flooding which may impede safe conditions of ingress and egress for owners and residents of property in the affected area as well as the traveling public, visitors, emergency responders and other public service providers. Some culvert owners may lack the resources to pay for improvements and repairs.
In 2021, the Board established a voluntary program, Ordinance No. 21-004, to which eligible property owners can apply for and receive funding to improve or repair culverts and then repay this funding through the imposition of a non-ad valorem special assessment against the improved property collected in annual installments on the tax roll.
The attached Resolution No. 2025-116 is the Assessment Resolution as required by County's Ordinance No. 21-004, as amended. The purpose of this resolution relates to the imposition and collection of special assessments to fund stormwater culvert improvements within the Culvert 2025-04 MSBU, determine that real property therein will be specially benefitted, establish the method of assessing the cost of the improvements, approve the assessment roll, and provide an effective date.

A commissioner requested staff place an item on the informal Board agenda to discuss the expansion of allowable uses within our Agricultural Zoning Districts. Specific to this discussion, there is an active Code Enforcement case on a parcel within the AG-2.5 zoning district, where a resident is operating a dumpster rental business. These standards include the proximity to Okeechobee Rd. and Orange Ave, increased buffering to screen the use from adjacent Rights-of-Ways and adjoining parcels, pavement and stormwater requirements, and identification of all proposed lighting and refuse collection. Additionally, the BOCC has the authority through the Conditional Use Permit process to place any other reasonable conditions on the proposed development to ensure compatibility with the surrounding uses.
Last month, the Board approved an applicant-initiated Land Development Code Text Amendment allowing for Utility Trade Contractors with Specialty Storage as an eligible Conditional Use within the AG-2.5 zoning district. The amendment requires the parcel to be located adjacent to and with direct access to State Roads 68 and 70, with a minimum lot size of four (4) acres and a minimum lot width of 250 feet.

attachments.name: Petition for Dissolution of Reserve Community Development District #2

description:
The Reserve Community Development District #2, a local unit of special-purpose government organized and existing in accordance with Chapter 190, Florida Statutes (the “District”), has filed the attached petition with the Board of County Commissioners of St. Lucie County, Florida, to adopt an Ordinance for the purpose of dissolving the District in accordance with Section 190.046(10), Florida Statutes. The Petition sets out that:
1. The District was established by St. Lucie County Ordinance Board of County Commissioners No. 99-029, amending Chapter 1-6.5, “Community Development” of the Code of Ordinances of St. Lucie County by adding Sections 1-6.5-70 through 1-6.5-73 to establish the District.
2. The boundaries of the District are located wholly within the boundaries of unincorporated St. Lucie County, Florida (the “County”) as set forth in the Legal Description (Exhibit “A”) and the Map of Reserve Community Development District (“Exhibit “B”), both of which Exhibits are attached hereto and incorporated herein by reference.
3. Section 190.046(10), Florida Statutes, provides that, upon petition of the District, the Board of County Commissioners may adopt an ordinance dissolving the District when the District has no outstanding financial obligations and no operating or maintenance responsibilities. Prior to the adoption of the ordinance dissolving the District, ownership of all infrastructure improvements owned by the District will be transferred to other entities and all other financial obligations of the District will be satisfied, so that at the time the District is dissolved, the District will have no further outstanding financial obligations or operating or maintenance responsibilities. A copy of an updated balance sheet for the District dated February 28, 2025, is attached hereto as Exhibit “C.”
4. The District Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution 2025-03 on November 21, 2024, authorizing the filing of this Petition to Dissolve, having determined that the District meets the criteria for dissolution as provided in Section 190.046(10), Florida Statutes, and the termination of the District will not harm or otherwise injure any interests of the landowners of the District, nor harm nor otherwise injure any interests of any other party within or without the District. A copy of Resolution 2021-09 is attached hereto as Exhibit “D” and incorporated herein by reference.
Also attached is a draft ordinance, which, if adopted, would dissolve the Community Development District. County staff has previously determined has no real property or other asset that it purposes to transfer to the County. All improvements funded by the District bonds are owned and maintained by one or more property owner associations within the District.

attachments.name: Contract for Sale and Purchase Signed

description:
The property consists of 399.50 +/- acres and lies west of Okeechobee Road and just east of the Okeechobee/St. Lucie County line. The parcel has a designation of AG-5 in the Future Land Use Map and Zoning District Map. The parcel is currently vacant, unmaintained and has previously been utilized for cattle grazing.
The property has been identified by the County as “Environmentally Significant Lands” and is immediately north of the County's Cypress Creek Preserve. The property and surrounding area represents a significant portion of the remaining hydric forest that once extended along the entire eastern edge of the Orlando Ridge south of Indian River County, through western St. Lucie County, to the end of the Alapatioka/Allapattah Flats Marsh System in southwest Martin County. This is a significant area for rural landscape conservation, natural storage, water quality improvement, habitat preservation and restoration, and supports the environmental and hydrological health of the Florida Everglades Ecosystem. This property and the surrounding area are also identified as a priority area for the State. For example, the area is targeted within the Florida Forever Projects (Bluefield to Cow Creek project), Rural and Family Lands Protection Program, Florida Wildlife Corridor and the Florida Ecological Greenways Network.
The Property Acquisition Division was contacted by the broker to see if the County had an interest in acquiring the subject parcel. The Environmental Resources Department requested the Property Acquisition Division obtain appraisals of the parcel.
The Property Acquisition Division contracted with Fuller-Armfield-Wagner and Parrish & Edwards, Inc. to perform appraisals of the subject parcel. Both appraisers identified a Fair Market Value of $6,000,000. The County presented a Contract for Sale and Purchase to Junior Louis Ranch, LLC for $6,000,000.
Attached for your review and approval is the signed Contract for Sale and Purchase.
The Kolter Group, LLC, (Kolter) is the main developer of the Oak Ridge Ranches Project (Project) located off Glades Cut Off Road and Range Line Road. The Project includes the preservation of 376.5 acres of environmentally sensitive lands, including wetlands, wetland buffers, upland habitats and the 101’ wildlife corridor onsite, via a recorded conservation easement. There is an additional approximately 107.5 acres of habitat to be mitigated plus the quantified acreage from the grading for drainage, which is currently estimated to be 125-130 acres inclusive of both impacts. The County has been coordinating with Kolter on satisfying its remaining preservation through the purchase of land off-site with the equivalent acreage and similar ecological value (i.e., comparable habitat). Kolter has indicated a desire to satisfy the remaining mitigation through a financial contribution to this purchase for the equivalent acreage required to be mitigated.

description:
In accordance with the requirements of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) Program Act (Sections 420.907-420.9079, Florida Statutes) and Rule Chapter 67-37, Florida Administrative Code, local governments must adopt a Local Housing Assistance Plan (LHAP) every three years to outline strategies for the use of SHIP funds. These funds are allocated by the State of Florida from documentary stamp tax revenue to support the development and preservation of affordable housing.
The LHAP for St. Lucie County covers fiscal years 2025-2026, 2026-2027, and 2027-2028 and includes strategies to address affordable housing needs for very low, low, and moderate-income households. Strategies include owner-occupied rehabilitation, purchase assistance, emergency repairs, disaster mitigation, new rental construction and rehabilitation, demolition and reconstruction, utility and security deposits, and code violation abatement.
The Plan also outlines the County’s approach to program administration, leveraging public and private funds, incorporating energy-efficient building practices, addressing special needs populations, and reducing homelessness.
The attached resolution authorizes submission of the 2025–2028 LHAP to the Florida Housing Finance Corporation for review and approval and designates the Chair to execute all necessary documents and certifications on behalf of the County.

description:
The “Work Camper” program was established for St. Lucie County Environmentally Significant Lands (ESL) program in 2002. This program provides a volunteer with a space and utility hook up for their recreational vehicle, or in the case of Becker Preserve, a 400 s.f. efficiency apartment, for use as a temporary residence in exchange for a minimum of twenty (20) hours of service each week assisting with preserve maintenance. Each Work Camper works 1,040 hours of work annually, benefiting the County with the equivalent of $34,829 of labor each year (based on the 2024 Independent Sector’s Value of Volunteer Time-=$33.49/ hour).
The work campers for the Becker Preserve will be responsible for tasks specified in the attached contract, including opening and closing gates, helping to maintain the parking lot, grounds, and nature trails in neat and clean condition, checking on campers, patrolling the preserve/site security, mowing, and exotic plant removal. The work camper presented for the Becker Preserve is Travis Brackney, a Deputy with the SL Sheriff's Office and experienced with procedure and protocol in emergency situations.
ERD manages over 11,000 acres of public preserves owned by the St. Lucie County Board of Commissioners. These preserves were purchased with funds from St. Lucie County’s Environmentally Significant Lands Bond Program, a local voter-approved bond program, and Florida Communities' Trust-Florida Forever Program, a State-funded program to preserve and provide passive public access to Florida’s remaining natural treasures.

description:
Chapter 50, Florida Statutes, Legal and Official Advertisements, provides that, effective January 1, 2023, a governmental agency may publish certain statutorily required legal advertisements, publications, or notices on the publicly accessible website of the county in which it lies if doing so would cost less than publishing legal notices in a newspaper. The County has determined that the cost of publishing legal advertisements and public notices on the publicly accessible website of the county is less than the cost of publishing legal advertisements and public notices in a newspaper.
The proposed ordinance creates a new Section 11.00.05 of the St. Lucie County Land Development Code to allow advertisements, publications or notices that are currently required or permitted to be published in a newspaper by county ordinance, resolution, board policy, or administrative procedure, or otherwise, to instead be published on the County’s official website or other private website designated by the County for the publication of legal notices and advertisements that is accessible to the public via the internet, pursuant to Chapter 50, Florida Statutes.
The proposed ordinance serves a public purpose by reducing the costs of County legal advertisements and public notices and by making County legal advertisements and public notices more accessible to the public.

description:
This amendment is a proposal to remove Special Condition #25 from the approved Class II mining permit for the Guettler Borrow Pit (±68.09 acres) located on the south side of State Road 70 (Okeechobee Road) in western St. Lucie County.
The BOCC approved a Class I mining permit for the Guettler Borrow Pit on June 6, 2006, which included Special Condition #14 that restricted the delivery of excavated material to the adjacent State Road 70 widening project. However, on November 27, 2007, the condition was removed through the issuance of Amendment #1 to the mining permit. The BOCC later approved an expansion to the mining operation for a Class II mining permit on March 6, 2012, which is valid for 20 years (March 6, 2032) unless revoked prior thereto, as provided in Sections 6.06.00 and 11.05.11 of the St. Lucie County Land Development Code. It is noted that the restriction on the delivery of excavated material to the State Road 70 project remained on the approved Class II mining permit as Special Condition #25.
On March 31, 2025, Guettler Brothers Construction, LLC, as the owners and operators of the Guettler Borrow Pit, presented a petition to modify the Class II mining permit to remove Special Condition #25, restricting the use of the mined material for the State Road 70 widening project.
The State Road 70 widening project between Summerlin Road and the County line was completed in approximately 2014. Guettler provided an updated description of the proposed haul route associated with the request to include the use of State Road 70 east to Midway Road, and then using Midway Road to either I-95 (northbound or southbound) or Glades Cut Off Road (northbound). Staff recommends approval of the proposed haul route roadways, as each roadway is identified on the Designated Freight Network per the St. Lucie Transportation Planning Organization.

description:
Chapters 125, and 163, F.S., require the adoption and enforcement of the comprehensive plan and codes; provide for the regulation of structures in the right-of-way limits of the county road system; and require enforcement to ensure development undertaken is consistent with the adopted plan and codes. Development proposals must be reviewed for compliance and consistency with the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code. These reviews are conducted by multiple County departments and divisions.
Government operations and services, including the technical and administrative activities for development review functions, demand a substantial amount of effort and resources by the County and establishing reasonable, necessary, and commensurate costs for providing those services to those parties deriving direct benefit is in the public interest. As such, it is necessary to further update and amend the schedule of fees to include charging the users of specific County services a fee for cost recovery which lessens the burden on taxpayers of St. Lucie County.
The updated schedule of fees was prepared based upon the estimated direct and reasonable indirect costs associated with the provision of services, including the review and processing of applications. The principal changes in the schedule of fees include creating fees for the review functions conducted by the Public Works Department and the Property Acquisition Division as well as formally creating a schedule of fees for the response to public record requests, consistent with Section 119.07, F.S. Updates have also been proposed for Planning & Development Services and Environmental Resources review functions. The effective date for the majority of the updated schedule of fees is proposed as July 1, 2025, to allow time to broadcast the updates as well as to provide time to implement the updates within the County’s online permitting system.
The effective date for Public Records Request fees and the discounted rates for Land Use amendments to AG-5, AG-2.5 and Cpub designations and the discounted rates for Zoning amendments to the AG-5, AG-2.5, AG-1, AR-1 and Cpub districts is proposed as the adoption date of the resolution.

description:
Chapter 125, F.S., provides for the enforcement of the Florida Building Code and to enforce local technical amendments to the Florida Building Code. Chapter 553, F.S., provides for the uniform adoption, updating, amendment, interpretation, and enforcement of a single, unified state building code, called the Florida Building Code. Section 125.56, F.S., specifically authorizes the Board of County Commissioners to establish a schedule of reasonable inspection fees in order to defer the costs of inspection and enforcement of the provisions of the Florida Building Code.
Government operations and services, including the technical and administrative activities for building permits, review and inspection functions, demand a substantial amount of effort and resources by the County and establishing reasonable, necessary, and commensurate costs for providing those services to those parties deriving direct benefit is in the public interest.
The updated schedule of fees was prepared based upon the estimated direct and reasonable indirect costs associated with the provision of services, including the review and processing of permit applications. The principal changes in the schedule of fees include the organization of residential permit types in alphabetical order, fee reductions on several residential permit types, an increase to the fee for a nonconforming lot of record request due to the workload associated with the research required, and establishing a fee for milestone inspection report submissions. The milestone inspection, or structural inspection of certain condominium and cooperative buildings, is a recent statutory requirement. The effective date of the updated schedule of fees is proposed as July 1, 2025, to allow time to broadcast the updates as well as to provide time to implement the updates within the County’s online permitting system.
Chapter 125, F.S., and the St. Lucie County Land Development Code Section 11.12.00 authorize the Board to establish a schedule of fees in order to cover the costs of technical and administrative activities required. Attached is a draft Resolution which, if adopted, would amend the schedule of fees to provide for the cost recovery of the technical and administrative review and issuance functions.

description:
In December 1986, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 85-02 creating regulations for the protection of sea turtles in St. Lucie County.
In March 1988, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 88-14 permitting horseback riding on the beach in areas authorized by permit and subject to further restrictions during sea turtle nesting season.
In 1991, the Board adopted Ordinance No. 91-21 amending the St. Lucie County Land Development Code and adopting Section 6.04.02 Sea Turtle Protection with Subsection D prohibiting activities disruptive to sea turtles. The ordinance provides that during sea turtle nesting season (Mar 1 - Nov 15), horseback riding shall be prohibited seaward of the primary dune, except when a special permit is issued by the County in accordance with regulations adopted by the Board.
Section 32-96 of the St. Lucie County Code and Compiled Laws authorizes horseback riding activities on the beach, if authorized by permit from the Director of Parks and Recreation of St. Lucie County.
In June 2024, the Board adopted Resolution No. 24-115 amending Resolution No. 11-056 which added John Brooks Beach Park as an additional site for horseback riding on the beach. The site was added to accommodate the relocation of the horseback riding on the beach program while Frederick Douglass Memorial Beach Park was closed due to renovations. Frederick Douglass Memorial Beach Park reopened on February 14, 2025.
Currently, in St. Lucie County, horseback riding on the beach is only permitted at Frederick Douglass Memorial Park Beach and John Brooks Beach Park.
Staff requests that the horseback riding on the beach program continues with amended rules and regulations. Changes to the amended rules and regulations include:Limit riding to occur after 8am and before 5pm, seven days a week (riding was previous sunrise to sunset)
Riders must ride north from Frederick Douglass Memorial Beach Park's designated horse access until reaching the end-of-the-trail marker that indicates the turnaround point (riders previously rode south from Frederick Douglass Memorial Beach Park)

description:
In November 2022, the Board accepted $100,000.00 from the U.S. Treasury’s Local Assistance and Tribal Consistency Fund (LATCF). LATCF was awarded to the County by the US Treasury in November 2022 as an eligible revenue-sharing county as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury; and for which, as determined by the Secretary, there is a negative revenue impact due to the implementation of a federal program.
At that time, it was agreed that the funds would be allocated to the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Ten Mile Creek Restoration/Oxbow Cleanout Project. The 10-Mile Creek project was initially designed using ARPA funds and was advertised for bid in 2024. However, construction was delayed due to increased costs and APRA obligation deadlines.
In late 2024, the Environmental Resource Department (ERD) identified an opportunity to partner with Ducks Unlimited and applied for a grant from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP). On March 26, 2025, FDEP notified ERD of the award for funding to support the 10-Mile Creek project.
This new grant funding for 10-Mile Creek creates an opportunity to reallocate the $100,000.00 LATCF funds to another eligible project, with transportation being an allowable use under LATCF guidelines. Staff recommend that these funds be reclassified to help offset the costs of the Keen Road Bridge Replacement project.

description:
The Florida Department of Health (DOH) in St. Lucie contracts with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to disperse rental assistance funds under the Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS (HOPWA) grant. On July 10, 2018, the County and DOH entered into an MOU that allowed St. Lucie County to assist DOH with processing rental and mortgage payments, including rental security deposits, first and last month’s rent and late fees as authorized by the DOH on behalf of clients deemed eligible for HOPWA services. Utilizing St. Lucie County to process rental and mortgage payments rather than the state payment system reduces the timeframe for payments to be issued thus reducing the possibility a housing payment is delinquent.
DOH provides all required documents to facilitate payment and the County requests reimbursement from DOH on a monthly basis. Included in the reimbursement is a 7% administrative fee paid to St. Lucie County. All reporting requirements are completed by DOH.
Both parties wish to enter into a new memorandum of understanding, as the current agreement expires on June 30, 2025.

description:
The Board of County Commissioners have expressed the desire to increase public participation in the planning process and has recommended requiring community participation meetings for certain development applications, prior to the application being heard at a Public Hearing.
The proposed Ordinance ensures community participation in the development review process and establishes requirements for public participation meetings within the Land Development Code.
The proposed Ordinance also establishes that uses which are permitted as-of-right, which do not require special permits or variances, can proceed as a minor site plan and are therefore eligible for administrative approval. Also, the proposal seeks to allow development applications that are in substantial conformity with a Preliminary Planned Development Plan approved by the Board of County Commissioners to be processed as a minor site plan.
This proposal also recognizes the Live Local Act, which was approved by the Florida Legislature in 2023 (Ch. 2023-17, LOF) and further refined in 2024 (Ch. 2024-188, LOF) to increase the availability of affordable housing options. The Live Local Act preempts local regulations for certain housing developments in areas zoned for commercial, industrial, or mixed use and requires administrative approval and no further action by the Board. Therefore, this proposal looks to update our Land Development Code accordingly by allowing all Live Local projects meeting the provisions of Section 125.01055, F.S. to be reviewed and approved administratively through a Minor Site Plan.
Lastly, the proposal includes deleting provisions pertaining to Developments of Regional Impact that are no longer consistent with Florida Statutes and updating obsolete department names and titles in Sections 11.02.04, 11.02.06, 11.02.08 and 11.02.09.

description:
On August 20, 2019, the St. Lucie County Water and Sewer District approved a contract with CDM Smith, Inc. to perform professional engineering services for Regional Water and Wastewater Treatment Plant Designs (RFQ No. 19-037). One of the elements of the project is the preliminary design of a Low-Pressure Reverse Osmosis (LPRO) Water Treatment Plant (WTP) at the Taylor Dairy Road site. The WTP will utilize mineralized raw water from the Upper Floridan Aquifer (UFA) to be treated with the Low Pressure Reverse Osmosis (LPRO) permeable membranes, which creates a mineralized concentrate as a by-product of the LPRO membrane treatment process. The mineralized concentrate must be properly disposed of by the District.
On September 7, 2021 the Board approved Amendment No. 1 to the August 20, 2019 contract to authorize a pilot testing program for the LPRO Membrane Treatment process using a pilot unit to collect operation data to corroborate the results of the software projections and to produce permeate samples for further testing (blending testing, corrosivity studies, etc.).
On November 2, 2021, the Board approved Amendment No. 2 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. The scope of services in Amendment No. 2 provided for the Underground Injection Control Class I Injection Well Septic Design, Permitting and Bidding Services for disposal of the mineralized raw water concentrate.
On December 6, 2022, the Board approved Amendment No. 3 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. The scope of services in Amendment No. 3 provided for increased compensation and extended the completion date of the project for Raw Water Pipeline and Offsite Production Wells 2 and 4 for Taylor Dairy Road Service Area.
On May 16, 2023, the Board approved Amendment No. 4 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. This amendment increased the compensation and extended the completion date of the project whereby adding the Regional Water Treatment Plant Design for Taylor Dairy Road Service Area to the scope of services.
On July 2, 2024, the Board approved Amendment No. 5 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. This amendment increased the compensation and extended the completion date of the project whereby adding the SFWMD Water Supply Facilities Work Plan update.
Attached is a copy of a proposed Amendment No. 6 to the August 20, 2019 Contract. The scope of services for Amendment No. 6 provided for increasing the compensation and extending the completion date of the project whereby adding additional engineering and Construction Administration services. The proposed cost of the amendment is an amount not to exceed $702,575.00. The new contract total as amended by Amendment No. 6 is $5,805,777.70.

In August 2023, Forest Place, immediately south of Cortez Boulevard, was closed to vehicular traffic due to the failure of a 48-inch diameter metal stormwater culvert pipe under the roadway. Kimley-Horn Inc. was issued a work authorization to perform the Engineering and Design services on November 7, 2023. description:
The 5310 program provides operating and capital assistance to eligible recipients that operate/contract public transportation services for seniors and the disabled population. The grant funds are provided by the Federal Transit Administration to the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT). The FDOT awards and reimburses the recipient for eligible expenses. The funding award will be used for vehicle purchases which provide public transportation for seniors and persons with disabilities.
Annually, the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) apportions funding to states for the purpose of assisting with the transportation needs of older adults and people with disabilities when the transportation service provided is unavailable, insufficient or inappropriate to meet these needs. Funds are apportioned to direct recipients; for rural and small urban areas, this is the state Department of Transportation, while in large urban areas, a designated recipient is chosen by the governor. Direct recipients have flexibility in how they select sub-recipient projects for funding, but their decision process must be clearly noted in a state/program management plan. In Florida, the Florida Department of Transportation administers the program through a competitive application process. The selection process is formula-based, competitive and discretionary, and sub-recipients can include state or local government authorities, private non-profit organizations, and/or operators of public transportation.
In the case of St. Lucie County, the county's Transit Department applied for capital assistance and the FDOT awarded funding to assist with the capital purchases. The total project cost is an estimated $583,281.00, with a federal share of $466,624.00, an estimated $58,328.00 comes from the state, and the remaining $58,329.00 comes from local funds. The local match will be met using funds from the Public Transit Municipal Services Taxing Unit (MSTU) Fund #130-9910-599332-910000. This project is in accordance with the Strategic Plan Policy RI 5.2.3.

description:
Stormwater culverts direct and channel the flow of stormwater under driveways, roads, sidewalks and other obstructions and are an integral component of stormwater management. Culverts fail over time due to maintenance, environmental or installation issues. Culvert failure can lead to localized flooding which may impede safe conditions of ingress and egress for owners and residents of property in the affected area as well as the traveling public, visitors, emergency responders and other public service providers. Some culvert owners may lack the resources to pay for improvements and repairs.
In 2021, the Board established a voluntary program, Ordinance No. 21-004, to which eligible property owners can apply for and receive funding to improve or repair culverts and then repay this funding through the imposition of a non-ad valorem special assessment against the improved property collected in annual installments on the tax roll.
The attached Resolution No. 2025-92 is the Assessment Resolution as required by County's Ordinance No. 21-004, as amended. The purpose of this resolution relates to the imposition and collection of special assessments to fund stormwater culvert improvements within the Culvert 2025-03 MSBU, determine that real property therein will be specially benefitted, establish the method of assessing the cost of the improvements, approve the assessment roll, and provide an effective date.

description:
Attached is a copy of a bond resolution prepared by the County's bond counsel. The proceeds of the Series 2025A Bonds will be used for the acquisition and construction of certain capital improvements relating to the water and wastewater system (the "2025A Project") owned by the St. Lucie County Water and Sewer District (the "District"). The proceeds of the Series 2025B Bonds will be used for the acquisition and construction of certain capital improvements relating to the solid waste disposal system (the "2025B Project") owned and operated by the County. The Series 2025A Project and the Series 2025B Project shall be referred to herein collectively, as the "Projects".
THE INTERLOCAL AGREEMENT
Pursuant to County Ordinance No. 04-023, enacted on June 15, 2004 by the County, the County established the Water and Sewer District for the purpose of implementing the utility service requirements of the County's Comprehensive Plan. The District owns utility assets comprising of a water and wastewater (the "System"). In order to permit the County and the District to make the most efficient use of their respective powers, resources and capabilities, the County and the District entered into the attached Interlocal Agreement to provide for the acquisition and construction of the 2025A Project. Under the terms of the Interlocal Agreement, the County shall issue the Series 2025A Bonds to construct the 2025A Project. The 2025A Project financed with proceeds of the Series 2025A Bonds shall become a part of the System, owned and operated by the District. The Interlocal Agreement authorizes the transfer of available District System revenues on an annual basis to the County for payment of debt service on the 2025A Bond used to finance the 2025A Project. Unless extended by mutual agreement or as otherwise provided, the Interlocal Agreement shall expire upon full payment of the Series 2025 Bonds.
SECURITY FOR THE SERIES 2025 BONDS
General
The Series 2025 Bonds shall be payable from and secured by a covenant to budget and appropriate from the total revenues of the County derived from any source whatsoever, other than revenues generated from ad valorem taxation on real or personal property, and which are legally available to make the payments required in the Resolution (the "Non-Ad Valorem Revenues").
THE SERIES 2025 BONDS SHALL NOT BE OR CONSTITUTE GENERAL OBLIGATIONS OR INDEBTEDNESS OF THE COUNTY AS "BONDS" WITHIN THE MEANING OF ANY CONSTITUTIONAL OR STATUTORY PROVISION, BUT SHALL BE SPECIAL OBLIGATIONS OF THE COUNTY, PAYABLE SOLELY FROM AMOUNTS BUDGETED AND APPROPRIATED BY THE COUNTY FROM NON-AD VALOREM REVENUES IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE RESOLUTION. NO HOLDER OF ANY SERIES 2025 BOND SHALL EVER HAVE THE RIGHT TO COMPEL THE EXERCISE OF ANY AD VALOREM TAXING POWER TO PAY SUCH SERIES 2025 BOND, OR BE ENTITLED TO PAYMENT OF SUCH SERIES 2025 BOND FROM ANY MONEYS OF THE COUNTY EXCEPT FROM THE NON-AD VALOREM REVENUES IN THE MANNER AND TO THE EXTENT PROVIDED IN THE RESOLUTION.
Covenant to Budget and Appropriate
Pursuant to the Resolution, the County has covenanted and agreed to appropriate in its annual budget, by amendment, if necessary, from Non-Ad Valorem Revenues available in each Fiscal Year, amounts sufficient to pay principal of and interest on the Series 2025 Bonds when due. Such covenant and agreement on the part of the County to budget and appropriate such amounts of Non-Ad Valorem Revenues shall be cumulative to the extent not paid, and shall continue until such Non-Ad Valorem Revenues or other legally available funds in amounts sufficient to make all such required payments shall have been budgeted, appropriated and actually paid. Notwithstanding the foregoing covenant of the County, the County does not covenant to maintain any services or programs, now provided or maintained by the County, which generate Non-Ad Valorem Revenues.
Such covenant to budget and appropriate does not create any lien upon or pledge of such Non-Ad Valorem Revenues, nor does it preclude the County from pledging in the future its Non-Ad Valorem Revenues, nor does it require the County to levy and collect any particular Non-Ad Valorem Revenues, nor does it give any Series 2025 Bondholder a prior claim on the Non-Ad Valorem Revenues as opposed to claims of general creditors to the County. Such covenant to appropriate Non-Ad Valorem Revenues is subject in all respects to the payment of obligations secured by a pledge of such Non-Ad Valorem Revenues heretofore or hereafter entered into (including the payment of debt service on bonds and other debt instruments). However, the covenant to budget and appropriate in its general annual budget for the purposes and in the manner stated in the Resolution shall have the effect of making available for the payment of the Series 2025 Bonds, in the manner described in the Resolution, Non-Ad Valorem Revenues and placing on the County a positive duty to appropriate and budget, by amendment, if necessary, amounts sufficient to meet its obligations under the Resolution; subject, however, in all respects to the payment of services and programs which are for essential public purposes affecting the health, safety and welfare of the inhabitants of the County or which are legally mandated by applicable law.

description:
Reva Kay Health Solutions, DST ("Reva Kay") has agreed to sell a building located at 8881 South US Highway 1 and ancillary facilities to the County for $12,550,000.00. The property includes a 64,000 ± square foot building, including a 10,000 square foot distribution/warehouse area with dock high loading, and associated parking.
Appraisals
The County retained Callaway & Price, Inc. and Parrish & Edwards, Inc. to perform appraisals of the property. The results of those appraisals are as follows:
Callaway & Price, Inc. $12,000,000.00
Parrish & Edwards, Inc. $13,100,000.00
The appraisals are available for review in the Property Acquisition Division.
Contract for Sale and Purchase and Contract Addendum #1
A copy of the proposed Contract for Sale and Purchase is attached. A summary of the Contract follows:
As indicated in the Contract, the proposed purchase price for Reva Kay's property is $12,550,000.00. The County intends to perform the following due diligence actions:Contract to perform a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment
Obtain a Boundary Survey of the property
Obtain a Title Insurance Commitment showing good and marketable title
Also attached is a copy of Contract Addendum #1 which provides for the following documents to be attached to the Contract: the Certificate of Amendment to the Declaration of Condominium of Liberty Lane Condominium Association, Inc., the Sixth Amendment to Declaration of Condominium, the Certificate of Approval for Sale and Use, and the First Amendment to Lease Agreement.
SMEP Survey and Roofing Survey
As part of its due diligence, the County retained the firm of RGD Consulting Engineers to perform an inspection of the existing structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, fire protection systems and roof. A copy of the written report is attached to this Agenda Request.
Discussion
The proposed purchase is beneficial for County use, as it would allow the County to sell the Walton Road Annex and repurpose the Logistics Center and combine those existing operations into one facility. The site has a prominent location on US 1 next to Crosstown Parkway for enhanced citizen access. The Tax Collector has toured the site and is willing to contribute to the purchase and renovation of the site at an amount to be determined and the large parking area is attractive for Driver's Testing. Additionally, the County has been in the planning phase for a secondary data center, with expected construction costs estimated to be at approximately $10,000,000; however, this property has an existing data center that can be repurposed as a County data center, potentially saving the County millions in construction costs.
If the County determines to purchase the property, the County will initially use funds from the future Government Center project and/or General Fund reserves and replenish some of those funds after selling the Walton Road Annex, which is appraised at $4,200,000. The purchase of this facility would also free up the Logistics Center, which may be repurposed to reduce the footprint needed for the proposed new campus. The return on investment realized after Walton Road Annex and combining resources to one campus equates to approximately $250,000 annually, as both the Walton Road Annex and the Logistics Center carry Operations and Maintenance costs (O&M) of nearly $500,000 annually and both need substantial capital improvements in the coming years.

description:
In 2023, St. Lucie County entered a grant agreement with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) for two Resilient Florida Program grant awards. These awards fund the development of a St. Lucie County Regional Resilience Vulnerability Assessment (RVA) to analyze current and future flood impacts on critical assets throughout the County.
The Resilient Florida Program was created by State Statute 380.093, F.S. The Program includes the requirement for the Florida Flood Hub (USF) to develop a statewide vulnerability assessment every five years, and FDEP to develop an annual Sea Level Rise and Flooding Resilience Plan.
In addition, the Statute created planning and infrastructure grant funding and developed specific criteria for conducting all vulnerability assessments, with the goal of having all counties conduct local / regional vulnerability assessments that align with the statewide effort.
This Draft St. Lucie County Regional Resilience Vulnerability Assessment was prepared based on the criteria and standards set forth in state law and provides the necessary data and corresponding analyses for the County and cities to be eligible for future Resilient Florida infrastructure funding.
The Draft SLC RVA assesses flooding impacts on critical assets – generally those local and regional assets that are considered critical to the health and safety of residents, the vitality of the economy and the integrity of the environment. Critical assets are defined in 4 categories within Section 380.093, F.S.: Transportation and Evacuation Routes; Critical Infrastructure; Community and Emergency Facilities; and Natural, Cultural and Historic Resources.
This project included interactive community presentations, and regular meetings of the St. Lucie Resilience Steering Committee which played a vital role in shaping the RVA. The Steering Committee represented various St. Lucie County, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce and St. Lucie Village departments, as well as local and regional agency staff.
The RVA represents the first step in developing a comprehensive approach to adapt to and mitigate the effects of extreme and disruptive flood events and is another tool that can be used in planning for a thriving and resilient community now and in the future.
This project furthers the goals and objectives of the St. Lucie County Strategic Plan, particularly: ES 6.1.1 – Develop a St. Lucie Regional Resilience Plan that addresses natural resources, citizen safety and well-being; RI 5.3.4 – Actively seek resilience and other funding opportunities to increase resiliency and sustainability of infrastructure and facilities; and HS 4.4.3 – Ensure that public infrastructure is well maintained, resilient and prepared to undergo the challenges of an emergency event.

description:
St. Lucie County Planning & Development Services and the St. Lucie Economic Development Council (EDC) are presenting this item to provide the Board of County Commissioners with information on the County's existing Economic Development (Targeted Industry) Incentives.
Presently, the County has three performance-based, monetary incentives available to new or expanding businesses that fall within the County's Targeted Industry list. These include the following:
Job Growth Investment Grant (JGIG) - Pays an expanding or relocating targeted industry per job created over 1–5 years. Based on the Company's average annual wages, the number of jobs created, number of St. Lucie County residents hired, and the use of local contractors for construction. The company must create a minimum of 10 new jobs, with an average wage of at least 107% of the County's average wage. Currently, 107% equals $25.52.
Requires an annual report to the County.
In 2015, new standards were adopted to encourage the expansion of locally-owned and operated small businesses.
Impact Fee Mitigation- Mitigates up to 100% of the County Impact Fees Due Based on the number of jobs created and the average annual wage.
Requires an annual report to the County.
Multiple different programs to become eligible Program One - Higher wage, plus the company must provide a benefits package to their employees ($3,500 - $7,500 per job created)
Program Two - Higher Capital Investment ($10M - $15M = 40% Impact Fee Mitigation, $15M - $20M = 50% Impact Fee Mitigation, $20M+ = 60% Impact Fee Mitigation)
Ad Valorem Tax Exemption - Section 196.1995, F.S. requires County voters to authorize exemptions. Voters approved in 1992, 2002, 2012, and 2022. Exempts an expanding or relocating targeted industry from the St. Lucie County portion of the Ad Valorem millage on a declining scale for a maximum of 10 years.Based on the average annual wages and the number of jobs created and their capital investment.
Applies to new or expanding businesses in SLC that make a positive contribution to the County's economy.
Requires an annual report to the County.
Items for the BOCC's consideration are as follows:
•Increase the average hourly wage above the current 107% ($25.52)
•110% ($26.24), 115% ($27.43), 120% ($28.62)
•Use or revise the scoring matrix to allocate points based on desired outcomes (higher wages, # of jobs, capital investment)
•Establish bonuses for certain Targeted Industry categories
•Establish sunset provisions for initial incentive offers
•Establish deadlines for construction of the project and creation of the committed jobs in the Job Growth Investment Grant (JGIG)
•Establish criteria for when a company can request amendments to approved agreements
•Establish Clawback provisions for Ad Valorem Tax Abatement if the Company fails to meet their commitments.

description:
On March 1, 2024, through an interlocal agreement with the St. Lucie County Sheriff, the County assumed management and oversight of inmate medical services at the St. Lucie County Jail. In order to assist in advising the County and Sheriff on inmate medical issues, St. Lucie County entered into a contract for Consulting/Professional Services with Dr. Roger Nicosia, Jr., D.O. Staff is seeking approval of new contract wtih Dr. Nicosia’s for one-year with an additional one-year renewal option.
Consulting services include:
Provide consultation on inmate medical matters on an as-needed basis.
Perform utilization review of medical care for inmates.
Assist the County in decreasing medical expenses, including but not limited to:Preventing inmate hospitalizations by identifying how to treat problems early while still in jail.
Facilitating appropriately rapid discharges from the hospital to jail.
Lowering the cost of outpatient testing and other therapies by suggesting competitive contracts.
As a result of Dr. Nicosia's services, the amount of time that inmates spend in the hospital has been reduced, thereby reducing the medical bills and the number of hours that deputies have to spend guarding inmates in the hospital, which translates into reduced deputy overtime expenditures and the ability to redeploy the deputies to other necessary functions. We estimate that getting inmates out of the hospital more quickly translates to a yearly deputy overtime savings of at least $80,000.00.

description:
The Environmental Resources Department (ERD) is working toward the goal of acquiring land adjacent to Turnpike Feeder Road. The area is identified in the 2004 SLC Native Habitat Inventory as an “A” based on high quality native habitat coverage and potential for rare and endemic species.
ERD was contacted by the property owner to see if the County had interest in acquiring the subject parcels. ERD requested the Property Acquisition Division obtain an appraisal of the parcels.
The County presented a Contract for Sale and Purchase to Friends I, LLC for $1,495,000, which is an average of two appraisals obtained by the Property Acquisition Division from Parrish & Edwards, Inc and Boyle & Drake, Inc.
On March 20, 2025, the St. Lucie County Land Acquisition Selection Committee (LASC) reviewed the two parcels owned by Friends I, LLC (Agenda Item 7.A, LASC Parcel Number ST 211). While there was not a quorum, the members present recommended that the County pursue acquisition of the subject parcels.
The property consists of two parcels, with a combined area of +/- 16.97 acres, which are bifurcated by Turnpike Feeder Road, and located approximately one-third (1/3) of a mile south of the Indian River County border. The west parcel is bounded by vacant wooded parcels to the north and west, by Turnpike Feeder Road to the east, and by a mobile home to the south. The east parcel is bounded by U.S. 1 to the east, Turnpike Feeder Road to the west, a mobile home park to the south, and by a vacant wooded parcel to the north. The parcels are currently vacant and unmaintained.
On January 11, 2022, the Board of County Commissioners granted developmental approval for a Preliminary Site Plan and Wetland Waiver for a project to be known as MMR RV Park.
An Environmental Assessment, conducted by EW Consultants in May 2021, concluded most of the site consists of native habitats with minimal disturbed/altered areas. Native upland habitat comprises 65% of the total site and native wetland habitat makes up 32% of the total site area. In general, the east parcel of the project site has a large willow slough that is oriented northwest-to-southeast in the center with pine flatwood uplands on either side. Mixed oak scrub upland habitat exists adjacent to U.S. 1. Disturbed areas on the eastern parcel include a stand of Brazilian pepper trees in the southern portion and a mowed strip adjacent to U.S. 1. The western parcel contains a willow slough in the northern portion which is connected to the willow slough east of Turnpike Feeder Road via a culvert. A large, high-quality wet prairie exists in the center of the western parcel, as does a smaller wet prairie in the southwestern portion of the western parcel. Uplands within the western parcel consist of native pine flatwoods.
The site potentially provides foraging and nesting habitat for a variety of state and federally listed wildlife species, including a myriad of wading birds such as wood stork, roseate spoonbill, sandhill cranes, various ibis, and herons; the federally protected scrub-jay; and the state-protected gopher tortoise. The presence of scrub habitat adjacent to U.S. 1 and on parcels east of the project site initiated a formal scrub-jay survey conducted by environmental consultants in accordance with the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service guidelines in March of 2021. This survey resulted in no scrub-jays observed or heard during the survey event. The sandy uplands serve as potential burrowing and foraging habitat for gopher tortoise. Several potentially occupied burrows were observed within the project site’s upland areas. Lastly, it should be noted that this region is known to host two federally endangered plant species; the four-petal pawpaw and Lakela’s mint, have been documented on nearby sites east of U.S. 1. Preliminary observations were made for both species, neither of which were identified at the time. A systematic survey for both species should be conducted within the scrub portion of the project site.
The primary purpose for ERD pursuing this acquisition is to protect high-quality native habitat within a critical scrub jay corridor. Future restoration will include exotic removal, prescribed fire, and potentially reintroduction of Lakela’s mint.
Attached for your review and approval is the signed Contract for Sale and Purchase.
