description:
On February 1, 2020, St. Lucie County Land Acquisition Selection Committee (LASC) reviewed the Jenkins Road Parcels (LASC Property ST205) located South of Jenkins Road and Edwards Road intersection along Ten Mile Creek. ST205 is currently listed for sale and staff has received confirmation that the property owner is a willing seller.
ST205 is approximately 39 acres and consists of 9 acres of hydric hammock, 8 acres of floodplain forest, including +/- 2,000 LF of shoreline along Ten Mile Creek, as well as 22 acres of disturbed upland habitat/fallow citrus grove. Through consideration of possible advantages to the future Jenkins Road extension, both in right-of-way and stormwater, as well as positive aspects associated with environmental preservation, water quality, connectivity, recreation, and resiliency, the committee unanimously ranked ST205 as a top tier "A" site and recommended that the Board pursue acquisition through a collaborative funding approach between Public Works and the Environmentally Significant Lands Program.
On February 23, 2021, the Board of County Commissioners approved the acquisition of the 39-acre Jenkins Road parcels with a collaborative funding approach for acquisition costs using Roadway Impact Fees to plan for the future Jenkins Road Extension Project and the Environmentally Significant Lands Program.
The Jenkins Road Extension from Midway Road to Orange Avenue is currently under analysis as part of a Project Development and Environmental (PD&E) study. The St. Lucie County Transportation Planning Organization (TPO) Smart Moves 2045 Long Range Transportation Plan lists Jenkins Road as a “Preliminary Roadway Deficiency” which indicates the corridor will experience congestion by 2045. Indeed, significant development along Jenkins Road from Edwards Road to Orange Avenue will continue to drive the need for a 4-lane divided section. The Jenkins Road PD&E project is funded by a partnership between St. Lucie County and the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT), using the transportation regional incentive program (TRIP) grant to pay for the non-local dollar share of the effort. The PD&E study is expected to be complete in late 2026.
Removing the “missing link” along the corridor from Glades Cut Off Road to Edwards Road will further serve the needs of the community by providing an alternate north-south connection between Midway Road and Orange Avenue.
The entire Jenkins Road corridor from Midway Road to Orange Avenue is intended to serve as a reliever for the Kings Highway corridor.
The segment of Jenkins Road from Glades Cut Off Road to Orange Avenue is a critical piece of infrastructure that will need supporting land to accommodate stormwater run-off from the roadway. The purchase of the 39 acres will provide a unique opportunity to acquire land for the stormwater needs of the Jenkins Road extension. This acquisition will minimize potential impacts to other properties along the corridor as the design analysis moves forward.
On April 23, 2024, the Board of County Commissioners accepted Grant Agreement Number WRP04 from the State of Florida Department of Environmental Protection under the Wetland Restoration and Protection grant program. The primary purpose of the grant funding is for protection of the wetland habitats and the floodplain, with the ability for future restoration and stormwater for water quality improvements in the region.
The proposed project is for acquisition, restoration and perpetual preservation of 39 acres of vacant land, including approximately 1,163 feet of Ten Mile Creek shoreline in St. Lucie County. Ten Mile Creek is a tributary of the St. Lucie River, which is the largest tropical riverine system in the United States and is the largest freshwater contributor to the Indian River Lagoon. As such, these waters serve as essential refuges for a multitude of fish species which utilize the riverine oxbows as nursery habitat as exemplified by the research completed by Dr. Grant Gilmore. The subject property contains approximately 16 acres of historic floodplain wetlands which are vital to the region for water quality, natural groundwater recharge, natural attenuation and storage, in addition to providing substantial habitat for a multitude of native species including state and federally listed species. In addition to the preservation of the natural communities onsite, St. Lucie County plans to reserve a future stormwater retention and treatment area within the disturbed portions of the site for additional water quality improvement and regional flood control, which will also provide additional wildlife habitat with the inclusion of native plantings and littoral zones for the future Jenkins Road project. If acquired, St. Lucie County restoration efforts including invasive exotic species control, hydrologic restoration of historic oxbows, and native replanting as needed.
The County had two appraisals prepared, per County policy, for properties estimated to exceed $500,000; Fuller-Armfield-Wagner fair market value was $3,750,000 and Callaway and Price's value was $3,975,000. Property Acquisition presented an offer of $3,862,500. M. T. Land made a counter-offer of $4,200,000.
The County requested Fuller-Armfield Wagner and Callaway & Price review the counter-offer to determine if it was in their range of value. Fuller-Armfield-Wagner and Callaway & Price indicated $4,200,000 was within their range of value and advised County staff to present a counter-offer of $4,200,000. A counter-offer was presented and accepted by M. T. Land. The signed Contract for Sale and Purchase is attached for your review and approval.

description:
The Housing Finance Authority of St. Lucie is proposing the issuance of Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds, in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $21,500,000.00 to provide financing for the rehabilitation of residential rental units known as Madison Cay Apartments, consisting of approximately 132 units located at 1655 N. 29th Street, Fort Pierce, FL 34947 to be occupied by persons of low to moderate income and owned and operated by Madison Cay Preservation, LTD, a Florida limited partnership, and/or its affiliates.

The St. Lucie County Housing Finance Authority (HFA) was established by the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners on July 22, 1980, via Ordinance No. 80-3 in accordance with the Florida Housing Finance Authority Law, Florida Statute 159-601, Part IV.
A local housing finance authority (HFA) is an agency or organization established at the local level, typically by a city, county, or regional government, with the primary goal of providing affordable housing options and promoting homeownership within the community. HFAs operate under state and federal regulations and are authorized to issue tax-exempt bonds or use other financial mechanisms to fund affordable housing initiatives.
Note that no county general funds are a part of this transaction.

description:
Pursuant to Section 288.9961(4)(b), Florida Statutes, the Office of Broadband is directed to build and facilitate local technology planning teams. On November 15, 2022, the Board created the Local Technology Planning Team (LTPT) for St. Lucie County as an advisory board. At the suggestion of the Office of Broadband representative and after conversations with other entities, it is recommended that the County clarify the purpose and function of the LTPT, specifically that the team does not have any decision-making authority, but rather serves in a fact-finding capacity.
This amendment amends and restates Resolution No. 2022-223 to remove language designating the LTPT as an advisory board and clarifies that the primary function of the team is to collaborate with community members, supporting the advancement of broadband service and infrastructure in St. Lucie County by gathering relevant data and providing it to the community and stakeholders. This amendment clarifies that the LTPT is not an advisory or recommending board, but rather gathers and disseminates information to the community. As such, this team is not subject to Florida Sunshine law and will be conducted informally in St. Lucie County as is done around the state.

description:
The Transit Department is seeking grant funding through the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Section 5339 Bus and Bus Facilities Competitive Grant for a Transit Operations and Maintenance (O&M) Facility. The proposed Transit O&M Facility will provide infrastructure to operate a modern public transit system which can accommodate repair of vehicles, provide fueling stations, and a bus wash. The Transit O&M Facility will provide a location for administration, maintenance and onsite storage to improve operational and safety efficiencies. This project supports improved service levels for residents and employment-generating businesses. The construction of a consolidated facility will provide cost-effective solutions to the current operations. Today, all major vehicle maintenance is currently outsourced, which is not efficient for the operations or cost-effective for part replacement and repairs. A centralized Transit O&M facility will allow public transportation programs in St. Lucie County to successfully evolve from a basic rural-suburban transit service to a comprehensive, modern public transportation system and reduce traffic congestion.
The total project cost is estimated at $35 million. The Transit Department would like to submit a competitive grant application for the FTA FFY 25 Section 5339 Bus and Bus Facilities Grant, which requires a 20% match of $7 million. The Transit Department currently has capital funds allocated for the Transit O&M Facility. The Transit Department will also use the value of the property, which is approximately $2 million, as a soft match for the grant. The FTA requires a resolution of support for the project and confirmation of matching funds available for the grant. This project is in accordance with Strategic Plan Policy RI5.2.3.

description:
In October 1998, the County acquired property from Murphy White Dairy for a purchase price of $1,028,000.00. A copy of a map locating the County property is attached as Exhibit "A". The property was an acquisition target and was ranked by the Land Acquisition Selection Committee as an "A" site. The County acquired the property using funds from the County's Environmental Lands Bond Program ($634,673.00) and a grant from Florida Communities Trust (“FCT”) ($631,885.00; FCT #96-017-P74). The site features one of the largest strands of pristine pine flatwoods in western St. Lucie County and is a destination on the State's Great Florida Birding Trail. The County designated the property "Pinelands Preserve".
When the County acquires property it is the County's standard practice to have an outside title agent examine title and provide title insurance to the County. The County retained a title agent and purchased title insurance when it bought the Pinelands Preserve property. Access to the Pinelands Preserve was through a 1991 Easement from Okeechobee Road approximately 2 1⁄3 miles in length (“1991 Easement”). The title insurance policy insured access to the Pinelands Preserve through this 1991 Easement.
On April 4, 2019, more than 20 years from the date the County acquired the Pinelands Preserve, a neighbor ("Plaintiff") sued the County (and another neighbor) seeking a declaration that the County could not use the 1991 Easement for either private or public access (“First Lawsuit”). Upon being served with the Complaint, the County forwarded the Complaint to the title insurance company with a request that the title insurance company defend the County under the terms of the title insurance policy. The title insurance company agreed to defend the County under a "reservation of rights" and retained an attorney to defend the County in the First Lawsuit.
A hearing was held on October 20, 2021, on the parties' Motions for Summary Judgment. On October 26, 2021, the Court entered the attached Order which is designated as Exhibit "B" (“2021 Order”). The 2021 Order held that the 1991 easement was invalid and prevented the County from using the 1991 easement to access the Pinelands Preserve. The Court deferred ruling on the issue as to whether the County is entitled to a prescriptive easement (an easement acquired by virtue of continuous public use) for the public to access the Preserve for the required 20-year prescriptive period.
The attorney representing the County in the First Lawsuit believed there were appealable issues and recommended that the County appeal the 2021 Order. The title insurance company agreed to fund the appeal under the terms of the policy. On November 16, 2021, the Board authorized the filing of a notice of appeal based on the recommendation. On January 3, 2025, the Court entered a Final Judgment in favor of the Plaintiff regarding the County's Prescriptive Easement Claims finding that the County was not entitled to a prescriptive easement over the property (“2025 Order”). The 2021 Order and 2025 Order prevents the County from using the 1991 Easement for private or public access.
The Plaintiff also filed a separate lawsuit against the County alleging tort and inverse condemnation claims (“Second Lawsuit”). That lawsuit is pending.
Alternate Access on SFWMD Parcel
Due to the uncertainty surrounding the County's right to use the 1991 Easement, the County entered into a temporary access agreement with South Florida Water Management District (“District”) to construct and use alternate vehicular access improvements located within a 50' Access Parcel easement extending southward from SR 70 approximately 2,400 linear feet to a 20' x 50' Parking Lot for a term of 5 years. If the County were to use this temporary access, it would require that the County design and permit pedestrian and equestrian access improvements to the Preserve from the parking lot, approximately 9,800 linear feet (~1.86 mi), to facilitate utilizing the Preserve for the benefit of County residents.
County staff continued to meet with District staff to discuss different forms of access. Currently, District staff, through its Executive Director, has agreed to recommend that the District Board allow the County to use the District property for permanent access. Hopefully, this item will go to the District Board in June for approval of the shared public access concept. County staff is scheduling coordination meetings with District project design staff to allow for shared public access to the reservoir and Pinelands Preserve. The District, through its staff, has indicated it will support allowing the County and the public to utilize the District's access at least to the location of the District's reservoir. From that point, the County may be required to construct a connection for public access from the District's access to the County Preserve at the County’s expense.
Proposed Settlement Agreements
County staff has been involved in settlement discussions with the various parties to see if a resolution of the litigation claims can be achieved. On March 27, 2025, the Plaintiff and County reached a written settlement agreement ("Global Litigation Settlement"), and the County and title company reached a separate written settlement agreement ("Title Company Settlement"), copies of which are attached. Both settlements are subject to Board approval. A summary of the settlement agreements follows:
Global Litigation Settlement
County agrees that it will not access Pinelands Preserve through Plaintiff’s property, including through the 1991 Easement.
County agrees to release the 1991 Easement, a 1988 easement previously given to Murphy White Dairy over the west 50’ of Plaintiff’s property and across the north 50’ of a neighboring property which has since been sold to Plaintiff, and a 1995 Amendment to a 1955 Easement which ratified the 1991 Easement (collectively the "Released Easements"). The County also agrees to promptly and diligently procure from FCT a release of any interest in the Released Easements and a duly executed acknowledgment of and consent to the County's release of Released Easements. At the option of Plaintiff, in the event the County fails to record its releases of the Released Easements and/or procure FCT's release of the Released Easements the Global Settlement Agreement may be terminated.
The settlement is conditioned upon County approving a modification to a mining permit (attached as Exhibit A to the Proposed Global Litigation Settlement) and associated conditional use permit (attached as Exhibit A to the Proposed Global Litigation Settlement) to remove conditions limiting the delivery of excavated soils to the State Road 70 widening project which has been completed. Staff has reviewed the proposed modifications and has determined the modification is appropriate and in compliance with the County Land Development Code. Upon receipt of a formal request for modification of the Mining Permit and Conditional Use Permit from Plaintiff, Staff shall schedule the modifications described above for the required public hearings and shall recommend approval of the said modifications to the Commission within ninety (90) days of the effective date of the Global Litigation Settlement (June 25, 2025). At the option of Plaintiff, if the modifications to the mining permit and conditional use permit are not approved by the Commission by June 25, 2025, the Global Settlement Agreement may be terminated.
The settlement is conditioned upon the administrative approval of a Minor Site Plan relating to a property affiliated with Plaintiff. The Minor Site Plan is currently pending applicant revisions. The Site Plan also identifies multiple access points along Sapp Road which require applicant to construct paved access. Applicant desires to reduce the requirement for the paving of Sapp Road to its southernmost access point. Within thirty (30) days of submission of the revised Minor Site Plan and Site Development Permit application for the Sapp Road construction which corrects all deficiencies identified by the County and which is consistent with the County Land Development Code and Comprehensive Plan provisions, the County shall administratively approve the corrected Minor Site Plan and issue the Site Development Permit for the Sapp Road construction. At the option of Plaintiff, if the Site Development Permit for the Sapp Road Construction and the TDC Minor Site Plan are not issued by the County within sixty (60) days of the effective date of the Global Settlement Agreement (May 26, 2025), the Global Settlement Agreement may be terminated. The County also agrees to promptly and diligently conduct reviews of submitted, complete applications for the Site Development Permit (for onsite improvements) and Building Permit for the same property to the extent within its authority
Upon fulfillment by the County of the terms and conditions of the Global Settlement Agreement, all claims and appeals between the parties are dismissed with prejudice and with each party bearing its own fees and costs.
The parties have agreed to abate all litigation proceedings in the First and Second Lawsuits for 120 days.
The Global Litigation Settlement is contingent upon the execution of the Title Company Settlement.
Title Company SettlementIn exchange for $400,000 paid by the title company to the County within 10 business days of all claims and appeals in the First and Second Lawsuits being dismissed with prejudice, the County agrees to release the title company from any claims relating to lack of access through the 1991 Easement.
The Title Company Settlement is contingent upon the execution of the Global Litigation Settlement.
Discussion
The First Lawsuit resulted in two court orders which have effectively invalidated the County’s private and public access to the Pinelands Preserve through the Plaintiff’s property. Based on the recommendation of outside counsel, the County has filed an appeal in the First Lawsuit. The title company contends that it is not obligated to pay for the cost of the appeal. Additionally, any success on appeal will likely result in the County obtaining private access. The County, however, requires public access as a condition of the FTC grant which helped fund the purchase of the Pinelands Preserve. Therefore, the expense of litigation in the appeal would likely not result in the public access needed. The parties are also actively litigating the Second Lawsuit, the continuation of which will result in substantial additional time and legal expenses. Plaintiff has indicated that it will not agree to allow County any form of access through its property. Thus, continuation of the litigation in the First and Second Lawsuit would at best result in private access at a substantial cost to the County.
A resolution of the First and Second Lawsuit without a resolution of the title claim would result in the County waiving its rights under the title insurance policy. Therefore, it is in the County’s best interest to simultaneously settle its claim with the title company to be able to reach a global settlement in the First and Second Lawsuits. The title company will also not settle the County’s claim without a global resolution of the pending litigation.
Although the County could litigate against the title company to try to obtain the full limits under the policy, the cost to the County of litigation combined with the risk of the title company prevailing in such litigation weigh in favor of an immediate monetary settlement. The monetary settlement would provide the County with funds to cover its out-of-pocket expenses to date as well as funds to go towards construction of public access through the District property.
A risk exists that the District could decline to allow the County public access through its property. However, if the County fails to resolve the litigation and title claim now, there is a strong chance that future resolution may not be an option, or the monetary settlement could be significantly reduced as the title company incurs more legal expenses. Discussions between County and the District staff have been positive and the District staff has indicated it will support the County’s request for permanent public access to the Pinelands Preserve through the District property and recommend such access to the District Board. Thus, although a risk exists that the County may not have public access to the Pinelands Preserve, failure to enter into the settlement agreements now could also result in no public access, substantial legal costs to the County, and no monetary settlement from the title company.
The attorneys representing the County in the various lawsuits have recommended that the County approve the Global Litigation Settlement and the Title Company Settlement.
Based on the foregoing, the staff recommends approval of the Global Litigation Settlement and the Title Company Settlement.

description:
Historically, St. Lucie County has been responsible for paying for inmate medical expenses incurred outside the jail, such as hospital treatment and specialist office visits. St. Lucie County's outside-the-jail inmate medical expenses have been higher than other counties with similar jail populations and in the past few years these medical expenses have risen sharply, approaching a level that would have been unsustainable.
In an effort to reduce inmate medical expenses, the County proposed legislation that would cap payments to inmate medical providers at 110% of the Medicare reimbursement rate. The County also sought to partner with a different inmate medical provider inside-the-jail who would help reduce offsite trips to the hospital and provide other efficiencies.
This presentation provides an update on the expense reductions from HB 1023 and other savings made possible through the County's partnership with its new inmate medical provider, NaphCare. The presentation also provides some examples of efficiencies and continuity of care benefits that have helped to further reduce total inmate medical expenses.

description:
Chapter 50, Florida Statutes, Legal and Official Advertisements, provides that, effective January 1, 2023, a governmental agency may publish certain statutorily required legal advertisements, publications, or notices on the publicly accessible website of the county in which it lies if doing so would cost less than publishing legal notices in a newspaper. The County has determined that the cost of publishing legal advertisements and public notices on the publicly accessible website of the county is less than the cost of publishing legal advertisements and public notices in a newspaper.
The proposed ordinance creates a new Section 1-12 of the St. Lucie County Code to allow advertisements, publications or notices that are currently required or permitted to be published in a newspaper by county ordinance, resolution, board policy, or administrative procedure, or otherwise, to instead be published on the County’s official website or other private website designated by the County for the publication of legal notices and advertisements that is accessible to the public via the Internet, pursuant to Chapter 50, Florida Statutes.
The proposed ordinance serves a public purpose by reducing the costs of County legal advertisements and public notices and by making County legal advertisements and public notices more accessible to the public.

description:
On October 2, 2022, responses to RFP No. 23-002, were opened. Six proposals were received; 371 companies were notified, and 60 RFP documents were distributed.
The purpose of this RFP was for qualified providers of ERP software to provide a robust solution to replace its 20+ year-old Banner System that currently provides support for the financial management, utility billing and HR/Payroll business processes.
On February 27, 2023, the following proposers were chosen to provide onsite demonstrations of their proposed solutions:Collaborative Solutions - Workday
Tyler Technologies, Inc.- EERP Powered by Munis
Highstreet, LLC - Oracle Fusion (SaaS)
From April 25, 2023, through May 10, 2025, onsite demos were held for each proposer to demonstrate their proposed solution.
On May 15, 2023, the selection committee met to evaluate, score and rank the three proposers but made the recommendation that site-visits were necessary. Site visits were scheduled with the City of Sarasota for the Workday solution, the City of Pinellas Park for the Munis solution and the City of Hollywood for the Oracle solution.
After the site visits were over, the selection committee met and decided that Highstreet, LLC, did not meet the County's minimum requirements and removed them from further consideration.
On January 10, 2024, the selection committee met to evaluate, score and rank the two proposals; the final score and ranking is included in Attachment A.
The County is entering into the contract negotiations phase, which resulted in the selection of a Software As A Service (SAAS) Agreement with Tyler Technologies. We are seeking the approval of the SAAS agreement which includes three years of software support, professional services and travel with Tyler Technologies with a contract total of $4,933,133 over a three-year period. We will also be requesting the approval of the Fourth Amendment to the advisory services agreement C22-0-201 with Plante Moran with a contract total of $986,400 and the approval of three full-time employees (FTEs) at an annual cost of $310,000. The three positions being requested are: two Application Administrators I at a pay grade of G204 and one Project Manager I at a pay grade of G205. The roles of these three positions include overseeing database integrity and database backups, application performance, solving application problems, and installing application upgrades. These positions will report to the IT Manager or designee. The additional funding needed to fulfill the one-time fees for implementation of the new ERP is $559,896.00. The recurring costs which will need to be added to Information Technologies' operating costs for FY25 are software support in the amount of $495,101 and the cost of the three positions in the amount of $310,000.00. However, since we are part way through FY25, only $155,000.00 is needed for the new positions. Funding will also need to be added to FY26 and FY27 for the recurring cost of the software support and all approved positions.

description:
On December 11, 2024, responses to RFQ No. 24-099, Homeless Veterans Shelter Operator, were opened. Three proposals were received; 37 companies were notified, and 34 RFP documents were distributed.
The purpose of this RFQ is for an eligible organization to provide management and operation services for the homeless veteran’s shelter located at 3455 N. US Highway 1 in Fort Pierce. The purchase of the shelter was funded in part by a State of Florida legislative appropriation from the FY23 budget.
The need for a homeless shelter specifically tailored to veterans arises from the distinct circumstances and challenges veterans often face upon returning to civilian life. Many veterans struggle with physical and mental health issues, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which can make it difficult to maintain stable housing. Additionally, the transition from military to civilian life can be challenging, leading to unemployment, financial difficulties, and social isolation. A homeless shelter for veterans can help our community by providing support, camaraderie, peer support, respect, dignity, and ultimately community integration. Veterans who can secure stable housing are more likely to become successful in reintegrating into civilian life, maintain steady employment, and experience improved mental and physical health.
By providing shelter and support services, the project seeks to reduce the number of veteran individuals and families experiencing homelessness in the community, ultimately working towards the goal of ending homelessness. The project aims to enhance the quality of life for homeless veteran individuals and families by providing a safe and supportive environment where they can access the resources, they need to rebuild their lives. In addition, the project seeks to promote community integration by fostering positive relationships between shelter guests and the surrounding community, encouraging shelter guests to participate in community activities and programs.
On February 25, 2025, the selection committee evaluated and ranked the proposals that were received. The committee members' scores and ranking for each firm are provided in Attachment A.
The short-listed firms in order of ranking are as follows:
Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council, Inc.
RiteLife Services, Inc.

attachments.name: Ex A to Resolution 25-063_Traffic Calming Policy

description:
The St. Lucie County Traffic Calming Policy addresses increasing traffic congestion, safety concerns, and livability issues in local neighborhoods. The policy outlines procedures to request, evaluate, and implement traffic-calming measures on County-managed roadways, ensuring a balanced approach to improving safety, reducing vehicle speeds, and enhancing quality of life.
Purpose and Goals
1. Reduce traffic speeds and improve safety for all road users.
2. Maintain neighborhood livability by mitigating noise, pollution, and traffic volume.
3. Engage the community in identifying and addressing traffic issues.
4. Implement cost-effective and consistent solutions while preserving emergency access.
Eligibility Criteria
Traffic-calming measures are eligible for local and collector roads in residential areas meeting specific conditions, such as:
1. Speed and volume thresholds, visibility, and accident history.
2. Exclusions: arterial roads, emergency routes, and roads not meeting support requirements (e.g., 75% resident approval within the affected area).
Traffic Calming Measures
Based upon the Eligibility Criteria, the policy will only consider implementing the following:
1. Physical Devices: Speed humps, speed tables.
2. Non-Physical Measures: Speed limit reduction, signage, pavement markings, radar speed feedback signs.
3. Education and Enforcement: Awareness campaigns, neighborhood flyers, variable message signs and law enforcement.
Implementation Process
1. Request Submission: Initiated by a neighborhood representative with a 75% support petition.
2. Review and Study: County staff conduct traffic studies and eligibility assessments.
3. Public Meeting: Residents provide feedback on conceptual plans.
4. Approval: Preliminary plan requires 75% resident approval and County Commission authorization.
5. Implementation and Evaluation: Final design, installation, and one-year post-implementation evaluation.
Funding and ModificationResidents or neighborhood associations may contribute to non-standard enhancements. Traffic-calming measures can be altered or removed based on changing conditions or resident petitions, subject to County Commission approval. Removal initiated by residents will be assessed to the properties within the Impact Area Boundary. Once removed, no petition for re-installation of traffic-calming shall be permitted for a period of five (5) years.

attachments.name: Old Dixie Bridge over Taylor Creek white paper - request to consider alternate

description:
In 2017, Hurricane Irma brought record rainfall to the northern part of St. Lucie County, overwhelming the natural systems and causing significant flooding. Inspections immediately after the storm showed that the flows in Taylor Creek during this event eroded embankments and undermined the approach slabs to the Old Dixie Highway bridge. The bridge was subsequently closed to traffic in January of 2018 due to safety concerns.
A damage assessment was performed and the resultant cost to repair the bridge was approximately $800,000 (2018 dollars). At the time, the budget for replacement with a new bridge was estimated to be $2,600,000 (2018 dollars). Due to the age of the bridge, constructed in 1962, and the lack of sidewalk or shoulder on the deck of the bridge, Public Works recommended, and the Board authorized a contract on March 23, 2021 in the amount of $688,937, to design the replacement of the bridge with an entirely new structure. The bridge project is identified as a priority in the infrastructure sales tax project list.
Several changes in the vicinity of the project since the time of the original consideration to replace the bridge are now underway and directly impact the value of replacing the bridge. The FDOT north causeway project will significantly decrease traffic on Old Dixie Highway and the port expansion creates uncertainty for multimodal configurations, connections and locations south of the bridge.
In the 2021 Bridge Inspection Report prepared by FDOT, it was noted that the undermining of the south approach was repaired by the contractors for the Brightline rail expansion project. Subsequent inspection reports have shown little to no change in the condition of the bridge, with the last inspection performed in 2024. The bridge is listed in “good to adequate” condition based on the latest FDOT inspection.
Current costs for replacement of the structure have escalated to nearly $4,000,000 (2024 dollars). A recent cost estimate to complete the repairs to the substructure of the bridge by filling the undermined slabs and other recommended repairs approximates the costs at $1,500,000 (2024 dollars).
As the costs of the replacement project have greatly increased, the bridge is expected to provide limited mobility and multimodal access, and there are uncertain configurations south of the bridge. Staff suggest it is not cost-effective to replace the bridge.
A memorandum with additional information has been prepared and is attached to this agenda item backup. Staff recommends Board approval to alter the project scope to repair the existing structure.
meeting: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting

description:
Tornados during Hurricane Milton caused severe damage, including uprooted trees, windblown debris, isolated washouts, and significant tree falls into, across, or over the drainage canal along the east side of Eastwood Drive in the Lakewood Park neighborhood of northern unincorporated St. Lucie County.
The Eastwood Canal provides critical drainage to the area and conveyance of stormwater runoff is currently impeded due to the amount of vegetative debris in the canal. The diminished capacity and hindered ability to convey stormwater runoff presents a real threat of potential flooding and public safety. Several existing canal bank washouts pose an ongoing threat of progressive canal bank sloughing and erosion adjacent to the roadway, which, if further aggravated, could close the road and risk longer response times for emergency services.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) has approved our application for canal restoration work within the Eastwood Canal through their Emergency Watershed Protection (EWP) program. As part of this program, St. Lucie County is required to enter into a cooperative agreement with the NRCS. The project will remove fallen trees, debris and vegetation from within the Eastwood Canal, restore the canal bank at washout locations and install some erosion protection measures over roughly 2.2 miles of canal.

description:
Stormwater culverts direct and channel the flow of stormwater under driveways, roads, sidewalks and other obstructions and are an integral component of stormwater management. Culverts fail over time due to maintenance, environmental or installation issues. Culvert failure can lead to localized flooding which may impede safe conditions of ingress and egress for owners and residents of property in the affected area as well as the traveling public, visitors, emergency responders and other public service providers. Some culvert owners may lack the resources to pay for improvements and repairs.
In 2021, the Board established a voluntary program, Ordinance No. 21-004, to which eligible property owners can apply for and receive funding to improve or repair culverts and then repay this funding through the imposition of a non-ad valorem special assessment against the improved property collected in annual installments on the tax roll.
The attached Resolution No. 2025-57 is the Assessment Resolution as required by County's Ordinance No. 21-004, as amended. The purpose of this resolution relates to the imposition and collection of special assessments to fund stormwater culvert improvements within the Culvert 2025-02 MSBU, determine that real property therein will be specially benefitted, establish the method of assessing the cost of the improvements, approve the assessment roll, and provide an effective date.

attachments.name: Fla. Stat. § 70.001. Private property rights protection.
Sand & Sea v. SLC BOCC - Denying Petition for Writ of Certiorari - Circuit Court Case No. 24-AP-01
Notice of $6,685,000 Claim Pursuant to Florida Statutes § 70.001, Bert J. Harris, Jr. Private Property Rights Act

description:
(Taken from the County's Response to the Petition)
The genesis of the issue concerns the actions of the Board in the adoption of an ordinance in 1994. On August 16, 1994, the Board adopted Ordinance 94-21 which established a maximum height of thirty-five (35) feet for all new structures on Hutchinson Island. Though the Ordinance created a new height limitation within the area, it also contained exceptions for structures that had previously been approved in excess of 35 feet and those proposed structures that had a vested right to construct at a height in excess of 35 feet as a result of a prior site plan approval. To implement the height limitation and identify the excepted properties, the Board directed staff to examine both existing and planned developments on Hutchinson Island that either exceeded or upon construction would exceed the 35 feet threshold and to map each of those locations.
On November 17, 1994, the Local Planning Agency/Planning and Zoning Commission (the "P & Z") held a public hearing on the proposed ordinance after publishing Notice in the Port St. Lucie News and the Tribune at least fifteen (15) days prior to the hearing and recommended that the proposed ordinance be approved. At the P & Z meeting a discrepancy was noted between the metes and bounds legal description and the map contained within the proposed Ordinance. As contained within the minutes of that meeting:
Mr. Murphy reviewed Draft Ordinance 94-026 and gave a detailed presentation using a series of color-coded maps displayed before the Commission. He stated that the draft ordinance provides for the creation of the Hutchison Island Building Height Overlay District. This district would establish two building height zones, effecting all of unincorporated Hutchinson Island. The first zone, "Zone B", would limit building heights to 35 feet, subject to meeting all applicable buildings spacing and setback standards. "Zone A" would establish maximum building height of 125 feet, subject to meeting all applicable building spacing and setback standards. There are also provisions for variance from these standards, subject to an applicant meeting the standard variance tests.
Chairman Klein asked where the 35 feet came from.
Mr. Murphy replied that 35 feet came from the direction of the County Commission as being consistent with single family or low-rise development.
Mr. Terpening noted an error in the ordinance's legal description.He stated that staff should make minor changes to correct the error.
Mr. Murphy stated that staff will make corrections.
Mr. Murphy stated that within Zone A on South Beach, staff made two text exemptions that will not be reflected in the map, the existing Sand Dollar Condominium project and the reactor area, or the main activity area of the power plan.
The P & Z passed a motion to recommend the Board of County Commissioners ("Board") approve the Ordinance subject to the correction of the legal description to conform to the incorporated maps. The error in the legal description referenced in the minutes and corrected by the P & Z at its November 17, 1994 meeting was an additional error to that which was subsequently addressed by the 2024 Ordinance.
On December 20, 1994, the Board held its first public hearing on the proposed Ordinance and adopted Ordinance No. 95-001 (the "1995 Ordinance") creating the Hutchinson Island Building Height Zones Overlay in the St. Lucie Land Development Code. Publication of the notice of the second public hearing was in the Port St. Lucie News and the Tribune on December 27, 1994. The 1995 Ordinance created Zone A in which the maximum height of structures could not exceed 125 feet and Zone B in which the maximum height of structures could not exceed 35 feet. However, though not discovered at that time, there was a discrepancy between the metes and bounds legal description (the "Legal Description") and the graphic boundary depiction (the "Map") contained within the 1995 Ordinance. The discrepancy existed at the point where Zone "A" ends (the 125 foot height limitation area) and Zone B begins (the 35 foot height limitation area). The area affected by the discrepancy consisted of three (3) narrow ocean lots, north of the Regency Condominium, one of which was the County's Normandy Beach Access. The Legal Description included the three ocean lots within the 125 foot height limitation area, while the Map reflected that the three lots were within the 35 foot height limitation area.
This discrepancy went largely unnoticed for several years and County staff applied the 1995 Ordinance utilizing the boundaries depicted on the Map. For example, in 2010 and again in 2016, potential developers made inquiries as to the developmental standards that would apply to two of the three properties impacted by the discrepancy in the 1995 Ordinance and in both cases they were informed that the 35 foot height limitation was applicable.
In approximately October 2021, the discrepancy between the Legal Description and the Map within the 1995 Ordinance was discovered. On September 19, 2023, County staff requested permission from the Board to advertise two alternative County initiated draft ordinances that would correct the scrivener's error between the Map and the Legal Description in the 1995 Ordinance. One alternative (Draft Ordinance 23-XXX-A) would amend the Legal Description to conform with the adopted Map. The second alternative (Draft Ordinance 23-XXX-B) would amend the Map to conform with the adopted Legal Description. The Board considered the two alternatives and directed staff to advertise both versions of the draft ordinances for the Board's consideration at the subsequent public hearing.
On October 19, 2023, County staff presented the two alternative versions of the ordinances correcting the scrivener's error between the Map and the Legal Description in the 1995 Ordinance to the P & Z at a noticed public hearing. County staff in setting forth the purpose of the two alternative versions, indicated to the P & Z that the goal of the draft ordinances was to reflect the intent of the 1995 Board when it adopted the 1995 Ordinance. At the meeting, the Petitioner made a presentation to the P & Z. The P & Z ultimately voted 6-2 to recommend to the Board to adopt the version of the Ordinance which would amend the Map to conform to the Legal Description and that the 3 narrow lots, including the County's Normandy Beach Access, would be included within the 125-foot height limitation of Zone A.
The Board held its initial public hearing on the two versions of the ordinances on November 7, 2023, and voted to continue the hearing to the regularly scheduled meeting of the Board on December 5, 2023. At the December 5th meeting, the Board conducted its first public hearing on the County initiated Ordinances. The Petitioner made a presentation to the Board. At the public hearing, the record included numerous minutes and materials related to the adoption of the 1995 Ordinance and subsequent applications. The material also included the Affidavit of Commissioner Cliff Barnes who served on the Board in 1995. Former Commissioner Barnes attested that it was his intent to rely upon the Map in the adoption of the 1995 Ordinance. Following the taking of public comment and discussion by the Board, the matter was approved to proceed forward with the County initiated Ordinance for a second public hearing to be held on January 9, 2024.
On January 9, 2024, the Board held its second public hearing on the County initiated Ordinances. The Petitioner again made a presentation to the Board. Following public comment and Board discussion, the Board adopted Draft Ordinance 2024-1A, which provided that the Map controlled over the Legal Description and that the parcels in question were within Zone B and subject to the 35-foot height restriction as depicted on the Map (the "2024 Ordinance"). The 2024 Ordinance corrected the Legal Description to conform to the Map. The vote at the Board was five to zero.
In the adoption of the Ordinance, the Board made four distinct findings supporting its decision that it was the intent of the Board in the adoption of the 1995 Ordinance that the Map would control over the Legal Description. Those findings were as follows:
A. There was no mention of the metes and bounds description in the staff report or the public hearing meeting minutes. The metes and bounds description may not back any relevance or bearing on the understanding or intent of the Commissioners.
B. The three (3) lots that are in the area affected by the discrepancy are narrow and long. The two (2) southernmost lots were vacant in 1995 and have remained vacant. The northernmost lot is a County Park (Normandy Beach Access) which was in existence at the time the Board adopted Ordinance No. 95-001. It appears contradictory for the Board at the time of adoption to include a County Park within Zone A, which would allow for higher building heights.
C. It is logical that the Board would have "grandfathered" the existing high-rise structures and limited the boundary of Zone A (125 feet) to the northernmost boundary of the existing high-rise building.
D. The rule of interpretation in Land Development Code Section 1.06.01 "Rules of Interpretation - Generally" is not applicable because Land Development Code Section 4.01.02.B "Hutchinson Island - Building Height Overlay Zone - Generally" provides, "Such zones are shown on the Hutchinson Island Building Height Overlay Plan as depicted in Figures 4.5a through 4.5e" (underlining supplied).
Ultimately, the Board found that the rule of interpretation set forth in Section 1.06.01 of the St. Lucie County Land Development Code providing that text would generally prevail over images was subject to the provision that "the rules of this section shall be observed except when the context clearly requires otherwise." (emphasis added). The Board determined that the context of the adoption of the 1995 Ordinance was such that the general interpretive rule was inapplicable in that situation.
On February 6, 2024, the Petitioner filed its Petition for Writ of Certiorari in the Circuit Court. On December 20, 2024, the Circuit Court denied the Petitioner's petition for writ of certiorari and issued a written opinion, a copy of which is attached. The Petitioner has appealed the Circuit Court decision to the Fourth District Court of Appeal (by filing a Petition for Writ of Certiorari) which appeal is pending.
Bert J. Harris, Jr. Private Property Rights Act Claim
On January 8, 2025, the County was served with a “Notice of $6,685,000 Claim Pursuant to Florida Statutes § 70.001, Bert J. Harris, Jr. Private Property Rights Act” by the attorneys representing Sand & Sea Development Group, LLC (“Sand & Sea”). A copy of the Claim is attached. As set out above, in 2024, Sand & Sea challenged the County’s adoption of Ordinance No. 2024-1A wherein the Board determined that the County Board in 1995 intended that the map controls over the text when the Board adopted height limitations on Hutchinson Island.
For the Board’s information, a general summary of the Bert J. Harris, Jr. Private Property Rights Protection Act (“Harris Act”) follows. A copy of the Harris Act is attached to this memorandum.
Harris Act
The Harris Act was enacted by the Florida Legislature in 1995. The Harris Act provided a new cause of action to private property owners when an action of a governmental entity has placed an “inordinate burden” on the existing uses or vested rights to specific uses of real property. “Inordinate burden” is defined in Subsection (3)(e) in the Harris Act.
The Harris Act provides for a 90-day-notice period before a property owner may file suit against a governmental entity. The governmental entity must provide written notice of the claim to all parties to any administrative action that gave rise to the claim as well as to owners of real property contiguous to the claimant’s property. The governmental entity must also report the claim to the State of Florida Department of Legal Affairs within 15 days after a claim is presented. Along with the claim, the property owner must submit an appraisal supporting the claim and demonstrating the loss in fair market value to the property. During the 90-day-notice period, the governmental entity must make a written settlement offer providing for any of the options listed in Subsection (4)(c) of the Harris Act, including the option of making no changes to the action of the governmental entity. If the settlement offer is not accepted by the property owner during the 90-day-notice period, the governmental entity must issue a written statement that identifies the allowable uses for the property.
In the absence of a settlement, the property owner may file suit against the governmental entity in circuit court. The circuit court first determines whether an existing use or a vested right to a specific use of the real property exists and whether action of the governmental entity has inordinately burdened the real property. If the court determines that the governmental entity’s action has inordinately burdened the claimant’s property, the court will empanel a jury to determine the amount of compensation to the claimant for loss in property value caused by the inordinate burden. If the claimant prevails, the claimant is entitled to receive reasonable costs and attorneys’ fees from the governmental entity.
Discussion
The Planning and Development Services Director and the Planning Manager will present a PowerPoint that discusses various options available under the statute.

description:
The County and DP Development, LLC (“DP”) entered into the contract to complete the construction of the Oleander Avenue sidewalk from Midway Road to South Market Avenue (the “Project”) on April 20, 2021 (the “Contract”). From the very beginning of the Project, DP struggled to perform the work in order to achieve timely substantial completion in accordance with the Contract. In a show of good faith, the County worked with DP to extend the Project schedules through a series of change orders. DP failed to adhere to the extended Project schedules and fell behind after some extensions. DP failed to provide and maintain a recovery schedule showing that it would achieve a firm completion date. DP disputed these points but the construction schedules and project delivery showed otherwise. The Project schedule was critical as the Project was being executed in accordance with the terms of the Local Agency Program Federally Funded Grant Agreement entered into by the County and the Florida Department of Transportation (“FDOT”). Under the Second Supplemental Agreement executed by the County and FDOT, the parties agreed to complete the Project on or before December 31, 2023.
Given the impending grant deadline, the timely completion of the Project was imperative and DP’s failures to adhere to its own schedules demonstrated its inability to complete the Project within the required timeframe. DP’s failure to advance the work so as to achieve timely completion per the express terms of the Contract was a default under the Contract and the General Conditions. As such, the County issued a Notice of Contractor Default and (Intended) Termination to DP on October 16, 2023, giving DP time to cure its default in accordance with the Contract’s procedures.
On October 20, 2023, DP sent its response to the County’s Notice of Contract Default and Termination and provided a revised recovery schedule. Almost immediately, DP failed to conform to its own recovery schedule, as evidenced by the fact that DP did not return to the site pursuant to that schedule. The County, in good faith, provided DP with time to show that it could abide by the cure plan and cure its deficiencies; however, DP continued to fail to be onsite, and the County issued its Notice of Termination to DP on November 2, 2023. The County then executed emergency contracts with Ranger Construction and PRP Construction in early 2024 to complete the Project and not default on the entire grant reimbursement requirements. The Project has since been completed in compliance with the FDOT grant.
In accordance with the Contract and the bond for the Project, the County provided DP’s Surety with proper notice during each step of DP’s ongoing issues on the Project. In its October 16 Notice of Default and again in the November 2 Notice of Termination, the County requested that the Surety perform its obligations under the bond. These requests went unanswered by the Surety until November 9 when counsel for the Surety reached out to dispute that it received proper notice of the default and termination. In its November 14 response, the County demonstrated that it had met the notice requirement for each of the Notices issued. The County informed the Surety that it had proceeded with hiring a replacement contractor to complete the Project but provided the Surety with a final chance to honor its bond obligations. The Surety did not respond to the November 14 correspondence from the County. The Surety’s failure to fulfill its bond obligations resulted in the County incurring additional costs to complete the Project.
The County has assessed its additional costs and damages in the wake of the completion of the Project. A breakdown of these costs is enclosed. The County currently holds $52,705.41 in retainage and $157,469.23 in other amounts due to DP.
Proposal for Settlement
The parties attended a mediation on February 18, 2025, in an effort to settle the dispute before litigation. The mediation resulted in the following proposed settlement for Board consideration:DP agrees that the County can retain the $210,174.64 (Retainage and cost that would otherwise be due to DP) that the County is currently holding.
In addition to the amount in #1, DP agrees to pay the County the amount of $350,000.00 payable $250,000.00 in 14 days and the balance ($100,000.00) 30 days thereafter.
Upon payment, the parties agree to general releases to each other for all claims relating to the Project including attorneys’ fees and costs.
Discussion
County staff believes that the proposed settlement is a fair resolution of the issues. The amount received from DP ($460,174.65) will virtually cover the County’s payments to PRP and Ranger to complete the Project. The alternative to settlement is litigation. One of the factors to consider in deciding to proceed with litigation is the cost of litigation including attorneys’ fees, expert witness costs and discovery costs. In this case, due to the complexity of the issues it will be necessary for each party to obtain Scheduling and Engineering experts. The combined cost (County and DP) to litigate the case could exceed $400,000.00 each. Although the construction contract provides that the prevailing party in the litigation will recover fees and costs from the other party, there is always risk of loss in proceeding with litigation. Settlement avoids that risk.
The County’s special counsel, Robert Alfert, who handled the mediation and settlement negotiations, strongly recommends that the County accept the settlement proposal. This is a very fair settlement for the County.

description:
The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) is a federally-subsidized flood damage insurance program administered by the Federal Emergency Management Agency enabling property owners in participating communities to purchase flood insurance in exchange for the community's adoption of floodplain management regulations to reduce future flood damages. Floodplain management is a community-based effort to prevent or reduce the risk of flooding, resulting in a more resilient community.
The NFIP Community Rating System (CRS) was implemented in 1990 as a voluntary program for recognizing and encouraging community floodplain management activities that exceed minimum NFIP standards.The CRS program uses a class rating system that is similar to fire insurance rating to determine flood insurance premium reductions for residents. CRS Classes are rated from 9 to 1. Each CRS Class improvement produces a 5% greater discount on flood insurance premiums.
St. Lucie County participates in the CRS program and has achieved a CRS rating of Class 5, which provides its residents with a 25% discount on flood insurance premiums. There are additional activities that the County can consider to preserve our Class 5 rating or possibly improve our CRS rating to a Class 4 (30% discount).
Unincorporated St. Lucie County has 6,049 National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) policies in place, with a total premium of $2,748,822. This premium reflects a 25% discount due to our CRS Class 5 rating. Without this discount, the total premium cost would be $3,665,096.
This means that our proactive floodplain management efforts and CRS participation are directly saving our residents $916,274 annually in flood insurance costs.
The St. Lucie County Building Division utilizes the services of Schwalls Consulting LLC. to assist with Floodplain Management. This presentation to the Board will be provided by Del Schwalls, PE, CFM, who will present various options for the Board's consideration to improve the County's flood resilience and improve our CRS class.
The topics that will be presented include:

description:
Recently, a Commissioner brought up the feasibility of requiring a "Community Participation Meeting" for certain types of development applications. Currently, PDS staff encourage applicants to hold a meeting with neighboring property owners to promote public participation; however, this is not a code requirement.
Staff is requesting Board input to determine if we should pursue a Land Development Code Text Amendment to outline the "Community Participation Meeting" as a requirement.
If the Board is interested in developing this new requirement, staff recommends "Community Participation Meetings" be required for the following applications:
• Planned Development (PUD, PNRD, and PMUD),
• Conditional Use Permits (New & Major Adjustments), and
• Development Agreements.
These applications typically include a site plan and conceptual development details which are reviewed by the Board through quasi-judicial public hearings, where the Board maintains the ability to provide input proposed plans to improve compatibility and design.
Additionally, staff recommends the following standards for these meetings, if required:
• The applicant must coordinate with the Planning & Development Services Director or designee regarding the date, time, and location of the proposed community meeting. All meetings shall be held on a weekday evening at a location close to the project site, between 20 and 60 days prior to the first of any public hearing required for the application.
• At least 15 days prior to the meeting, surrounding property owners shall be noticed through a mailed notice.
• The applicant shall pay the cost of advertising for the community meeting and provide proof of notice to the Planning & Development Services Director or designee.
• The meeting shall be facilitated by the applicant or designated representative and the Planning & Development Services Director or designee shall be invited to the meeting.

description:
This is a request for an additional FTE (full-time employee) for the Planning & Development Services (PDS) Department – Planning Division. The Planning Division has the significant responsibilities of maintaining and implementing the County Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code; reviewing all proposed development applications to ensure compliance with the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code; and providing assistance and guidance to other County Departments and the public to advance a high quality of life and improve the health, safety and welfare of the community.
With the continuing heavy workload due to development submittals, recent legislation that alters or requires faster review procedures, Land Development Code amendments, research requests, informal meeting discussion requests and the ongoing efforts to complete the Evaluation and Appraisal Report of the Comprehensive Plan, impact fee studies, mobility infrastructure plan study, and USB traffic study, the Planning Division is overloaded and juggling significant responsibilities. Additionally, present staff are currently addressing requirements related to lawsuits as well as reviewing the economic development incentive program.
The ongoing studies mentioned above, and the Evaluation and Appraisal Report of the Comprehensive Plan are significant responsibilities that require a more experienced staff member. A Senior Planner role primarily focuses on complex planning projects, analysis, develops policies and leads major planning initiatives. The Planning Division has three senior planners, but based on the current heavy workload and the lean staffing (12 total in the division, including 3 administrative positions), their assigned responsibilities are mainly focused on the review of development applications due to demands.
As a note, the PDS Department continues to monitor the current legislative session, which includes proposals that have the potential to increase workload even further and drastically reduce timeframes for local government review.
The continuing contracts for Planning Services include fees ranging from $140.00-$250.00 per hour for a Senior Planner. In comparison, the Senior Planner FTE has a pay grade (G206) scale of $36.49 (min) - $45.62 (mid) - $54.74 (max). The County Administrator has requested we present this request to the BOCC for consideration of cost savings and providing the resources needed for the PDS Department to maintain a consistent level of service.

description:
On April 18, 2023, St. Lucie County, the City of Fort Pierce, and the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency entered into an interlocal agreement for the Moore’s Creek Redevelopment Project, also known as the Avenue D Model Block Project. This initiative aims to foster affordable workforce housing, job creation, economic growth, expanded commerce, enhanced public services, and an increased tax base. The project is located near Avenue D and 7th Street in Fort Pierce, with St. Lucie County leading the procurement process.
To facilitate the redevelopment efforts and leverage the benefits of the Live Local Act, the properties included in the project are undergoing a future land use amendment to designate them as general commercial while preserving the area’s rich cultural history.
As part of the project’s preliminary planning, St. Lucie County issued Request for Information (RFI) No. 23-054 on June 11, 2023, seeking input from the development community regarding the design and construction of a mixed-use development. Responses were due by August 25, 2023, and two firms submitted preliminary project proposals.
Following the RFI, the County released Request for Proposals (RFP) No. 24-044 on April 14, 2024. The RFP was widely distributed, with notifications sent to 740 companies and 80 document requests. Two proposals were ultimately received. On December 3, 2024, the selection committee evaluated the submissions, with scoring details provided in Attachment A.
On February 3, 2025, and February 11, 2025, the Fort Pierce City Commission and the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, respectively, approved the selection of Pinnacle Communities II, Inc. for the project and authorized staff to enter into negotiations.

description:
In August of 2024, the Indian River Lagoon Council was awarded a $9.4 million NOAA Transformational Habitat Restoration grant. The grant includes 10 sub-grantees; with these partners implementing habitat restoration across 14 locations throughout the Indian River Lagoon. Indian River State College (IRSC), with a partnership with ERD, was selected for a project at the Walton Scrub Preserve. The project proposal featured a strong community engagement aspect and IRSC as the sub-grantee, utilizing capstone students and interns to help implement the restoration projects. The grant deliverables are to utilize 200 volunteers and reach 6,000 volunteer hours, install 3 quarter-acre oyster reefs, restore 2,015 linear feet of shoreline and plant one acre of seagrass. The County benefits from the environmental restoration and engagement in the project and offered to leverage the existing $1M Walton Scrub Preserve Observation Tower project as match. As such, IRSC and ERD successfully secured $924,974.00 over a three-year period to install the oyster reefs, restore the eroded shoreline and plant one acre of seagrass.
Since the award to the IRL Council, a discrepancy has been identified between the IRL Council and IRSC during the sub-grantee contract negotiations regarding an additional $52,000 requested to cover IRSC’s overhead costs of managing the grant. The IRL Council does not have additional funds in the grant budget to accommodate the request, so the agreement was declined. ERD believes this project has significant value and will serve as an engaging service-learning project for community volunteers, local partners and students, and as a beacon of demonstration and inspiration for residents along the Indian River Lagoon who want to improve their properties with resilient shorelines. To save the project, ERD is requesting permission to assume the role of sub-grantee and manage the grant directly.
The grant period is for three years and requires quarterly reporting. ERD’s primary project manager, Tessa Roberts, Sr. Outreach Coordinator, will be committing the same amount of time as originally intended, however, now ERD will also be enlisting our Administrative Operations Coordinator to help with grant reporting, budget management, and invoicing.
ERS has the ability to manage this project effectively and believes the return on investment will be significant for both the environment and the community.

description:
White City Park is one of St. Lucie County's oldest parks and is located in the middle of the County off Midway Road on the St. Lucie River. Over the years this Park's shoreline on the east side of the park along the St. Lucie River has experienced significant erosion largely due to the constant flow of the river, tidal changes, and boat traffic. The shoreline is relatively unprotected from tide and wave action other than by vegetation. No structure currently exists to protect or stabilize the shoreline. In recent years, this erosion has become severe enough to encroach on the Park's entrance road leading to the boat ramp. Therefore, it is crucial that this shoreline is stabilized to restore the shoreline, entrance road and prevent further erosion.
Parks and Recreation previously submitted and was awarded a FIND WAP (Florida Inland Navigational District Waterway Assistance Program) Grant to help cover the costs for Phase I of this project which was survey, design and engineering. Phase I was completed in FY'24.
In order to help fund Phase II, construction, St. Lucie County Parks and Recreation Department applied and was awarded a matching $400,000 FIND (Florida Inland Navigational District) Grant. If accepted, this matching grant along with County funds will allow for $800,000 to be available to complete this project which includes: design, Shoreline Stabilization structures to be constructed per design, and the original access road to be restored to original condition and use.

(“Replay”) for software and hardware maintenance and support services, and remote quality assurance services of the County’s 911 emergency communications, and the NICE Inform Voice Logging Solution Upgrade, which is the public safety radio system recorder.
On October 31, 2023, NICE Public Safety Regional Account Executive notified the County via e-mail that they would be ending their business relationship with Replay as a reseller and service provider of NICE Solutions, which means Replay can no longer perform service and/or support of the County’s 911 Center NICE software and equipment.
The Replay Agreement allows the County to terminate the agreement, in whole, without cause upon 30 days written notice to Replay.
Based on a review of the existing service provided by Replay, County staff believes that it is in the best interest of the County to exercise its right to terminate the August 20, 2019, Agreement with Replay, and all related agreements without cause. The agreement allows for termination without cause upon 30 days’ written notice. A buyout penalty applies only if termination occurs within the first four years of the 10-year agreement. As the agreement was executed in August 2019, therefore the County should not be subject to any penalty under this clause.

attachments.name: Prima Vista Access Management Agenda Project Summary
Prima Vista Blvd Access Management Project Scope-Signed

description:
Prima Vista Boulevard between Airoso Drive and US-1 is a County maintained roadway that serves as a urban principal arterial roadway, evacuation route, and strategic freight corridor. The roadway is a five-lane section, with a center opposing left-hand turn lane with no median from Aldea Street west to Airoso Boulevard. While the center opposing left-turn lane can improve the flow of traffic and safety in certain contexts, it also introduces various issues such as increased collision risks, confusion for drivers, and possible disruptions to traffic and pedestrian flow.
This project will analyze and design raised medians for vehicles that will provide safe and efficient movement of people and goods along the corridor. The design will utilize the principles of the latest edition of the Multimodal Access Management Guidebook of the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT). Additionally, the project will evaluate the condition of the existing pedestrian sidewalks and ramps and bring them up to compliance as necessary.
As a median will restrict access to the many driveways along the corridor, the project includes significant public involvement activities that will provide information to and obtain input from the citizens, businesses, and private and governmental agencies, to ensure that the design reflects the values and needs of the community. The scope of work will also include but not be limited to landscaping, signing and pavement markings, signal evaluation, maintenance of traffic, and regulatory permitting.
A request for qualification (RFQ) process was utilized for the selection of the most qualified firm to perform professional engineering services and Kimley-Horn & Associates was the top-ranked firm by the selection committee.

attachments.name: North FFA Road at NSLRWCD C-44 and C-45 Emergency Culvert Lining and Replacement Summary
C25-01-093 PRP Construction - N FAA Rd @ C44 and C45
24-24M N. FFA Rd Culverts Emergency Memo

description:
North FFA Road, north of Orange Avenue has several culvert pipes that convey surface water (stormwater) beneath the roadway, generally from west to east at the locations of canals owned and maintained by the North St. Lucie River Water Control District (NSLRWCD). The NSLRWCD’s system of canals is essential for providing proper management of stormwater throughout this area of the County.
Staff have been monitoring two of these critical culvert crossings under North FFA Road at NSLRWCD Canals 44 and 45, with video inspection (most recently performed on June 25, 2024) and periodic visual inspections of the roadway at the crossings. Canal 44 is located approximately 0.5 miles north of Orange Avenue and Canal 45 is located along the north side of Orange Avenue. Over the past few years, both locations have exhibited small depressions recurring just outside the edge of the pavement, above or alongside the culvert pipes, which is indicative of soil traveling into a severely deteriorated section of the aged metal pipes and/or a partial collapse of the pipe.
Recent rainfall events, including Hurricane Milton, have increased the intensity of the depressions at these two culverts, to the point where the roadway's integrity is threatened and requires immediate action to protect the health and welfare of the traveling public.
The attached memorandum, signed by the County Administrator, declares this an emergency and is in accordance with the provisions of the County's purchasing manual.
meeting: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting
title: North FFA Road at North St. Lucie River Water Control District Canals C-44 and C-45 - Emergency Culvert Lining and Replacement

Photos of Main Terminal Renovations Change Order#1 for 2-18-25 Board Agenda

description:
The Airport Main Terminal is undergoing renovations for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and future commercial air service. The existing terrazzo in the terminal has about 8 strips from the main entrance to the back passenger seating area that are a different color of terrazzo that were poorly done, are unlevel, and have cracks in them. The Airport is removing the existing terrazzo to install a single uniform floor. While other flooring options were investigated, terrazzo is the only type of flooring that can withstand a high volume of people with luggage and is used in major airports throughout the world. The cost of terrazzo is high, but this type of floor can last up to 40 years or more. Additionally, the current plans had the bathroom vestibules continuing with a slippery light tan tile. This change order will remove light tan tile and replace it with the new uniform terrazzo in the main terminal.
During demolition, a Concrete Masonry Unit (CMU) Wall (aka precast concrete blocks) was found underneath the drywall on the wall leading into the former administration conference room. This wall is likely original to the building from 1962 and needs to be demolished to achieve the floor plan necessary for the TSA and future commercial air service. The area also includes a concrete column which is load bearing to the roof and that portion will be maintained and cleaned to ensure a smooth surface to receive the new metal stud partition wall.
meeting: Board of County Commissioners Regular Meeting

description:
The St. Lucie County Environmental Resources Department (ERD) manages over 11,000 acres of public preserve owned by St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners. These preserves were purchased with funds from the St. Lucie County’s Environmentally Significant Lands (ESL) Bond Program, a local voter approved bond, and Florida Communities' Trust-Florida Forever Program, a State funding program to preserve and provide passive public access to Florida’s remaining natural treasures. The “Work Camper” program was established for the ESL program in 2002.
