description: The Information Technology Department is continuing its efforts to standardize and modernize the County's security infrastructure across all sites for The Board of County Commissioners. We are embarking on the second phase of this project. Phase two builds upon the foundation laid in previous efforts completed in fiscal year 2024, where the Keri Access Control security system was installed county-wide, however, the Digital Watchdog closed circuit television system (CCTV) camera system was installed at only approximately 25% of Board of County Commissioner sites. The ultimate goal for the county is to replace all legacy CCTV cameras with the standardized Digital Watchdog system which will seamlessly integrate with the Keri Access Control security system. The Keri Access Control system is designed with flexibility and interoperability in mind, enabling smooth integration with a variety of gate automation systems. Through advanced relay modules and programming options, Keri Access Control systems can control and monitor gate access points efficiently. The Keri Access Control system software is compatible with DW Spectrum™ IPVMS, creating a unified platform for access control and video surveillance. This integration delivers the following advantages, event-based recording, enhanced monitoring and streamlined investigations. The first phase of this project was previously approved by the Board in April of 2024 granting Gearface, LLC as a sole-source solution due to emergency circumstances as a result of a safety audit. This integration of the Keri Access Control System with Digital Watchdog ensures a cohesive, efficient, and secure system across all sites. Per Section 8.1(a)(2); of the Purchasing Manual, if there is only a single source for goods or service a waiver of formal sealed bids may be requested. The Information Technology department is requesting the waiving of the bid process and the granting of Gearface, LLC as the sole source provider for items related to the Keri Access Control System and the Digital Watchdog integration. Per a letter received from Keri System, Gearface, LLC is the sole integrator in the Treasure Coast geographical area that is a Keri partner through their Integrated Partner Program (IPP). We recommend utilizing a single vendor to install and maintain the system, including Keri Access Control and DW Spectrum™ IPVMS. Working with a single vendor ensures unified support, seamless integration, cost efficiency and consistency in quality. For St. Lucie County, adopting this integrated solution thru Gearface, LLC will provide a centralized and efficient approach to managing access control and video surveillance across various facilities. We believe this approach aligns with the county's goals for enhanced security, streamlined operations, and cost-effective system management.

description:
In 1996, a bond referendum was approved by St. Lucie County BOCC to purchase what now is Harbour Pointe Park (f.k.a. the Cotton Property). The 20-acre tract of land was purchased with the understanding that the property would be used for "...marine commercial, recreation, and tourism...". Since then, this park has been primarily dormant, being operated as a passive recreational park and as a lay-down area (periodically) for County initiated marine construction activities and our artificial reef program. The park includes a stormwater pond that services some of North 2nd Street roadway improvements.
The County's purchase of the Port Terminal (previously known as the Indian River Terminal) in 2018 included a 10% stake in the adjacent port land owned by Destin Beach Incorporated (DBI Inc.); this land is immediately north of the current port terminal and south of Harbour Pointe Park. An exchange agreement was recently completed between St. Lucie County and DBI, Inc., which included the conveyance of approximately 6 acres of land to the County. This land is contiguous to the existing park and will help the County establish a formal roadway corridor to park land and a proposed boat ramp facility.
There is a growing demand for boat ramp facilities in the County and the City of Fort Pierce has expressed similar observations. In response to this, the 2020 Port of Fort Pierce Master Plan and Reinvestment Strategy identified a recreational boat ramp facility at Harbour Pointe Park to help curb this growing demand; a demand spurred by population growth within the County and limited launching options within our inlet complex. This plan was adopted by the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners (BOCC), and funding was provided for the design and permitting of the proposed facility in the County's FY-2023/24 budget.
Anticipating this project, consulting services for design and permitting of the new facility were pursued (RFQ No. 24-032 - Harbour Point Regional Boat Ramp) and a consultant (Taylor Engineering) was selected. Grant funding opportunities with the Florida Inland Navigation District (F.I.N.D.) and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) - Florida Boaters Improvement Program (FBIP) are also being pursued to offset the cost of design and permitting efforts. The County was recently successful last year in attaining a $250,000.00 grant from F.I.N.D. but fell short in our FBIP application rankings for supplemental design funding. Upon gathering feedback from FWC, and making minor changes to the 2024 application, it was recommended by FWC that staff resubmit during the 2025 FBIP funding cycle. Staff anticipate submitting a FWC-FBIP application prior to April 8, 2025, and it will include detailed information regarding the proposed project and an anticipated design/permitting schedule.
The attached Resolution is required for grant application completeness.

description:
In approximately 2013, the Public Works Department learned of the existence of five box culverts beneath Orange Avenue. These culverts are situated within five miles of the St. Lucie and Okeechobee County line and were constructed in the 1960s when FDOT owned and built the roadway. The culverts are identified as follows: Culvert A (MP2.2), Culvert B (MP2.3), Culvert C (MP2.7), Culvert D (MP3.0), and Culvert E (MP4.0).
In 2015, an engineering evaluation was conducted and completed on the five culverts to assess their construction, conditions, hydrologic and hydraulic functions, as well as their maintenance needs. This evaluation also examined how these culverts perform during rainfall events and provided a summary of potential alternatives to address any concerns.
Stephen Cooper, PE & Associates, Inc. (SCPE) was awarded the total contract of $174,888.80 for the design and preparation of construction plans. The project includes the removal of four existing box culverts on Orange Avenue (Culverts A, C, D, and E) and the removal and replacement of Culvert B with a 121.5 LF of 36” reinforced concrete pipe (RCP). Subsequently, it was decided to remove Culvert C from the project due to the need for a more thorough analysis, coordination with the adjacent Wescott Groves property, and budget considerations.
The project was advertised for construction on November 10, 2024. On December 18, 2024, a total of seven bids were received. The bids were reviewed by staff to confirm the numbers and rankings are accurate. Telephone conferences were held with SoCal Shaker Plates & Construction Site Services, LLC, and Ferriera Construction Company, Inc., the two lowest bidders respectively. However, both companies withdrew their bids after discussing the construction of a bypass road as a requirement for the project. The telephone call with Johnson-Davis, Inc., the third lowest bidder, determined that their bid of $1,518,000.00 meets the project's requirements, making it the lowest responsive and responsible bid.
Additionally, a proposal from Andersen Andre Consulting Engineers, Inc. for geotechnical and testing services was received in the amount of $16.620.00.
The Total Construction Project Budget is established as follows:
Construction Contract: $1,380,000.00
Construction Contingency (10%): $138,000.00
Construction and Materials Testing: $16,620.00
Project Budget Total: $1,534,620.00

attachments.name: South 25th Street Pond Outfall Repair at Lake Forest Park Board Acceptance Summary (final draft)

description:
A County-owned stormwater pond is located on the west side of South 25th Street, north of Edwards Road and immediately south of the Lake Forest Park facility. An 84-inch corrugated metal pipe extends from the control structure at the southwest corner of the pond west to the North St. Lucie River Water Control District (NSLRWCD) Canal No. 9. The east end of the outfall pipe near the control structure was inadvertently damaged during pond maintenance activities.
An inspection found the pipe in overall fair to poor condition as the pipe was nearing its design service life. An engineering consultant performed an analysis to evaluate whether the pipe should be repaired or replaced. It was determined that rehabilitation of the damaged pipe with a Cured-In-Place Pipe (CIPP) liner would be the most economical and effective option to repair the pipe. The CIPP option is typically a fraction of the cost to replace the pipe and provides for an extended service life equivalent to or greater than that of a replacement pipe.
On May 26, 2024, Bid No. 24-070 was advertised for the selected CIPP method repair of the damaged outfall pipe. On June 26, 2024, the three received bids were opened. The lowest responsive and responsible bidder was Hinterland Group, Inc. of Stuart, Florida, with a bid in the amount of $205,480.00. The total amount spent on this project was $194,220.00, including $7,420.00 of the $18,680.00 used from contingency.
Staff monitored the construction and determined the project was completed in conformance with the plans and specifications. The project was completed under budget with a remaining amount of $11,260.00.

description:
Indian River Estates is an existing 1,300 acres subdivision located in unincorporated St. Lucie County. Indian River Estates is bounded by North St. Lucie River Water Control District (NSLRWCD) Canal 22 to the west, Midway Road to the north, and the Savannas Preserve State Park (Savannas) to the south and east. Drainage within the subdivision is divided along a north-south axis. Most of the subdivision drains east toward the Savannas, but a portion of the stormwater runoff flows west to the North St. Lucie River Water Control District Canal 22 and Canal 23.
Development of the subdivision started in the 1950s and is still not completely built out to this day. Since Indian River Estates predates modern stormwater regulations, the development does not have the typical stormwater management facilities associated with newer subdivisions. In the past the subdivision frequently experienced flooding issues due to inefficient drainage collection and conveyance, flat topography, high groundwater levels and tailwater influences from the Savannas. Additionally, high stages within Indian River Estates can result in untreated stormwater discharges to the Savannas, contributing to degradation of water quality. Easy Street, the southernmost street in the subdivision, historically experienced the worst flooding issues due to lower elevations and proximity to the Savannas.
The County has designed and constructed a large-scale drainage retrofit to improve drainage and reduce flooding occurrences. Phase 1 improvements, including a stormwater pump station, force main and treatment pond, were completed in 2009. Phase II improvements, designed by Inwood Consulting Engineers, were completed in 2015. Phase 2 added a gravity storm sewer collection system, swale grading improvements, and modifications to the outfalls to the Savannas. These projects have improved drainage conditions within Indian River Estates, but flooding and inefficient drainage is still a concern in the most low-lying areas along Easy Street and in western portions of the subdivision.
Phase 3 improvements are a continuation of the St. Lucie County’s investments to date. The project seeks to build on the improvements initiated under previous phases by addressing three main elements:
• Evaluate the drainage along Easy Street. Provide recommendations to reduce road flooding during heavy rain events.
• Address interaction of flow between Indian River Estates and the Savannas. Evaluate options to reduce/ prevent backflow from the Savannas.
• Address internal block drainage systems that are located outside the limits of Phase 2. Provide cost-effective recommendations and designs to improve drainage efficacy.
On October 17, 2023, the Board was presented and approved the three alternatives.
August 11, 2024, RFQ 24-092 was advertised for Design-Build of the Easy Street/Buchanan Drive project. Responses were received on September 11, 2024, with one proposal. Due to the lack of market participation, it was determined that the project would pivot to a traditional design-bid-build delivery, with Inwood completing the design.
Inwood has submitted a proposal to complete the design (Amendment 7). Staff has reviewed the attached Scope and Fee Proposals. Staff is recommending the Board award Amendment 7 to Inwood Consulting Engineers in the amount of $226,801.63 and authorize the Chair to sign documents approved by the County Attorney.

description:
On October 15, 2024, the BOCC approved an Option Agreement with Ashley Capital Pursuant to RFP No. 22-092, to purchase 111 acres within the Treasure Coast Research and Education Park. The agreement includes a 180-day removal period to be completed by the County to:• Amend Land Development Code Section 4.03.00 to exclude the Property and the Purchaser’s Property from the Research and Education Park Overlay Zone, modifying the boundaries of the Overlay map as specified in §4.03.02(A) to reflect this removal, and modifying the text of any other sections of the County Code as required to achieve the purpose.
• Amend the TCERDA Lease to exclude the property therefrom.
• Amend the Declaration to exclude the property therefrom.
The Research Park was originally developed in the early 2000s by the County to promote additional agricultural research and education already occurring in the area. Together, with the State of Florida, the County assembled 1,600 acres that presently make up the Research Park.
The County and partners sought to attract additional research facilities and companies to the Research Park to complement the ongoing activities of the Indian River Research & Education Center (“IRREC”) of the University of Florida’s Institute of Food & Agricultural Sciences (“IFAS”), the Hayslip Biological Control Research and Containment Laboratory and the United States Department of Agriculture (“USDA”) Agricultural Research Service. All three continue to be tenants in the Research Park.
For a variety of reasons, the original vision for the Research Park never materialized, such as changes in federal research funding and the great recession contributed significantly to why the Research Park never realized the research development goals. In recognition of the changes, the TCERDA Board authorized staff to hire a consultant and provide analysis and recommendations on next steps for the Research Park.
In 2018, John Rhodes of Moran, Stahl and Boyer was hired to provide a series of strategic recommendations to improve the likelihood of development in the Research Park. Three of the main strategic recommendations were to expand the allowable uses in the Research Park, sell rather than lease land and lessen the architectural rules for new buildings in the Park (the Research Park is subject to that certain Declaration of Covenants and Restrictions for Treasure Coast Education, Research and Development Park, dated February 7, 2012, and recorded March 16, 2012, in Official Records Book 3371, Page 2418, in the Public Records of St. Lucie County, Florida (the “Declaration of Covenants”). The rationale for the changes was that the original list of allowed uses was very restrictive, potential developers prefer to buy rather than lease land and the design rules significantly increased the cost of development.
Amendments to the Land Development Code were processed to expand the number of allowable uses and amend the architectural requirements. Both the TCERDA Board and the Board of County Commissioners adopted the changes. An RFP was also published to offer the Research Park land for sale. The sole respondent to the RFP was Ashley Capital.
Quad 1A within the Research Park is where the Sunshine Kitchen is located, and the County has previously put the six parcels surrounding the Kitchen on the market for developers to purchase. Since those various actions, the vision for the Research Park has changed further and the BOCC approved an exchange agreement with the Fire District to build a Fire Station on Quad 1A-Lot 3 on December 14, 2022.
The County is also working on the designs for a proposed Animal Safety Facility, with land to house agricultural animals, within Quad 1A.

description:
In 2021, the Board of County Commissioners approved Ordinance 2021-009, which amended the Land Development Code pertaining to Planned Development Site Plan submittal requirements, allowing certain items to be provided at the Final Site Plan Stage instead of at the time of Preliminary Planned Development review. This action stemmed from a request from the St. Lucie County Chamber of Commerce and their Development Review Taskforce, who were interested in promoting efficiency, local economic development and the Planned Development process. At the time, the development community approached the County and discussed the need for cost containment during the Preliminary Planned Development review process, prior to spending considerable time and capital in the preparation of more detailed development application requirements before the proposal is considered by the Board.
Ordinance 2021-009 shifted some of the more detailed submittal requirements for Preliminary Planned Development approval from the Preliminary stage to the Final Site Plan stage. The amendment deferred the following submittal requirements to the Final Site Plan application:
1) A topographic survey - The existing grade conditions and contours of the proposed development sites are used to create detailed drainage plans. As a result, during the Preliminary Planned Development submittal, only a conceptual utility and drainage plan is required, since more detailed survey work and engineering would be completed as a part of a sufficient Final Site Plan application.
2) A final landscape plan - Typical landscape sections, including proposed buffers are reviewed as a part of the Preliminary Planned Development application and defers the detailed site specific landscape plan to the Final Site Plan stage.
3) The approximate location and dimension of all proposed lots and all yard requirements - The Preliminary Planned Development plan allows for a developer to provide a "Bubble Plan" identifying areas where certain lot types will be located and provide "Lot Typical" details identifying specific lot types, including dimensions.
It should be noted that the LDC allows for the Planning & Development Services Director to request any other information deemed necessary for the reasonable review of the proposed development at the Preliminary Planned Development application stage.
Planning staff generally promotes the Planned Development process as it allows for creativity in design, identification of designated open space, and adherence to architectural standards. Land Development Code (LDC) Section 7.01.00 - Planned Unit Development (PUD) and Section 7.02.00 - Planned Non-Residential Development (PNRD) provides that the purpose of Planned Developments is intended to achieve residential and non-residential land development of superior qualify through the encouragement of flexibility and creativity in design options. Planned Developments are intended to allow for creative approaches to the development of land reflecting changes in the technology of land development. Planned Developments also lead to a more efficient use of land, which can result in smaller networks of utilities and streets and thereby lowering costs and enhancing neighborhoods through the preservation of natural features, provisions for underground utilities, and provisions for recreational and open space areas.
Comprehensive Plan Objective 1.1.8: Planned Developments. state that the County shall continue to support and encourage innovative land use development patterns including planned developments through the adequate provision in the County's Land Development Code including Planned Unit Developments (PUD), Planned Non-Residential Developments (PNRD) and the Planned Mixed Use Development (PMUD) zoning designations.

description:
St. Lucie County developed the Sunshine Kitchen Food Business Incubator (Sunshine Kitchen) in 2018 with a US Economic Development Administration grant. The Sunshine Kitchen Food Business Incubator, a 10,000-square foot facility providing year-round, 24-hour-a-day access to users to prepare, produce, package, and market food business items, has been operating since September 2018. The Sunshine Kitchen was created as a community kitchen concept where food entrepreneurs could develop their products in a commercially-equipped shared-use kitchen. The concept follows other business incubation methodologies that provide start-up businesses with management guidance, technical assistance, and relatively low-cost facilities in which the entrepreneur can develop their venture until the company is strong enough to secure its own brick-and-mortar or conventional commercial space. The Sunshine Kitchen continues to grow and serve numerous entrepreneurs, with over 100 clients currently.
The use of kitchen facilities directly impacts costs related to staff workload, contract labor, utilities, supplies, equipment maintenance, cleaning and security. As such, the Board adopted a fee schedule via Resolution 2024-184 on October 1, 2024. The adoption of a uniform fee schedule with a uniform effective date and term is necessary for the efficient administration of the Sunshine Kitchen and is in the public interest. It is in the best interests of the general public to charge a fee for services provided by the County, so that those parties deriving the benefit(s) from County-provided services pay for the costs of providing those services. It is appropriate to maintain a fee schedule to properly reflect the technical and operational costs incurred by the County in providing use of the kitchen facilities and rates that are sustainable to the community.
It is also in the best interest of the general public to provide an opportunity for a reduced kitchen user membership fee for non-profit organizations and governmental organizations providing services to the citizens of the County. Non-profit organizations and governmental organizations may qualify for a 50% reduction to the Kitchen User Membership Fee (discount not applicable to any other fee) for use of facility only between 7:00PM and 7:00AM on any day or between 7:00AM and 11:00AM on Wednesdays. The reduced fee is limited to the use of the facility for a maximum of two (2) hours per week. Additional usage will not be provided the fee reduction. The non-profit organizations and governmental organizations will be evaluated to ensure the organization is not benefitting financially from the use of the kitchen and to ensure it is providing services to the citizens of the County, such as preparing meals to the homeless; teaching cooking to middle/high school students; holding hospitality or cooking sessions for 4-H members; providing baking lessons to seniors or kids; teaching formerly incarcerated individuals with basic kitchen skills (practical work skills); preparing meals for the elderly and/or disabled; preparing meals for free prekindergarten programs; and similar beneficial services to the St. Lucie County community.
Further, based on feedback and engagement with the kitchen clients, it is in the best interest of the general public to establish a fee and opportunity for food truck clients to prep food and kitchenware in the production space as well as amend the needed kitchen membership hours from 101 to 91 to qualify for a parking space lease.

description:
Road Impact Fees in St. Lucie County were first adopted in 1985 and implemented in 1986. Since then, the County has continued to periodically update its Road Impact Fee Study, last updated and adopted on April 19, 2022. The County engaged Nilgün Kamp, AICP, with Tindale Oliver (n.k.a. Benesch) to provide the latest update.
The County has also strived to work with municipalities to streamline the collection of County Impact Fees whereby a developer or builder pays only the permitting agency. The County's Road Impact Fee Interlocal Agreement with the City of Fort Pierce has been in place since September 13, 2005, and with the City of Port St. Lucie (PSL) since April 19, 2022.
Additionally, the current County Road Impact Fee only assesses impacts to State and County Roads proportionally by Municipality based on VMT (vehicle miles traveled).
In 2024, the FL Legislature passed HB 479, requiring cities and counties to enter into an interlocal agreement to define any fees for transportation impacts and determine a methodology for the distribution of any revenues. If there is no agreement in place by October 1, 2025, or if an existing agreement is terminated, only the local government issuing the building permit may collect for transportation impacts based on a developer's traffic impact study or a city or county's mobility fee less a 10% discount to the developer.
At the December 10, 2024 Informal meeting, Benesch presented mobility plan and impact fee information as well as discussed recent legislative changes and provided various solutions to meet the County’s growing travel demands. The Board discussed multiple options during the Informal meeting. As such, Benesch provided a scope of work to conduct a Transportation Study that includes methodologies for Mobility Fees, Impact Fees, and Multimodal Fees. Including all three (3) options allows the Board to consider alternative methods to capture travel demand revenue from future development. The scope of services also includes six (6) in-person meetings and a preliminary project schedule for the adoption of the County's Roads Transportation Impact Fee by September 2025.
The current project budget of $135,000.00 will need to be increased by $9,525.00 for a total project budget of $144,525.00. Funds are available in Roads Impact Fee Reserves.

description:
The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) recently executed Public Transportation Grant Agreement (PTGA) G2S29 for the Port of Fort Pierce Terminal Improvements Initiative. This grant was pursued in direct response to proposed terminal improvements proffered by Derecktor Shipyards. The paving and drainage improvements (known as Areas 1-4) are essential for streamlining and scaling current Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) operations and will help Derecktor better utilize the recently completed Utility Loop (which was funded by Derecktor Shipyards).
The newly acquired grant funding in PTGA G2S29 is similar to FDOT grant funding in PTGA G1W17 (C20-08-547) and G1804 (C19-04-420), both of which were previously secured by the County (for use by Derecktor) and set to expire. The County proactively requested consolidation of the balance of these grant funds from the Florida Seaport Transportation and Economic Development (FSTED) Council and FDOT on July 19, 2024. That petition was supported by Derecktor Shipyards and subsequently approved by the FSTED Council. This consolidation will result in an available balance in PTGA G2S29 of $2,058,963.00 from FDOT, requiring a $2,058,963.00 local match (to be provided by Derecktor Shipyards). A total of $4,117,926.00 is available for Areas (1-4) Pavement and Drainage Improvements, and use of the consolidated funding have been approved through December 27, 2027.
Please note that all funds secured for this project have been previously acknowledged by Derecktor Shipyards in various grant funding agreements, most recently in the Amended and Restated Grant Funding Agreement (FDOT Grant No.’s G2204, G1W17, G1804, and G2S29) between St. Lucie County and Derecktor Shipyards on July 19, 2025. The Amended and Restated Seaport Grant Funding Agreement (FDOT Grant No.’s G2204, G1W17, G1804, and G2S29) with Derecktor Shipyards ensures active communication between both parties through the life of the grants and includes an acknowledgement from both parties to work in good faith to maintain the status of each grant and execute the proposed improvements.
Preliminary cost estimates provided by Derecktor Shipyards put the cost of Area 1-4 improvements at approximately $4,198,137.21.

description:
In July of 2024, St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners approved the St. Lucie Transit Development Plan (TDP). The TDP serves as a guiding document with a ten-year planning horizon and contains a list of prioritized projects and the overall budget for the transit program. The project list includes capital and operating investments such as new service routes, expansion of service, and enhanced infrastructure. The county's existing bus route seven was identified as early as 2009 in the TDP for regional economic development by providing cross-county connectivity. Route seven was implemented in 2015 and is currently in the fourth iteration of route modifications to increase ridership and enhance regional connectivity.
The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Corridor Development Program (CDP) is designed to relieve congestion and improve capacity within an identified transportation corridor by increasing the people carrying capacity of the transportation systems through the use of high occupancy conveyances. In St. Lucie County, the CDP is intended to strengthen the initial project with improved efficiencies and increased ridership. The CDP covers up to 100% of the total eligible cost of the project.
A local match is not required. FDOT allocated funds in the amount of $300,000.00.

description:
On October 15, 2024, the BOCC approved an Option Agreement with Ashley Capital Pursuant to RFP No. 22-092, to purchase 111 acres within the Treasure Coast Research and Education Park. The agreement includes a 180-day removal period to be completed by the County to:• Amend Land Development Code Section 4.03.00 to exclude the Property and the Purchaser’s Property from the Research and Education Park Overlay Zone, modifying the boundaries of the Overlay map as specified in §4.03.02(A) to reflect this removal, and modifying the text of any other sections of the County Code as required to achieve the purpose.
• Amend the TCERDA Lease to exclude the property therefrom.
• Amend the Declaration to exclude the property therefrom.
The Research Park was originally developed in the early 2000s by the County to promote additional agricultural research and education already occurring in the area. Together, with the State of Florida, the County assembled 1,600 acres that presently make up the Research Park.
The County and partners sought to attract additional research facilities and companies to the Research Park to complement the ongoing activities of the Indian River Research & Education Center (“IRREC”) of the University of Florida’s Institute of Food & Agricultural Sciences (“IFAS”), the Hayslip Biological Control Research and Containment Laboratory and the United States Department of Agriculture (“USDA”) Agricultural Research Service. All three continue to be tenants in the Research Park.
For a variety of reasons, the original vision for the Research Park never materialized, such as changes in federal research funding and the great recession contributed significantly to why the Research Park never realized the research development goals. In recognition of the changes, the TCERDA Board authorized staff to hire a consultant and provide analysis and recommendations on next steps for the Research Park.
In 2018, John Rhodes of Moran, Stahl and Boyer was hired to provide a series of strategic recommendations to improve the likelihood of development in the Research Park. Three of the main strategic recommendations were to expand the allowable uses in the Research Park, sell rather than lease land and lessen the architectural rules for new buildings in the Park (the Research Park is subject to that certain Declaration of Covenants and Restrictions for Treasure Coast Education, Research and Development Park, dated February 7, 2012, and recorded March 16, 2012, in Official Records Book 3371, Page 2418, in the Public Records of St. Lucie County, Florida (the “Declaration of Covenants”). The rationale for the changes was that the original list of allowed uses was very restrictive, potential developers prefer to buy rather than lease land and the design rules significantly increased the cost of development.
Amendments to the Land Development Code were processed to expand the number of allowable uses and amend the architectural requirements. Both the TCERDA Board and the Board of County Commissioners adopted the changes. An RFP was also published to offer the Research Park land for sale. The sole respondent to the RFP was Ashley Capital.
Quad 1A within the Research Park is where the Sunshine Kitchen is located, and the County has previously put the six parcels surrounding the Kitchen on the market for developers to purchase. Since those various actions, the vision for the Research Park has changed further and the BOCC approved an exchange agreement with the Fire District to build a Fire Station on Quad 1A-Lot 3 on December 14, 2022.
The County is also working on the designs for a proposed Animal Safety Facility, with land to house agricultural animals, within Quad 1A.

description:
The ARC of the Treasure Coast was incorporated in 1956 and has provided programs and services to individuals with disabilities in our community for nearly 70 years. From its grassroot beginnings, the ARC of the Treasure Coast evolved into a comprehensive community organization, focusing on providing services to people with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (I/DD), as well as advocacy and education for the community.
Presently, the ARC of the Treasure Coast has sixteen community-based group homes with six homes in St. Lucie County and plans to acquire two new homes in Port St. Lucie in the next 6 to 12 months. The community-based homes provide the opportunity for people with disabilities to live in affordable housing that is rehabilitated to meet their physical challenges and provide for their long-term health care needs.
ARC is seeking funding to create a Therapeutic Intervention Program (TIP) Center, to be located in Port St. Lucie. The TIP Center will serve residents and families of Port St. Lucie (PSL) and St. Lucie West, as well, as individuals residing in ARC group homes and other smaller residential providers located in PSL that have no other day program operations. The TIP center will assist individuals with I/DD and their families, by providing intensive therapeutic interventions and meaningful day activities through a comprehensive array of programs. This service expansion is key as PSL remains the most densely populated area on the Treasure Coast, one of the fastest growing cities in the country, and no similar center or program exists in the 29-mile stretch between Stuart and Ft. Pierce.
The ARC of the Treasure Coast is seeking contributions up to $300,000.00 towards the purchase of the Port St. Lucie Therapeutic Intervention Program Center. The ARC has received a State Appropriation from the Florida Legislature of $1,000,000.00. They have also received contributions and commitment pledges for the project in the amount of $400,000.00 from several foundations and donors. They anticipate an additional $900,000.00 to be received by additional donors by the closing date in January 2025 or shortly thereafter. Additional contributions in grants are anticipated within the first year for various programs that will run within the TIP center of $500,000, but the ARC has a $375,000.00 gap in the purchase price of $2,600,000 and buildout cost of $75,000.00.

description:
At an Informal Meeting on July 14, 2020, the Board of County Commissioners discussed the collection process for code enforcement liens. The Board directed staff to solicit an RFP for debt collection. Upon research, our neighboring jurisdiction, the City of Port St. Lucie uses a collection agency to collect outstanding debts on code enforcement liens and we are able to piggyback on their contract. Therefore, staff requested to piggyback on the City's contract for debt collection with CrediTech. On April 20, 2021, St. Lucie County entered into a contract with CrediTech to collect Code Enforcement Liens.
In 2019, a lawsuit was filed against Palm Beach County. Initially it was a single code violator, but on November 29, 2022 the Court certified a class action lawsuit for similarly situated Palm Beach County Code violators with liens. The Class filed a Motion for Summary Judgment asserting that Palm Beach County’s policy and procedure of charging and collecting interest and collection agency fees as part of code enforcement penalty, prior to the County filing a foreclosure action was improper. The Court found that the County was authorized to impose the daily fine but was not authorized to charge interest and collection agency fees. The Court stated, “This lack of any legislative authority to charge interest and collection fees results in a violation of the Eight Amendment Excessive Fine Clause.”
Based on this Court ruling, staff and CrediTech have agreed to amicably terminate their agreement.

description:
In 2021, ACCEL International Holdings, Inc. ("ACCEL"), which manufacturers high performance conductors, applied for a Job Growth Incentive Grant ("JGIG") as a qualified target industry. On May 18, 2021, the Board approved JGIG Agreement No. 21-003, wherein ACCEL committed to the creation of 125 new jobs with an average hourly wage of $22.59 over a four-year period. The agreement provided for the company to receive a JGIG in an amount not to exceed $165,625.00 on a 7-year payout schedule based upon the number of jobs created. In addition, the agreement recognized the County's $125,000.00 local contribution to the State of Florida Qualified Target Industry ("QTI") tax refund program.
These new jobs were phased on the following schedule:
Year One-a minimum of 60 jobs.
Year Two-a minimum of 40 jobs.

On January 11, 2022, the Board approved the First Amendment to JGIG 21-003, to change the start of the payout period from January 1, 2022, to January 1, 2023.
Second Amendment to JGIG 21-003
On December 13, 2022, the Board approved the Second Amendment to JGIG 21-003, to change the start of the payout period from January 1, 2023, to January 1, 2024.
Third Amendment to JGIG 21-003
On February 20, 2024, the Board approved the Third Amendment to JGIG 21-003, to revise the job creation schedule provided by the JGIG Agreement, as follows:
Year One, ending December 31, 2024 -a minimum of 63 jobs.

description:
The County has entered into a Contract for Sale and Purchase with SHER-BRT, LLC for an 80' wide strip of land adjacent to the future connection of Laidback Way, north of Orange Avenue and west of Rock Road.
Segments of Orange Avenue west of Kings Highway and Kings Highway between Orange Avenue and Angle Road are anticipated to operate over capacity based on the 2045 St. Lucie County TPO’s approved long range transportation plan (LRTP). The distance from parallel north-south connections between Orange Avenue and Angle Road is approximately 2 miles. Kings Highway east of I-95 is the nearest paved north-south connection, and North FFA Road west of the Florida Turnpike is a chip-sealed unimproved roadway not well suited for high volume travel.
The acquisition of the right-of-way of Laidback Way may provide a transportation benefit to the entire vicinity should a link to Old FFA Road, therefore Angle Road, be achieved in the future. The potential roadway helps create an alternative north-south route to help avoid over-burdening Kings Highway. Additionally, the potential roadway can provide a more direct alternative for residents to Angle Road and Orange Avenue, and to provide options for a future roadway system to serve the +/-1,307 acre land area located inside the Urban Services Boundary and between the FL Turnpike and I-95 and between Angle Road and Orange Avenue. Additionally, a potential K-8 School Site for the St. Lucie County Public School District could benefit from this roadway.
The County had an appraisal prepared by Fuller-Armfield-Wagner that valued the 80' strip of right-of-way at $43,150. Mr. Benjamin, the representative of SHER-BRT, LLC, provided an appraisal performed by Callaway and Price, Inc., which valued the right-of-way at $119,300. Due to the difference in valuation, the County had an appraisal review performed by Parrish & Edwards, Inc., which identified a value of $98,000-$100,000. The County presented a Contract for Sale and Purchase to SHER-BERT, LLC. for $99,000, which is the fair market value of the parcel, as identified by Parrish & Edwards, Inc. Mr. Benjamin submitted a counteroffer of $100,000, which is in the range of value identified by the County's appraiser. The appraisals are available in the Property Acquisition Division.
Attached for your review and approval is the signed Contract for Sale and Purchase.
For reference, in 2006 the BOCC approved Resolution 2006-051 for a rezoning from AG-1 (Agricultural-1) to PUD and a Preliminary Plan for the Sunnyland Farms PUD. This prior approval provided for 458 detached, single-family dwellings (1.99 dwelling units per acre), preservation of 35.2 acres of native upland habitat (more than twice the required minimum), and preservation of the entirety of the 12.53 acres of on-site wetlands, and the construction or bonding of paved improvements to Laidback Way (Emerson Avenue) from Orange Avenue to Sunnyland Drive as a two-lane facility and turn lanes at Orange Ave. In 2007, the BOCC approved Resolution 07-044 granting a major adjustment to the approved Sunnyland Farms PUD to adjust the phasing the project. The Sunnyland project had a similar roadway connection as depicted above. The project approvals, including a phasing modification, expired without construction commencing.
Based on the existing and already growing population of the county and the potential school site, the acquisition of the right-of-way helps create an option for an alternative north-south route.

description:
The Fiscal Year 2025 budget included $600,000 in funding to support the Housing Hub operated by the Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council (TCHSC).
St. Lucie County proposes to enter into an agreement with Treasure Coast Homeless Services Council, Inc. (TCHSC) to operate the Housing Hub program for homeless individuals. This initiative provides separate shelters for men and women, offering services such as case management, benefit enrollment, healthcare access, mental health services, employment support, and rental assistance. The agreement allocates $600,000 in funding for fiscal year 2025, with up to 15% available for administrative costs. The program aims to facilitate the transition of participants into permanent housing through comprehensive support and outreach efforts. TCHSC will adhere to rigorous reporting, compliance, and monitoring requirements under this cost-reimbursement arrangement. The men's Housing Hub is located at 609 N. 7th Street in Fort Pierce. The women's Hub consists of 5 cottages located at the intersection of Dundas Court and Avenue B in Fort Pierce.
Summary of Outcomes for Fiscal Year 2024Rental Assistance & Other Homelessness Services: Assisted 322 individuals, providing critical support to those experiencing homelessness.
SOAR Services - Social Security Disability Applications: Processed and supported 9 applications for Social Security Disability benefits.
Benefits Enrollment - Food Stamps: Assisted 91 individuals with enrollment in food assistance programs to address food insecurity.
Medical Service Referrals: Referred 104 individuals to medical services, connecting them with necessary healthcare resources.
Residency Services: Processed 74 applications for the men's residency program, with 64 individuals successfully transitioning to permanent housing. Similarly, processed 17 applications for the women's residency program, resulting in 13 successful transitions to permanent housing.

description:
This agreement authorizes Elaine M. Wood and Michael S. Irey to plant and maintain native plants, provided by St. Lucie County (SLC), within a specific area within the Ocean Bay Preserve, immediately adjacent to their property (see Exhibit B). Upon execution of this agreement, ERD will deliver a minimum of 60 pitch apple (Clusia rosea) plants, a minimum of 60 seagrape (Coccoloba uvifera) plants, and a minimum of 5 key thatch palms (Thrinax morrisii) to be installed and maintained at the property owner's expense, per the terms of the agreement. ​
Ocean Bay Preserve is a 24.79-acre County owned property located on South Hutchinson Island and managed by the Environmental Resources Department (ERD). The site also contains a County Water Treatment Plant managed by the Utilities Department. ERD commonly manages non-native plants (exotics) by treating with herbicide and leaving it in place to degrade over time, allowing the soil to remain intact and benefit from the nutrients, as well as allowing native plants to recruit naturally and restore the native habitats. ERD received a $62,720 grant in late 2023 to treat the exotics within Ocean Bay Preserve and Walton Rock's Beach.
In early 2024 an attorney for Wood and Irey contacted the County requesting removal of standing dead exotics citing concerns of potential fire hazard, exposure to hurricane damage, and disturbance from the now visible water treatment facility (lights and alarms). Wood and Irey also requested replanting of the area and offered to pay a reasonable portion of the costs as well as providing continued maintenance by a licensed arborist/company. In August 2024, ERD contracted with a company to remove the dead, previously treated exotics in the area adjacent to the property for an amount of $10,875 and the Utilities Department fixed the alarm, programmed the lights to turn off at night, and repaired the odor control system.
meeting: BOCC Regular Meeting
title: Ocean Bay Preserve Agreement - Elaine M. Wood and Michael S. Irey

description:
The Florida Indian Heritage Association, formerly the Florida Indian Hobbyist Association, was founded in Fort Pierce with an interest in Native American traditions and culture. The group is comprised of both natives and hobbyists. They have hosted a 3 day Pow-Wow each year at the Fairgrounds and previously at the Savannas Recreation Area. This is the 56th Annual Pow-Wow hosted in St. Lucie County and it is the longest continually running Pow-Wow in the Southeastern United States. The request is to return to the Fairgrounds for the 2025 Pow-Wow.
The Pow-Wow highlights Native American traditions, dances, food, crafts, and many vendors. The organization strives to perpetuate the Native American Heritage. This is accomplished by several dances held daily with participants in full regalia representing many different tribes and providing educational seminars. On average, the festival draws an estimated 5,000 attendees from all over the United States.
The Florida Indian Heritage Association is a registered local 501(C)3 organization. The organization and event meet the requirements of the St. Lucie County Facility Use Policy for fee waivers. The organization is requesting to host the event March 28-30, 2025 at The St. Lucie County Fairgrounds. The organization is requesting that the County waive the Adams Arena rental fees of $5,250.00 and have agreed to reimburse the County $2028.00 for staff and equipment costs associated with the event, as required by Board Policy.

description:
The Transportation Alternatives Program (TAP) provides funding for programs and projects defined as transportation alternatives including on and off-road pedestrian and bicycle facilities, infrastructure projects for improving non-driver access to public transportation and enhanced mobility, recreational trail program projects, community improvement activities, and environmental mitigation.
This item request Board approval for a resolution to submit a Transportation Alternatives Program (TAP) grant application to the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) for funding the work program to construct a six-foot-wide sidewalk along the south side of Easy Street from US Highway 1 to Canal 22 at the future SunTrail regional connection (+/- 0.5 Mile). This sidewalk will provide multimodal connectivity for local residents of Indian River Estates. The project would provide a 6 ft. wide concrete sidewalk to connect US 1 to the future Sun Trail regional system. Students who do not have school bus service in the immediate vicinity would have the ability to use the sidewalk to have a safe walking route to a school bus stop on US 1. If the grant is successfully approved, funding would be available in FY2028/29.
Easy Street sidewalk is identified on the Transportation Planning Organization’s (TPO) Pedestrian Facility Needs Plan and the List of Priority Projects (LOPP) on the Transportation Alternatives (TA) Projects. The project is ranked second on the TPO’s LOPP Transportation Alternatives Projects.

description:
Stormwater culverts direct and channel the flow of stormwater under driveways, roads, sidewalks and other obstructions and are an integral component of stormwater management. Culverts fail over time due to maintenance, environmental or installation issues. Culvert failure can lead to localized flooding which may impede safe conditions of ingress and egress for owners and residents of property in the affected area as well as the traveling public, visitors, emergency responders and other public service providers. Some culvert owners may lack the resources to pay for improvements and repairs.
In 2021, the Board established a voluntary program, Ordinance No. 21-004, to which eligible property owners can apply for and receive funding to improve or repair culverts and then repay this funding through the imposition of a non-ad valorem special assessment against the improved property collected in annual installments on the tax roll.
The attached Resolution No. 2025-17 is the Assessment Resolution as required by County's Ordinance No. 21-004, as amended. The purpose of this resolution relates to the imposition and collection of special assessments to fund stormwater culvert improvements within the Culvert 2025-01 MSBU, determine that real property therein will be specially benefitted, establish the method of assessing the cost of the improvements, approve the assessment roll, and provide an effective date.

description:
Discussion on a Pilot Program for an adjusted Board of County Commissioners meeting time in an effort to provide for the efficient and orderly functioning of board business; to protect the right to be heard; and to enhance effective government operations for the public and public engagement in alignment with Strategic Plan Objective FCT 1.2.2 (Community Trust).
Currently, the Board of County Commissioners hold formal meetings on the first Tuesday of every month at 6:00 pm and the third Tuesday of every month at 9:00 am. Historically, items requiring a public hearing have only been placed on evening meeting agendas in an effort to allow as many members of the public as possible an opportunity to attend the meeting and speak during public comment.
Unfortunately, county staff has received negative feedback from the community due to the quantity of business being conducted during the evening (6pm) meetings, causing these meetings to stretch beyond 10:00 pm, and at times last as late as 2:00 am the following morning. Board members have also expressed concerns related to the late meetings and suggesting that meetings should not extend beyond 11:00pm. For many members of the public, these meetings are too late in the day to comfortably attend in their entirety. Members of the public have asked why the county meetings are not scheduled at similar times as the adjacent counties (note: Indian River County both meetings are at 9:00am; Martin County multiple meetings are at 9:00am; Okeechobee County both meetings are at 9:00am; and Palm Beach County both meetings are at 9:30am). It is unclear if an early morning start time, such as 9:00am, would be too drastic a change. As such, as a measured approach to the proposed pilot program, an afternoon start time is proposed as a potentially mutually beneficial solution which can be tried out, will allow for feedback and be adjusted or undone, if needed.
In response to these questions and feedback, staff is proposing a 6-month pilot program featuring both formal Tuesday board meetings to begin at 2:00 pm and revise the agenda format (blue text indicates changes) to the following order:
2:00pm on the first and third Tuesday of each month, unless otherwise advertised:1. Call to Order
2. Invocation
3. Pledge of Allegiance
4. Approval of the Agenda - Additions, Deletions, Revisions
5. Presentations
6. First General Public Comment Opportunity (not pertaining to public hearings)
7. Proclamations
8. Approval of Minutes
9. Consent Agenda
10. Regular Agenda
11. Public Hearings
If the meeting is lengthy, recess at 5:00 pm
Reconvene the meeting at 6:00pm
12. Second General Public Comment Opportunity (not pertaining to public hearings)
13. Continue with Public Hearings
14. Upcoming Meetings
15. Announcements
16. Adjournment
This would allow regular business to be conducted during business hours and keep more engaging topics (such as the public hearings) to the general public after the general business but at reasonable hours. It also allows for those who would like to comment, but can’t stay late into the evening, the opportunity to participate. Additionally, by having both meetings start at the same time, staff would be able to more evenly distribute public hearing items, resulting in more efficient and shorter meetings and agendas.
Further, several Board members have mentioned wanting to be more involved earlier in the development review process and have suggested reviewing Section 163.3174, F.S., which provides the Board may designate itself as the local planning agency. If the Board determines to also sit as Planning and Zoning Commission/local planning agency, they would be attending meetings four days per month. The Board could consider adjusting the meeting schedule further by having a formal board meeting at 2:00 pm on the first Tuesday as well as an informal board meeting at 9:00am and a formal board meeting at 2:00pm on the third Tuesday. In so doing, the Board would maintain attending meetings three days per month. Alternatively, the Board could consider moving the meeting times to 2:00 pm (1st meeting) and 9:00 am (2nd meeting), or any other timeslots the Board of County Commissioners so desire.
Upon a review of what other counties across the State of Florida are doing in terms of formal meeting times, staff found that there are examples across the spectrum to support varying options. In general, the larger the community, the more likely it was that meetings began in the morning given the length of the agendas.
The proposed pilot program is in alignment with Strategic Plan Objective FCT 1.2.2. “Expand meaningful community engagement and participation in the government process with our diverse community through effective communication, collaboration and public outreach.”

description:
Several Board members have expressed an interest in having more involvement earlier in the development review process. One way to accomplish this would be for the Board to designate itself as the local planning agency, as provided in Section 163.3174, F.S.
Section 163.3174, F.S., specifically states "The governing body of each local government, individually or in combination as provided in s. 163.3171, shall designate and by ordinance establish a “local planning agency,” unless the agency is otherwise established by law. Notwithstanding any special act to the contrary, all local planning agencies or equivalent agencies that first review rezoning and comprehensive plan amendments in each municipality and county shall include a representative of the school district appointed by the school board as a nonvoting member of the local planning agency or equivalent agency to attend those meetings at which the agency considers comprehensive plan amendments and rezonings that would, if approved, increase residential density on the property that is the subject of the application. However, this subsection does not prevent the governing body of the local government from granting voting status to the school board member. The governing body may designate itself as the local planning agency pursuant to this subsection with the addition of a nonvoting school board representative."
The County currently designates the County Planning and Zoning Commission as the Local Planning Agency for the unincorporated area of the County.
A draft amendment to the County Land Development Code is attached for review and discussion purposes. This draft amendment proposes to adjust the Planning and Zoning Commission membership to: not less than five (5) nor more than seven (7) members, who shall be the five (5) members of the Board of County Commissioners and two (2) at-large appointments made by the Board of County Commissioners.
Additionally, the Florida Association of Counties (FAC) completed a survey in September 2024 and assembled a list of Local Planning Agencies for counties across the State. A copy of the FAC list is attached, with nine (9) counties identified with the BOCC serving as their Local Planning Agency.

description:
Strategic planning and budgeting are integral components of successful fiscal management and meeting the County’s vision of Endless Opportunity by Design. The Strategic Plan provides direction, while the Budget allocates resources to implement the plan. County divisions and departments concentrate their actions and resources on the focus areas, goals and objectives of the Strategic Plan to move the county towards its vision through implementation of the plan.
The Board of County Commissioners (BOCC) originally adopted a Strategic Plan in June of 2020. In 2024, the BOCC approved the refreshed Strategic Plan with the BOCC’s priorities, and it was utilized for the preparation of the Fiscal Year (FY) 25 Budget.
The Strategic Plan has the following six focus areas: Foster Community Trust; Resilient Infrastructure; Thriving Community; Advance Opportunity; Environmental Stewardship; and Health & Safety.
Annually, the BOCC convenes to refresh and align its priorities with the community needs. For FY 25, the BOCC identified the following 10 priorities for the County:Housing Affordability/Workforce Housing
Airport & Seaport Development
Infrastructure (water, sewer, stormwater)
Natural Environment
Balancing Impacts of Development
Economic Development
Community Engagement & Messaging
County Government Campus Assessment
Medical Examiner’s Office
Water Quality
The preparation of the FY26 Budget will begin in early 2025 and staff is seeking the BOCC’s input and guidance for the priorities for FY 26.

description:
On September 5, 2023, the Board approved the selection of Wharton-Smith, Inc. as the Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR) for the Water Treatment Facility at Taylor Dairy Road. This was based on their submittal in response to RFQ No. 23-050. The CMAR Services shall include all necessary pre-construction, construction and close-out services to deliver a successful building project. The intent of the CMAR delivery method is to establish an environment of collaboration, trust, and partnership between the CMAR Contractor, the Design Team (CDM Smith), St. Lucie County Utility, and the appropriate regulatory agencies.
On October 17, 2023, the Board approved the Wharton-Smith, Inc. contract (C23-10-893). That initial contract only included pre-construction services.
On September 17, 2024 the Board approved amendment No. 1 in the amount of $6,757,484.00. The scope of services for that amendment covered the drilling of the upper Floridan aquifer (UFA) raw water wells #2 and #3 as well as the raw water pipeline between the well locations #2 and #3 and the water treatment facility site.
Attached is a copy of the draft proposed amendment No. 2 in the amount of $9,900,000.00 covering phase 1. The scope of services for this amendment covers the majority of the construction services needed to build the water treatment facility. The following components are included in this amendment: mechanical, structural, building, roofing, HVAC, coatings, signage, canopy, electrical, plumbing, sitework, subsurface, instrumentation, various pumps, chemical, storage tank, odor control, degassifier, CO2, generators, and several allowances for miscellaneous systems.
The remaining amount of $38,318,500.00 will be presented on a third amendment sometime in the second quarter of 2025, that will cover phase two of this scope of work.
Selection of the final subcontractors will be made by both Wharton-Smith and the County as described in the original contract documents. This will allow the County to accept certain bids that may be received after the initial package deadline and come in at a lower cost than previously estimated. These areas are currently listed as allowances within the amendment documents. One benefit of the CMAR (Construction Manager at Risk) process allows the County to review specific line items and subcontractors, allowing for a lower overall cost.

description:
In July of 2024, St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners approved the St. Lucie Transit Development Plan (TDP). The TDP serves as a guiding document with a ten-year planning horizon and contains a list of prioritized projects and the overall budget for the transit program. The project list includes capital and operating investments such as new service routes, expansion of service, and enhanced infrastructure. One of the projects outlined in this document is improvements to the Port St. Lucie Intermodal Passenger Area.
The Port St. Lucie Intermodal project is currently in Phase III of facility development. Phase I, completed in 2013, includes 4 open bus bays, a platform for passengers, parking for 24 cars, pedestrian connectivity to the Community Center, and a 1,200 square foot covered seating area. The facility serves as a connection point for four fixed routes and two microtransit zones that serve the City and provide regional connectivity. Phase II of the project involved several public workshops to ensure the design of the facility met the needs of both residents and other stakeholders. The conceptual plan was presented to County and City elected officials to obtain feedback and the project is currently in the final design phase.
When constructed this project will meet the St. Lucie County Transit Department’s vision to create a destination. This project also aligns with the City of Port St. Lucie’s vision to create high-performing public spaces and the desire to create neighborhood green spaces/parks as indicated in the City’s Parks & Recreation Master Plan.
The Florida Department of Transportation Intermodal Access Development Program provides assistance for upgrades and safety improvements for Intermodal Centers. Funding from this grant supports the improvements to the Port St. Lucie Intermodal Facility. The grant is matched with Federal Transit Administration 5307 CARES funding that was previously set aside for this project. No additional local match is required.

description:
The St. Lucie County Planning & Development Services Department, on behalf of the Board of County Commissioners, is proposing text amendments to the LDC to address and clarify provisions for fence height on various properties within unincorporated St. Lucie County.
The proposed Ordinance seeks to clarify that the Agricultural, Residential - 1 (AR-1) zoning district is a residential zoning district and subject to fence heights associated with other residential zoning districts within unincorporated St. Lucie County. Additionally, the draft amendment provides flexibility in determining fence height where significant grade changes exist between the centerline of the adjacent roadway and the elevation on which the fence is to be constructed. A good example of this situation is the residential parcels along Indian River Drive.
The amendments also seek to provide flexibility in allowable fence height when it is necessary to contain a public use or facility for safety or security purposes, for example, a public water/wastewater treatment facility, an electrical substation, or a public airport facility. Also, staff has drafted the proposed Ordinance to include higher fence heights for the purposes of containing athletic activity, such as a tennis or basketball court.
In 2023, the Board of County Commissioners developed standards for residential fence materials, effectively prohibiting the use of cattle wire, chicken wire, and barbed wire within the RE-1, RE-2, RS-2, RS-3, RS-4, RMH-5, RM-5, RM-7, RM-9, RM-11, RM-15 and HIRD zoning districts. Since the adoption of the 2023 Ordinance, property owners who are contiguous to preserve areas where existing cattle or chicken wire fences were installed by local, state, or federal agencies have desired to utilize a similar fence material within their side and rear yards to allow for consistency. One example of this scenario are properties within Indian River Estates that abut the State's Savannas Preserve State Park.
Additionally, the County is seeking to clarify its requirement for the construction of a permanent 4ft. tall fence or wall around all residential swimming pools not enclosed with a screen within unincorporated St. Lucie County, in addition to the current standards of F.S. § 515.27 - Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act. The State's Residential Swimming Pool Safety requirements specify certain pool safety features, which must be in place in order to pass a final inspection and receive a certificate of completion. These include one of the following:(a) The pool must be isolated from access to a home by an enclosure that meets the pool barrier requirements of s. 515.29;
(b) The pool must be equipped with an approved safety pool cover;
(c) All doors and windows providing direct access from the home to the pool must be equipped with an exit alarm that has a minimum sound pressure rating of 85 dB A at 10 feet;
(d) All doors providing direct access from the home to the pool must be equipped with a self-closing, self-latching device with a release mechanism placed no lower than 54 inches above the floor; or
(e) A swimming pool alarm that, when placed in a pool, sounds an alarm upon detection of an accidental or unauthorized entrance into the water. Such pool alarm must meet and be independently certified to ASTM Standard F2208, titled “Standard Safety Specification for Residential Pool Alarms,” which includes surface motion, pressure, sonar, laser, and infrared alarms. For purposes of this paragraph, the term “swimming pool alarm” does not include any swimming protection alarm device designed for individual use, such as an alarm attached to a child that sounds when the child exceeds a certain distance or becomes submerged in water.
In many instances, compliance with the state's requirements is met through the installation of a pool barrier, also known as a baby gate, which can be removed following the issuance of a certificate of completion. To provide for increased public safety, the County has historically required an additional level of protection through the installation of a permanent fence or wall located between the pool and the property line. The Draft Ordinance seeks to clarify this requirement as an item that is in addition to the requirements of F.S. § 515.27 - Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act.
Lastly, the draft ordinance amends the code to allow for an administrative waiver from the additional pool fencing requirements. The current procedure requires an application to the Board of County Commissioners to waive the requirement of Section 8.00.05.A, for fencing. The amendment shifts this process to an administrative approval, granted by the Planning & Development Services Director, as long as the owner demonstrates that the proposed built or natural conditions provide equal or greater protection than the required 4ft. high permanent fence. Previously, the BOCC has approved pool fence waivers where a seawall was determined to be an adequate barrier in lieu of a fence.

description:
At the May 15, 2024, Board of County Commissioners Informal Meeting, the subject of mining permit exemptions was discussed with the Board. Mining permit exemptions are used for land development projects that request to haul material in excess of 100 cubic yards from the site. These land development projects are not commercial mines; however, they must follow the same public hearing, noticing, and other requirements similar to a commercial mine based on the current codified language.
To streamline the process, Staff recommended increasing the threshold for applications that must enter the public hearing process for consideration by the Board from 100 cubic yards to 30,000 cubic yards. Small and medium-sized projects that haul below 30,000 cubic yards offsite would be administratively approved.
This action would propose alternate language to land development code section 11.05.11 – Mining Permits.
Words in strike through type are deletions from existing text.
Words in underlined type are additions to existing text.
11.05.11. Mining Permits.
A. Requirement for Permit; Exemptions.
1. Except as provided in this Section, no mining or excavation operation shall be conducted in the unincorporated areas of St. Lucie County without a mining permit or mining permit exemption from the Board of County Commissioners or an administratively approved mining permit exemption. As used in this Section, the terms "mining" and "excavation operation" include any operation that entails the excavation or removal of earth off-site in excess of one hundred (100) cubic yards.
2. The following activities shall be exempt from the mining permit requirement provided that all applicable federal, state and local permits and/or authorizations have been obtained and the removal of the material remains on-site and is required to support development on-site:
a. Removal of material for installing utilities;
b. Removal of material from a site for the construction or removal of any foundations for any building or other structure;
c. Removal of material for digging drainage or mosquito control ditches and canals by authorized units and agencies of government;
d. Removal of material for digging drainage or mosquito control ditches and canals by private persons when construction is permitted by all authorizing agencies, if any, and when the excavated material is not removed from the involved tract of land;
e. Removal of material for existing agricultural operations;
f. Removal of material for accessory uses of land, such as septic tanks, graves, etc., that are designed to be filled and graded upon completion of excavation; and
g. Removal of material for a swimming pool when construction is permitted by all authorizing agencies.
h3. The removal of material less than thirty thousand (30,000) cubic yards shall require administrative approval of a mining permit exemption. This is limited to the removal of material less than thirty thousand (30,000) cubic yards for approved development in which the material is being excavated to provide on-site stormwater management and/or on-site fill for elevating roads, houses, buildings, sidewalks, driveways, parking areas, or other features customarily associated with on-site development. ; however, the The property owner or authorized agent shall submit the following for the County Engineer's approval:
1a. A sketch plan indicating the size, shape and location of the proposed excavation amount and disposition of excavated material.
2b. Setback of twenty-five (25) feet from any adjacent property line.
c. A sketch of the haul route with the proposed dates and times for the hauling operations.
d. Copies of all applicable federal, state and local permits and/or authorizations.
e. Sufficient evidence to demonstrate the removal meets the standards in Section 11.07.03(B), standards for review of conditional Use - Effects on Adjacent Properties. The application may be determined to comply with the provisions of this Code and the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan by the County Engineer, under certain conditions or exceptions, in consideration of existing site conditions, location, and potential for impact on public facilities, natural resources, and health and public safety. In such case, the County Engineer or designee shall provide a written statement to the applicant setting forth any applicable conditions or exceptions.
Action. Within 20 working days of receiving the complete mining permit exemption application, the County Engineer shall request additional clarifying information, approve, approve with conditions, or deny the application for removal of material. The conditions may include certain restrictions to the proposed operation, a maintenance agreement bond or line of credit and specific provisions for revocation of the approval.
Notice of Action. Notification of the decision of the County Engineer shall be provided to the Board of County Commissioners at a regularly scheduled Board of County Commissioners meeting, and the decision shall be filed with the Office of the Planning and Development Services Director in accordance with Subsection 11.00.04(F), notification and recorded in the Public Records of St. Lucie County.
34. All off-site removal of material in excess of one hundred thirty-thousand (100) (30,000) cubic yards shall require a public hearing and action before the Board of County Commissioners in accordance with the provisions of Section 11.00.03, notice of public hearing. The public hearing held on the application for removal of materials in excess of one hundred thirty-thousand (100) (30,000) cubic yards shall be in accordance with Section 11.00.04, hearing procedure. In reviewing the request for the removal of material in excess of one hundred (100) thirty-thousand (30,000) cubic yards, the Board of County Commissioners shall consider the report of the Growth Management Director County Engineer to determine whether the removal meets the standards in Subsection 11.07.03(B), standards for review of conditional use - Effects on Adjacent Properties. The property owner or authorized agent shall submit the following for the County Engineer's approval:
a. A sketch plan indicating the size, shape and location of the proposed excavation amount and disposition of excavated material.
b. Setback of twenty-five (25) feet from any adjacent property line.
c. A sketch of the haul route with the proposed dates and times for the hauling operations.
d. Copies of all applicable federal, state and local permits and/or authorizations.
e. Sufficient evidence to demonstrate the removal meets the standards in Section 11.07.03(B), standards for review of conditional Use - Effects on Adjacent Properties. The application may be determined to comply with the provisions of this Code and the St. Lucie County Comprehensive Plan by the County Engineer, under certain conditions or exceptions, in consideration of existing site conditions, location, and potential for impact on public facilities, natural resources, and health and public safety. In such case, the County Engineer or designee shall provide a written statement to the applicant setting forth any applicable conditions or exceptions.
Action. Within a reasonable time of the conclusion of the public hearing, the Board of County Commissioners shall approve, approve with conditions, or deny the application for removal of material in accordance with Subsection 11.00.04(E). The decision on the application shall be by resolution setting forth the findings of the Board of County Commissioners and any condition, limitation, or requirement of such decision
Notice of Action. Notification of the Board of County Commissioners' decision shall be mailed to all parties, and the decision shall be filed with the Office of the Growth Management Planning and Development Services Director in accordance with Subsection 11.00.04(F), notification.
Revocation of Permission to Removal Material. In addition to any other penalty and remedy for violation of this Code, it shall be a condition of every removal of material approval that such approval may be revoked for:
(1) Violation of any condition imposed upon such approval; and
(2) Upon complaint and proof of adverse effect on adjacent properties. The permit may be revoked only after the Board of County Commissioners holds a public hearing in accordance with Section 11.00.04 unless the permittee consents to a revocation of the permit. If the permittee provides written consent to the revocation to the Growth Management Director County Engineer, the Director County Engineer shall revoke the permit and notify the Board of County Commissioners of the revocation.

The FPRA grant funds may only be used to pay the cost to engineer, design, permit, construct and inspect the Project.
Attached to this memorandum is a copy of a proposed Funding Agreement between the County and FPRA that provides for the reimbursement grant described above. The FPRA approved the Funding Agreement on December 10, 2024.

description:

As consideration for the First Amendment to the 2010 Interlocal Agreement (TCERDA), the City agrees that it will not annex the Airport Property as described and shown in Attachment A to the Agreement on Non-Annexation of Airport Property ("Non-Annexation Agreement").
Pursuant to the Non-Annexation Agreement, the parties must enter into the First Amendment to the 2010 Interlocal Agreement within 45 days of the Effective Date of the Non-Annexation Agreement. The City and FPUA have already signed the First Amendment to the 2010 Interlocal Agreement.

description:
The County, the Treasure Coast Education, Research and Development Authority ("TCERDA"), the Fort Pierce Utilities Authority ("FPUA"), and the City of Fort Pierce ("City) entered into an interlocal agreement dated June 1, 2010 (2010 Interlocal) relating to deferred annexation of certain parcels located in the Treasure Coast Research Park ("Park") as shown in Exhibit B to the 2010 Interlocal.
As a condition of water and wastewater service, the FPUA and City require a water and/or wastewater service user to enter into an annexation agreement whereby the user voluntarily agrees to annex into the City at the City's discretion.
FPUA is the water and wastewater service provider to those parcels located within the Park. As county-owned parcels within the Park require water and wastewater services, the County is required to enter into annexation agreements.
Pursuant to the 2010 Interlocal, the City agreed to defer annexation of the County-owned parcels within the Park to a future date at least 10 years from the date that a certificate of occupancy is issued for a parcel subject to an annexation agreement.
The First Amendment to the 2010 Interlocal ("First Amendment") reduces the deferment period to allow annexation of the county-owned parcels identified in Exhibit B of the First Amendment ("TCERDA Properties") 2 years from the effective date of the First Amendment.
As consideration for the County reducing the deferment period for annexation of the TCERDA properties, the City has agreed that it will not annex the Airport Property as shown in Exhibit A of the attached draft of the Agreement on Non-Annexation of Airport Property.
